The people of Zarahemla recognize that the spirit of the Lord rests upon Mosiah because he can interpret sacred records—public confirmation of authority through demonstrated prophetic gift.
The Lord declares that the president of the Church shall receive the words of the Lord through the Holy Ghost—the spirit rests upon the prophet to guide the people.

commentary.historical_context: The prophetic guild system (benei hanevi'im) was a formal institution in ancient Israel, with prophets trained, housed, and organized into communities. These schools were headquartered at major cities: Bethel, Jericho, Ramoth-gilead. Archaeological evidence from the broader ancient Near East suggests that prophetic or priestly training centers were common in Mesopotamia and Egypt as well. The acceptance of a new leader by the prophetic guild was a significant social and religious validation. In ancient Mediterranean societies, legitimacy of leadership came through public recognition by peers and priests. Jericho was a major religious center in the Jordan Valley, significant from the time of Joshua onward. The fact that the Jericho prophets first see Elisha and first recognize his authority makes Jericho the starting point of his recognized ministry.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 46, Moroni presents the title of liberty, and the people recognize his cause and rally to his leadership. Like the sons of the prophets bowing to Elisha, the people of the Book of Mormon communities often recognize true authority through public signs and through the testimony of the Spirit. In Ether 12, Moroni's power is confirmed when the Jaredites witness the spiritual gifts manifesting through him.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:12 lists apostles and prophets as foundational officers of the Church. The public recognition of Elisha by the prophetic community at Jericho parallels the sustained and supported authority of modern prophets and apostles—they are sustained by the body of the Church, not merely appointed from above. The priesthood is organized, hierarchical, and publicly acknowledged.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, new initiates are presented before witnesses and covenants are made public. Similarly, Elisha's authority over the prophetic community is confirmed publicly before the sons of the prophets. Covenant authority is not secretive or private; it is witnessed and sustained by the community of the faithful.

commentary.christological_typology: The prophetic community's recognition that 'the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha' prefigures the declaration at Christ's baptism: 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased' (Matthew 3:17). In both cases, the spirit of God visibly rests upon the chosen successor, confirming to witnesses that authority has passed. The bowing of the prophetic community before Elisha typifies the recognition of Christ's authority by all who witness His works—the spirits acknowledge Him, creation obeys Him, and the faithful bow before Him. Elisha's assumption of the prophetic mantle, publicly confirmed, typifies Christ's assumption of the role of Prophet, Priest, and King, sealed by the Holy Ghost.
commentary.application: The sons of the prophets did not appoint Elisha; they recognized what God had done. In your own sphere of influence—whether as a parent, teacher, leader, or member of a quorum—genuine authority is not self-proclaimed but publicly recognized and confirmed by those with eyes to see. Are you living in such a way that the Spirit's presence in your life is evident to those around you? The modern covenant equivalent is the sustaining of priesthood leaders and prophets: we do not appoint them, but we sustain (acknowledge and uphold) those whom God has called. Conversely, if you are uncertain whether a calling or authority is genuine, the test is the same as the prophets': Does the Spirit rest upon this person? Is their life and work consistent with God's character? Is the community of the faithful willing to submit to their leadership?

text_kjv: And they said unto him, Behold now, there be with thy servants fifty strong men; let them go, we pray thee, and seek thy master: lest peradventure the Spirit of the LORD hath taken him up, and cast him upon some mountain, or into some valley. And he said, Ye shall not send.

commentary.narrative:
Immediately after acknowledging Elisha's authority, the sons of the prophets propose a search expedition for Elijah. They have fifty 'strong men' (anashim benei chayil, literally 'men of strength/valor')—trained, capable individuals ready to scour the countryside. Their reasoning reveals their theological understanding: the ruach YHWH can physically transport a prophet from one place to another. They know the accounts of Elijah's miraculous movements (cf. 1 Kings 18:12, where Obadiah fears Elijah will be taken away). So they reason: perhaps Elijah has not died; perhaps the Spirit has carried him off and set him down somewhere on a mountain or in a valley, and they can find him and bring him back.

Elisha refuses: 'Ye shall not send.' The refusal is absolute and immediate. He does not explain, he does not negotiate, he does not offer an alternative. His single word of command—'Do not send'—asserts his authority and his knowledge. Elisha knows what the sons of the prophets do not: that Elijah's departure is permanent and final. The ascent into heaven was not a displacement but a translation, a taking up to God's presence, not a deposit on some remote mountain. Elisha's refusal is not arbitrary or haughty; it is the knowledge of one who saw what happened and understands its meaning. The new prophet's first act of actual leadership over the Jericho community is to prevent a futile, misguided effort and to direct their understanding toward the truth.

word_study.meaning: To take up, to lift, to carry away. The verb root nasa means to bear, carry, lift—often used for God carrying or lifting up individuals (cf. Psalm 91:12).
word_study.significance: The sons of the prophets use the language of transportation and displacement. They assume the Spirit has lifted Elijah and deposited him elsewhere, not removed him from the earthly realm entirely. Their understanding is incomplete—they know the Spirit can move people, but they do not grasp that Elijah has been taken up to heaven itself, not merely relocated on earth. Elisha's refusal corrects this misunderstanding.

word_study.meaning: Men of valor, might, or strength. The word chayil refers to military strength, capability, and power. These are not merely volunteers but trained fighters and capable individuals.
word_study.significance: The irony is striking: the prophets offer fifty men of physical strength to find one prophet of spiritual power. The assumption is that Elijah might be lost somewhere and needs to be found by human effort. Elisha's refusal implies that Elijah's fate is not a mystery requiring a search party, but a known and accomplished fact.

word_study.meaning: Do not send, do not dispatch. The negation combined with the imperative creates an absolute prohibition without qualification or negotiation.
word_study.significance: This is Elisha's first command to the prophetic community as their new leader. It is a simple but firm assertion of authority. He does not argue or explain; he speaks as one who knows. The Covenant Rendering reflects this bluntness: 'Do not send them.' This is leadership through knowledge and authority, not persuasion.

cross_references.connection: Obadiah fears that the Spirit of the Lord will carry Elijah away while he is searching for him—the sons of the prophets at Jericho are operating from a similar understanding of the Spirit's power to transport prophets.
The Spirit lifts up Ezekiel between earth and heaven—the Spirit can indeed transport prophets, but this verse shows the transport is visionary and heavenly, not earthly displacement.

The Spirit of the Lord catches away Philip after baptizing the Ethiopian, transporting him to Azotus—a New Testament parallel showing the Spirit can relocate prophets, validating the sons of the prophets' general understanding even as Elisha's refusal implies Elijah's case is different.

Enoch was translated that he should not see death, and he was not found because God had translated him—the ultimate precedent for a prophet being taken up to heaven, which is what Elisha understands has happened to Elijah.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, search parties for missing persons were common and expected. The proposal of fifty men reflects both the resources available to the Jericho prophetic community and the seriousness with which they took the possibility of Elijah's disappearance. The mention of mountains and valleys reflects the actual topography of the Jordan Valley region—rugged terrain where someone could be lost or stranded. The prophetic community's willingness to mount an extensive search also reflects their authority and independence as an institutional body. However, their misunderstanding reveals a gap in their comprehension: they know the Spirit can move prophets, but they do not grasp the concept of translation to heaven. This reflects a broader ancient Near Eastern context where afterlife beliefs varied and were often unclear, even among the faithful.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 3 Nephi 28, the Savior allows nine disciples to die and be resurrected, but the other three disciples ask to remain and minister. Their understanding is incomplete until Christ explains to them that they will be translated—taken from mortality to immortality without passing through death. Like the sons of the prophets misunderstanding Elijah's fate, these disciples initially misunderstand what translation means. Elisha's knowledge and refusal to search parallels Christ's revelation to those three disciples: sometimes only the Lord and His chosen prophet understand the full dispensational implications of events.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 45:58 speaks of the righteous being caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord—a Restoration teaching that clarifies what Elijah experienced and what the sons of the prophets did not yet understand. D&C 133:55 specifically references Elijah being taken up without tasting death, a doctrine made clear only in the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, participants pass through gates and veils that represent transitions between earthly and heavenly realms. The sons of the prophets understood the Spirit's power to move people horizontally (from place to place on earth), but Elisha knows the Spirit can move people vertically (from earth to heaven). The temple teaches that such transitions are real and that the veil is permeable by God's power. Elisha's authority rests partly on his comprehension of invisible reality that others do not yet see.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's statement in John 3:13, 'No man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven,' reflects a similar teaching: ascension to heaven is not an accident of displacement but a transaction accomplished by God. As Elisha alone understands Elijah's translation, the disciples alone understand Christ's ascension. The risen Christ will be taken up into heaven before many witnesses (Acts 1:9), validating the reality of translation. Elisha's refusal to search and his calm assertion of knowledge parallels Christ's post-resurrection appearances, where He knows what the disciples do not yet comprehend and must teach them to understand new reality.
commentary.application: Elisha's refusal to search teaches a difficult principle: sometimes the right thing to do is to let go and stop searching. The sons of the prophets' desire to find Elijah was natural and well-intentioned, but it was misdirected because their premise was wrong. In modern covenant life, this applies to grief, to questions about death, to loss. When someone passes away in faith (or is called beyond our reach), the right response is not to search for them in earthly terms or to deny the reality of their departure. Elisha teaches that the prophet leads by understanding God's larger purposes, even when the community's immediate instinct is different. Are you, as a believer, willing to accept the prophet's authority to redirect your understanding of difficult events? Are you, as a leader, willing to command obedience based on knowledge the community does not yet possess?

text_kjv: And when they urged him till he was ashamed, he said, Send. They sent therefore fifty men; and they sought three days, but found him not.

commentary.narrative:
The sons of the prophets do not simply accept Elisha's refusal. They press him, urging him again and again until he is ashamed. The Hebrew phrase ad bosh ('until embarrassment, until shame') suggests mounting pressure and repeated entreaties. Elisha stands firm initially, but eventually the weight of the community's insistence, his own position as newly recognized leader, and perhaps the desire to maintain good relations with the prophetic community begin to erode his resolve. He capitulates: 'Send.' In a single word, he reverses his command and grants their request.

The irony is profound and instructive. Elisha yields not because he has changed his mind about Elijah's fate, but because maintaining community cohesion feels more pressing than enforcing his knowledge. He is not wrong to yield—he is recognizing that he must lead a community, not simply command it. Yet the outcome proves him right from the start: three days of searching yield nothing. The fifty men traverse the region thoroughly ('they sought'), but Elijah is gone. The text does not say they found him dead or alive; it simply states they found nothing. When they return (verse 18), Elisha's gentle rebuke—'Did I not say to you, do not go?'—is not harsh anger but a correction rooted in knowledge. He waited in Jericho knowing they would return, knowing the search would fail, knowing the lesson would be painfully learned.

word_study.meaning: To press, urge, entreat persistently. The root relates to insistent pressure, repeated request, or passionate pleading.
word_study.significance: The verb captures the relentless social pressure the community applies. This is not a single polite request but waves of insistence. Modern readers often overlook the communal and social dimension of prophetic authority—prophets do not exist in isolation but must navigate community expectations, even when those expectations conflict with true understanding.

word_study.meaning: To be ashamed, embarrassed, put to shame. The emotion of shame involves loss of face or standing in the community.
word_study.significance: Elisha experiences social pressure that his position as new prophet has not entirely insulated him from. He is vulnerable to community opinion, to the fear of appearing unreasonable or autocratic. This makes him human and relatable, even as it shows the complexity of prophetic leadership. The word choice reveals that Elisha's capitulation is motivated by shame, not by reconsideration of the facts.

word_study.meaning: They sent, they dispatched. The verb represents the community acting on Elisha's permission, moving from request to action.
word_study.significance: Once permission is granted, the community acts immediately. There is no delay, no further discussion. This shows the eagerness with which they pursued the search—they were ready to go and only needed the new prophet's approval.

cross_references.connection: The initial proposal and Elisha's refusal; verse 17 shows the pressure mounting as the community persists despite the refusal.
Saul admits to Samuel, 'I have sinned... I was afraid of the people and obeyed their voice'—similar tension between personal conviction and community pressure that compromises the leader's integrity.
Paul recounts confronting Peter at Antioch because Peter was swayed by social pressure from the Judaizers, a parallel to leaders being moved by community opinion despite better knowledge.

The Zoramites reject Alma's preaching, and Alma and his companions must leave, only later learning that their departure was right and that the Spirit had guided them—a parallel to a leader's original direction being vindicated even when the community resists it.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern societies, leadership was often a negotiation between individual authority and communal will. Elders, priests, and prophets held power but were not absolute monarchs; they had to maintain relationships with other power centers. The sons of the prophets at Jericho were not Elisha's subordinates but peers or colleagues in a guild structure. His authority was newly established and not yet fully consolidated. The three-day search reflects the distance that could be covered in that time by a determined party. The Jordan Valley region is not vast, but it is rugged enough that a person could evade searchers or be genuinely lost. The failure to find Elijah in three days of searching was not unusual; it validated that Elijah was not simply hidden nearby.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 29, Mosiah counsel against a king and encourages the people to elect judges instead—the people experience tension between desiring a king and Mosiah's conviction that judges are better. Though the parallel is not exact, both narratives show leaders wrestling with community pressure to do what the community wants rather than what they believe is right.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 52:9 commands leaders to be meek and to humble themselves, not to be overbearing or tyrannical. Elisha's willingness to listen to the community and to yield when the pressure becomes intense reflects this principle. Leadership is not about rigid insistence on personal knowledge but about building community consensus where possible.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple ceremony includes moments where the initiate is tested and pushed back by gatekeepers before being allowed to proceed. Similarly, Elisha is tested by the prophetic community's resistance; he must learn to lead not through force but through the willingness to engage with the community's will, even when his own knowledge suggests a different course.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ in Gethsemane prayed, 'Not my will, but thine, be done' (Luke 22:42), submitting His will to the Father's even at great personal cost. Though Christ does not yield to community pressure, He does yield to the Father's will and accepts the burden that the community's lack of understanding will place on Him. Similarly, Elisha yields—not to the prophetic community's understanding, but to their request, accepting that they will learn through experience what he already knows. This parallels Christ's acceptance of being misunderstood and His willingness to allow events to unfold so that believers can witness and learn.
commentary.application: Verse 17 teaches a subtle but important leadership lesson: sometimes the right thing to do is to allow the community to learn through their own experience rather than to force compliance with the leader's knowledge. Elisha knows the search will be futile, yet he allows it to happen. In your own leadership—as a parent, teacher, or priesthood holder—this raises a difficult question: when should you insist, and when should you permit the community to experience the consequences of their misunderstanding? There is wisdom in knowing the difference. Elisha's capitulation is not weakness; it is the recognition that authority sustained by force is brittle, while authority that allows for community input and learning is stronger. However, the lesson also works in reverse: do you, as a member, press leaders past their conviction out of desire for what you want, rather than trusting their knowledge and direction?

text_kjv: And when they came again to him, (for he tarried at Jericho,) he said unto them, Did I not say unto you, Go not?

commentary.narrative:
The search party returns to Jericho after three days of fruitless seeking, exactly as Elisha knew they would. He has waited for them in Jericho, not anxiously but with the calm knowledge of one who knows how events will unfold. His greeting is neither vindictive nor gloating; it is a gentle but firm reminder: 'Did I not say unto you, Do not go?' The question is rhetorical but not harsh. It is the voice of someone saying, 'I told you this would be the outcome. I knew.' The Covenant Rendering renders it simply: 'Did I not tell you not to go?' The repetition of his original words emphasizes the point without requiring him to say 'I told you so.' The implicit message is clear: you now have empirical proof that my original direction was right.

This moment establishes Elisha's authority on firmer ground than before. It is not based on the miracle of the parted Jordan alone, not on the community's initial acknowledgment, but on knowledge demonstrated. He knew what would happen; it happened exactly as he said. The sons of the prophets have now learned—through experience—that Elisha's understanding of reality is reliable and trustworthy. Going forward, when Elisha speaks, the prophetic community will have cause to listen, because he has proven himself to know things they do not. The gentle rebuke becomes the foundation of genuine prophetic authority.

word_study.meaning: To sit, to dwell, to remain. The word suggests a settled presence, not temporary lodging but an establishment of place.
word_study.significance: The parenthetical note that Elisha remained in Jericho is significant. He did not flee or hide; he stayed publicly in the city, waiting for the search party to return. This demonstrates confidence and calm knowledge. He was not worried about his standing or his authority being challenged; he was simply waiting for events to unfold as he knew they would.

word_study.meaning: Did I not say? The negative particle combined with the past tense creates a rhetorical question that assumes agreement and recalls previous words.
word_study.significance: This is not an accusatory demand but a pedagogical question. Elisha is helping the prophetic community remember his original directive and connect it to the result they have just experienced. He is teaching through Socratic method: drawing them to the conclusion that his original knowledge was sound.

cross_references.connection: These verses record the search that failed; verse 18 shows the return and Elisha's response.
The heart of the prudent gets knowledge, and the ear of the wise seeks knowledge—the search party is learning to listen to Elisha's knowledge rather than relying on their own assumptions.
Samuel's authority is established because his words prove reliable and never fall to the ground—similarly, Elisha's authority grows as his words are consistently proven true.

The Lord promises that those who receive the president of the Church receive the Lord, and that the president shall receive understanding and knowledge by the Spirit—Elisha's knowledge demonstrates the pattern of prophetic understanding.

commentary.historical_context: Jericho was an established city with a prophetic community centered there (verse 5 mentions a company of prophets at Jericho). The city was significant as the first city Joshua conquered (Joshua 6) and maintained religious importance throughout the monarchical period. Elisha's decision to remain in Jericho rather than move on to other centers (such as Bethel, where another prophetic community is mentioned in 2 Kings 2:23) shows his establishing his base of operations there. The three-day search was standard length for such expeditions in the ancient Near East. After three days, the searchers would return, assuming the person was either dead or beyond reach. Elisha's knowledge that the search would be futile in three days specifically shows prescient understanding of how the search would develop.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 37:33-35, Alma counsels his son Helaman to keep the commandments, and the promises given come to pass. Similar to Elisha's establishment of authority through the reliability of his words, prophetic leaders in the Book of Mormon establish credibility through the fulfillment of their words.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 30:11-12 describes how to discern true prophets: they will say the word and it shall be done. Elisha's word regarding the futility of the search is proven reliable, establishing him as a true prophet in the community's understanding.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the endowment, the participant is taught to recognize true messengers and false ones by their words and authority. The sons of the prophets learn to recognize Elisha's true authority not through emotional persuasion but through the reliability of his knowledge. This is the pattern for recognizing priesthood authority in the modern Church: does the leader's direction prove true?

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's fulfillment of Old Testament prophecy establishes His authority as the promised Messiah. Matthew 5:17, 'I am not come to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfill,' shows that authority is demonstrated through the fulfillment of words spoken. Similarly, Elisha's words about the futility of the search are fulfilled, proving his prophetic knowledge and establishing his authority. Christ's resurrection and ascension validate everything He taught, much as Elijah's translation is the ultimate validation of everything Elijah taught, and Elisha's words about that translation prove his authority to lead.
commentary.application: The closing rebuke in verse 18 invites modern believers to consider how they discern true prophetic authority. It is not enough that a leader claims authority or performs isolated miracles; true authority is demonstrated through knowledge that proves reliable over time. Elisha did not berate the sons of the prophets for their disobedience; he simply reminded them: 'I told you.' This is the voice of a prophet who is secure in his understanding and trusts that experience will teach the community. In your own life, when a priesthood leader or prophet gives counsel that you do not immediately understand, Elisha's example suggests patience. The fulfillment of their words will establish their authority. Conversely, if you are a leader, your authority rests ultimately not on position but on the reliability of your words and direction. Earn the community's trust by knowing what others do not and by allowing your knowledge to be validated over time.

text_kjv: And the men of the city said unto Elisha, Behold, I pray thee, the situation of this city is pleasant, as my lord seeth: but the water is naught, and the ground barren.

commentary.narrative:
The men of Jericho approach Elisha with a paradox: their city enjoys an excellent location with fertile soil and pleasant surroundings, yet something fundamental is broken. The water—essential to all life—is polluted, and the ground itself is becoming barren and unproductive. This is not a minor inconvenience but a crisis of sterility affecting both human and animal fertility. The people recognize Elisha as a prophet ('my lord') and appeal to him for divine intervention. They are not demanding but requesting humbly, addressing him with respect and making their case clearly.

What The Covenant Rendering clarifies is the severity of the word meshakkelet ('causing miscarriage'). This is not water that tastes bad or lacks minerals; it actively causes death and miscarriage in both humans and livestock. The Hebrew term meshakkelet comes from shakal, meaning to be bereaved of offspring or to suffer loss of children. The people are facing a crisis in which the source of life itself has become a source of death. The irony is sharp: Jericho, the first city conquered by Israel under Joshua, sits in one of the most geographically privileged locations in Canaan, yet its water—the most essential resource—has become toxic.

word_study.meaning: Causing sterility, miscarriage, bereavement of offspring; from shakal, to be bereaved. The term describes a condition in which fertility itself is negated at the biological level.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering reveals that Jericho's crisis is not merely about poor water quality but about the destruction of reproductive capacity in the land. This sets up Elisha's miracle as not just a practical fix but a restoration of life-giving power itself—a prophetic sign that through the word of God, what is barren can become fruitful again.

word_study.meaning: Bad, evil, wicked, harmful. Literally 'evil waters,' indicating quality that is morally or practically hostile.
word_study.significance: The waters are not merely unpleasant but actively hostile to life—a condition that requires not repair but transformation by divine power.

word_study.meaning: Dwelling place, settlement, location. A term emphasizing the physical position and environment of a place.
word_study.significance: The people acknowledge that geographically and geologically, the city is ideally situated, yet this advantage cannot overcome the corrupted water source—a reminder that physical advantages mean nothing without spiritual and practical provision.

cross_references.connection: Jericho is the city whose walls fell before Israel at Joshua's command; now it faces a different kind of judgment—the life-giving water within has become destructive, requiring a prophet's healing.
At Marah, Israel's water was bitter and undrinkable, and God commanded Moses to cast a tree into the waters to make them wholesome—a typological precedent for Elisha's healing of Jericho's waters.
The geography of Jericho as a city in the Jordan valley, whose water sources are crucial to survival in a desert environment, underscores the severity of the contamination the people face.
The water that brings forth death rather than life mirrors the spiritual decay that comes when the word of God is rejected—both require divine restoration.

commentary.historical_context: Jericho sits in a fertile oasis in the Jordan Valley, one of the lowest and most intensely cultivated regions in Canaan. Archaeological evidence shows that Jericho was continuously inhabited, with natural springs feeding its agricultural economy. The Ein as-Sultan spring (the traditional site of Jericho's water source) is fed by groundwater that can become contaminated by mineral deposits, particularly salts, which would indeed cause the toxic effects described. Ancient peoples understood that water quality was connected to mineral content and salinity. The mention of barrenness suggests either saline water poisoning livestock and causing miscarriage, or mineral deposits in the soil making cultivation difficult. Elisha's act of throwing salt into the spring seems paradoxical until we understand the symbolic and covenantal significance of salt as a purifying and preserving agent—the salt is not a chemical solution but a prophetic sign.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon records similar instances of divine healing and restoration: in Alma 9:10, the people of Ammonihah reject the prophets and face judgment; conversely, in Mosiah 8:7-9, King Benjamin's people are healed and restored when they receive the word from prophets. Elisha's restoration of Jericho's water parallels the spiritual restoration that comes when a people receive prophetic guidance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:8 teaches that the word of God, spoken by prophets, has creative and restorative power: 'And the Lord said unto me, I am Jesus Christ...Wherefore, I say unto you, that ye shall be my disciples.' The prophet's word, spoken in God's name, carries authority over creation itself—as Elisha's word will heal the water.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Water in temple theology represents the purifying and life-giving power of covenants. Jericho's contaminated water represents a people or place cut off from the covenant blessings of life and fertility. Elisha's healing of the water foreshadows the restoration of covenant relationship and the return of divine blessings—fertility, health, and life flow from renewed covenant connection.

commentary.christological_typology: Jericho's death-dealing water represents the spiritual condition of humanity without Christ—sources of life corrupted by sin and separated from the fountain of living water. Christ, in John 4:10-14, offers 'living water' to the woman at the well, contrasting it with water that leaves one thirsty. Elisha, as a prophet-type prefiguring Christ's healing ministry, brings restoration to the source of life itself. His action at the spring parallels Christ's work: healing at the source, restoring what is barren to fruitfulness, and making what was destructive into that which sustains life.
commentary.application: When we face what seems like a fundamental corruption in our circumstances—a relationship, a situation, a pattern of life that produces only barrenness—the first step is to recognize the problem clearly, as the men of Jericho did. They did not deny or minimize their crisis; they brought it to the prophet and asked for divine intervention. In our modern covenant life, when we recognize that something foundational is broken (finances, health, relationships, spiritual condition), we must similarly bring the matter to God through prophetic counsel and seek His healing at the source, not merely addressing symptoms. Like the men of Jericho, we must respect the authority of the living prophets and be willing to follow their direction, even when the remedy (like salt cast into the spring) seems strange or insufficient. We must believe in the restorative power of the word spoken in God's name.

text_kjv: And he said, Bring me a new cruse, and put salt therein. And they brought it to him.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha's response is immediate and specific. He does not pray at length, does not engage in elaborate ritual, but issues a straightforward command: bring a new bowl and fill it with salt. The people obey without question or hesitation. This brevity and directness contrast sharply with the elaborate actions of some miracle workers in ancient religious texts. There is no fanfare, no dramatic invocation, no preparation of special materials—only the selection of a new vessel and the addition of salt, two elements that carry profound covenant and purification significance in Hebrew tradition.

The command reveals the nature of prophetic authority: the prophet speaks, and those who recognize his authority act. The people do not delay, do not ask for explanation, do not test the prophet's instructions. Their immediate obedience signals their faith in Elisha's authority as a successor to Elijah. The new cruse (or bowl) is crucial—it must be unused, ritually clean, bearing no contamination from prior use. This newness suggests that God is initiating something fresh, not merely patching a broken system. Salt, which preserves and purifies, will become the instrument through which the prophet addresses the source of death.

word_study.meaning: A new, unused vessel or bowl. Tzlochit may derive from a root meaning 'to pour out' or 'to be round'; chadashah means 'new.' The emphasis is on an object with no prior history or contamination.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering notes, the newness is essential—the vessel must be unspoiled and unused. In ancient Near Eastern practice, new vessels were required for sacred purposes. This signals that what Elisha is about to do is not a human engineering solution but a divine act that requires a ritually appropriate vessel.

word_study.meaning: Salt; from a root meaning 'to be strong' or 'to preserve.' In Hebrew, salt is associated with covenant, preservation, purification, and divine judgment.
word_study.significance: In Numbers 18:19 and 2 Chronicles 13:5, salt is called 'the covenant of salt,' signifying an eternal, inviolable covenant. As The Covenant Rendering emphasizes, the salt here is not a chemical solution but a covenantal sign—it represents God's work of restoration and the establishment of a new covenant relationship between God and Jericho. The salt also connects to purification: in ancient practice, salt was used in burnt offerings and purification rituals to make something acceptable to God.

cross_references.connection: God commands that the covenant between Himself and the Levites be sealed with a 'covenant of salt'—an eternal, unchangeable covenant. Elisha's use of salt invokes this covenantal meaning: the healing of the water is not temporary but permanent.

The phrase 'covenant of salt' appears again, describing the covenant between God and David's dynasty. The salt in Elisha's miracle carries the weight of this covenant theology—what is being restored is not just physical water but covenant relationship and divine blessing.
All grain offerings must be seasoned with salt, a sign of the covenant. Salt makes an offering acceptable to God; here, salt will make the corrupted water acceptable for life-giving use.

Christ calls His disciples 'the salt of the earth,' indicating that salt represents the transformative, preserving power of divine truth. Elisha, as a prophet-type, becomes through the salt an instrument of transformation.
The Lord promises that the faithful will be preserved and protected—salt as a preserving agent symbolizes God's covenant promise to preserve His people.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern cultures, salt was extraordinarily valuable and symbolically laden. It was a principal preservative for food in a world without refrigeration, making it essential for survival. Salt was also used in purification and sacred rituals throughout the ancient world. The Ugaritic, Egyptian, and Mesopotamian texts all reference salt as both a practical and ritual substance. The use of a new vessel suggests awareness of ritual purity practices—in Israelite law, new vessels were appropriate for sacred use, while used vessels might be considered contaminated. The specificity of Elisha's command—new cruse, salt—suggests a ritual propriety that would have been recognized and respected by ancient audiences. The simplicity of the act (a handful of salt thrown into a spring) would have appeared insufficient by natural causation alone, thus highlighting the miraculous nature of what follows.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 3:5-7, the angel announces Christ as 'the Lamb of God' who will atone for sin and 'work mighty miracles among the children of men.' The miraculous healing of Jericho's water through a simple prophetic act parallels the simple yet mighty power of the Atonement—what appears small in human terms carries infinite power when spoken by one authorized of God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-6 establishes that the words spoken by the Lord's spokesman are 'the will of the Lord, and the word of the Lord, and the power of the Lord.' Elisha's command to bring salt and cast it into the water demonstrates this principle: the prophet's word, not the physical substance, is the true agent of change. The salt is merely the outward sign of the inward covenant power.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, salt is used in purification and in the offering of sacrifices. Elisha's use of salt in a new vessel invokes temple theology: the restoration of Jericho's water parallels the sanctification and purification of a people through covenants made in the temple. The new vessel represents the renewal of covenant relationship.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha, empowered with Elijah's mantle and speaking in God's name, prefigures Christ as the one who heals and restores. The new vessel suggests the need for a fresh start, a new creation—in 2 Corinthians 5:17, Paul writes that 'if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature.' Salt, as a preserving and purifying agent, represents Christ's work of purification and preservation of the faithful. The command itself reflects Christ's authority—He speaks, and creation responds (as in the calming of the storm in Mark 4:39).
commentary.application: When we seek prophetic guidance for our spiritual healing, we must be prepared to act immediately and completely on what the prophet instructs, even if the remedy seems simple or insufficient by worldly standards. The people of Jericho did not question Elisha's command for salt and a new bowl—they obeyed. In our covenant life, when living prophets counsel us through General Conference, official communications, or the Spirit's prompting, we must respond with the same faith and obedience. We cannot demand that the remedy make sense by human reasoning; we must trust in the authority of those called to lead. Additionally, the emphasis on the 'new' vessel reminds us that spiritual healing often requires starting fresh—letting go of old patterns, old habits, old thinking—and allowing God to work through us as new vessels, purified and ready for His purposes.

text_kjv: And he went forth unto the spring of the waters, and cast the salt in there, and said, Thus saith the LORD, I have healed these waters; there shall not be from thence any more death or barren land.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha takes decisive action. He does not perform the act at the city gate or in a public square, but goes directly to the motza ha-mayim—the source or outlet of the water. This is theologically significant: healing happens at the source, not downstream. By addressing the fountain itself, Elisha is not offering a temporary fix or treating symptoms; he is restoring the very origin point of life for the entire region. The act is simple and swift: he casts the salt into the spring and immediately speaks a declaration in the name of the Lord.

The declaration itself is remarkable for its use of what Hebrew grammar recognizes as the 'prophetic perfect'—Elisha speaks of the healing as already accomplished ('I have healed') even though the physical manifestation is just beginning. This is not presumption but the language of divine certainty: when God speaks through His prophet, the thing is as good as done. The reversal is total and absolute: death (mavet) and miscarriage (meshakkelet) will no longer come from these waters. The prophet does not speak of gradual improvement or partial remedy; he announces complete, permanent restoration. The phrase 'thus saith the LORD' frames this as a divine utterance, not a personal act by Elisha. The prophet is merely the instrument through which the Lord's creative and restorative word flows.

word_study.meaning: The place where water comes forth, the source or outlet; from yatza, to go out or come forth. Emphasizes the originating point of the water flow.
word_study.significance: The prophet goes not to where the corruption is most evident but to where the problem originates. Spiritual and physical healing in biblical thought happens at the root, the source, the foundation. By going to motza ha-mayim, Elisha demonstrates that prophetic power works at the fundamental level, transforming the very source of life.

word_study.meaning: I have healed, cured, mended; from rapha, to heal. In the prophetic perfect tense, indicating an action that is certain in God's sight even before its physical completion.
word_study.significance: The use of the past tense ('I have healed') rather than 'I will heal' or 'I am healing' reflects the Hebrew understanding that God's word accomplishes what it declares. When a prophet speaks in God's name, the thing is already done in the divine reality, even if the physical manifestation follows. This is the power of the dabar YHWH—the word of the Lord.

word_study.meaning: Death, the state of being dead; from the root meaning 'to die.' Indicates not just the fact of death but the condition and power of death in a place.
word_study.significance: The waters had become a source of mavet—not just that people and animals occasionally died, but that death itself emanated from the spring. The healing reverses this: the waters transition from being agents of death to being sources of life.

word_study.meaning: Miscarriage, bereavement of offspring, barrenness at the biological level; from shakal, to be bereaved.
word_study.significance: As noted in verse 19, this term describes not mere infertility but active destruction of reproductive life. The healing restores fertility and the capacity for life at its most fundamental level—in the womb and in the animal herds.

cross_references.connection: Moses is commanded to cast a tree into the bitter waters of Marah, making them wholesome and sweet—a clear typological precedent for Elisha's healing of the water. Both prophets address the source and use a material object as the sign of divine healing.

The psalmist longs for God 'as the hart panteth after the water brooks'—water as a symbol of life, healing, and divine sustenance. Jericho's healing water restores this symbol of God's life-giving presence.
Christ offers the Samaritan woman 'living water' that quenches thirst eternally. Elisha's healing of Jericho's water prefigures this living water that comes through the prophet and the word of God.

The prophet declares that God's word 'shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please.' Elisha's declaration of healing, spoken in God's name, demonstrates this principle: the prophetic word is creative and accomplishes its purpose.

The Lord teaches that He speaks and creation responds: 'All things were made by him; and by him all things consist...and he received all things, that he might be glorified.' The prophet, as God's voice, participates in this creative power.

commentary.historical_context: The Ein as-Sultan spring (modern Tel Jericho) emerges from an underground aquifer and creates a natural oasis in the arid Jordan Valley. The spring's mineral content and seasonal variation could indeed cause the problems described: high salt or mineral concentration would poison livestock, cause miscarriage in pregnant animals and women, and render the soil difficult to cultivate due to salt accumulation. Elisha's throwing of salt into the spring would be, from a chemical standpoint, the opposite of what would help; this underscores that the healing is not natural but miraculous. The prophetic declaration and the casting of salt are inseparable—it is the word, not the material, that accomplishes the healing. Ancient Near Eastern religious texts often describe gods or divine representatives addressing the source of water, mountains, and natural phenomena, treating them as entities that respond to divine power. Elisha's action fits this cultural framework while pointing to the supremacy of Israel's God.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 32:28-29, Alma teaches that faith that works must be accompanied by works: 'Now, as I said concerning faith—faith is not to have a perfect knowledge of things; therefore if ye have faith ye hope for things which are not seen, which are true...Now we will compare the word unto a seed.' Elisha's faith (speaking the declaration before the visible healing) coupled with his action (casting the salt) demonstrates the principle that faith and works together bring forth the miracle. The word itself, when spoken by a prophet, is the seed of transformation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 teaches: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the prophecies and promises which are in them shall all be fulfilled. What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken...whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' Elisha's declaration carries the weight of God's own word. When the prophet speaks, God speaks; the healing flows from divine utterance, not from human agency.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In Latter-day Saint theology, the font in the temple represents the healing waters of Zion—waters that wash away sin and restore the covenant relationship. Jericho's healed waters symbolize the purifying, life-giving power of temple covenants. The waters, once destructive, become the means of sustenance and blessing—paralleling how broken covenant relationships are healed through renewed temple worship and commitment.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate source of healing water. In John 7:37-39, Christ stands in the temple and cries, 'If any man thirst, let him come unto me, and drink...out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.' Elisha, by healing the spring at its source, prefigures Christ's office as the fountain of living water. The waters that once brought death are restored to bring life—a type of Christ's Atonement, which transforms death into resurrection and opens the way to eternal life. The 'prophetic perfect' language ('I have healed') reflects Christ's declaration in Revelation 22:13: 'I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end'—the past, present, and future are encompassed in Christ's eternal work of redemption.
commentary.application: When we face a situation where the source itself is corrupted—whether in our character, our relationships, our community, or our spiritual condition—we must understand that surface fixes are insufficient. We must seek healing at the source, just as Elisha went to motza ha-mayim. This may require repentance, restructuring of fundamental habits or relationships, or a complete recommitment to covenant principles. We must believe in the power of the prophetic word spoken in God's name. The living prophets today carry the same authority as Elisha; their words, though they may seem simple or insufficient by worldly reasoning, carry the power to transform when spoken in God's name and in faith. We must act on prophetic counsel immediately and completely, without hesitation or demand for explanation. Finally, we must understand that our healing, like Jericho's, is not temporary or provisional but permanent and total—'even unto this day.' The Lord does not offer patch-work solutions; He offers complete restoration.

text_kjv: So the waters were healed unto this day, according to the saying of Elisha which he spake.

commentary.narrative:
The narrator adds a footnote that confirms the permanence of Elisha's miracle. The phrase 'unto this day' (ad ha-yom ha-zeh) is a historical notation indicating that at the time of writing, the water of Jericho remains healed and wholesome. This is not a dramatic affirmation of a temporary wonder, but a statement of fact: the healing persists, generation after generation. The waters that killed are now life-giving. The narrator explicitly attributes this ongoing miracle not to the salt (which is never mentioned again) but to 'the saying of Elisha which he spake'—the prophetic word itself.

This verse establishes an important principle: the power of the miracle resides entirely in the word spoken by the prophet in God's name. The salt was merely a sign, a physical action that accompanied the utterance. What matters is the dabar Elisha—the word of Elisha—which flows from the dabar YHWH—the word of the Lord. The narrative does not explain the mechanism of the healing, nor does it claim that the salt chemically altered the water. Instead, it attributes the miracle to the prophetic declaration. This is consistent with biblical theology: God speaks creation into existence (Genesis 1); God's word accomplishes what He purposes (Isaiah 55:11). The narrator's comment anchors the miracle in history: it is not mythological or legendary, but a matter of documented fact.

word_study.meaning: Until this day, even now; a temporal marker indicating that the condition described continues into the present moment of the narrator.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears throughout the Hebrew Bible as a historical assertion—the narrator is claiming eyewitness or documented knowledge that the condition persists. It is a claim about history and continuity, not mythology. The healing is real, verifiable, and permanent.

word_study.meaning: According to the word, in accordance with the saying; from davar, word, thing, matter.
word_study.significance: The healing is attributed not to natural causes or to the physical action (the salt) but to the dabar—the word spoken. In Hebrew thought, davar carries both the meaning 'word' and 'thing'—the word is the thing; it accomplishes reality. Kidvar Elisha ('according to the word of Elisha') means the healing flows from the prophetic utterance.

cross_references.connection: God's word accomplishes what He purposes and does not return empty; similarly, Elisha's word, spoken in God's name, accomplishes the healing and continues to sustain it through history.

Moses is told that a prophet like him will arise, and 'whosoever will not hearken unto my words which he shall speak in my name, I will require it of him.' Elisha, as that prophet-type, speaks with divine authority; the healing persists as evidence of his prophetic authenticity.

The stones of Gilgal are set up as a memorial 'that all the people of the earth might know the hand of the LORD, that it is mighty.' The healing of Jericho's water serves a similar function—a sign of God's mighty hand working through His prophet.

The Lord teaches that His word is 'quick and powerful, sharper than a two-edged sword,' accomplishing what He purposes. Elisha's word, as the Lord's prophet, carries this same creative and sustaining power.

commentary.historical_context: The phrase 'unto this day' is a common historical notation in ancient Near Eastern literature, indicating that the narrator is writing at a significant temporal distance from the event described. This suggests that the text of 2 Kings was composed centuries after Elisha's ministry, during the Judean monarchy or possibly after the exile, when a return to the land was contemplated. The persistence of the healing would have been a matter of historical record—the water of Jericho would have been known and used for generations. The Ein as-Sultan spring does indeed flow to the present day, making this claim historically plausible. The attribution of the healing to the 'saying' rather than the salt or any natural cause reflects a sophisticated understanding: the narrator distinguishes between the physical accompaniment of the miracle (the salt, the action) and its true cause (the word of the prophet).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 8:13-14, the prophets among the Nephites are called 'the stumbling block of the people,' yet their words 'shall be preserved.' Similarly, Elisha's word is preserved in history through the continuing miracle; his prophetic authority is confirmed by the lasting effect of his utterance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 states that the Lord's word, whether spoken by His own voice or by the voice of His servants, is binding and sure. The continuing healing of Jericho's water is living proof that the prophet's word, when aligned with God's purpose, endures forever.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, covenants made are eternal and persist through all generations. The continuing healing of the water is analogous to the eternal nature of temple covenants—once made and sealed, they abide in perpetuity. The water, made wholesome through the prophetic word, becomes a type of the continuing blessing that flows from covenant relationship.

commentary.christological_typology: The permanent nature of the healing points to Christ's eternal work. His Atonement, once wrought, continues to operate 'even unto this day' and forever. Hebrews 10:12 states that Christ 'sat down on the right hand of God...his enemies made his footstool,' indicating that His work is complete and its effects endure. The healing of Jericho's water, attributed entirely to the prophetic word, prefigures the way that Christ's word—His teachings, His sacrifice, His promises—continues to heal and sustain creation.
commentary.application: The narrator's confirmation that the waters remain healed 'unto this day' teaches us to have confidence in the permanence of prophetic counsel and divine promises. When we receive guidance from living prophets and follow their counsel, the effects are not temporary or conditional; they establish lasting change in our lives and in our posterity. We should look for evidence of the enduring power of the Lord's word in our own experience: the blessings that flow from obedience, the healing that comes from repentance, the transformation that results from accepting prophetic guidance. These effects compound and persist through generations, just as the healing of Jericho's water blessed all who drank from it for centuries. When we question whether prophetic counsel is still relevant or powerful in our modern world, we can return to verse 22's simple assertion: the word spoken in God's name accomplishes reality and continues to sustain that reality through time.

text_kjv: And he went up from thence unto Bethel: and as he was going up by the way, there came forth little children out of the city, and mocked him, and said unto him, Go up, thou bald head; go up, thou bald head.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative shifts abruptly from a miracle of restoration to a scene of mockery and contempt. Elisha leaves Jericho and travels northward to Bethel, a city with deeply negative theological significance in the northern kingdom of Israel. As he walks along the road, a group of youths—The Covenant Rendering clarifies that ne'arim and ne'arim qetannim likely refer to young men rather than 'little children,' probably adolescents to young adults—emerge from the city to mock and taunt him. The taunt is two-fold: 'Aleh qereach'—'Go up, baldhead'—with 'go up' (aleh) possibly referencing Elijah's recent ascension to heaven, which all of Jericho and Bethel would have witnessed or heard about. The repetition of the taunt emphasizes the viciousness: they are not merely insulting his appearance but apparently mocking his assumption of Elijah's prophetic role.

Bethel carries particular weight in this context. It was the site where Jeroboam I established one of the golden calf temples (1 Kings 12:29), making it a center of religious apostasy and rejection of the Jerusalem temple and the Davidic covenant. The youths emerging from Bethel represent a generation raised in idolatry, who mock the prophet of the true God. Their mockery is not innocent childhood jest but a deliberate repudiation of prophetic authority. By mocking Elisha, they mock the Lord whose word he speaks. The physical reference to baldness might indicate Elisha's age or appearance, but in context, it represents an assault on the prophet's dignity and authority. The fact that the youths are from Bethel—a city of calf worship—suggests this is not a random encounter but a confrontation between the kingdom of man and the kingdom of God.

word_study.meaning: Young men, youths, servants; from na'ar, to shake, to shout. Ne'arim covers a wide age range from adolescents to young adults. The addition of qetannim ('small, young') may emphasize their youth but does not necessarily mean they are young children. In military contexts, ne'arim can refer to soldiers or fighting men.
word_study.significance: As The Covenant Rendering emphasizes, the term is better translated 'young men' or 'youths' rather than 'little children.' This changes the nature of the offense: these are not innocent children but young men old enough to act with deliberate malice. They are capable of understanding what they are doing when they mock a prophet.

word_study.meaning: To go up, to ascend, to climb. Can be literal (ascending a mountain) or metaphorical (ascending to heaven, being promoted). The same verb is used of Elijah's ascension in 2 Kings 2:11.
word_study.significance: The double use of 'aleh in the taunt may be deliberately mocking Elijah's ascension—'Go up, like your predecessor, you bald-headed fraud.' The youths may be expressing disbelief in Elijah's ascension or contempt for Elisha's claim to have inherited his mantle. The command to 'go up' in mockery becomes, ironically, a statement about what the Lord will do through judgment.

word_study.meaning: Bald, bare, hairless head; from qarah, to make bare. Used literally to describe baldness and metaphorically of shame or humiliation.
word_study.significance: The insult may reference Elisha's actual baldness (he may have been older than Elijah when he assumed the mantle) or may be a metaphorical denunciation of weakness or shame. In the ancient Near East, hair was associated with strength and virility; baldness could suggest weakness, age, or shame. However, in context, the insult is more about rejecting the prophet's authority than commenting on his appearance.

word_study.meaning: To mock, to jeer, to ridicule, to make sport of. From qalal, to be light, to be of little value, to despise.
word_study.significance: The verb indicates a deliberate, contemptuous act. The youths are not innocently making fun but are deliberately ridiculing and despising Elisha. They are treating the prophet as worthy of contempt.

cross_references.connection: Jeroboam established the golden calf temples at Bethel and Dan, leading the northern kingdom into idolatry. The youths of Bethel, raised in this apostasy, represent the spiritual corruption that results from rejection of the true God and His prophets.

Christ rebukes the Pharisees for being the descendants of those who mocked and killed the prophets: 'Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees...ye build the tombs of the prophets.' Mockery of prophets is a mark of spiritual rebellion recurring through history.

The epistle recalls that prophets were 'mocked...and scourged, and moreover bound and imprisoned,' yet 'were not worthy' of their suffering because they were servants of God. Elisha's mockery fits this pattern of prophetic persecution.

The Lord promises that His spokesman 'shall have all the writing of the prophets,' and 'Wherefore, meaning the church, thou shalt give heed unto all his words and commandments.' Those who mock the prophet mock the Lord Himself.
Mormon warns against those who mock the prophets and the Church, stating that such mockery brings judgment. The youths of Bethel, in mocking Elisha, set themselves against the kingdom of God.

commentary.historical_context: Bethel sits in the hill country of Ephraim, about twelve miles north of Jerusalem. It was a major religious center in the northern kingdom, and Jeroboam's establishment of the golden calf cult there was a deliberate rival to the Jerusalem temple. By the time of Elisha (9th century BCE), Bethel would have been fully integrated into the northern religious economy, with multiple generations raised in the calf worship. The youths emerging from Bethel would have been indoctrinated in rejection of the Jerusalem temple, the Davidic covenant, and the authority of YHWH's prophets as those prophets appeared in Judah. Their mockery of Elisha represents not mere personal rudeness but a religious and political statement: rejection of the prophet who represents God's true authority. The reference to the road suggests that Elisha was traveling publicly, making him visible to whoever emerged from the city. In ancient Near Eastern culture, a prophet's journey was itself a form of proclamation—to encounter a prophet was to encounter the divine presence. The youths' mockery is thus a direct affront to divine authority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 17:11-12, Abinadi is mocked by King Noah's priests before his martyrdom. Like Elisha, Abinadi is a prophet of the true God confronting a community in apostasy. The Book of Mormon establishes that mockery of prophets is endemic to apostate communities and that prophets have consistently been rejected by those who have turned from the covenant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:14 teaches that the Lord's word comes 'whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants...that the unjust might be condemned.' Those who mock the prophet condemn themselves by rejecting the voice of God. The judgment that follows Elisha's curse reflects the principle that rejection of the prophet brings condemnation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Bethel, as a center of false worship (the golden calf), represents the opposite of temple covenant. Those who maintain false worship systems inevitably come into conflict with the true prophets of God. The youths' mockery represents the hostility that always arises between those committed to false religion and those who call people to return to true covenant relationship.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's mockery prefigures Christ's suffering at the hands of those who reject His authority. In Matthew 26:67-68, Christ is spat upon and struck during His trial; in Luke 23:35-37, He is mocked while on the cross: 'He saved others; let him save himself.' Both Elisha and Christ face mockery from those who represent spiritual rebellion against God. Christ's ultimate rejection and execution represents the deepest form of the prophet-mockery that begins with contempt and culminates in violence. Yet both Christ and Elisha (through the judgment that follows) demonstrate that rejection of the prophet brings judgment.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern covenant members with a difficult reality: mockery of the prophets, and contempt for prophetic authority, remains a temptation even in our day. The youths of Bethel represent not ancient history but a recurring human tendency to reject authority, to mock those who call for repentance, and to organize communal support for that mockery. We may not face the violent rejection that some prophets have faced, but we live in a culture that increasingly mocks religious authority and prophetic counsel. The question is: are we aligned with Bethel or with Elisha? Do we defend and honor the living prophets, or do we position ourselves among those who distance themselves from prophetic guidance? The Covenant Rendering's clarification that these are 'youths' or 'young men,' not innocent children, reminds us that there comes an age when mockery becomes a moral choice, not innocent behavior. When we hear our peers, our colleagues, or our media culture mock the prophets, we must understand this as a spiritual and moral issue: it is mockery directed against God Himself.

text_kjv: And he turned back, and looked on them, and cursed them in the name of the LORD. And there came forth two she bears out of the wood, and tare forty and two children of them.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative reaches a point of crisis and judgment with stunning directness. Elisha turns back toward the youths. His first action is to look at them—a deliberate gaze that signifies his awareness and will. He then speaks a curse in the name of the LORD (be-shem YHWH). The curse is not an expression of personal anger or retaliation but an invocation of divine authority and judgment. The prophet is not acting on his own but as God's instrument of judgment. Immediately—and with no time for escape—two she-bears emerge from the forest (ya'ar) and maul (wavataqqa'enu) forty-two of the youths.

This is one of the most jarring and difficult narratives in the Old Testament, and it deserves serious theological reflection. The violence is real and terrible. Yet the text presents it not as a random tragedy but as a precise act of divine judgment. The number forty-two may carry symbolic weight (it appears in several judgment contexts in Scripture) or may simply indicate a large group. The detail that the bears are female (dubbim, the feminine form) is notable—female bears would be particularly protective and aggressive if they had cubs, making the attack both more ferocious and more comprehensible. However, the text does not claim to explain the mechanism of the bears' appearance; it presents them as a divinely sent instrument of judgment.

The significance lies in what the narrative asserts about the relationship between the prophet's authority and divine judgment. When the prophet, speaking in God's name, pronounces a curse, that curse carries weight. The youths were not simply rude; they mocked the prophet who represents God. In the theology of ancient Israel, such mockery had consequences. The passage teaches that contempt for prophetic authority carries real spiritual and temporal consequences. The precise nature of those consequences lies with God, not with the prophet (who does not direct the bears); the prophet simply invokes God's justice, and God responds.

word_study.meaning: To curse, to revile, to invoke evil upon; from qalal, to be light or insignificant. A curse is a spoken pronouncement calling down judgment or evil.
word_study.significance: Elisha's curse is not a personal wish for harm but a prophetic invocation of divine judgment. In biblical theology, a curse spoken in God's name has binding power because God backs it. The prophet does not create the judgment; he pronounces it, and God executes it.

word_study.term_english: in the name of the LORD
word_study.meaning: In the name of the LORD; a formula indicating that the speaker acts with divine authority and that the LORD stands behind the utterance.
word_study.significance: This phrase appears throughout Scripture when prophets perform miracles or pronounce judgments (cf. Elisha's healing of the water in verse 21). The formula 'in the name of the LORD' distinguishes between personal action and prophetic authority. Elisha is not cursing in his own strength but invoking the name and authority of YHWH.

word_study.meaning: Bears, wild beasts; from dab, the root for bear. The feminine form (dubbim in this context, though the standard plural is dubbim) emphasizes that these are female bears.
word_study.significance: The specificity that these are female bears may indicate that they were protecting cubs or were in a particularly aggressive state. Bears in ancient Near Eastern literature are creatures of wilderness and divine judgment. Their emergence from the forest (ya'ar) is presented as a response to the prophet's curse.

word_study.meaning: Tore, mauled, ripped open; from baqa', to split, to break open, to tear apart.
word_study.significance: The term is violent and final, indicating thorough and fatal attack. There is no ambiguity about the severity of the judgment: it is complete and decisive.

word_study.meaning: Children, young ones, youths; from yalad, to bear, to give birth. Technically refers to young people, though the passage uses three different terms (ne'arim, qetannim, yeladim) to describe the group, suggesting they are young men rather than small children.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that the repeated use of different age-descriptive terms suggests a group of youths or young men. This is significant because it means the judgment falls on those old enough to understand the nature of their mockery—not innocent children but young men capable of deliberate rebellion.

cross_references.connection: The Lord declares: 'See now that I, even I, am he...if I whet my glittering sword, and mine hand take hold on judgment; I will render vengeance to mine enemies.' Elisha's curse invokes this divine principle that judgment belongs to God and flows through His chosen instruments.

Samuel rebukes Saul, saying 'rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry.' The youths' mockery of the prophet represents rebellion against God's authority, which is presented in Scripture as equivalent to witchcraft or idolatry.

The law commands: 'Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man.' While this specifically addresses the elderly, it reflects a broader principle of respect for authority. The youths' mockery of Elisha, a prophet, violates the honor due to God's representative.

A wise proverb states: 'The eye that mocketh at his father, and despiseth to obey his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, and the young eagles shall eat it.' The principle is that those who mock authority face judgment.
The Lord teaches that He comes 'to vindicate my Zion and my people'—those who reject the word spoken by His servants reject the Lord Himself and incur judgment.

Mormon warns those who mock the prophets and the Zion of the latter days that judgment awaits them. The Book of Mormon echoes the Old Testament principle that rejection of the prophet brings condemnation.

commentary.historical_context: Bears inhabited the forested regions of ancient Palestine and Mesopotamia. The forests around Bethel and the Jordan Valley would have provided habitat for wild bears, which were known to be dangerous to humans, particularly if defending cubs or in a defensive posture. In ancient Near Eastern literature and texts, wild animals are sometimes depicted as instruments of divine judgment—a way of expressing that God controls creation and can direct natural forces against those who rebel against His purposes. The number forty-two is significant in biblical numerology: forty often represents judgment or testing, and forty-two appears in other judgment contexts (e.g., Revelation 11:2). Whether the number is symbolic or historical, it indicates a substantial group—not merely two or three offenders, but a significant number of youths participating in the mockery. The location in Bethel, a center of apostasy, adds theological weight: the judgment falls in the very city that has rejected the Lord's covenant and true worship. Bethel becomes the site not only of false religion but of judgment against those who mock the prophet.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 14:1-10, Alma and Amulek are persecuted and imprisoned by the people of Ammonihah, who mock them and burn the faithful. The scriptures record that 'the Lord suddenly showeth his power' and judgment comes upon the city. The pattern is consistent: mockery and persecution of the prophets brings condemnation. However, the Book of Mormon also emphasizes that judgment can be averted through repentance (Alma 10:22-23)—the youths of Bethel had no such opportunity to repent.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 and D&C 21:4-6 establish that the Lord's word through His servants is binding and carries divine authority. When the prophet speaks in God's name, God backs that word. Elisha's curse, spoken in the name of the LORD, is not a personal judgment but a prophetic pronouncement that invokes divine justice. D&C 84:77 teaches that 'whoso receiveth you, receiveth me; and the same will feed you, and clothe you, and give you money.' By extension, those who mock or reject the prophet mock and reject the Lord.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The contrast between Bethel (a center of false worship) and Elisha (a representative of true covenant relationship) reflects the temple theology that permeates Restoration scripture. Those who turn from the true covenant and embrace false worship place themselves in opposition to God's prophet and suffer judgment as a result. The animals that emerge from the wilderness represent the chaos and judgment that result when covenant is broken.

commentary.christological_typology: The judgment that falls on those who mock Elisha prefigures the judgment that comes to those who reject Christ. In Matthew 23:29-35, Christ tells the Pharisees that they will 'fill up the measure of your fathers' in persecuting prophets and righteous men, and judgment will come upon that generation. Christ's authority as God's prophet and Son carries divine backing. However, Christ's emphasis is on repentance: 'How often would I have gathered thy children together, even as a hen gathereth her chickens under her wings, and ye would not' (Matthew 23:37). While Elisha's curse is immediate and absolute, Christ calls first for repentance, and judgment only follows continued rebellion. Both demonstrate that rejection of the prophet's word has consequences—either repentance and blessing, or continued rebellion and judgment.
commentary.application: This is a verse that demands serious contemplation in our modern context. It teaches several principles that are often uncomfortable but biblically essential: First, contempt for the prophets is not a light matter. The youths of Bethel were not ignorant; they were from a city that deliberately rejected covenant worship. Their mockery was deliberate and willful. In our day, when prophets counsel us, opposition to that counsel is not merely intellectual disagreement—it is a spiritual choice with consequences. Second, the judgment is swift and absolute. There is no period of grace, no opportunity for these youths to repent or reconsider. This reflects the seriousness of choosing open rebellion against the prophet. Third, the judgment is not proportional by ordinary standards—it seems harsh and terrible to modern ears. But the text presents it not as cruelty but as the inevitable consequence of mocking God's representative. We must ask ourselves: What is our response when we encounter contempt for the living prophets? Do we join the mockers, remain neutral, or defend the covenant? Fourth, the Covenant Rendering's clarification that these are 'youths' or 'young men,' not children, reminds us that there is a point at which innocence gives way to moral responsibility. Contempt for prophetic authority, chosen and deliberate, comes with consequences. Finally, this verse teaches that the prophet's word—whether a blessing (as in verse 21) or a curse (as here)—has binding power. Elisha does not direct the bears; he pronounces the judgment, and God executes it. We would do well to consider: Am I aligned with or against the purposes of God as declared through His prophets?

text_kjv: And he went from thence to mount Carmel, and from thence he returned to Samaria.

commentary.narrative:
This final verse of 2 Kings 2 marks the geographic and spiritual completion of Elisha's succession narrative. After the dramatic events at the Jordan River, the translation to heaven, and the miraculous multiplication of the widow's oil, Elisha now travels to Mount Carmel — the very site where Elijah had performed his most famous miracle, the contest with the prophets of Baal (1 Kings 18). This is not a random journey; it is a deliberate pilgrimage to the place of Elijah's greatest triumph and vindication. By visiting Carmel, Elisha symbolically claims his position as Elijah's legitimate successor and reconnects himself to the prophetic tradition Elijah embodied.

The journey from Carmel to Samaria completes the internal geography of the chapter and establishes Elisha's base of operations. Samaria was the capital of the Northern Kingdom, the seat of royal power and political authority. By positioning himself there, Elisha moves from being a solitary disciple following a master to being an established prophet in the kingdom's center. This transition is crucial: Elisha is no longer defined by his relationship to Elijah alone, but by his role as a prophet who will interact with kings, speak to nations, and shape the political and spiritual future of Israel. The chapter's ending leaves him poised and ready, having completed the succession ritual and the initial miracles, now established in the place where he will exercise his prophetic authority.
