The Psalmist remembers how Israel's ancestors 'sacrificed their sons and their daughters unto devils' and 'shed innocent blood.' This history shows why the law so strictly forbade the practice—it was Israel's perpetual temptation.

commentary.historical_context: Child sacrifice, particularly of royal or elite children in times of extreme crisis, appears in several ancient Near Eastern sources. The Moabite Stele, discovered in 1868 and dating to Mesha's reign (circa 9th century BCE), confirms the historical reality of this period and Mesha's rule. While the Stele records Mesha's perspective on his conflicts with Israel, it does not specifically mention the child sacrifice, leaving 2 Kings as our primary source for this act. The practice of offering a king's heir in crisis appears in other ancient Near Eastern texts as an act of ultimate desperation—the parent offering what is most precious to secure divine intervention. Archaeological evidence from Carthage and other sites shows evidence of child sacrifice in the ancient world, typically to gods like Molech or Chemosh in times of military crisis. The placement of the sacrifice 'upon the wall' in full view would maximize its psychological impact on both the besieging army and the Moabite population, serving as a final act of defiance and invocation. The term 'great wrath' arising in response is unprecedented in the biblical account and has generated centuries of theological speculation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon provides parallels to the desperation that drives people away from God. King Noah's flight and ultimate death (Mosiah 19) shows a king who, when his kingdom crumbles, goes to increasingly desperate and shameful ends. Mesha's willingness to destroy his own dynasty mirrors the self-destruction that comes from covenant rejection. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that 'the wicked shall perish' (1 Nephi 22:16), which can include the perishing of their own seed if they do not repent.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 63:32-34 warns that 'delight in the shedding of innocent blood' is an abomination; Mesha's sacrifice is precisely this. The revelation also teaches that those who do such things 'cannot be saved in the kingdom of God.' Mesha has placed himself beyond redemption by this act.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The contrast between Mesha's offering and the temple worship of Israel is absolute. The temple sacrifice was offered to the true God and symbolized covenant renewal and forgiveness. Mesha's sacrifice is offered to a false god in an act of ultimate rebellion. The temple represents the Lord's redemptive path; Mesha has chosen the opposite path, leading to destruction.

commentary.christological_typology: Mesha's willingness to sacrifice his own son contrasts sharply with the Father's willingness to sacrifice His Son for redemption. Where Mesha offers his son to a false god in desperation and rebellion, the Father offers His Son to accomplish universal redemption (John 3:16). Mesha's sacrifice represents the nadir of human rebellion—offering what is precious to demons. Christ's sacrifice represents the apex of divine love—offering what is infinitely precious for salvation. The passage thus, through contrast, illuminates the uniqueness and redemptive power of Christ's offering.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern members with the ultimate consequence of rejecting God's word: the destruction of everything one holds dear, including the future one has built. Mesha's attempt to preserve his dynasty through desperation—by sacrificing the crown prince—is paradoxical and tragic. It is precisely what the person clinging to idolatry does spiritually: in refusing to surrender to God's will, they ultimately sacrifice their own spiritual offspring, their own future, their own redemption. The application is not about literal child sacrifice but about the spiritual destruction that comes from covenant-breaking taken to its logical end. The 'great wrath' that follows Mesha's act is left unexplained because the narrator wants readers to understand that such rebellion brings judgment from a power the person cannot control or predict. For covenant members, the lesson is clear: the path of least resistance in the moment—refusing the word of the prophet—leads to the greatest loss in the end.

text_kjv: Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets unto Elisha, saying, Thy servant my husband is dead; and thou knowest that thy servant did fear the LORD: and the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen.

commentary.narrative:
This verse opens a story of desperate need and righteous appeal. A widow whose husband was part of the prophetic community—a group presumably devoted to serving the Lord—now faces a crisis that tests whether faithfulness has a place in a harsh economic reality. Her husband is dead, and she has no means to pay the debt he left behind. Under Israelite law, creditors had the right to take children as debt-slaves to recover what was owed (Leviticus 25:39; Nehemiah 5:5). She approaches Elisha not as a stranger but as someone whose household was known to the prophet—her husband feared the LORD, a statement that carries weight in the prophet's community.

The woman's appeal is carefully constructed. She uses the language of servanthood (your servant, my husband; your maidservant) to establish both her humility and her legitimacy. She is not demanding; she is petitioning. She reminds Elisha that her husband was a righteous man—'feared the LORD'—yet righteousness did not protect him from debt or death. This is the painful reality of being a prophet's family during a time when the northern kingdom was turning away from God. Those who stood for righteousness often paid a material price.

The creditor (noseh) comes to take her two sons. This is not merely a financial matter; it is a family being torn apart. The widow's cry is an appeal not just to Elisha's authority as a prophet, but to his compassion as a man who understands the cost of faithfulness. Her situation embodies a larger theological question: Does the fear of the LORD secure provision, or does it sometimes lead to loss?

word_study.meaning: To cry out, to call aloud with urgency and distress; often used for a cry that demands attention and response. Not a whisper or a polite request, but a desperate shout.
word_study.significance: The widow's cry is not tentative; it is urgent and demanding. This word choice elevates her situation to one requiring immediate intervention. In the Hebrew Bible, tzaaqah often precedes divine action or prophetic response (e.g., Exodus 3:7, where God hears the cry of Israel). The widow's cry stands in that tradition.

word_study.meaning: To reverence, respect, and obey God; the foundational posture of covenant fidelity. Yare carries both awe and obedience.
word_study.significance: The widow emphasizes that her late husband possessed the most fundamental qualification in Israelite theology—fear of the LORD. She is not asking for charity for the lazy or unworthy; she is asking for help for a family of the righteous. This distinction matters to Elisha and to the narrative. Righteousness alone, however, did not prevent hardship.

word_study.meaning: One who lends; a creditor. From nasah, meaning to lend or advance. The noseh has legal standing to recover debt.
word_study.significance: The creditor is not portrayed as wicked or unjust; he is operating within the law. The tragedy is systemic: the law permits the seizure of children to pay debts. Elisha's intervention will not dispute the law but will provide an alternative path—divine provision rather than legal coercion.

cross_references.connection: The Law of Moses permitted Israelites to become debt-slaves but required their eventual release in the Jubilee year. The widow's situation exemplifies the harsh reality of debt in ancient Israel, where families could be broken up before relief could come.

Elijah provided for a widow and her son by multiplying meal and oil during famine. The widow in 2 Kings 4 echoes the same crisis of provision, suggesting a pattern in how the prophets respond to the needs of the faithful poor.
The LORD 'relieveth the fatherless and widow.' The widow's appeal assumes God's covenantal concern for the vulnerable, and Elisha acts as an instrument of that divine care.
Nehemiah confronts the practice of creditors taking children into debt-slavery, showing this was a recurring injustice in Israel's history that righteous leaders opposed.

Though New Testament, this passage on Christ becoming poor to make us rich resonates with the theology implicit in this narrative: divine provision often flows through reversals of fortune for the faithful.

commentary.historical_context: The widow is described as one of the wives of the sons of the prophets (bnei ha-nebi'im), a phrase that appears several times in Elisha's narrative. These were likely members of prophetic guilds or communities—men devoted to the service and worship of the LORD, often in opposition to the idolatry spreading through Israel under kings like Ahab and Jehoram. Her husband's membership in this community would have brought him respect but not necessarily material security; prophets often lived modest or even impoverished lives, especially when they stood against the tide of royal policy. Debt-slavery was a legal remedy in ancient Near Eastern societies, including Israel. The practice was regulated (Leviticus 25:39-43 and Deuteronomy 15:12 required debt-servants to be released in the seventh year), but the law offered little comfort to a widow facing immediate loss of her children. The absence of a male protector (her husband) made her particularly vulnerable in patriarchal Israelite society.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon frequently emphasizes the obligation of the righteous community to care for widows and the poor. Alma 4:13 describes how the Church members 'were generous to all, both old and young, both bond and free, both male and female, being filled with the Spirit.' The widow's crisis in 2 Kings 4 represents a failure of community care—her righteous husband has died without leaving provision, and the community (represented by the creditor) is prepared to claim his children. Elisha's intervention restores what the community's ordinary structures should have provided.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 52:40 teaches that the Lord gathers 'the poor and the meek' and makes their 'faces to shine.' The widow's story illustrates how divine power is often channeled to address injustice and provide for those whom earthly systems have failed. D&C 78:5-6 establishes that the Lord's people should 'be organized in families' and that provision should be adequate; the widow's family is being dismantled by debt, and Elisha's miracle will reconstitute her household.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The widow's appeal for help in preserving her family echoes temple themes of sealing and family preservation. Her desperate attempt to keep her sons connects to the doctrine that the family unit is sacred and inviolable in God's eyes. The miracle that follows will restore family bonds that law and circumstance had threatened to sever.

commentary.christological_typology: While the widow herself is not typically typed as a messianic figure, her situation—a righteous but vulnerable person facing loss—sets up a pattern of redemptive intervention that foreshadows Christ's work. Just as she cries out in distress and a prophet responds with miraculous provision, humanity's spiritual bankruptcy and cry for help are answered by the Savior's infinite atonement. The removal of her sons from their family prefigures spiritual death and separation from covenant blessings; Elisha's intervention—through a humble miracle—restores what was lost, as Christ's redemptive work restores all things.
commentary.application: Modern members of the Church face their own versions of the widow's crisis: situations where righteousness has not prevented loss, where faithful people find themselves in economic distress, where circumstances threaten to tear apart what we hold dear. This verse invites us to see our own cries of need as legitimate petitions—not shameful, but part of the covenant relationship. It also invites us to consider whether our community structures adequately protect the widow, the widower, and the vulnerable. The widow did not wait silently; she cried out to the prophet. In our own lives, seeking help from Church leaders, trusted confidants, and community is not a failure of faith but an expression of it—and it often precedes divine intervention.

text_kjv: And Elisha said unto her, What shall I do for thee? tell me, what hast thou in the house? And she said, Thine handmaid hath not any thing in the house, save a pot of oil.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha's response is neither dismissal nor automatic provision. Instead, he asks a diagnostic question: 'What can I do for you?' His second question—'What do you have in the house?'—reframes the entire situation. The widow has come to him focusing on what she lacks: money to pay the debt, means to support her family, protection against loss. Elisha redirects her attention to what she possesses. This is a pedagogical moment. The prophet is not simply going to hand her a solution; he is going to draw her into a process that will deepen her faith and align her with divine principle.

The widow's answer is striking in its minimalism: 'Your servant has nothing at all in the house except a small jar of oil.' The asukh (a small flask or container) is so humble that she almost apologizes for mentioning it. In her eyes, a jar of oil is not wealth; it is a cooking ingredient, a minor household item. Yet Elisha seizes upon it as the foundation for a miracle. This establishes a profound principle: God's miracles do not begin from nothing; they begin from what you already have, however small. The widow is not being asked to conjure provision from emptiness but to offer what little remains and watch God multiply it.

The interaction between Elisha and the widow models the relationship between prophet and people. The prophet asks questions that shift perspective; he does not assume control but draws the widow into active participation. Her acknowledgment of what she has—even though she frames it as 'nothing except'—becomes the starting point. This jar of oil represents her last resource, and she is being invited to offer even that to God's work.

word_study.term_english: What shall I do for thee?
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'What shall I make/do for you?' A question that opens possibility and draws the other person into conversation. E'ese (I will do/make) is future tense, indicating intention and capacity.
word_study.significance: Elisha's question asserts his willingness and ability to help, but it invites the widow to define what 'help' means. This is not the patronizing gesture of a powerful figure offering charity; it is a genuine inquiry. The prophet's power is directed toward understanding the widow's actual need.

word_study.term_original: אֵין לְשִׁפְחָתְךָ כׇל בַּבַּיִת (ein le-shifchatekha khol ba-bayit)
word_study.meaning: 'There is not to your maidservant anything in the house.' Ein (there is not) + khol (everything, all things). The widow uses absolute language to convey her destitution.
word_study.significance: The widow's statement is an expression of total deprivation. Yet the very next breath contradicts it: 'except a jar of oil.' The Covenant Rendering captures this well: she has 'nothing at all... except.' This exception becomes everything. Her willingness to acknowledge the oil—to refuse to dismiss it as insignificant—is the spiritual posture that opens the door to miracle.

word_study.meaning: A jar, flask, or container of oil. Asukh is a small vessel, often used for olive oil or precious liquids. Shamen (oil) in ancient Israel was both a commodity and a symbol of blessing, anointing, and provision.
word_study.significance: Oil appears throughout Scripture as a symbol of the Holy Ghost, blessing, and healing (see Leviticus 8:10-12; 1 Samuel 16:13; James 5:14). The widow's jar of oil, though humble and nearly exhausted, becomes the vessel through which divine multiplication flows. In temple and covenant contexts, anointing oil represents the bestowal of the Spirit's gifts. This jar of oil is not just cooking material; it is the widow's last connection to the provision and blessing of God.

cross_references.connection: Elijah's widow of Zarephath also has nothing except a little oil and meal, and Elijah declares that these will not be consumed until the Lord sends rain. Like Elisha's widow, she is invited to offer her last resource as an act of faith.

The widow's mite: Jesus commends the widow who gives her last two coins, noting that she has given more than the wealthy because she gave 'all that she had.' Elisha's widow, like the widow of the temple, will offer what little she has.

Paul writes that if there is a willing mind, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have. The widow's willingness to acknowledge her jar of oil, small as it is, reflects this principle of offering what one possesses.

'The prudent see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty.' The widow's oil, though seemingly insignificant, represents a preserved resource—something prudently kept even in desperation—that becomes the basis for God's provision.
Oil is a key component in the holy anointing oil prescribed for the tabernacle. The widow's jar of oil, when multiplied by divine power, will have redemptive purpose—saving her family from servitude.

commentary.historical_context: Oil was a staple commodity in ancient Israelite households. Olive oil served multiple purposes: as cooking fat, as fuel for lamps, as cosmetic and medicinal application, and as a component of religious ritual. A small jar of oil (asukh shamen) would have been a valuable resource, but by itself insufficient for trade or payment of significant debt. The widow's possession of this one item suggests she has stripped away everything else already—food stores, household goods, anything of value—leaving only this last essential. The prophet's question about what she has in the house is therefore not trivial; it is an invitation to inventory what remains and to recognize that even the smallest possession has potential when offered to God's purpose.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32 teaches the parable of the seed, where Alma invites the poor and afflicted Zoramites to plant a small seed of faith and watch it grow. Like the widow's jar of oil, a seed seems insignificant, yet when nurtured it grows into a tree of eternal life. The widow in 2 Kings 4:2 is in a similar position—she has something small (a jar of oil) and is about to exercise faith by offering it, which will result in exponential growth and provision.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 84:33-34 speaks of the Spirit giving 'treasures of knowledge even hidden treasures' to those who are faithful. The widow's jar of oil, hidden in her house and seemingly worthless, will become the conduit through which hidden treasures of provision flow. D&C 6:7 teaches that 'virtue shall go forth from you'; the widow is about to discover that what little she has retains virtue and power when combined with faith.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, oil is used in the anointing process to set apart and sanctify. The widow's jar of oil, when multiplied, will serve to anoint and sanctify her family by preserving it from the indignity and separation of debt-slavery. The miracle is not merely material but covenantal—it preserves the sanctity of the family unit.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ emphasized that God works with willing hearts and offered resources, however small. In the Sermon on the Mount, he teaches that 'from the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh' (Matthew 12:34), and later he commends the widow who gives her last coins. The widow in 2 Kings 4 foreshadows the principle that Christ embodies: divine multiplication begins with humble offering. Christ himself would feed five thousand with five loaves and two fishes—a multiplication that begins with a boy's small lunch offered in faith.
commentary.application: In our modern lives, we often focus on what we lack—inadequate savings, insufficient income, unpaid debts—and we may feel ashamed to approach the Lord or Church leaders with such small resources. This verse invites a different perspective: to account for what we have, however humble, and to offer it as part of the solution. We may not have much, but we have something—time, effort, faith, a willingness to work—and these offered in the right spirit become vessels through which divine provision flows. The widow does not solve her problem through her jar of oil; she solves it by offering what she has and partnering with the prophet's guidance. Similarly, modern covenant members are invited to take inventory of their actual resources (spiritual and material), offer them in faith, and participate in God's solution rather than waiting passively for rescue.

text_kjv: Then he said, Go, borrow thee vessels abroad of all thy neighbours, even empty vessels; borrow not a few.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha's instruction is paradoxical and demands active faith. The widow is in debt; the last thing her neighbors would expect is for her to come borrowing vessels. Yet this is precisely what the prophet commands. She must go to her neighbors—the very community that has presumably watched her decline into poverty—and ask for empty containers. The instruction 'borrow not a few' is crucial: Elisha is not telling her to borrow a reasonable number of vessels but to ask boldly, to gather as many as possible. This command tests her faith in multiple ways. First, it requires her to humble herself publicly. Second, it sets up a direct correlation between her initiative and the scope of God's provision: more vessels means more oil; fewer vessels means less oil. The widow's willingness to ask determines the extent of the miracle.

This principle—that human initiative and faith shape the dimensions of divine provision—is radical. God is not simply going to pour oil whether or not vessels exist; the miracle will be limited by the widow's capacity to prepare. In theological terms, this reflects the principle of agency: humans are not passive recipients of grace but active participants in their own redemption. The widow must do something that costs her pride and effort before the multiplication can occur. She must expose her condition to her neighbors, admit her need, and ask for help. This is not easy for someone who has lost everything.

Elisha is also teaching something about receptivity. The vessels are not filled with anything yet; they are empty. This emptiness is essential—it is the capacity to receive. Just as Elisha's opening question asked the widow to identify what she had, now he is asking her to create space for what she will receive. An empty vessel is a posture of readiness. The more vessels she borrows, the more space she creates for reception. This is a principle that will appear throughout Elisha's miracles: divine abundance meets human receptivity, and the two together create provision.

word_study.meaning: Request/ask for vessels on your behalf. Sha'al means to ask, request, or petition. Kelim (vessels, containers) is the plural of kli, meaning any kind of utensil or vessel.
word_study.significance: The verb sha'al (to ask) is the same verb used throughout Scripture for prayer and petition (Hannah in 1 Samuel 1:27 sha'alti—'I asked'). The widow's act of borrowing vessels is thus framed as a form of petition, not merely a practical errand. She is practicing the spiritual discipline of asking, which is foundational to receiving.

word_study.term_original: מִן־הַחוּץ מֵאֵת כׇּל־שְׁכֵנָיִךְ (min ha-chutz me-et khol she-khenayikh)
word_study.meaning: 'From outside, from all your neighbors.' Ha-chutz (the outside, the street, the external community) indicates she must go beyond her household to the broader community.
word_study.significance: The widow must engage with her community, overcoming the shame and isolation that poverty often brings. The miracle is not worked in isolation but in the context of community participation. Her neighbors, who watched her decline, will now be witnesses to her restoration.

word_study.meaning: Vessels that are empty, void, hollow. Reqim (empty) emphasizes complete lack of contents.
word_study.significance: In Hebrew, reqim (empty) carries the sense of nothingness, void. Genesis 1:2 describes the earth as tohu va-vohu (formless and void) before creation. Empty vessels are vessels awaiting divine creative work. The widow is being invited to gather vessels of nothingness so that they can be filled with something—a powerful metaphor for the receptive posture required for miracle.

word_study.meaning: 'Do not make few.' Tam'it comes from maat, meaning to become small or few. The imperative form with negative (al tam'iti) is an emphatic command: 'Do not limit yourself to a small number.'
word_study.significance: This command places faith and boldness squarely on the widow. She is being told not to ask modestly but to ask maximally. The size of the miracle is directly proportional to the size of her request and her faith. This reverses the normal pattern where the powerful dictate terms to the powerless; here, the widow's willingness to ask greatly determines what God will do. It is a stunning affirmation of human agency in divine work.

cross_references.connection: Christ teaches 'Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find.' Elisha is teaching the widow this same principle in action—that asking is the precondition for receiving, and the extent of asking shapes the extent of receiving.
The lazy soul desireth and has nothing, but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat. The widow must go and actively borrow vessels; her diligence in gathering empties is rewarded with abundance.

The Lord tells Adam that Satan deceives those who 'come unto me and do not come unto me.' The principle of active participation in one's own salvation is central to LDS theology, mirrored here in the widow's required activity.

Nephi declares that the Lord gives no commandment without preparing a way to accomplish it. Elisha's command to borrow vessels is achievable—the neighbors will lend—and its accomplishment will establish the ground for the miracle.

Christ teaches that 'Give, and it shall be given unto you; good measure, pressed down, and shaken together, and running over, shall men give into your bosom.' The principle of pressing down and filling full is enacted in the widow's miracle: as she prepares vessels, God will fill them pressed down and overflowing.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite society, borrowing and lending were communal activities governed by covenant and custom. A person asking to borrow from neighbors would have been engaging in a normal economic practice, but for a destitute widow to do so would have required considerable humility. The term kelim (vessels) is broad and could include anything from water jugs to cooking pots to storage containers. The widow's neighbors would have understood her request as unusual—why does a poor widow suddenly need many empty containers?—but they would likely have granted the request out of goodwill or curiosity. The act of going to 'all thy neighbors' suggests a small village or urban neighborhood where people knew each other's circumstances. This was not a society where poverty could be hidden; the widow's neighbors were already aware of her crisis.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, receiving divine blessings repeatedly requires preparation and faith. The people of Alma the Younger 'did repent and prepare' themselves (Mosiah 27:28-29). The widow in 2 Kings 4 is similarly preparing—gathering vessels—as an act of repentance and faith that precedes the blessing. Her preparation is not earning the miracle but aligning her will with God's, creating the conditions in which it can occur.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:123 teaches that 'it is impossible for a man to be saved in ignorance,' and more broadly that knowledge and preparation are prerequisites for blessing. The widow's gathering of vessels is a form of practical knowledge and preparation—she is positioning herself to receive what she cannot yet see. D&C 130:18-19 establishes that 'whatever principle of intelligence we attain unto in this life, it will rise with us in the resurrection,' and similarly, the widow's initiative and faith in this moment are spiritual principles that will define her eternal standing.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple preparation, initiates are taught to present themselves as clean vessels ready to receive sacred ordinances and covenants. The widow's gathering of empty vessels mirrors this spiritual preparation—presenting oneself as empty and ready to be filled with divine purpose and blessing.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ taught his disciples to 'take up the cross and follow me' (Luke 9:23), emphasizing that discipleship requires active participation, not passivity. The widow's obedience to gather vessels, which requires visible effort and humbling herself before her community, is a type of this principle. Just as Christ required his followers to do something difficult as a condition of discipleship, Elisha requires the widow to do something that costs her pride. The result will be not just material provision but a transformed understanding of her place in God's economy and her capacity to receive divine gifts.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members are often counseled to prepare themselves for blessings. President Russell M. Nelson has taught the importance of spiritual preparation, temple attendance, and living righteously as preparations for receiving the full measure of God's blessings. The widow's instruction to gather vessels is a scriptural model for this principle: blessings require preparation, not passivity. In our own lives, this might mean: gathering knowledge before making decisions, setting up structures and systems to support the changes we want to see, reaching out to community for support and participation, and taking visible steps of faith even before we see the result. We are not empty vessels sitting and waiting; we are active gatherers, preparing ourselves and our families to receive what God desires to give.

text_kjv: And when thou art come in, thou shalt shut the door upon thee and upon thy sons, and shalt pour out into all those vessels, and thou shalt set aside that which is full.

commentary.narrative:
The instruction to shut the door marks a shift from public action to private miracle. The widow has done her part in the community—asking neighbors for vessels, gathering what she could—but now she withdraws into the domestic space of her home with her sons. This closed-door setting is theologically significant. In the Gospel accounts, Christ often performs miracles in private or semi-private settings: healing Jairus's daughter behind closed doors, casting demons out of the Gadarene demoniac away from the crowds, performing the miracle of the feeding of the five thousand in a remote place. The miracles are not spectacles designed to impress crowds but redemptive acts that address specific human need.

The instruction that the widow shall pour the oil is crucial: the widow is not a passive recipient of divine action but an agent of it. She does the pouring; the oil multiplies through her hands. This is different from miracles where a prophet commands something to happen and it does (like Elisha calling fire from heaven). Here, Elisha gives power to the widow to be the instrument of her own salvation. She acts, and as she acts, the miracle occurs. She is responsible for the pouring; she must be attentive to setting aside full vessels. This requires both physical labor and spiritual attention. She cannot be careless or distracted; she must tend to the pouring with care.

The phrase 'set aside that which is full' implies ongoing discernment. As each vessel fills, she must remove it and prepare for the next. This prevents overfilling and breaking vessels and ensures that the oil is properly distributed among all the vessels she has gathered. The instruction reveals a God who cares about order, completeness, and proper stewardship. She is not being asked to pour randomly but to manage the process with wisdom.

word_study.term_english: shut the door upon thee and upon thy sons
word_study.term_original: סָגַרְתְּ הַדֶּלֶת בַּעֲדֵךְ וּבְעַד־בָּנַיִךְ (sagarat ha-delet ba'adekh u-ve'ad banayikh)
word_study.meaning: 'You shall shut the door after you and after your sons.' Sagar (to shut, close, enclose). The door (delet) seals the space, creating privacy and separation from the outside world.
word_study.significance: The closed door is not about hiding shame but about creating sacred space. Throughout Scripture, doors close when intimate or sacred moments occur: the Angel of the Lord enters a shut door (John 20:19), and the marriage chamber is entered with closed doors. The widow and her sons are about to witness and participate in a miracle in the privacy of their home. This is not a public sign but a personal covenant-renewal experience.

word_study.meaning: To pour, to flow, to cast (as in pouring molten metal). Yatzaq carries the sense of continuous, deliberate pouring—an active, sustained action.
word_study.significance: The widow is not given oil to dispense passively; she must pour actively. The verb yatzaq emphasizes her agency and labor. In the context of the miracle, her pouring becomes the channel through which divine multiplication flows. Her action is not peripheral to the miracle; it is essential to it.

word_study.term_english: set aside that which is full
word_study.meaning: 'The one that is full, set aside/remove.' Maleh means full, complete, filled. Tassi'i comes from nasa, meaning to lift, bear, carry away.
word_study.significance: The widow must be attentive and active in managing the miracle. As each vessel fills (maleh), she must remove it and set it aside. This requires her to recognize when fullness has been reached, to stop pouring, and to prepare the next vessel. The instruction implies a rhythm: fill, recognize fullness, set aside, refill. This is not magical automaticity but partnered action between human and divine.

cross_references.connection: Christ teaches that prayer should occur in a closed room, addressing the Father in secret rather than for public display. The widow's private miracle mirrors this principle: true miraculous work occurs in hidden places and intimate moments.

Elijah raises the widow's son 'and went in therefore [to the chamber] and shut the door upon them both, and prayed unto the Lord.' Elisha's widow scene recalls this pattern of miracles occurring behind closed doors with family present.

The virtuous woman 'riseth also while it is yet night, and giveth meat to her household.' The widow in 2 Kings 4 rises to her labor with her sons—pouring oil, managing vessels—embodying the active, purposeful housekeeping that Scripture commends.

Paul teaches 'work out your own salvation with fear and trembling: For it is God which worketh in you.' The widow works (pours) while God works (multiplies); salvation is not passive reception but active partnership.

Members are to use their gifts as faithful stewards of God's manifold grace. The widow stewards the miracle by managing the vessels, recognizing fullness, and ensuring order—she is a faithful steward of divine provision.

commentary.historical_context: The domestic interior of an Israelite home in the Iron Age would have been relatively small and intimate. A widow and her two sons together in a closed room would have created an atmosphere of concentration and witness. The door (delet) typically consisted of wooden planks and could be secured from the inside, creating a barrier to the outside world. The act of pouring oil would have been familiar labor to a woman in an agricultural society—she would have prepared meals, maintained household supplies, and managed resources. What would have been unfamiliar is the continuous flow of oil from a small jar into many vessels. The miracle would have been immediately obvious—she would have felt the abnormality as she poured, vessel after vessel filling beyond what the original jar could contain.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 32, Alma teaches that faith is like planting a seed, and the seed grows as we nourish it with attention and care. The widow's pouring of oil, her setting aside of full vessels, her continued attention to the work—these are forms of tending and nourishing. Like Alma's farmer who must water the seed and watch it grow, the widow must pour and tend, and as she does, growth and multiplication occur. The principle is active partnership: God provides the power, but we provide the labor and attention.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-29 teaches that all things are spiritual to the Lord and that labor, properly understood, is part of covenant living. The widow's pouring of oil is spiritual work, not merely mechanical action. D&C 136:32-33 further teaches that the Lord gives commandments that require sustained effort and attention: 'Let all thy doings be done in soberness.' The widow's care in pouring and setting aside vessels reflects this soberness and spiritual seriousness.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, patrons are anointed with oil as a symbol of the Holy Ghost and covenantal blessings. The widow's oil, when multiplied, takes on this covenantal significance—it becomes a sign of God's willingness to bless and sustain those who are faithful. The private, intimate setting mirrors temple experience, where sacred work occurs in separated, holy space.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ instructed his disciples regarding prayer: 'When thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret' (Matthew 6:6). The widow's entering into her house and shutting the door is a type of entering into intimate communion with God. Just as prayer in secret opens access to divine blessing, so the widow's private pouring opens access to miraculous provision. Christ also taught that the greatest commandments are kept in the heart, in the privacy of intention (Matthew 15:19)—the widow's miracle occurs not on a stage but in the hiddenness of home and family, yet it will transform her entire circumstance.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members often seek visible, dramatic evidence of God's work—expecting miracles to be public and undeniable. This verse teaches that God's greatest work often occurs in the quiet, private sphere of home and family. The widow's miracle is not broadcast; it occurs behind closed doors. This invites us to recognize that our own miracles—spiritual growth, family healing, answered prayers, personal redemption—are often experienced in private. We do not need public validation for God's work in our lives. Additionally, the instruction to pour and tend teaches that receiving divine blessing requires our active participation and attention. We cannot sit passively and expect provision; we must work, tend, and manage what God provides. This aligns with the principle of agency that is central to Latter-day Saint theology: we are not saved by grace alone, nor by works alone, but by grace coupled with our willing, active participation in our own redemption.

text_kjv: So she went from him, and shut the door upon her and upon her sons, who brought the vessels to her; and she poured out.

commentary.narrative:
This verse records the widow's obedience to Elisha's instruction and then transitions into the miracle itself. She departs from the prophet's presence and enters into her home with her sons. The narrative voice shifts from direct instruction to narration of action. The Hebrew tense forms indicate continuous, repeated action: hem maggishim eleha (they were bringing to her) and hi motzaqet (she was pouring). This is not a one-time act but an ongoing process. The sons bring vessels; the mother pours. The rhythm is established: receive vessel, pour oil, set it aside, receive next vessel, pour again.

The participation of the widow's sons is significant. They are not passive observers but active participants in the miracle. They bring vessels to their mother. This mirrors the structure of household labor in ancient Israel, where children contributed to the family's economic and domestic activity. The miracle occurs within the framework of family work, not apart from it. The sons will witness their mother's provision of salvation for the household, and they will have played a part in it by bringing vessels. They become collaborators in their own deliverance.

The widow's obedience is immediate and complete. She does not question, delay, or modify Elisha's instructions. 'So she went' (vattelekh) indicates a straightforward transition from instruction to action. This obedience—without argument or hesitation—is the posture that opens the door to miracle. Elisha has taught a principle through his instructions: gather vessels, shut the door, pour, tend. The widow now lives that principle. As she does, she will discover that the jar does not empty. The miracle unfolds not through external intervention but through the widow's faithful execution of what she has been told to do.

word_study.meaning: 'And she went from his presence.' Halakh (to go, walk) + me'itho (from him, from his presence). The verb vattekh is past tense, indicating completed action.
word_study.significance: The widow does not remain in the prophet's presence but departs to act independently. She takes the instruction away from the prophet and enacts it in her own space. This represents a transfer of agency and authority: Elisha gives direction, but the widow must walk it out in her own household.

word_study.term_english: who brought the vessels to her
word_study.meaning: 'They were bringing to her.' Maggish (bringing, presenting) is a participle form indicating continuous, ongoing action. The plural 'they' refers to her sons.
word_study.significance: The participle form hem maggishim is imperfective, indicating an action that was repeated or sustained throughout the miracle. The sons did not bring all vessels at once but continuously brought them as needed. This reflects the rhythm of the household miracle: continuous need met by continuous supply, with the sons' labor integral to the process.

word_study.meaning: 'And she was pouring.' Motzaqet is a feminine participle, again indicating continuous, sustained action. The verb yatzaq means to pour, to flow.
word_study.significance: Like the sons bringing vessels (maggishim), the widow's pouring (motzaqet) is rendered as a continuous, repeated action through the use of the imperfect participle. The narrative is capturing not a single moment but a sustained process: the widow pouring repeatedly, continuously, as long as vessels were available. The miracle is not instantaneous magic but a process of faithful labor meeting divine multiplication.

cross_references.connection: The virtuous woman 'looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.' The widow, by immediately obeying Elisha and setting to work with her sons, exemplifies this virtuous attention to household welfare.

Joshua is told to meditate on the law 'day and night' and 'thou shalt observe to do according to all that is written therein: for then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success.' The widow's obedience to Elisha's instruction—her careful execution of what she has been told—leads to prosperity and success.

Mary responds to the angel Gabriel: 'Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word.' The widow similarly accepts and enacts the prophet's word without reservation or negotiation.

At Cana, Mary tells the servants regarding Jesus: 'Whatsoever he saith unto you, do it.' This principle of obedience to the word of God or his spokesman is exemplified in the widow's immediate action.

Nephi declares: 'I will go and do the things which the Lord hath commanded, for I know that the Lord giveth no commandments unto the children of men save he shall prepare a way for them.' The widow embodies this faith: she goes and does what Elisha commanded, trusting that the way will be prepared.

commentary.historical_context: The scene depicted here—a widow and her two sons working together in a household task—reflects the normal division of labor in ancient Israelite families. Children, especially sons, were contributors to household labor from a young age. A boy would assist his mother in various domestic and economic tasks. The fact that both sons are present and participating suggests they are old enough to carry vessels but not yet grown or engaged in their own households—perhaps ranging from early adolescence to young adulthood. The continuous activity (they were bringing, she was pouring) implies a sustained period of labor. The miracle would not have occurred instantaneously but over a period of time during which the widow and her sons worked steadily, filling vessel after vessel. This sustained miracle is more impressive than an instantaneous one, as it demonstrates God's patient, ongoing care and the widow's sustained faith and labor.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 7, King Benjamin addresses his people about the requirements of covenant living: 'For the sake of retaining a remission of your sins from day to day, that ye may walk guiltless before God—I would that ye should impart of your substance to the poor, every man according to that which he hath' (Mosiah 4:26). The widow, though poor, is being shown that she has a substance—oil—and that by giving it in faith, she will receive back multiplied. Additionally, the Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that family unity is essential to salvation and redemption. The widow's miracle occurs within her family unit, with her sons as active participants, reflecting the LDS understanding that families are the basic unit of covenant life.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 58:27-28 teaches: 'Verily, verily, I say unto you, ye must practice virtue and holiness before me continually. Even so I say unto you again, all my saints, that they shall be gathered unto one place, and have all things in common; and they shall not depart from my law.' The widow's household becomes a place where 'all things' are held in common (the oil is distributed among family members), and she practices the virtue of obedience before the Lord. D&C 84:36-37 further connects obedience to receiving: 'Ye are not able to abide the presence of God now, neither the ministering of angels; wherefore, continue in patience until ye are perfected.' The widow's patient, continuous pouring is a form of that patience and obedience that leads to perfection and receipt of divine blessings.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple ceremony, the pattern of continuous, repeated action is significant—washing and anointing are done with ritual precision and repetition. The widow's continuous pouring of oil into vessel after vessel mirrors this pattern of sacred, repeated action. The oil itself, as noted, symbolizes the Holy Ghost and covenantal blessing. The widow's sustained pouring is a type of the sustained bestowal of the Spirit upon the faithful.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ himself modeled obedience coupled with continuous, sustained work. In Gethsemane, he prayed not once but three times, maintaining his supplication and aligning his will with the Father's. The widow, like Christ, does not perform her work once but maintains it, continuously bringing her will and effort into alignment with what the prophet (and through him, God) has instructed. Christ also taught that discipleship involves 'taking up the cross' daily—not a one-time act but a continuous commitment. The widow's continuous pouring is a daily enactment of faithfulness to her household and covenant.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members are often inspired and moved by stories of dramatic conversion or miraculous intervention. This verse teaches a different principle: miracles often unfold through sustained, continuous obedience and work. The widow did not receive her provision in a flash of light but through the steady, repeated action of pouring vessel after vessel. In our own lives, we receive blessings not typically through sudden divine intervention that bypasses our effort but through showing up day after day, doing what we have been instructed, and continuing in faith. Whether in marriage, child-rearing, education, health, or spiritual growth, the principle is similar: continuous, faithful action coupled with trust in God's promise. The widow's work with her sons also teaches the importance of family participation in spiritual growth and provision. We are not isolated individuals receiving isolated blessings; we are members of families and communities through which God's provision flows. Engaging our children in meaningful work, including the work of faith and prayer, invites them into the experience of divine provision and strengthens family bonds.

text_kjv: And it came to pass, when the vessels were full, that she said unto her son, Bring me yet a vessel. And he said unto her, There is not a vessel more. And the oil stayed.

commentary.narrative:
The climax of the miracle arrives when the flow of oil ceases. The widow, continuing her work, turns to her son and asks for another vessel. His answer—'There is not a vessel more'—signals the end. At that precise moment, the oil stops. The Hebrew statement 'va-ya'amod ha-shamen' (and the oil stood, stopped) indicates that the multiplication halted. This is not because the original jar of oil was finally exhausted but because there were no more empty vessels to receive it.

The ending of the miracle is the ultimate revelation of its principle. Had the widow borrowed fewer vessels, less oil would have been produced. Had she borrowed more, more oil would have remained. The scope of the miracle was determined by her faith and initiative—by the number of vessels she was willing to ask her neighbors for. This is a profound theological statement: God's abundance is not limited, but our capacity to receive it is. The widow did not hit a ceiling imposed by God but by the number of receptacles she had prepared. The miracle reveals that God gives generously, but provision requires preparation. In this case, the widow's preparation took the form of gathering empty vessels—creating space for what God desired to give.

The stopping of the oil is not a failure but the perfect completion of the miracle. Every vessel is full. Nothing is wasted. The oil did not run out prematurely; it stopped precisely when it had filled every vessel the widow had gathered. This speaks to God's perfect calibration: the supply matched the need and the preparation exactly. God did not give too little (leaving vessels empty) or too much (spilling over and wasting). The miracle was not arbitrary but precisely measured to the widow's circumstances and faith.

The verse is structured with elegant simplicity: request for another vessel, answer that none remains, cessation of the oil. The rhythm of the narrative mirrors the rhythm of the miracle: bring vessel, pour oil, set aside; bring vessel, pour oil, set aside; ask for vessel, none available, oil stops. The widow and her sons performed the action; the oil responded to their action. Now the action is exhausted; the oil stops.

word_study.meaning: 'As the filling of the vessels' or 'when the vessels were filled.' Malot is an infinitive construct form of male (to be full, to fill), indicating the point at which fullness was achieved.
word_study.significance: The moment of fullness is marked precisely. The narrative is not vague about when the miracle ends; it ends when fullness is achieved. In Hebrew thought, 'full' (male) carries connotations of completeness and sufficiency. When the vessels became male (full), the work was complete.

word_study.term_english: There is not a vessel more
word_study.meaning: 'There is not yet/still another vessel.' Ein (there is not) + od (still, yet, any more) + keli (vessel). The phrase literally means no additional vessel remains available.
word_study.significance: The son's answer is definitive. All available vessels have been gathered and filled. The Hebrew ein od conveys both absence and the sense that further action is impossible—there is literally nothing more to bring. This marks the boundary of the miracle: not a boundary imposed by God's supply but by human preparation and capacity.

word_study.meaning: 'And the oil stood, stopped, ceased.' Ya'amod comes from amad, meaning to stand, take a stand, come to a halt. The perfect tense (vaya'amod) indicates completed action in the past.
word_study.significance: The verb amad is the same verb used for standing up, standing firm, or standing still. The oil did not dissipate or disappear; it stood—it ceased flowing, it came to rest. The image is of motion halting, of a stream stopping. This is the precise moment the miracle ended: when there was nowhere left for the oil to go. The Covenant Rendering's phrase 'the oil stopped flowing' captures this sense of cessation, of the flow halting. Notably, the text does not say the oil was exhausted or the jar was empty—it says the oil stopped. The original small jar still contained oil potentially, but there was no vessel left to receive it, so the multiplication ceased.

cross_references.connection: Christ teaches that 'unto whomsoever much is given, of him shall be much required.' The widow received much (many vessels full of oil), and the miracle calibrated itself to her preparation—she was given according to what she had prepared to receive.

Paul writes that 'we have different gifts according to the grace given to each of us.' The widow's gift of multiplication was given in proportion to her faith and preparation—her 'grace' was calibrated to her receptiveness.

The Lord promises that if the people bring tithes, 'I will...open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it.' The widow's miracle is a microcosm of this promise: abundant blessing poured out until there is no more room to receive it—in her case, until all vessels are full.

Joseph Smith revealed that 'when we obtain any blessing from God, it is by obedience to that law upon which it is predicated.' The widow obtained her blessing (oil) by obedience to Elisha's instructions (gathering vessels, shutting the door, pouring). The blessing was contingent on obedience to the law of preparation and faith.

Nephi teaches that God 'granteth unto the children of men line upon line, precept upon precept.' The widow's miracle unfolds line upon line—vessel by vessel, instruction by instruction—not all at once but through a progressive, measured process.

commentary.historical_context: The story of the widow's oil resonated with the Israelite audience because it addressed a real social crisis. Economic hardship and debt were common, and the seizure of children as debt-slaves was a legal reality that most listeners would have encountered or feared. Yet the narrative promises that divine intervention, when sought through a prophet and received through faith and preparation, can overturn seemingly inevitable social tragedy. The miracle works through ordinary means—borrowed vessels, a small jar of oil, a household—not through extraordinary external displays. This made it believable to an ancient audience while also being genuinely wonderful. The principle that abundance flows to the extent that one has prepared to receive it is also consistent with ancient wisdom literature (Proverbs) and ancient Near Eastern understandings of providence: the gods provide for the righteous who prepare and act, not for the idle.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 32:40-43, Alma teaches that the seed of faith grows and develops fruit 'that ye may pluck and eat.' The widow's miracle is similar: she plants her faith (by gathering vessels, obeying Elisha), and it grows and produces fruit (oil). The point at which the fruit is mature and ready to harvest (all vessels full) is the point where she can enjoy what she has grown. Just as Alma emphasizes that the seed must be nourished and tended to produce fruit, so the widow must pour and tend to bring the miracle to fruition.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:32-34 teaches that 'the earth rolls upon her wings, and the sun giveth his light by day, and the moon giveth her light by night' according to law and order. Similarly, the widow's miracle operated according to principle and order: the oil flowed according to the law of faith and preparation. D&C 59:16-17 further teaches that all things that come of the earth are made 'for the benefit of man...to be used, with judgment, not to excess, neither by extortion.' The widow's oil, perfectly proportioned to her vessels and her need, exemplifies this principle of measured, non-excessive provision.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple worship, blessings are bestowed in sequence and order according to the patron's readiness to receive them. Just as temple ordinances cannot be administered without the person's preparation and willingness to covenant, so the widow's oil flows only to the extent that she has prepared vessels (spiritual or physical containers) to receive it. The stopping of the oil when vessels run out is a principle of sacred limits: blessing flows within appropriate bounds, respecting both the giver's wisdom and the receiver's capacity.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's teaching about the kingdom of heaven often uses containers and measuring metaphors. In Mark 4:24-25, he teaches 'Take heed what ye hear: with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you: and unto you that hear shall more be given. For he that hath, to him shall be given: and he that hath not, from him shall be taken even that which he hath.' The widow's miracle illustrates this principle: she prepared vessels (measuring), and she received more (the oil was multiplied) according to her preparation. Christ also teaches in Matthew 13:52 that 'every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is a householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.' The widow, bringing forth oil from her small jar (old) in a multiplied and continuous stream (new), exemplifies this bringing forth of treasure.
commentary.application: The cessation of the oil at the precise moment when all vessels are full teaches several lessons for modern covenant life. First, it affirms that God provides abundantly but not wastefully. The oil did not run out before all vessels were full, nor did it spill over uselessly. This teaches us to trust that God's provision will be exactly calibrated to our need—no more, no less. In an age of anxiety about scarcity, this is a powerful promise. Second, the principle that the extent of the miracle depended on the number of vessels the widow gathered teaches us about personal responsibility and preparation. We cannot expect to receive blessings we have not prepared to receive. If we want to be filled with spiritual gifts, we must 'gather vessels'—through prayer, study, temple attendance, service, and moral preparation. Third, the stopping of the oil when no more vessels remain teaches us about boundaries and contentment. The widow did not complain that the oil stopped or try to pour into already-full vessels; she recognized that the work was complete. This teaches us to recognize sufficiency and completion, to be grateful for what God has given rather than to perpetually demand more. In our consumer culture, which constantly encourages us to want more, to take more, to receive more, this verse's quiet affirmation of satisfaction and completeness is countercultural and healing.

text_kjv: Then she came and told the man of God. And he said, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest.

commentary.narrative:
The widow returns to Elisha with news of the miracle — the oil has stopped flowing, and she now possesses far more than she could have imagined. Elisha's response is remarkably practical and threefold: sell the oil, pay the debt, and live on what remains. This is not merely a miraculous provision; it is an economically complete solution to her crisis. In ancient Israel, debt slavery was a terrifying reality. A widow with unpaid debts faced the loss of her sons to creditors — they would become servants to her debtors for years, potentially forever. Elisha's instruction directly addresses this legal threat first, then secures her livelihood.

The structure of his command reveals his understanding of her actual needs. He does not say, 'Rejoice in God's abundance' or 'Trust in the Lord.' He says: pay what you owe (restoring your legal status and your sons' freedom), then use the surplus to sustain yourself and your children. The miracle is complete only when it results in restored dignity and economic stability. This is a picture of redemption that is both spiritual and material.

word_study.meaning: The verb shallem means 'to complete, to pay in full, to repay.' Neshiyah refers to debt or obligation. The imperative form indicates this is Elisha's first priority for her — not enrichment, but restoration of legal standing.
word_study.significance: In ancient Israel, unpaid debt meant the loss of freedom for the debtor's children. Elisha's command prioritizes the widow's sons' freedom over her comfort. This reflects both the law (Exodus 21:2-4) and covenant values of jubilee and liberation (Leviticus 25).

word_study.meaning: Tichyi is second-person feminine singular of 'to live' (hayah). Ba-notar means 'in/from what remains, what is left over.' The verb is in future tense — she will live; her life is secured.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes that this is 'economically comprehensive' — not a gift that runs out, but a sustainable means of living. She and her sons have a future, not merely a temporary rescue.

cross_references.connection: The law of debt slavery in Israel: after seven years, a Hebrew slave was released, but if he had married and had children, they remained the master's property. Elisha's command to pay the debt immediately protects this widow's sons from this fate.

The covenant obligation to help a poor brother or sister in financial distress, not by lending at interest, but by restoration of dignity and means. Elisha's instruction embodies this covenantal principle.
The proverb that 'the borrower is servant to the lender' — the widow's debt has enslaved her legally and psychologically. The miracle frees her from this bondage.
Nephi observes that the Lord brings temporal and spiritual salvation together. The widow's rescue is both material (debt paid, provision secured) and spiritual (God's covenant care manifest).

The law of consecration in latter-day revelation teaches that surplus belongs to the poor — a modern echo of the principle that Elisha applies: meet basic needs, then the surplus sustains the community.

commentary.historical_context: Debt slavery in the ancient Near East was a common mechanism for wealth consolidation and social stratification. The Code of Hammurabi allowed creditors to enslave debtors' children for up to three years. Israelite law theoretically limited this (Exodus 21:2), but the practice was widespread and brutal. A widow without male protectors was especially vulnerable. She had no one to mediate with creditors, no family honor to protect her. The economic system was structurally designed to dispossess women and children. Elisha's intervention is not sentimental charity; it is direct resistance to a system of exploitation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin teaches that one's salvation depends partly on being 'willing to submit to all things which the Lord seeth fit to inflict upon [you], even as a child doth submit to his father' (Mosiah 3:19), yet his own society included specific laws protecting the poor from debt slavery. The Nephite law code, rooted in Mosaic tradition, reflected the same value Elisha demonstrates: economic justice is part of covenant fidelity.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 52:39-40 teaches that Saints should consecrate surplus for the poor. Elisha's instruction to pay debt and live on the remainder embodies this principle: not hoarding, not desperation, but right use of God's provision.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The widow's restoration through oil mirrors the anointing of priests and kings in the temple — oil as a sign of God's setting apart, consecration, and blessing. Her deliverance through oil is her own spiritual anointing for restored life.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ is the ultimate satisfier of debt. 'Blotting out the handwriting of ordinances that was against us, which was contrary to us, and took it out of the way, nailing it to his cross' (Colossians 2:14). The widow's complete redemption — both from legal bondage and from material desperation — is a type of Christ's atonement, which liberates from both the penalty of sin (debt) and from spiritual destitution.
commentary.application: This verse calls modern disciples to examine whether our economic decisions honor both justice and mercy. When we encounter someone in financial crisis, do we seek only their spiritual comfort, or do we address the structural injustice that oppresses them? Do we help them pay their debts, or merely offer temporary relief? The lesson is: true charity restores dignity and creates sustainable freedom, not dependency.

text_kjv: And it fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where was a great woman; and she constrained him to eat bread. And so it was, that as oft as he passed by, he turned in thither to eat bread.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative shifts from the widow of the oil to a woman of entirely different status. The 'great woman' (ishah gedolah) is not poor or desperate; she is prominent, wealthy, and influential in the town of Shunem. Yet she also recognizes something in the traveling prophet. She 'constrains' him — the Hebrew verb is forceful, suggesting she seizes the opportunity and insists on his acceptance of her hospitality. What begins as a single meal becomes a pattern: every time Elisha passes through Shunem, he comes to her house. This is the beginning of a relationship of spiritual patronage, rooted in ordinary acts of feeding and welcome.

The narrative's emphasis on bread and eating should not be overlooked. In the ancient world, sharing a meal was a covenantal act. To invite someone to your table, to feed them regularly, was to enter into relationship and obligation. The woman's persistent hospitality is not mere kindness; it is an act of discernment and commitment. She perceives something in the prophet that makes her willing to break social conventions — a prominent woman pursuing a traveling holy man, inviting him into her home repeatedly. This would invite speculation and gossip. Yet she does it anyway, which suggests she sees something others miss.

word_study.meaning: Ishah means 'woman.' Gedolah (from gadal, 'to be great, to grow, to become mighty') refers to social status, wealth, and influence. She is not merely 'great' in age or wisdom, but prominent, a woman of standing in her community.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'prominent woman' to capture that this is social and economic status. This is a woman with resources, a household, servants, property. Her choice to serve the prophet is not born of desperation but of conviction.

word_study.meaning: Tachazek is from chazak, 'to seize, to hold, to strengthen, to prevail.' The reflexive form (tachazek bo) means 'she took hold of him,' 'she urged him strongly,' 'she prevailed upon him.' It is an active, insistent verb.
word_study.significance: This is not a polite invitation. The woman seizes the prophetic moment. She recognizes Elisha and is determined that he will receive her hospitality. The verb suggests spiritual and social boldness — qualities the narrative will reveal as crucial to what comes next.

word_study.term_english: as oft as he passed by
word_study.term_original: מִדֵּ֥י עׇבְר֖וֹ יָסֻ֥ר שָׁ֖מָּה (midei ovro yasur shammah)
word_study.meaning: Midei ('according to,' 'whenever') ovro ('his passing through') yasur ('he would turn aside, turn in') shammah ('there'). The repeated action is habitual and intentional — a regular pattern.
word_study.significance: This establishes that Elisha's visits become routine, reliable, expected. The relationship deepens through repetition and trust. The woman has created a 'prophet's chamber' — a sanctuary where the man of God finds rest and nourishment.

cross_references.connection: Abraham's hospitality to the three visitors (who are angels/the Lord) parallels the Shunammite's recognition and welcome of the prophet. Both stories affirm that faithful hospitality toward God's servants is a pathway to divine blessing.
Mary and Martha's reception of Jesus. Like the Shunammite, Martha is 'cumbered about much serving' — hospitality is an outward expression of spiritual attentiveness and love.
'Be not forgetful to entertain strangers: for thereby some have entertained angels unawares.' The Shunammite's hospitality to the prophet is an embodiment of this New Testament principle.

The widow of Zarephath fed Elijah during famine and was blessed with continuous provision. Like her, the Shunammite recognizes and serves God's prophet, though she comes from a place of abundance rather than desperation.

Paul commends widows who have 'lodged strangers, washed the saints' feet, relieved the afflicted' — acts of hospitality as evidence of faith. The Shunammite's regular provision of food and shelter to Elisha exemplifies this covenantal virtue.

commentary.historical_context: Shunem was a town in the Jezreel Valley, in the northern kingdom of Israel, roughly 15 miles northwest of Bethshan. It was a prosperous agricultural region. A 'great woman' in such a setting would have owned land, perhaps livestock, and would have had servants. She would have had social standing to defend. The fact that she persistently invites a prophet into her home — especially given the turbulent religious and political climate under the later Omride kings (Ahab's dynasty, which was hostile to prophetic figures) — suggests both courage and spiritual conviction. Prophets were often viewed with suspicion; harboring one could invite political risk. Yet she does so anyway, suggesting she saw Elisha as trustworthy and worth the social cost.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 17:3 describes how Ammon and his brothers 'were instruments in the hands of God in bringing so many of the Lamanites to the knowledge of the truth.' The Shunammite becomes an instrument in God's hands by recognizing and sustaining the prophet. King Benjamin teaches that 'the worth of souls is great in the sight of God' (D&C 18:10) — the woman's service shows her understanding of the worth of the prophet who bears God's word.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:6-7 teaches 'If thou lovest me thou shalt serve me and keep all my commandments.' The Shunammite's repeated, voluntary service to Elisha is an expression of love for the Lord and his servant. D&C 88:125 promises that those who provide for the Lord's servants shall receive a reward in the resurrection.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The 'prophet's chamber' the Shunammite prepares (verse 10) anticipates temple service — a dedicated space set apart for sacred purposes, furnished with specific items of holiness (bed, table, chair, lamp). Her act of hospitality is proto-temple work: creating a sanctuary for the work of God.

commentary.christological_typology: The woman's discernment and service foreshadow the faith of those who recognized and served Christ. Just as she 'perceived' Elisha's holiness (verse 9) without explicit declaration, so did others recognize in Jesus something divine that official Israel missed. Her hospitality is a type of discipleship — recognizing the servant of God and sustaining him in his work.
commentary.application: Modern disciples are called to recognize and honor those who serve God's purposes — not just prophets, but teachers, missionaries, priesthood leaders, and all who labor in the Lord's vineyard. The Shunammite's example invites us to ask: Do I recognize the spirit in those whom God has called? Am I willing to sacrifice time, resources, and social comfort to sustain them? Do I create 'chambers of rest' for the servants of God — both literally (hospitality) and figuratively (prayers, support, encouragement)?

text_kjv: And she said unto her husband, Behold now, I perceive that this is an holy man of God, which passeth by us continually.

commentary.narrative:
The woman turns to her husband and shares her spiritual discernment. She begins with 'Behold now' — a call to his attention, to take her seriously. Her perception is not a guess or sentiment; it is knowing (yadati, 'I know'). She has discerned something about Elisha that is not obvious to casual observers: he is a 'holy man of God' (ish Elohim qadosh). The phrase combines both his functional role (man of God, prophet) and his essential character (holy, set apart, consecrated). She perceives that he 'continually' passes by, establishing that she has observed a pattern and recognized its significance.

This verse is crucial to understanding the Shunammite's character. She is not naïve or manipulated by a charming stranger. She has actively observed, discerned, and recognized spiritual truth. She has the gift of spiritual perception — the ability to see beyond the surface of things to the reality of the divine. In the biblical tradition, this is a hallmark of faithful women: Sarah, Rebekah, Ruth, Hannah, Mary Magdalene — they perceive truths that elude others. The woman's discernment is not presented as extraordinary or miraculous; it is the natural fruit of attentiveness and faith. She looks at the prophet and sees the Holy Ghost attending him. She speaks to her husband not as one seeking permission, but as one sharing knowledge that should inform their household's choices.

word_study.meaning: First-person singular perfect of yada, 'to know.' In Hebrew, yada is not merely intellectual knowledge; it is knowledge from experience, from relationship, from discernment. It can mean 'to know by sight,' 'to recognize,' 'to perceive,' 'to be aware.' Here it carries the sense of spiritual recognition — she has come to know, through observation and intuition, who Elisha is.
word_study.significance: This is not 'I think' or 'I suspect.' It is 'I know.' The woman's perception is grounded in certainty, not conjecture. The Covenant Rendering renders it 'I am certain,' capturing the confidence and clarity of her knowing.

word_study.meaning: Ish Elohim is a standard phrase for 'prophet, man of God, God's servant.' Qadosh (from qds, 'to be set apart, sanctified, holy') means 'holy, sacred, consecrated.' It describes someone or something separated from the common and devoted to the sacred. Applied to the prophet, it indicates both his consecration and the divine presence that attends him.
word_study.significance: The woman's use of both titles — 'man of God' and 'holy' — shows she understands both his function and his essence. She perceives not just that he is a prophet, but that holiness radiates from him. In Latter-day Saint terms, she recognizes the Holy Ghost is with him.

word_study.meaning: An adverb meaning 'perpetually, continually, always, constantly.' It refers to habitual or unceasing action. Here it emphasizes the regularity of Elisha's passage through Shunem.
word_study.significance: The woman's observation is not based on a single encounter. She has watched the pattern develop, noted his regularity, and drawn a sustained conclusion. Her faith is informed by consistent observation of his character and presence.

cross_references.connection: Samuel is recognized as 'a prophet of the LORD' because 'the LORD was with him' and his words did not fall. The Shunammite's recognition of Elisha parallels this: she perceives that God is with him.

The Samaritan woman at the well recognizes Jesus as a prophet: 'Sir, I perceive that thou art a prophet.' Like the Shunammite, she discerns spiritual reality through spiritual perception, not through credentials.

John the Baptist declares, 'Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world.' His perception of Jesus' true identity parallels the Shunammite's recognition of Elisha's holiness — both are moments of spiritual discernment.

Modern revelation teaches that 'every soul who forsaketh his sins and cometh unto me, and calleth on my name, and obeyeth my voice, and keepeth my commandments, shall see my face.' The Shunammite's ability to perceive the holy man of God is the fruit of her own faithfulness and attentiveness.

Moroni promises that God will 'manifest the truth of it unto you by the power of the Holy Ghost.' The Shunammite's discernment is an example of how the Holy Ghost manifests truth — she knows Elisha is holy because the Holy Ghost witnesses to her.

commentary.historical_context: In the religious world of northern Israel during Elisha's time (mid-9th century BCE), the prophetic office was contested. There were false prophets, court prophets who served kings, and independent prophets like Elijah and Elisha. Distinguishing a true prophet from a charlatan was a genuine challenge. The criterion the woman uses — holiness, the presence of God — reflects the Old Testament standard: a true man of God demonstrates the reality of God's presence through his words, actions, and spiritual aura. In a culture saturated with religious claims and political manipulation, her ability to perceive Elisha's true nature reveals both spiritual maturity and a heart attuned to the divine.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 18:24-25 describes how King Lamoni perceived that Ammon 'was a great man, and a man of God' through observing his actions and spiritual presence. The Shunammite's discernment mirrors Lamoni's — perception of God's power attending a servant of God.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 teaches that the president of the Church speaks as 'the mouthpiece of the Lord' and that 'his word ye shall receive, as if from mine own mouth.' The principle is that when the Holy Ghost attends a servant of God, discerning souls will recognize it. The Shunammite exemplifies this kind of recognition.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Holiness (qadosh) is a central temple concept — the temple is the holy house, the sanctuary of the holy presence. The woman's recognition that the prophet is 'holy' is her acknowledgment that the divine presence (the Holy of Holies) attends him.
