Her choice to build him a chamber is thus a temple-like act: creating space for the holy one to dwell.

commentary.christological_typology: Just as the Shunammite perceives the holiness of Elisha and is drawn to serve him, so do faithful souls perceive in Jesus Christ the holiness and power of God incarnate. 'Truly this was the Son of God' (Matthew 27:54) is the centurion's moment of similar perception. The woman's discernment is a type of the faith that recognizes the divine in the midst of the ordinary.
commentary.application: Modern disciples are invited to cultivate the gift of discernment the Shunammite demonstrates. In a world of competing voices and claims, can we perceive the presence of the Holy Ghost with God's true servants? The test is not credentials alone, but the fruit of the Spirit: holiness, integrity, the presence of God. Where do we see such holiness? Are we willing to prioritize support of such people over social comfort or convenience? The woman's example challenges us to develop spiritual perception and act on it.

text_kjv: Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall, and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither.

commentary.narrative:
The Shunammite moves from discernment to action. She proposes to her husband that they build a 'little chamber on the wall' — a small upper room, likely constructed on the flat roof of their house or as an extension of the upper story. This is not a guest room in the ordinary sense; it is a dedicated, permanent space specifically for the prophet. The furnishings are carefully enumerated: a bed (for rest), a table (for meals), a stool or chair (for sitting), and a lamp or candlestick (for light).

Each of these items is significant. They represent basic provision — comfort, hospitality, dignity. But together, they also represent completeness. The woman has thought through what a holy man would need: rest, sustenance, a place to sit (place of authority, contemplation), and light (both literal and spiritual). The Covenant Rendering notes that these four items constitute 'complete provision for a guest.' The phrase 'it shall be, when he cometh to us' reveals her confidence that he will continue to come — she is not preparing for a single visit but establishing a pattern of refuge and rest. This is prophetic patronage at its finest: the woman provides the material conditions that allow the prophet to continue his work, traveling without burden, knowing he will find rest and nourishment.

The proposal to build on 'the wall' (aliyyat qir) suggests a room built on or into the exterior wall of the house, accessible perhaps by its own stair. This gives the prophet privacy while keeping him within the household's spiritual orbit. It is a generous gesture that respects his holiness — providing space and separation, not forcing integration into family life, yet making it clear he is cherished and expected.

word_study.meaning: Aliyyah (from alah, 'to go up') means 'upper chamber, upper room.' Qir means 'wall.' Qetannah (from qatan, 'to be small') means 'small, little.' So: a small upper room built on or extending from the wall of the house.
word_study.significance: The specificity of the Hebrew indicates a structure known in ancient Israel — a room built on the roof or as a lean-to on the exterior wall, providing privacy while maintaining connection to the household. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes 'on the wall' to preserve this architectural detail, which reflects the woman's thought and care.

word_study.term_original: מִטָּ֥ה וְשֻׁלְחָ֖ן וְכִסֵּ֣א וּמְנוֹרָ֑ה (mittah, shulchan, kisei, menorah)
word_study.meaning: Mittah: bed (for sleeping, resting). Shulchan: table (for eating, sustenance). Kisei: chair, stool (for sitting, comfort, authority). Menorah: lamp, candlestick (for light, clarity, holiness). These four items form a complete provision for a resident guest.
word_study.significance: The enumeration is deliberate and reflects covenant care. In ancient Israel, providing these four items to a guest — especially a holy person — was an act of profound honor and recognition. The menorah, in particular, carries spiritual significance: it is the item that appears in the tabernacle and temple, suggesting the woman understands the prophet as carrying sacred light.

word_study.meaning: Yasur (from sur, 'to turn aside, to withdraw, to turn in') means 'he will turn in, turn aside.' Shammah means 'there.' The future tense indicates this is a projected pattern.
word_study.significance: The woman's language assumes Elisha will accept and use the chamber — not as a request, but as a certainty. Her faith in his continued visits and his acceptance of her hospitality is implicit in the grammar itself.

cross_references.connection: Elijah goes up to a 'chamber' (aliyyah) to raise the widow of Zarephath's dead son. The chamber serves as a place of prophetic power and divine work — the Shunammite's chamber may serve similar purposes.

Jesus teaches: 'He that receiveth you receiveth me...and whosoever shall give to drink unto one of these little ones a cup of cold water only...shall in no wise lose his reward.' The Shunammite's provision for the prophet embodies this principle.

'Let brotherly love continue...be not forgetful to entertain strangers...remember them that are in bonds.' The Shunammite's care for the prophet reflects the covenant virtue of hospitality grounded in love and remembrance.

The description of the golden candlestick (menorah) in the tabernacle. The woman's provision of a menorah for the prophet's chamber suggests she understands the chamber as a space where holy light (God's presence) dwells.

'Behold, I say unto you, concerning the properties of the church...all things shall be consecrated unto this people.' The Shunammite's dedication of a space to the prophet reflects the covenant principle of consecration — setting apart for sacred purposes.

commentary.historical_context: Rooftop rooms were a standard feature of Palestinian houses in the Iron Age. Archaeologists have found evidence of wooden structures built on house roofs, used for storage, sleeping (in summer), and work. The Shunammite's proposal reflects realistic building practices. The furnishings (bed, table, chair, lamp) represent the essential goods that show honor to an important guest. In ancient Near Eastern hospitality codes, the quality and completeness of provisions reflected the honor given to the guest and the host's means. By providing all four items, the woman demonstrates both generosity and proper hospitality protocol. The fact that she coordinates this with her husband also reflects the domestic authority structure: major household decisions (building projects, resource allocation) involved both spouses, though the narrative prioritizes her insight and initiative.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin gathers his people and teaches from a tower (watchtower) constructed for the purpose of proclamation and covenant renewal. The Shunammite's prophet's chamber is, in miniature, a similar covenantal space — built to facilitate the prophet's work and the household's connection to God's word.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:1-7 teaches that the Church should care for the poor and provide for missionaries. The Shunammite's provision for Elisha anticipates this modern revelation: the community sustains the messenger of God through material provision.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The items in the chamber echo temple furnishings: bed (altar of rest), table (table of showbread), stool (seat of judgment and authority), lamp (menorah, source of light and holiness). The Shunammite's chamber is a domestic sanctuary — a space set apart for the work of God and the rest of God's servant.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ offers believers a similar provision: 'Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest' (Matthew 11:28). Jesus himself received hospitality (Martha's house, Zacchaeus's home, the Passover supper) and blessed those who offered it. The Shunammite's chamber is a type of the spiritual rest and provision that Christ offers — a place of refuge, nourishment, light, and dignity.
commentary.application: The Shunammite's example challenges modern disciples to ask: What structures of support do I create for those who serve God? Is my hospitality generic and occasional, or have I built a deliberate, recurring space of care? Do I provide not just food, but rest, comfort, light, and a seat of honor? The verse invites us beyond casual kindness to covenantal commitment — creating conditions where God's servants can be sustained in their work. For parents, this might mean creating a home environment that supports a child's service in the Church; for ward members, it might mean reliable support for missionaries or young people in service; for all, it might mean the spiritual provision of prayer, encouragement, and believing faith.

text_kjv: And it fell on a day, that he came thither, and he turned into the chamber, and lay there.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative is economical and spare. The Shunammite's preparation is complete; Elisha's acceptance is immediate. He 'came,' 'turned into the chamber,' and 'lay there.' There is no elaborate gratitude, no emotional scene, no lengthy conversation. The prophet simply uses what has been prepared. The Covenant Rendering notes that 'the narrative is spare' — this is intentional. The prophet's dignity is preserved; he accepts what he needs without fawning or excessive thanks. The hospitality is so natural and established that it requires no commentary.

This simplicity reflects mature spiritual relationship. There is no awkwardness, no performative gratitude, no sense of burden on either side. The Shunammite has built something so thoughtful that the prophet can simply receive it. He comes, goes to the chamber, and rests. The verb 'lay' (shkb) has connotations of repose and peace. After his labors of traveling, prophesying, and ministering, Elisha finds a place of genuine rest. The verse demonstrates that one of the prophet's real needs is physical rest — the spiritual work of prophecy depends on the body's restoration. The Shunammite understands this and provides for it without fanfare.

The phrase 'it fell on a day' (wayehi hayom) is a standard Hebrew narrative formula marking a new scene or development. It suggests this is not the first time — that this pattern has been established and is now becoming routine. The prophet comes, uses the chamber, rests. The domestic miracle is unfolding quietly, almost invisibly: a man finds rest, a woman finds purpose and blessing, a household touches the divine through simple care.

word_study.meaning: Va-yavo is third-person masculine singular past tense of ba, 'to come, to go into.' Shammah means 'there, thither.' The simple verb form and adverb convey the straightforward fact of his arrival.
word_study.significance: The lack of elaboration in the Hebrew mirrors the lack of elaboration in the action. This is routine, expected, natural. No drama, no surprise.

word_study.meaning: Va-yasar is from sur, 'to turn aside, to withdraw, to turn in.' El ha-aliyyah means 'into the chamber.' The verb suggests a deliberate turning aside, a choice to enter the prepared space.
word_study.significance: The use of 'turned into' (rather than 'entered' or 'went to') suggests familiarity. He knows where it is and goes directly to it. The chamber has become 'his' space in the household.

word_study.meaning: Va-yishkab is from shkb, 'to lie down, to recline, to rest.' Shammah means 'there.' This is the verb used for sleep, rest, and intimacy.
word_study.significance: The choice of shkb emphasizes not just lying down but finding rest. For a man of God constantly in motion, traveling, teaching, ministering, this is significant. Physical rest is presented as legitimate and necessary, not a luxury or failure of faith.

cross_references.connection: Jacob 'lighted upon a certain place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set; and he took of the stones of that place, and put them for his pillows, and lay down in that place to sleep.' Like Jacob, Elisha finds rest in a provided place, and it becomes a site of divine encounter.

Jesus says, 'The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head.' Elisha's finding of rest and lodging in the Shunammite's home contrasts sharply with Christ's homelessness, yet both exemplify dependence on others' hospitality.

'He maketh me to lie down in green pastures...he restoreth my soul.' The Shunammite's chamber provides the restful place where the prophet's soul can be restored — a fulfillment of the psalmist's promise.
Jesus 'lay...in a manger' — a humble bed provided by faithful people. Elisha's acceptance of simple lodging parallels Jesus' humility in accepting provision from his people.

'And the elders of the church...shall appoint unto him a member of the church, by common consent...who shall feed him, or impart unto him of the church, every member shall contribute according to what he hath.' The principle of providing for the Lord's servants is codified in modern revelation and exemplified in the Shunammite's care.

commentary.historical_context: Rest was not a luxury in the ancient Near East, particularly for holy men who traveled constantly. Prophets like Elijah and Elisha were itinerant, moving between towns, living outdoors, depending on hospitality. They slept on hard ground, in caves, under trees. A prepared chamber with a bed would have been genuine comfort. The social reality is that such comfort was not universal — Elisha would have often slept rough. When he was offered a bed in a good house, the acceptance would have been genuine relief. The narrative's lack of elaboration may partly reflect ancient narrative style, but it also reflects the prophet's acceptance of need and rest without guilt. In some religious traditions, ascetic renunciation is valorized to the point that accepting comfort is seen as spiritual failure. The biblical narrative here normalizes rest as necessary and good.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 7:23 teaches that the Church should give 'succor to the poor and the needy.' The Shunammite's provision of a chamber for rest is concrete succor — care that addresses real, bodily needs of God's servant.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 81:5 teaches that the presidency should 'strengthen one another in the work of the Lord.' The Shunammite strengthens Elisha through material provision, enabling him to continue his prophetic labors. This is a principle of mutual strengthening.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Rest is a covenant theme, from the Sabbath rest (Exodus 20:11) to the promised 'rest' of entering the covenant (Hebrews 4). The prophet's rest in the Shunammite's chamber is a type of the covenant rest promised to the faithful.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's rest — in the boat asleep during the storm (Mark 4:38), in the tomb, promised to the faithful (Matthew 11:28) — is a type of the peace and security found through trusting God and receiving care from faithful people. The Shunammite's chamber is a type of the sanctuary Christ provides.
commentary.application: This verse invites disciples to recognize that caring for God's servants includes attending to their physical needs. Rest, food, shelter, and comfort are not luxuries in covenant community; they are necessities. For institutional leaders, this means creating sustainable systems of support for those in service. For individuals, this means recognizing when God's servants are weary and providing relief without requiring elaborate gratitude or performance. The naturalness of Elisha's rest — no big ceremony, just acceptance and sleep — suggests that true hospitality is so complete that the recipient can simply receive and be restored.

text_kjv: And he said to Gehazi his servant, Call this Shunammite. And when he had called her, she stood before him.

commentary.narrative:
Having rested, Elisha moves to respond to the woman's kindness. He calls for his servant Gehazi and instructs him to summon the Shunammite. This is the first mention of Gehazi in this narrative, though he is known from other passages as Elisha's trusted attendant. The introduction of Gehazi here is significant: he functions as the intermediary between the prophet and the petitioner, just as Elisha once functioned between Elijah and the people. This is a representation of prophetic succession and institutional stability — the prophet has a trained servant who carries out his instructions and mediates his relationships.

When Gehazi calls her, 'she stood before him.' The verb 'stood' (amad) carries the sense of standing ready, standing in obedience, standing prepared. The phrase 'before him' (lifnav) indicates her formal posture: she is before the prophet, awaiting his word. This is not a casual conversation; it is a formal audience. The woman comes expectantly, but with respect and deference. She has served the prophet; now she is about to receive from him. The narrative positioning is significant: the giver becomes the receiver. The Shunammite has given freely, without expectation of return, but the prophet recognizes her generosity and seeks to honor it. Elisha's instinct is to bless her. What blessing he will offer remains to be seen, but the narrative trajectory is clear: her hospitality will be met with prophetic blessing.

word_study.meaning: Gehazi is a proper name (etymology uncertain, possibly 'valley of the prophet'). Na'ar means 'young man, servant, attendant, apprentice.' In the context of a prophet's household, the na'ar is a trained assistant who carries out instructions, manages hospitality, and learns the prophet's ways.
word_study.significance: Gehazi is Elisha's na'ar — his apprentice and servant, just as Elisha was Elijah's na'ar (1 Kings 19:21). The term represents institutional continuity and training in the prophetic tradition. The Covenant Rendering identifies Gehazi simply as 'servant,' preserving the functional relationship.

word_study.meaning: Kra is imperative of qra, 'to call, to summon, to name.' La-Shunammit means 'the Shunammite (woman)' — she is identified by her origin and status. Ha-zot means 'this one.' So: 'Call this Shunammite woman.'
word_study.significance: Elisha identifies the woman by her geographic origin and her distinctiveness ('this one'). She is known to him not by name (we never learn her personal name) but by her role in his life. The anonymity is significant — she is 'the great woman,' 'the Shunammite,' a representative figure whose identity is bound to her faithfulness and her place.

word_study.meaning: Va-ta'amod is third-person feminine singular past tense of amad, 'to stand.' Lefanav means 'before him, in front of him.' The posture is formal and respectful.
word_study.significance: Standing before the prophet is the posture of one receiving instruction or blessing. The narrative positions the woman as attentive, ready, obedient. She does not demand or presume; she responds to the summons and stands ready to hear what the prophet will say.

cross_references.connection: Elijah calls Elisha to be his servant and successor. Elisha was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen when Elijah threw his mantle upon him. Gehazi now serves Elisha in the same capacity Elisha once served Elijah — a cycle of prophetic succession.

The angel Gabriel is sent to Mary and she is troubled by his greeting. 'Hail, thou that art highly favoured.' Similarly, the Shunammite is about to receive a word from the prophet that will honor her. Both women are about to be elevated through divine word.

Eli the priest speaks a blessing over Hannah: 'Go in peace...the God of Israel grant thee thy petition that thou hast asked of him.' Hannah leaves 'in peace' and soon conceives. The Shunammite is about to receive a similar prophetic blessing that will reverse her barrenness (as the next verses will reveal).

Boaz tells Ruth, 'All the city of my people doth know that thou art a woman of excellence.' The Shunammite, like Ruth, is recognized as a woman of remarkable character, and the man of authority (Boaz/Elisha) moves to bless her.

'If ye forgive one another your trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you.' More broadly, the principle of reciprocal blessing — that the giver shall be blessed in return — is taught throughout covenant scriptures. The Shunammite gave without expectation, and now the prophet seeks to bless her.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient household structure, servants like Gehazi were responsible for hospitality management, message delivery, and daily care. They were trained in their master's ways and often became trusted counselors. Gehazi's role here — summoning the woman, presumably at Elisha's direction — illustrates how a prophet's household functioned. The formal summons, the woman standing before the prophet, the anticipation of his word — these reflect the social protocols of ancient Israel, where meeting with a man of authority or wisdom was a formal affair. The woman's standing posture suggests she has not been invited to sit (she has not yet received that honor), but she is fully present and attentive.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin's people 'stood and gave thanks' (Mosiah 2:15) — standing before authority, especially spiritual authority, is the posture of the covenant community. The Shunammite's standing before Elisha anticipates this covenant posture.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:26-27 teaches that 'the Lord requireth the heart and a willing mind' and 'every man shall receive according to his labor.' The Shunammite has labored in service to the prophet; now she stands before him to receive according to her labor.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Standing before the Lord (or his representative) is a temple concept. The Shunammite stands before the prophet in the posture of one standing before the altar, ready to receive blessing and covenant.

commentary.christological_typology: Jesus frequently commended those who served others, saying 'Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me' (Matthew 25:40). The Shunammite's service to Elisha is service to God's anointed. Now she stands before the prophet as one about to receive the blessing of Jesus, who promises that 'every one that hath forsaken houses, or brethren, or sisters, or father, or mother, or wife, or children, or lands, for my name's sake, shall receive an hundredfold' (Matthew 19:29).
commentary.application: This verse invites reflection on the cycle of giving and receiving in covenant community. The Shunammite gave generously, without seeking return. Now she receives. The lesson is not that we give in order to get, but that faithful giving opens us to receive blessing in unexpected ways. Modern disciples are invited to stand before their prophets and authorities with the same attentiveness the Shunammite demonstrates — ready to hear, open to blessing, prepared to act on prophetic instruction. What does it mean to 'stand before' the prophet today? It might mean attending to General Conference, reading prophetic words, or standing in faith with Church leadership. When we stand in faith and obedience, we position ourselves to receive the blessing the Lord desires to give.

text_kjv: And he said unto him, Say now unto her, Behold, thou hast been careful for us with all this care; what is to be done for thee? wouldest thou be spoken for to the king, or to the captain of the host? And she answered, I dwell among mine own people.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha, recognizing the profound hospitality the Shunammite woman has shown him, asks Gehazi to inquire what he can do in return. This is not merely politeness—it reflects the ancient Near Eastern honor system where hospitality creates a debt of gratitude that must be repaid. Elisha offers the most valuable currency in a monarchy: access to power. He can speak to the king or the military commander on her behalf, which in the ancient world meant protection, favor, influence, material advantage.

Yet the woman's response is remarkable: she declines all worldly patronage. She says she dwells among her own people—she is embedded in her community, secure in relationships rather than politics. This is not false modesty or cultural constraint; it is a genuine statement of self-sufficiency. She lacks what power can provide. However, as Gehazi will soon perceive, there is one thing she lacks that power cannot give: a son.

word_study.meaning: To be anxious, careful, diligent; to show concern or solicitous care. The root חָרַד conveys both emotional anxiety and practical diligence—she has fretted over Elisha's welfare.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering notes this emphasizes not just the acts of hospitality but the emotional labor and concern behind them. She has been diligent with genuine care, not mere duty.

word_study.meaning: To sit, dwell, remain in a place. In the perfect tense, it suggests ongoing, settled habitation—not temporary residence but established rootedness.
word_study.significance: Her answer 'betokh ammi anokhi yoshevet' ('among my own people I am dwelling') reflects a woman secure in her social position through family and community ties rather than through political patronage. She is already established, already safe, already belonging.

word_study.meaning: My people, my kin, my community. In ancient Israel, one's people were one's primary source of identity, security, and belonging.
word_study.significance: Her identity is rooted in community rather than ambition. This makes her different from those who seek political elevation. She is content with what she has—except for the one thing she cannot create for herself.

cross_references.connection: The promise to Sarah of a son at the appointed season of life (ka-et chayyah) uses the same language that will appear in verse 16. The Shunammite's story echoes the barren matriarch's experience.
Access to the king and military commander represented the ultimate form of patronage in an ancient monarchy—the very structures of power Elisha offers and the woman refuses.
The Shunammite woman's contentment in her community and her husband's trust parallel the virtuous woman of Proverbs, rooted in family rather than public ambition.
Her refusal of external patronage in favor of inner security and community belonging foreshadows New Testament teaching on true worth found in relationships rather than status.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near Eastern monarchy, proximity to the king and military commander was the primary pathway to wealth, protection, and honor. Elisha's offer would have been extraordinary—a direct line to the throne or the military establishment. The Shunammite's refusal indicates she already possesses wealth (implied by her ability to provide lavish hospitality), a secure husband, and social standing. Her contentment with her community status, rather than seeking elevation through political patronage, was countercultural. Women's security typically came through male relatives or powerful patrons; her independence through community embeddedness was unusual.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The theme of one possessing wealth and position yet lacking what truly matters appears in the Book of Mormon. See Alma 32:8-15, where those who are 'rich and proud' and 'lifted up in the pride of their hearts' lack the broken heart that receives the seed of the gospel—a spiritual poverty amid material sufficiency.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 59:15-16 teaches that the Lord gives 'all things' for the benefit of His people, yet many 'notice not the worth of the blessings'—like the Shunammite, who has not yet received the one blessing that will matter most.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Shunammite's journey parallels the temple progression: she begins in the worldly courts (refusing political patronage) and will ultimately receive the covenant blessing of posterity—a temple principle of eternal increase.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's offer of patronage and the woman's refusal foreshadow the nature of Christ's kingdom. Christ offers not political power (John 6:15) but covenant blessings—the kind that cannot be obtained through the world's systems of influence. The woman's wisdom in recognizing that true fulfillment comes not from proximity to earthly power but from covenant relationship anticipates the reorientation Christ brings.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to examine what we seek from the Lord. Are we asking for worldly advantage, political favor, and protective patronage? Or are we willing to receive the deeper covenant blessings—family, posterity, spiritual increase—that cannot be obtained through the structures of worldly power? The Shunammite's contentment with community before receiving the covenant promise suggests that spiritual readiness comes partly through freedom from worldly ambition. What are we refusing to seek, so that we are open to what the Lord truly wants to give?

text_kjv: And he said, What then is to be done for her? And Gehazi answered, Verily she hath no child, and her husband is old.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha's question—'What then is to be done for her?'—suggests he is searching for the real lack, the thing beneath the surface. Gehazi's answer reveals the crucial insight. The Shunammite has wealth, community, position, and her husband's love, but she lacks a son. In ancient Israel, this was not a sentimental lack but an existential one. Childlessness meant the family line would end; it meant there would be no heir to inherit the ancestral property; it meant that in old age, she would have no one to care for her and her aging husband. Moreover, in Hebrew culture, childlessness was often interpreted as a sign of divine disfavor (see Hannah's story in 1 Samuel 1), even when the cause was natural infertility.

Gehazi's observation is acute: her husband is old, which makes the possibility of natural conception increasingly remote. Gehazi knows what Elisha needs to know—this woman has one need that money, community, and social position cannot solve. Only a prophetic word can address it. This sets up the structure of the narrative: the woman has everything the world values except the one thing only God can give.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'a son—she does not have.' The construction with ben in the accusative emphasizes the specific thing lacking: a son (not merely offspring, but a male heir).
word_study.significance: In Hebrew thought, ben (son) carries connotations of inheritance, continuity, and family legacy. The absence is structural, not incidental.

word_study.meaning: Old, aged; can refer to physical age or to the wisdom that age brings. Here it clearly indicates advanced years.
word_study.significance: Zaqen emphasizes that the window for natural conception is closing. The couple's years of fertility are behind them. This detail makes the subsequent promise of a son supernatural, not merely fortunate.

cross_references.connection: Hannah's childlessness in the context of Peninnah's fertility parallels the Shunammite's lack. Both women face the cultural shame of barrenness despite their virtue.
Sarai is introduced as barren before God promises her a son. The pattern of the righteous woman without children awaiting God's miracle is established in Genesis.
Elizabeth's childlessness 'well stricken in years' with Zechariah parallels the Shunammite's situation—a couple whose natural years of fertility have passed, yet who will receive a promised child.
Children are described as 'a heritage of the Lord' and 'a reward'—the one thing the Shunammite lacks that all the world's patronage cannot provide.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, childlessness was not only a personal sorrow but a family catastrophe. Without an heir, the family line would end, the ancestral land would pass to collateral relatives, and the couple would have no support in old age. There was no social safety net; one's children were one's pension and legacy. Moreover, the law of levirate marriage (Deuteronomy 25:5-10) indicates that childlessness was such a critical issue that special provisions existed for a brother-in-law to father a child with a widow. The Shunammite's situation, with an old husband, would likely have seemed beyond remedy—she would have resigned herself to a childless old age and the attendant loss of dignity and security.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In the Book of Mormon, barrenness appears as a divine test and blessing. Lehi's wife Sariah initially questions Lehi's calling and is comforted; later, she bears children in the wilderness (1 Nephi 5:6-8). The theme of the righteous woman who receives covenant blessings despite natural hardship appears throughout.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 131-132 emphasizes that the fulness of the priesthood includes the sealing of families and eternal increase—the very principle symbolized by the son promised to the Shunammite. A son in this context foreshadows eternal posterity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The inability to have natural children and the need for divine intervention mirror the temple principle of new birth and regeneration. As one is born again through covenant at the temple, so the barren woman receives a new kind of birth through the prophet's word.

commentary.christological_typology: The barren woman awaiting a miracle foreshadows Elizabeth, mother of John the Baptist, who was barren until Gabriel brought her the promise (Luke 1:36). More broadly, it points to the Church as the Bride without children until Christ grants her spiritual fruit. The pattern of divine favor coming to the seemingly hopeless is central to the Gospel.
commentary.application: Gehazi perceives what the woman does not yet know she needs: not what she lacks in worldly terms but what she lacks in covenant terms. The Spirit often knows what we truly lack—not what we are striving for. This verse invites self-examination: Are there needs we have ceased to voice because we have made peace with their absence? Are there prayers we have stopped praying? Gehazi's simple observation—'She has no son, and her husband is old'—suggests that recognizing the real lack is the first step toward receiving the covenant blessing.

text_kjv: And he said, Call her. And when he had called her, she stood in the door.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha commands Gehazi to call the woman, and she responds by standing in the doorway. This positioning is significant. The doorway (petach in Hebrew) is a threshold space—she is not fully inside the private room where Elisha rests, nor is she outside in the public space. She stands poised between her current reality and something unknown. Doorways in ancient Near Eastern narrative often represent liminal spaces where transformation occurs, where one stands on the boundary between two states of being.

The woman's obedience to the summons shows her respect for Elisha and her openness to receive whatever word he has for her. She does not delay, does not send a servant, does not hide. She comes immediately and stands in the doorway—vulnerable, visible, ready to listen. This stance of availability is essential to what follows. She has positioned herself to receive, even though she does not yet know what is coming.

word_study.meaning: An opening, entrance, doorway. In architectural terms, it refers to the threshold between spaces. Figuratively, it can represent a point of entry or transition.
word_study.significance: The woman stands ba-petach ('in the doorway'), suspended between the privacy of Elisha's room and the public world outside. This is a threshold position, literally and symbolically, between her present life and the promise about to be spoken. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes this spatial positioning as theologically loaded—she stands at the border of transformation.

cross_references.connection: Abraham sits at the tent door (petach) when the three visitors arrive. Like the Shunammite, Abraham and Sarah are on the threshold where a life-changing promise will be delivered.
The doorpost (mezuzah) marks the threshold where God's protective presence stands. The doorway is a sacred boundary in Hebrew thought.

Christ describes himself as 'the door'—the threshold through which transformation and new life enter. The Shunammite standing in the doorway anticipates those who come to the door to receive blessing.
The promise 'I have set before you an open door' uses the doorway as a symbol of opportunity and divine readiness to bless. The woman's standing in the doorway represents her openness to receive.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite houses, the doorway between the andron (public reception area) and the interior living quarters was a significant architectural and social boundary. Women of respectable standing did not freely circulate in the male reception area where guests were received. The Shunammite's willingness to come to the doorway of Elisha's room shows the exceptional regard in which she is held—she is invited into the liminal space where a private word can be spoken. This is a sign of her status and the prophet's respect for her.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The threshold space appears in the Book of Mormon in Alma 32:28, where the seed begins to grow—a process of transformation that begins at a point of entry into new understanding.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 77 and temple theology emphasize that thresholds and doorways represent entry into higher understanding and covenants. The woman standing in the doorway mirrors the soul standing at the threshold of new revelation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The doorway is a central image in temple theology—one passes through doors to access higher degrees of the covenant. The Shunammite's position at the petach suggests she is about to be invited into a deeper understanding of God's covenant promise.

commentary.christological_typology: The doorway through which the woman stands is a type of the threshold Christ represents. Just as she must stand at the boundary to receive Elisha's word, so all must come to the threshold of faith to receive Christ's promise. Her openness and readiness reflect the spiritual posture necessary to receive covenant blessings.
commentary.application: Standing in the doorway suggests a posture of readiness and openness. The woman does not know what Elisha will say, yet she comes when summoned and stands ready to listen. In our own spiritual lives, this verse invites us to consider whether we are positioned to receive the Lord's word. Are we standing at the threshold, ready to listen, open to transformation? Or do we hide ourselves away, resistant to what God might say? The simplicity of her response—she came, she stood, she listened—models the availability that precedes covenant blessing.

text_kjv: And he said, About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son. And she said, Nay, my lord, thou man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha delivers the promise: at this appointed time next year, according to the season of life (ka-et chayyah), she will be holding a son. This language—'the season of life'—deliberately echoes the promise to Sarah in Genesis 18:10 and 14. The connection is unmistakable to any Israelite reader familiar with the Torah. Just as Sarah laughed when told she would bear a son in her old age, the Shunammite responds with resistance. But her resistance is not mockery; it is self-protection.

Her response is heartbreaking in its realism: 'Do not deal falsely with your maidservant.' She has learned, over the years of childlessness, to protect herself from hope. The pain of longing that ends in disappointment is worse than the numb acceptance of permanent loss. She would rather not hope than to hope and have her hope destroyed. She calls Elisha 'man of God'—acknowledging his spiritual authority—yet pleads with him not to speak words that will raise false expectations. Her resistance reveals the depth of her previous suffering.

word_study.meaning: An appointed time, season, fixed time, or festival. The root conveys the idea of something fixed and reliable, a point in time when something is designated to occur.
word_study.significance: The use of mo'ed ('appointed time') indicates that this is not mere wishful thinking but a fixed, covenantal promise. God designates and appoints the time; it will occur when He determines.

word_study.meaning: According to the season of life, the living season, the time of fertility and vitality. Chayyah refers to life, vitality, and renewal.
word_study.significance: This exact phrase appears in Genesis 18:10 and 14, the promise to Sarah. The Covenant Rendering notes this linguistic connection is intentional—the Shunammite's story is meant to evoke and echo Sarah's. Both are promises of life coming to the barren; both invoke the same covenantal language.

word_study.meaning: To embrace, hold, clasp. The participle form suggests ongoing action—she will be holding, embracing, cradling the child.
word_study.significance: Chobeqet is tender and physical. It is not merely 'have' a son but actively hold and embrace him—an image of intimate maternal possession and love.

word_study.meaning: To lie, deceive, deal falsely, speak untruth. In some contexts, it carries the sense of disappointing expectations.
word_study.significance: Her plea is not that Elisha would intentionally deceive but that he would not raise hopes that experience has taught her will be dashed. She has been deceived by false hopes before; she begs him not to compound that deception.

cross_references.connection: The promise to Sarah uses the identical phrase 'at the season of life' (ka-et chayyah). Both barren women receive the promise of a son when conception seems naturally impossible. The Shunammite's story is a deliberate echo of Abraham and Sarah's covenant.
Sarah laughs inwardly at the promise; the Shunammite directly protests. Both women respond with skepticism rooted in the natural impossibility of what is promised.

Hannah, also barren, receives a promise from Eli the priest: 'Go in peace, and the God of Israel grant thee thy petition.' Both Hannah and the Shunammite experience deliverance from barrenness through prophetic utterance.
Mary's response to Gabriel—'How shall this be?'—parallels the Shunammite's resistance. Both involve impossible situations where the woman must choose to believe the word spoken by God's messenger.
The faith of Sarah 'who was past age' to bear a child is upheld as an example of faith. The Shunammite's journey from doubt to faith in receiving a promised son likewise demonstrates covenant faith.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israel, as in many pre-industrial societies, barrenness was a profound social tragedy. A woman's primary value and security came through her reproductive function and her role as matriarch of a family household. A childless woman was pitied, sometimes blamed, and always at risk of neglect in old age. The Shunammite, wealthy and well-regarded as she is, would have experienced decades of this social deficit. Her emotional self-protection is understandable; hope in the face of years of disappointment is psychologically costly. The phrase 'do not lie to your maidservant' reflects her vulnerability—she is not skeptical of Elisha's power but terrified of her own heart's capacity to hope and then break.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon's emphasis on faith during waiting periods appears in 2 Nephi 4:31-35, where Nephi struggles with faithfulness despite years of hardship. The Shunammite's resistance to hope parallels the difficulty of maintaining faith when circumstances seem unchanged.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 101:4 promises deliverance 'that my people may be taught to pray and to have faith.' The Shunammite must learn faith in receiving the promise of a son—faith that God's word will not deceive her.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, the sealing of families and the promise of eternal increase center on God's power to create posterity. The son promised to the Shunammite foreshadows temple covenants that guarantee eternal family increase.

commentary.christological_typology: The promise of life coming forth—a son born when natural generation is impossible—prefigures Christ, the promised Son born of Mary in what seemed impossible circumstances (Luke 1:26-37). Both the Shunammite's son and Christ's birth represent God's power to bring forth life against natural odds. More broadly, the pattern of divine promise and human doubt leading to miraculous fulfillment runs through the Gospel narrative.
commentary.application: The Shunammite's plea—'Do not deceive your maidservant'—speaks to a widespread spiritual condition: the exhaustion that comes from hoping and being disappointed. Many have hoped for blessings that never came, have prayed for circumstances to change and seen them remain static, have believed promises that seemed not to materialize. Her resistance is not faithlessness but the self-protective response of the spiritually wounded. Yet Elisha's word comes anyway. This verse invites us to consider what we have stopped hoping for. What dreams have we put away as too painful to carry? Are we willing to let the Lord's word revive hope, even at the risk of disappointment? The Shunammite must choose to believe despite her hard-won caution. That choice is the threshold of faith.

text_kjv: And the woman conceived, and bare a son at that season that Elisha had said unto her, according to the time of life.

commentary.narrative:
The promise is fulfilled with absolute precision. The woman conceives, bears a son, and does so at exactly the appointed season—just as Elisha had spoken. There is no ambiguity, no partial fulfillment, no near-miss. The prophetic word produced reality. The language recalls Genesis 21:2, where Sarah conceived and bore Isaac 'at the set time of which God had spoken to her.' The Shunammite's experience is presented as a perfect parallel to Sarah's—a covenant promise fulfilled at the appointed time.

The repetition of the phrase 'according to the time of life' (ka-et chayyah asher dibber eleha Elisha—'at the season of life which Elisha had spoken to her') frames the promise and its fulfillment. The word spoken becomes the word fulfilled. Between verses 16 and 17 lies all the drama of waiting, believing, carrying the pregnancy to term. But the text compresses this entire journey into a single statement: she conceived, she bore a son, exactly as spoken. The simplicity of the statement underscores the reliability of the prophet's word.

word_study.meaning: She became pregnant. The verb tahar is used throughout biblical narrative to describe conception.
word_study.significance: The word is straightforward and physical. Conception is not metaphorical or spiritual but bodily real. The miracle is written into her flesh.

word_study.meaning: She gave birth to a son. Teled is the standard term for childbirth; ben emphasizes the male heir she lacked.
word_study.significance: The birth of a son fulfills the specific lack identified in verse 14. Not merely a child, but a son—an heir, a continuance of the family line, the one thing that wealth and community could not provide.

word_study.term_english: at that season...according to the time of life
word_study.term_original: לַמּוֹעֵד הַזֶּה כָּעֵת חַיָּה אֲשֶׁר־דִּבֶּר אֵלֶיהָ אֱלִישָׁע (la-mo'ed ha-zeh ka-et chayyah asher dibber eleha Elisha)
word_study.transliteration: la-mo'ed ha-zeh ka-et chayyah asher dibber eleha Elisha
word_study.meaning: At this appointed time, at the season of life, which Elisha had spoken to her—the phrase links promise to fulfillment through the language of the prophetic word (dibber = spoke, uttered).
word_study.significance: The triple reference to the appointed time and Elisha's word emphasizes that this is covenant-language. The fulfilled promise validates the prophet's word as reliable and divinely backed.

cross_references.connection: Sarah conceived and bore Isaac 'at the set time of which God had spoken to her.' The Shunammite's conception and birth mirror Sarah's, establishing continuity in God's covenant promises to barren women.
Hannah 'conceived, and bare a son, and called his name Samuel.' Like the Shunammite, Hannah's barrenness is ended through divine intervention, and she bears the promised child.
Elizabeth 'was delivered of a son' and her neighbors rejoiced. The pattern of the barren woman bearing a promised son continues into the New Testament.
The psalm celebrates that God 'maketh the barren woman to keep house, and to be a joyful mother of children.' The Shunammite's fulfillment illustrates this psalm's theme.

The Restoration emphasizes that through sealing covenants, partners can have 'a continuation of the seeds forever and ever.' The Shunammite's son represents the continuation of seed that covenant promises ensure.

commentary.historical_context: The text's compression of pregnancy and birth into a single verse was conventional in ancient narrative but also carried theological weight. The focus is not on the woman's experience but on the fulfillment of the prophetic word. In the ancient world, pregnancy and childbirth were the most dangerous periods of a woman's life; infant mortality was high. The successful delivery of a living son would have been not merely joyful but miraculous—a triumph of grace over the biological and medical realities that claimed many women and infants. The Shunammite's joy would have been profound, vindicated after years of longing and (perhaps) social suspicion.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes that God's word unfailingly produces the promised result. See Alma 37:40: 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass'—the miraculous fulfillment of the covenant word through ordinary means (conception and birth) demonstrates God's power.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:37-38 states, 'Whether by mine own voice or by the voice of my servants, it is the same.' The Shunammite's fulfillment validates Elisha's word as equivalent to God's own voice—whatever Elisha spoke, God caused to come to pass.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple covenants promise eternal increase and continuation of the family unit. The Shunammite's son is a type of the eternal posterity promised through temple marriage—the covenant of sealed families that ensures continuation 'forever and ever.'

commentary.christological_typology: The conception and birth of the promised son is an Old Testament type of the Incarnation. Just as the Shunammite's son was born in fulfillment of a prophetic word spoken at an appointed time, so Christ was born of Mary in fulfillment of the messianic promises spoken by the prophets. Both involve the miraculous bringing-forth of life through the power of God's word.
commentary.application: Between verse 16 and verse 17, the woman has made the journey from doubt to belief to fulfillment. The text does not record her internal transformation, but we can infer it: she chose to believe the prophet's word despite her protective skepticism. She let herself hope again. And the promise came true. This verse is a vindication of faith. For those who have struggled to believe God's promises—whether of healing, of direction, of protection, of family blessing—the Shunammite's experience is assurance that the Lord's word does not return empty. The appointed time comes. The seed grows. The promise bears fruit. The application is simple: believe the prophet's word, even when circumstances seem to contradict it. The Shunammite conceived and bore because she ultimately said yes to what Elisha spoke. Our spiritual fruitfulness depends on the same assent to God's covenantal promises.

text_kjv: And when the child was grown, it fell on a day, that he went out to his father to the reapers.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative shifts abruptly from the miraculous birth to a seemingly ordinary moment years later. The boy has grown—the Hebrew compresses all the years of childhood into two words (va-yigdal ha-yeled, 'the child grew'). We move from the covenant gift to its maturation. The boy is old enough to go to the harvest fields, old enough to work alongside the adults, old enough to be useful. The phrase 'it fell on a day' (va-yehi ha-yom) is deliberately casual, suggesting an ordinary day, nothing remarkable. He goes out to his father, who is among the reapers. This is a normal scene of agricultural life in ancient Israel—a son joining his father's work at harvest time.

Yet the reader familiar with biblical narrative knows that this ordinariness masks a precipice. After years of waiting, after the miraculous gift, after the joy of the child's growth and vitality, a crisis approaches. The verse ends in peace and normalcy, but it is the calm before a storm. The Covenant Rendering notes this precisely: 'The casualness of the opening—a normal day, a boy going to see his father at work—makes the crisis that follows more devastating.' The boy enters the harvest field in health and vigor, and he will leave it gravely ill. The contrast between this verse's serenity and what follows (verse 19-20) is designed to shatter the reader's sense of security.

word_study.meaning: He grew, became great, increased in size and maturity. The verb suggests healthy, normal development.
word_study.significance: The text does not describe the child's infancy or childhood in detail—only that he grew. Years of maternal care, watching him develop from infant to boy, are compressed into this single past-tense verb. The growth is assumed, normal, expected.

word_study.meaning: And it came to pass, a day it was. This is a standard temporal marker in biblical narrative, indicating the passage of time and the beginning of a new episode.
word_study.significance: The formula va-yehi ha-yom is used throughout the Old Testament to introduce both momentous and mundane events. Its neutrality here makes the subsequent crisis more jarring—the text gives no warning that this particular day will be different from other days.

word_study.meaning: He went out to his father—the simple statement of a normal action, a son seeking his parent.
word_study.significance: The verb yatza ('went out') is unremarkable. The action is filial, dutiful, ordinary. Nothing here suggests what is about to happen. The boy's walk to the reapers is as innocent as any other morning's errand.

word_study.meaning: Those who reap or harvest grain. In ancient agricultural society, harvest time brought together all family members and laborers for the critical work of bringing in the crops.
word_study.significance: The harvest setting places the boy in a working context—he is old enough to be useful, to learn his father's livelihood, to participate in the family's survival. The setting is one of productivity and vitality, which will shortly contrast with illness and death.

cross_references.connection: Hannah brings her son Samuel to serve the Lord at Shiloh: 'For this child I prayed...as long as he liveth he shall be lent to the LORD.' The Shunammite's son, like Samuel, is a child of covenant promise whose life is not fully the parents' to control.

Jacob sends Joseph to the fields to check on his brothers: 'Go, I pray thee...and bring me word again.' The journey to the fields sets in motion events of captivity and separation. The Shunammite's boy likewise goes to the fields, only to encounter sudden calamity.
Elijah, exhausted, falls asleep in the wilderness, and is touched by an angel who provides sustenance. The theme of sudden crisis and divine intervention appears throughout Elisha's narrative world.
Job's eldest son's house falls upon his children during a feast, killing them all. The text's placement of disaster immediately after describing the child's normalcy recalls Job's sudden loss.
The immediately following verses describe the boy's sudden illness. Verse 18 is the bridge between peace and crisis.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite agricultural society, harvest was the critical period when survival for the coming year was determined. The entire household participated—men, women, and children who were old enough to work. A child of perhaps 8-12 years (old enough to be useful but still young enough to be vulnerable to the heat and physical demands of harvest work) would naturally accompany his father to the fields. Harvest time was urgent, exhausting work conducted in the intense heat of late spring or early summer in the Levant. The fields could be several miles from home; a child working in such conditions without modern medicine or easy access to water and rest was vulnerable to sudden illness from heat exposure, dehydration, or illness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains narratives where covenant promises are tested by crisis. Lehi's family receives the promise of reaching a promised land, yet faces recurring threats and trials. Similarly, the Shunammite receives the promised son but will face the test of losing him.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 122:7-8 teaches that trials refine faith: 'And if thou shouldst be cast into the pit, or into the hands of murderers, and the sentence of death passed upon thee...thou art still chosen.' The Shunammite's coming trial will test her faith in the covenant God made with her.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology emphasizes that covenant blessings are eternal but may require proving and testing. The Shunammite's receipt of a promised son and the trial that follows (his death and resurrection) mirror the pattern of covenant gift and covenant testing that structures the temple experience.

commentary.christological_typology: The young boy, the product of miraculous promise, going about his ordinary work and about to face sudden death, prefigures the innocent suffering of righteous individuals in scripture. More specifically, the pattern of a covenanted child in danger appears in the Gospel narrative—the child Jesus, product of virgin promise, is endangered by Herod's sword (Matthew 2:13-16). The Shunammite's son's predicament will evoke the theme of innocent suffering redeemed through divine intervention.
commentary.application: Verse 18 is deceptively peaceful. It describes what seems to be a normal day—a child growing, maturing, doing normal work. But the reader is positioned at the threshold of crisis. The text teaches us that trials often come not after seasons of hardship but in the midst of blessing. The Shunammite has received her promised son, watched him grow healthy and strong, seen the covenant fulfilled—and now, on an ordinary day, everything will be tested. This verse prepares us for the reality that covenant blessings may be tested in ways we do not anticipate. The application is not primarily about pessimism but about spiritual readiness: the trials that test our faith may come on ordinary days, when we least expect them. The Shunammite will need to remember the miracle of the boy's birth when she faces the crisis of his death. So too, we must hold fast to God's covenant promises when circumstances seem to contradict them.

text_kjv: And he said unto his father, My head, my head. And he said to a lad, Carry him to his mother.

commentary.narrative: The son of the Shunammite woman, born through Elisha's prophetic word (2 Kings 4:17), suddenly collapses while working in the harvest fields. His cry—"My head, my head!"—is immediate and distressing. The repetition of roshi ('my head') is not poetic but symptomatic: it suggests acute physical trauma, likely sunstroke or heatstroke. This is a brutal moment of irony. The miraculous child, the gift promised and delivered, falls without warning in the heat of the day. The father, present at the scene, does not attempt to care for the boy himself but sends him to his mother. This reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding that child-rearing and the care of sick children belonged primarily to the mother's sphere of responsibility and expertise. The father's action is not neglectful but conventional—yet it opens the way for the mother to become the central figure in what follows.

word_study.meaning: The repetition of the word for head signals acute distress and physical pain. In Hebrew, doubling a word often intensifies emotion or sensation. Rosh (head) in this context refers not merely to the anatomical head but to the center of sensation and consciousness. The boy is not saying his head aches; he is crying out that his whole center of being is in pain.
word_study.significance: This is clinical and realistic detail embedded in the narrative. The symptoms point to heat exhaustion or sunstroke during harvest labor. The repetition mirrors the desperate, uncontrolled cry of a suffering child. In the context of Elisha's miracle-working power, the cry also sets up the devastating contrast: the impossible gift is subject to the same fragile mortality as any child.

word_study.meaning: Sha'ah means to lift, carry, or bear. The father orders the servant to lift the boy and bring him to his mother. This action presumes the mother's role as healer and caregiver. In the ancient Near Eastern household, the mother was the one versed in remedies, care, and the management of illness.
word_study.significance: The Shunammite is positioned from the outset as the active agent in the story. While her husband is present but passive, she will be the one to move toward the prophet, to take initiative, to speak faith into being. This verse plants the first seed of her extraordinary role.

cross_references.connection: This verse introduces the promised son now dying—the word Elisha spoke has come to pass, but so has the boy's mortality. The miracle of conception is now shadowed by the reality of death.

Elijah's raising of the widow's son follows a similar pattern: a child dies, the mother grieves, and the prophet restores life through divine power. This typological parallel would have been recognized by ancient readers.
Jesus is interrupted on his way to heal a synagogue ruler's daughter, paralleling Elisha's later journey to the Shunammite's home. In both cases, faith precedes visible signs of restoration.

The father's delegation to the mother reflects the cultural understanding that parents bear responsibility for raising and caring for children, with the mother taking the primary role in the immediate nurture of the young.

commentary.historical_context: Harvest in ancient Palestine (likely barley harvest in spring or grain harvest in early summer) was intensive outdoor labor. Heatstroke was a genuine occupational hazard for workers in the fields. The mention of the specific time (the boy collapses during daytime work) and the specific symptom (head pain) anchors this miracle story in the realistic textures of peasant life. The division of medical care by gender—mothers tending children, likely using folk remedies, herbal preparations, and cooling techniques—was standard practice in the ancient household. The Shunammite's wealth (she could afford to build a room for the prophet) would have given her access to better resources and knowledge than a poorer family might have had.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The principle that faith often precedes visible deliverance appears in the Book of Mormon. The Shunammite's calm exterior (verse 22) despite internal crisis mirrors Nephi's willingness to act in faith when circumstances seem impossible (1 Nephi 3:7, 1 Nephi 4:6). Both stories teach that covenant people move forward trusting in divine power even when human understanding fails.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:5-10 describes how revelation comes 'line upon line,' often through seasons of trial. The Shunammite's promised son, now dead, represents the stripping away of visible blessings—a season in which faith must be recalibrated from trust in the promise itself to trust in the promiser (Elisha, and ultimately the God who works through him).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Shunammite's built a room for Elisha (4:10) as an act of covenant hospitality. That room becomes the setting for the climax of this story. In temple theology, the sacred space we prepare (whether literal or spiritual) becomes the arena where divine power operates most directly.

commentary.christological_typology: The boy's death and promised resurrection foreshadow Christ's own death and resurrection. Like Christ, the boy is the promised son of impossible circumstances, and his restoration will come through the prophet's identification with death (Elisha will lie upon the boy's body, verse 34). The Shunammite's faith that the prophet can address death itself prefigures the faith required to believe in resurrection through Christ.
commentary.application: This verse introduces a crisis that every parent fears and few discuss in faith community contexts: the sudden, inexplicable loss of a child. The Shunammite's story teaches that covenant life does not exempt us from suffering or mortality. The immediate application is to recognize that when crisis comes—unexpected, devastating, seemingly to contradict all God's promises—our first response should be to seek the prophet (figuratively or literally, through the living prophets and apostles of the Restoration). We do not sit passively with grief. We move.

text_kjv: And when he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees till noon, and then died.

commentary.narrative: The servant carries the boy from the field to the house. Upon arrival, the mother takes him onto her lap—a posture of comfort and closeness, the natural place a dying child would seek. The narrative specifies "until noon," marking the passage of time and emphasizing the heat and brightness of the hottest part of the day. The boy sits on his mother's knees, held close, while his life ebbs away. Then, in a single Hebrew word, va-yamot (and he died), the narrative pivot occurs. The promise dies with the child. The Shunammite has spent hours holding a living being who is becoming a corpse. The intimacy of that image—a child on his mother's lap, then death—carries unbearable weight. What makes this verse theologically significant is what it does not do: it does not explain away the death as God's will, does not spiritualize the loss, does not soften the reality with theological language. A child dies. His mother holds him. That is the text, and it is devastating.

word_study.meaning: Yashav means to sit, dwell, or settle. Birkaim (knees) refers both to the anatomical knees and, metaphorically, to the lap—the place where a child is held. The phrase describes a child held close to his mother's body, resting against her.
word_study.significance: This is maternal intimacy at its deepest. The image of a child on the mother's knees appears in contexts of comfort, nurture, and blessing (Job 3:12, Isaiah 66:12). Here the same posture frames death. The Covenant Rendering's choice to use 'lap' rather than 'knees' captures the personal warmth of the image more directly than the anatomical term.

word_study.meaning: Tsohorayim is the noon hour, the height of daylight and heat. Va-yamot is the simple past tense of dying: 'and he died.' The brevity of the verb—a single syllable in the Hebrew (mot)—mirrors the sudden finality of death.
word_study.significance: The timing (noon) connects the death to the heat that likely caused the collapse. The simplicity of va-yamot undercuts any temptation to elaborate. He died. The son of promise, held in his mother's arms, died at the brightest hour of the day. There is no softening the blow.

cross_references.connection: Job laments being born, asking why he did not die in the womb or at birth. Like the Shunammite, Job grapples with the reality that birth and life do not guarantee continued existence. Job's speeches model the anguish this mother now faces.

Phinehas's wife goes into labor at news of her husband's death and her father-in-law's death; she dies in childbirth after bearing a son. Both she and the Shunammite experience the intersection of birth and death, promise and loss.

Lamentations describes children fainting in the streets from hunger. While not identical, the image of children dying while mothers look on reflects the vulnerability and grief that this verse invokes.

Jesus raises a widow's son at Nain. The parallel is striking: a widow, a dead son, Jesus's compassion and power to restore. The Shunammite's story (like Elijah's with the widow of Zarephath) prefigures Christ's resurrection power.

Lehi teaches that mortality and death are consequences of the Fall, and that redemption comes through Christ. The Shunammite's son dies as all mortals do; redemption will come through prophetic power that points toward Christ's ultimate victory over death.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, infant and child mortality rates were extraordinarily high. Perhaps one-third or more of children died before reaching adulthood, often from infectious disease, malnutrition, or environmental causes like heat exposure. While loss was more common, it was no less devastating. A mother holding her dead child at noon would have been a sight repeated in countless households. The Shunammite's extraordinary response (composure, faith, action) stands out precisely because her suffering is so ordinary. That a wealthy, faithful woman experienced this loss underscores that covenant status and material resources do not shield the faithful from mortality.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes that mortality is a universal experience. Alma describes the power that restored the Nephites to God as inclusive of overcoming the bonds of death (Alma 5:15, Alma 22:14). The Shunammite's son now lies dead, awaiting the faith and power that will overcome what has happened. Her subsequent actions (verse 21 onward) will model the kind of active faith the Book of Mormon advocates.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 138:14-16 describes the Savior's ministry among the dead. The promise implicit in this verse is that death is not final—that even when we experience loss, the power exists to restore. Joseph Smith taught that the Resurrection encompasses all who have lived (D&C 88:14-16), giving context to the Shunammite's later assertion that Elisha's prophetic power can reverse death.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Temple theology teaches that the veil between the living and the dead is not absolute, and that those who hold priesthood keys can act on behalf of both the living and the dead. Elisha's later action (lying on the child's body) will operate in this space of intimate connection between the living prophet and the dead child.

commentary.christological_typology: The death of the promised son on the mother's lap anticipates the death of the Promised Son in the arms of his mother (John 19:26-27, though Mary stands rather than holds). Both stories center on the loss of a son of impossible origin (the Shunammite's through Elisha's word; Jesus through the Virgin Birth) and both lead to resurrection. The child held in his mother's arms becomes the child who will be restored, prefiguring the pattern of Christ's death and resurrection.
commentary.application: This verse speaks directly to parents and caregivers who have experienced the death of a child. It validates the depth of that loss without explanation or comfort. The text does not say 'the child went to a better place' or 'God needed another angel.' It says: he sat on his mother's knees, and he died. The application is to grieve fully, to sit with the reality of loss, and to understand that the Shunammite's next move—seeking the prophet—is the covenant response to devastation. We move toward those who hold prophetic power, even (or especially) when all hope seems lost.

text_kjv: And she went up, and laid him on the bed of the man of God, and shut the door upon him, and went out.

commentary.narrative: The Shunammite now acts with extraordinary purpose and faith. She carries her dead son upstairs to the prophet's room—the room she herself had built and furnished for Elisha. She places him on Elisha's bed, the very place where the prophet would have rested. This is not a random choice but a deliberate act of faith. In placing her dead son on the prophet's bed, she is making a statement: this child belongs here; this bed, saturated with the prophet's presence, is the proper place for restoration. She then shuts the door—not in despair but as if sealing a transaction, closing off the space, making it private and inviolable. Only after this does she leave. Her silence to her husband (verse 22) now becomes clearer: she has already determined that she will not process this death through normal channels (mourning, burial, extended family consultation). Instead, she will bring it to the prophet himself. The woman who built a room for Elisha now uses that room as the stage for an act of faith. Every detail demonstrates psychological and spiritual acuity: she is calm, purposeful, and acting on an intuition that the prophet's presence and power can transcend death.

word_study.term_english: laid him on the bed of the man of God
word_study.term_original: va-taskibehu al-mittat ish ha-Elohim (וַתַּשְׁכִּבֵ֙הוּ֙ עַל־מִטַּ֣ת אִ֣ישׁ הָאֱלֹהִ֔ים)
word_study.meaning: Taskib is the causative form of lying down; she causes her son to lie on the bed. Mita (bed) refers to both a sleeping place and a place of intimacy. Ish ha-Elohim (man of God) is the standard title for Elisha in this narrative, emphasizing his role as God's representative.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering captures the deliberation in 'laid him'—this is an intentional placement, not a hasty action. By choosing the prophet's bed specifically, the Shunammite is appealing to the sanctity of that space and, implicitly, to Elisha's authority and connection with the divine. She is acting on the principle that proximity to holiness, even by proxy, can affect restoration.

word_study.meaning: Sagor means to shut, close, or bar. Ba'ado means 'behind him' or 'after him.' The phrase indicates a decisive closing of the door, sealing the space.
word_study.significance: This closing is not a gesture of despair or finality. Rather, it is a sealing—the Shunammite is creating sacred space, marking off this room as dedicated to restoration. The door closing becomes a boundary between the world of death and the prophetic space where life can be restored.

word_study.meaning: To go out, depart, exit. A simple verb, but in context it signals the Shunammite's exit from her role as mourner and her entrance into her role as a woman on a mission.
word_study.significance: She leaves the room and will leave her home to seek the prophet. Her exit is not a retreat but a launch point. She will not sit with the body; she will go to the one who can undo death.

cross_references.connection: The Shunammite had built this very room for Elisha with her own initiative and resources. She now uses her creation as the vessel for faith in the prophet's power. Her previous generosity toward the prophet becomes the infrastructure for her present crisis.

Elijah carried the widow's dead son 'into a loft where he abode,' a sacred or separated space within the house. The Shunammite follows the same pattern: removing the body to a private, elevated space associated with the prophet.

When Jesus arrives at the synagogue ruler's house to heal the dead daughter, he sends out the crowds and enters the room alone with the child. The Shunammite's closing of the door mirrors this principle: the space of restoration must be set apart.

The closed temple room where Joseph Smith and Oliver Cowdery see the Savior models the concept of sealed, sacred space where divine power operates directly. The Shunammite's closed room functions similarly in this narrative.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern houses, an upper room (aliyah in Hebrew) was often the cooler, more private space, sometimes reserved for guests of honor. The Shunammite's room for Elisha would have been such a space. Placing a dead body in an upper room was not standard practice for immediate burial; bodies were usually wrapped and placed in tombs or graves relatively quickly (though sometimes delay occurred for important persons, allowing time for family to gather). The Shunammite's action—placing her son in the prophet's bed rather than in a burial context—breaks protocol and reflects her extraordinary faith that the situation is not yet final.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Benjamin teaches that when we serve God's servants, we serve God (Mosiah 2:17). The Shunammite had served Elisha; now she appeals to that relationship and to the prophetic power resident in the room she built. The Book of Mormon emphasizes faith as action—moving toward the source of healing rather than away from it (Ether 12:6).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:45-48 outlines the Lord's law for the sick and dying, emphasizing the role of priesthood holders in healing. The Shunammite does not yet know that Elisha will come; she is positioning her son and her faith in a way that makes healing possible when the prophet acts.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The room becomes a type of holy place—a space where covenant relationship (the Shunammite had made covenant hospitality with Elisha) enables divine power to work. In temple context, sacred space is where ordinances on behalf of the dead become possible. The Shunammite is acting as if she understands this principle.

commentary.christological_typology: The dead body laid on the prophet's bed anticipates the body of Christ laid in the tomb. Both are placed in a space that will become the stage for restoration. The sealing of the door mirrors the stone rolled before Jesus's tomb—but in both cases, the sealing precedes resurrection, not final entombment.
commentary.application: This verse challenges the notion that faithful prayer is passive. The Shunammite does not sit and weep; she acts decisively, making use of every resource at her disposal (the room, the bed, the prophet's presence in her home). For modern readers, this teaches that faith includes taking steps, making changes, positioning ourselves where divine power can work. We do not wait passively for deliverance; we move toward the source of healing and power. For parents who have lost children, this models dignifying loss—placing the child in a place of honor, in covenant space, then pursuing restoration through those who hold prophetic authority.

text_kjv: And she called unto her husband, and said, Send me, I pray thee, one of the young men, and one of the asses, that I may run to the man of God, and come again.

commentary.narrative: The Shunammite now speaks to her husband for the first time since the child's death. She does not tell him that their son is dead. Instead, she makes a request: send her a servant and a donkey so she can go to the prophet and return quickly. The deliberation here is extraordinary.
