The closed door and the solitary space reflect the belief that intimacy with the divine requires separation from the mundane and from public view. However, the biblical narrative emphasizes that this separation is not for the prophet to conjure power but for the prophet to humble himself before God. The space is not a locus of power but a place of vulnerability and appeal. Many ancient prophets claimed to access power through technique, ritual, or inherited authority. The biblical prophet accesses power through prayer—through asking God directly.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Enos 1:3-4 describes Enos's prayer in the wilderness: 'I cried unto him in mighty prayer and supplication for my own soul; and all the day long did I cry unto him.' The wilderness (or the closed chamber) becomes the space where the prophet or believer gains direct access to God's power through earnest, solitary supplication.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:63-64 teaches that those who seek shall find, and those who knock shall have the door opened to them. Elisha's closed door and prayer embody this principle: he knocks at the door of heaven, seeking God's direct intervention. The closed earthly door opens the way to communion with God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The closed chamber parallels the holy of holies—the most sacred space in the temple, accessible only to the High Priest, where he stands directly before God's presence. Elisha, as a prophet, accesses a similar covenant intimacy through prayer in the closed chamber. This prefigures the temple endowment, where the faithful are brought into sacred enclosures to commune with God directly.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's prayer in Gethsemane occurs in a withdrawn place (Luke 22:41), where He faces the reality of death—His own impending death. Like Elisha with the dead child, Christ approaches death through prayer, appealing to the Father. Both demonstrate that the power to overcome death flows not from might or technique but from intercession and submission to God's will. Elisha's closed door and prayer anticipate Christ's prayer before raising Lazarus: 'Father, I thank thee that thou hast heard me' (John 11:41)—acknowledging that resurrection power comes from God the Father, accessed through prayer and faith.
commentary.application: You cannot solve spiritual death—your own or another's—through effort, technique, or delegated authority alone. Like Elisha, you must step into a place of private prayer and vulnerability before God. Shut out the noise of the world, the expectations of others, the pressure to appear in control. In that closed space, appeal directly to God. The power to heal, restore, and resurrect spiritually dead conditions flows through prayer—through asking, beseeching, interceding. This is not weakness but the highest form of strength.

text_kjv: And he went up, and lay upon the child, and put his mouth upon his mouth, and his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands: and he stretched himself upon the child; and the flesh of the child waxed warm.
text_kjv_note: The TCR rendering of this verse: 'He went up and lay on the child, placing his mouth on the child's mouth, his eyes on the child's eyes, and his hands on the child's hands. He stretched himself over the child, and the child's body grew warm.'

commentary.narrative: This is perhaps the most extraordinary moment in the Elisha cycle. After prayer comes action, but it is an action unlike any other in Scripture: the prophet lies down upon the dead child and enacts a complete body-to-body correspondence. His mouth covers the child's mouth; his eyes align with the child's eyes; his hands correspond to the child's hands. The Hebrew root for 'stretched himself' (va-yighar) suggests pressing down, bending over with full weight and intention. This is not a gentle touch but an intense, intentional pressing of the living prophet's body upon the dead child's body. The result is the first sign of returning life: va-yachom besar ha-yeled, 'the flesh of the child grew warm.'
commentary.narrative_continuation: The warmth precedes full resurrection—it is the first physical sign that life is returning. But the action itself is shocking in its intimacy and physicality. Many ancient resurrection accounts involve words or gestures; Elisha's method is one of radical identification. The prophet becomes, in a sense, a conduit through which the life of the living passes to the dead. Some interpreters understand the mouth-to-mouth contact as the transfer of breath (ruach), the very essence of life. The threefold correspondence (mouth, eyes, hands) is complete and total—not a partial contact but full bodily identification. This echoes Elijah's method (1 Kings 17:21) and establishes prophetic continuity: life restoration requires the prophet's willingness to make himself one with the dead, to cross the boundary between life and death through his own body.

word_study.meaning: mouth; also the opening, entrance, or edge of something. Metaphorically, the mouth is the source of words and breath.
word_study.significance: In the context of life-giving, mouth-to-mouth contact suggests the transfer of breath (ruach), the vital essence. The mouth is not merely the organ of speech but the opening through which the breath of life flows. Elisha's mouth upon the child's mouth implies the prophet's own breath—his life force—given to the dead child.

word_study.meaning: eye; also consciousness, awareness, attention. In Hebrew thought, the eyes are the seat of perception and intention.
word_study.significance: Eyes-to-eyes contact suggests a transfer of consciousness, awareness, and intention. The prophet's living awareness is brought into direct contact with the dead child's unseeing eyes. This is spiritual and physical identification simultaneously.

word_study.meaning: palm of the hand; also strength, power, capacity. The hands represent the instrument of action and power.
word_study.significance: Hands-to-hands contact represents the transfer of power and capacity for action. The prophet's hands, which have done God's works, are laid upon the child's hands, transferring the capacity for life and action.

word_study.meaning: to stretch over, to bend down, to press down upon. A verb suggesting full weight and intention.
word_study.significance: The TCR translation captures the sense better than the KJV's 'stretched himself'—va-yighar suggests an intense pressing down, a bending over with the full body and will. This is not a resting or lying beside but a pressing down, a total commitment of physical presence.

word_study.meaning: to become warm, to grow warm. The verb suggests the gradual return of vital heat to the body.
word_study.significance: Warmth is the first physical sign of life returning. In ancient understanding, the absence of warmth (the body being 'cold') was associated with death. The return of warmth indicates the return of life's vital processes. The Covenant Rendering's 'the child's body grew warm' emphasizes the gradual restoration of vital function.

cross_references.connection: Elijah performs the identical action with the widow's son: 'And he stretched himself upon the child three times, and cried unto the Lord.' The precedent is exact, establishing that body-to-body contact is the prophetic method for resurrection.

Paul lies upon the dead Eutychus and embraces him, and the young man is revived. Even in the New Testament era, the prophetic or apostolic method maintains this intimate physical contact with the dead.

When Jesus raises Lazarus, He calls him forth by name: 'Lazarus, come forth.' Christ's method differs—His word alone is sufficient—foreshadowing that His is a higher and more direct authority over death.

Paul teaches that through baptism we are united with Christ's death and resurrection. The body-to-body identification in verse 34 prefigures the covenant unity through which we participate in Christ's resurrection power.

The Lord teaches that 'the spirit and the body are the soul of man,' and that glory is obtained through the union of spirit and body. Elisha's action demonstrates that bodily resurrection requires the intimate reintegration of spirit and body, which occurs through the prophet's bodily presence and prayer.

commentary.historical_context: The body-to-body contact was not a standard medical practice in ancient Israel. This is a prophetic action, not a therapeutic technique. However, in ancient Near Eastern magical and religious texts, there are accounts of contact-healing and restoration through physical proximity or touch. The biblical account differs crucially: Elisha's power comes not from his body or technique but from God, accessed through prayer. The physical contact is the means through which the prophet makes himself a conduit for God's resurrecting power. The act requires vulnerability, humility, and absolute faith—the prophet identifies so completely with the child's condition that he lies down as if dead himself, then becomes the vehicle of restored life.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 36:26-27 describes how Alma was 'racked with eternal torment' and cried out unto Jesus Christ, being 'harrowed up by the memory of my sins.' The recovery from spiritual death involved an inward wrench—a soul-to-soul identification. Similarly, Elisha's body-to-body contact suggests the necessity of complete personal identification with the dead one's condition. Modern Temple covenants teach that we become 'one' with God and each other through sacred ordinances—a spiritual parallel to Elisha's physical identification.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:1 teaches that 'light cleaveth unto light; therefore, your bodies cannot be glorified without your spirits.' Elisha's action illustrates this principle physically: the prophet's living spirit, working through his body, awakens the dead child's spirit back into covenant relationship with the body. The bodily resurrection requires this exact kind of union and identification.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple endowment teaches patterns of covenant union and identification—the initiate is taken through stages of intimacy with God, progressively 'clothed' in sacred covenants, ultimately standing before God in direct communion. Elisha's body-to-body contact is a type of the temple's movement toward greater and greater intimacy with the divine. The prophet becomes, temporally, a mediator of that relationship for the child.

commentary.christological_typology: This verse anticipates Christ's resurrection power most directly. Jesus does not need to lie upon the dead; His voice alone awakens them. Yet the principle of complete identification remains: Christ 'became like unto us, that we might be made like unto him' (Helaman 14:13). He took upon Himself a mortal body and submitted to death so that He might have power to raise all bodies from the dead. Elisha's laying upon the dead child foreshadows Christ's voluntary submission to death and His power to resurrect. The warmth that returns to the child's flesh echoes the resurrection—'O death, where is thy sting?' (1 Corinthians 15:55).
commentary.application: True spiritual restoration requires your whole self—not just your prayers from a distance or your good intentions, but your genuine, embodied presence. If you are called to minister to someone spiritually dead (in despair, loss of faith, alienation from God), you cannot do it by proxy or by technique alone. You must be willing to enter their pain, to identify with their condition, to 'lie down' with them in their spiritual death through genuine compassion and presence. Then, as the prophet's action was preceded by prayer, your presence combined with sincere intercession before God becomes the conduit through which resurrection power flows. You are not the source—God is—but you are the vessel.

text_kjv: Then he returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes.

commentary.narrative: The resurrection does not occur in a single moment. After the first pressing down upon the child, Elisha rises and paces. Va-yelekh ba-bayit achat hennah ve-achat hennah—'he walked in the house, one way here and one way there.' The pacing is significant. It may indicate prayer, agitation, the building of spiritual intensity, or discernment. Elisha does not declare victory or move on; he returns to the child a second time and presses down again (va-yighar einav, the same verb as in verse 34). Then, remarkably, the child sneezes—not once but seven times. Va-yezorer ha-na'ar ad sheva pe'amim, 'the child sneezed seven times.' The sneeze is a violent expulsion of breath, the body's violent reassertion of living function. It is the body saying 'I am alive again.' The number seven suggests completion, fullness—not merely a sign but a complete and utter restoration of the body's vitality. Finally: va-yifqach et einav, 'he opened his eyes.' The child's eyes open. Consciousness returns. Life is fully restored.
commentary.narrative_continuation: The process unfolds in stages: warmth (verse 34), pacing and prayer (verse 35a), second pressing down (verse 35b), sneezing (verse 35c), opening of eyes (verse 35d). This is not an instantaneous miracle but a gradual return to life, as if the child is slowly awakening from the deepest sleep. The sneeze—that most involuntary and bodily of reflexes—is the turning point. It shows that the body's own vital functions are reasserting themselves. The child is not merely moved or touched but is truly alive again, breathing, conscious, aware. The opening of the eyes is the final seal: the child sees and is restored to the world of the living.

word_study.meaning: to walk, to go, to proceed. Can suggest movement with intention or the passage of time.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests not idle movement but purposeful walking—the pacing of one engaged in prayer, discernment, or spiritual waiting. Elisha does not sit idle; he moves as if carrying the weight of intercession.

word_study.meaning: to sneeze; to make a sudden, violent expulsion of breath through the nose.
word_study.significance: The sneeze is listed among the involuntary bodily functions—it demonstrates that the child's body is now operating on its own, without the prophet's direct pressure. The return of involuntary function is the sign that life has fully returned. In some ancient cultures, the sneeze was considered a sign of blessing or divine favor (cf. the Hebrew term 'bless you' after a sneeze, which may derive from this passage).

word_study.meaning: seven times; the number seven signifies completeness, fullness, perfection in biblical numerology.
word_study.significance: The child does not sneeze once or twice but seven times—a complete and perfect restoration. Nothing partial or ambiguous remains. This echoes the biblical pattern of sevenfold completion (seven days of creation, seven years, seven churches, etc.).

word_study.meaning: to open (especially the eyes); to make seeing; to make conscious or aware.
word_study.significance: The opening of eyes is the final return to consciousness and awareness. The child is not merely alive in body but alive in awareness—seeing, knowing, present in the world.

cross_references.connection: After Elijah stretches himself upon the widow's son three times, 'the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.' The gradual process of Elijah's three-fold action parallels Elisha's two-fold pressing down.
Jesus commands Lazarus to 'Come forth' and 'Loose him, and let him go.' Unlike Elish's gradual process, Christ's word is instantly effective—demonstrating a higher authority over death.

Ezekiel prophesies over the dry bones, and 'there was a noise, and behold a shaking, and the bones came together.' The restoration of the bones is described in stages: coming together, flesh growing, skin covering, breath entering. Like Elisha's stepwise restoration, spiritual resurrection has a process.

The Lord teaches that 'all things are spiritual unto me, and not carnal,' and that spirit and body together constitute the soul. Elisha's bringing together of spirit and body in the restored child reflects this principle—full life requires both.

Christ declares, 'I am alive for evermore, and have the keys of hell and of death.' The keys of resurrection power are Christ's alone, yet He delegates that power to prophets like Elisha who act in His name through faith and prayer.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient understanding, the sneeze was sometimes interpreted as a sign of the departure of an evil spirit or the arrival of blessing. The seven-fold sneeze would have been understood as a complete and unmistakable sign that the child was fully alive and restored to normal function. The gradual nature of the restoration—not an instantaneous awakening but a progressive return of bodily functions, consciousness, and awareness—aligns with ancient Near Eastern resurrection narratives in which the return of life is sometimes described as a gradual process. However, the biblical account is remarkable in its emphasis that the process depends on the prophet's prayer, presence, and repeated pressing down, not on magical incantations or spells.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:34-35 teaches that faith is 'like a seed.' If it is good, it will begin to enlarge your soul. The seed grows, takes root, and eventually brings forth fruit. Elisha's resurrection of the child parallels this growth process: first warmth, then the body's own vital functions reasserting (the sneeze), finally consciousness returning (the opening of eyes). Spiritual resurrection similarly unfolds in stages as faith takes root and grows.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 121:45 teaches that 'let thy bowels also be full of charity towards all men, and to the household of faith.' Elisha's return to the child a second time shows his unwavering charity and refusal to accept partial success. His patient, repeated pressing down mirrors the Lord's repeated invitations and opportunities for repentance and restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple's pattern of progressive initiation mirrors this stepwise restoration: the initiate enters, is clothed in covenants, moves through stations, is tested and refined, and finally stands in the presence of the Lord. Elisha's methodical restoration—warmth, bodily function, consciousness—echoes the temple's movement from preparation toward fullness of covenant presence.

commentary.christological_typology: The seven sneezes and the opening of eyes herald the resurrection of Christ Himself. When Jesus rose from the dead, He showed the apostles His hands and His feet (Luke 24:40)—the same hands and feet that had lain in the tomb. His eyes opened to resurrection reality; His body functioned in newness of life. The child's restoration foreshadows Christ's—both require the prophet/Messiah's direct intervention, both include the restoration of bodily consciousness and awareness, both are signs to those who witness them that death has been overcome.
commentary.application: Spiritual restoration may not happen all at once. You may experience seasons of increased warmth (the feeling of God's presence returning), followed by seasons when you must wait and pace, returning repeatedly to prayer before breakthrough comes. Do not despair if the resurrection is not instantaneous. The sneezing—the involuntary, bodily reassertion of life—is the sign that your own spiritual vitality is beginning to function again without your forced effort. When the eyes open, you will see clearly. Trust the process. Return repeatedly to God in prayer. The restoration will come.

text_kjv: And he called Gehazi, and said, Call this Shunammite. So he called her. And when she was come in unto him, he said, Take up thy son.

commentary.narrative: With the child fully restored, Elisha summons Gehazi and instructs him to call the Shunammite mother. The servant who failed earlier is now given a role in the restoration—to serve as the messenger who brings the mother to her revived son. Gehazi calls her, and she comes. The moment is supremely understated in its power. Elisha says only six words: se'i venekh—'Pick up your son.' No explanation, no theological commentary, no recitation of what happened or how. Just the simple imperative: take your son. The mother who came to the prophet in verse 27 and cast herself at his feet, who declared her faith in verse 23 that 'all shall be well' even as her son lay dead—that mother now hears the most extraordinary words possible. The child she buried in her heart is alive. She is instructed to take him up, to hold him again, to claim him as her own.
commentary.narrative_continuation: The command se'i venekh completes the covenant arc that began when the Shunammite gave hospitality to the prophet. She provided the upper chamber and bed. She was promised a son (verse 16). She witnessed her son's death. She came to the prophet in faith. Now, through the prophet's direct prayer and bodily identification with the dead child, the son is restored. Her faith is vindicated. Her covenant relationship with the household of God, mediated through the prophet, has borne fruit. The brevity of Elisha's final words mirrors the simplicity of the Gospel: take up your son. Take the gift God has restored. The prophetic work is done; now the mother must receive and cherish what has been given back to her.

word_study.meaning: to take up, to lift, to bear, to carry. The imperative form is a command or strong invitation.
word_study.significance: The verb se'i carries multiple layers: physically take up your son (lift him, hold him); bear him (carry the responsibility of motherhood); receive him (accept the gift of restored life). The command is an invitation to full participation in the miracle—the mother is not merely a witness but an actor, the one who receives and bears the restored child.

cross_references.connection: The Shunammite's initial hospitality to Elisha—her willingness to provide the upper chamber and sustenance—was the foundation for the covenant of blessing. Now that covenant is fulfilled in the restoration of her son.

Elisha's word of promise—'About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son'—is now fulfilled beyond the natural death of the child. The promise is not merely for birth but for the eternal restoration of the son.

Jesus tells the widow of Nain, 'Weep not.' He touches the bier and says, 'Young man, I say unto thee, Arise. And he that was dead sat up, and began to speak.' Like Elisha, Christ restores the son to the mother.

Martha declares to Jesus, 'Lord, I believe that thou art the Christ, the Son of God.' Jesus then goes to Lazarus's tomb and raises him. Martha's faith, like the Shunammite's, precedes and makes way for the miracle.

The Lord teaches, 'And if it so be that you should labor all your days in crying repentance unto this people, and bring, save it be one soul unto me, how great shall be your joy with him in the kingdom of my Father!' Elisha's restoration of the Shunammite's son is joy in its fullest expression—a soul restored to covenant relationship.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Israelite culture, the death of an only son (or a precious son) was understood as the severance of the father's name and memory. The son was the continuation of the father's covenant and house. The Shunammite, though named in only a few verses, is presented as a woman of faith and wisdom—she recognized Elisha as 'a holy man of God' (verse 9) and acted on that recognition through hospitality. Her action of giving to the prophet brought covenant blessing. The restoration of her son was not merely an act of compassion but a validation of her faith and the reward of covenant relationship. The prophet's willingness to go to her son, to lay upon the dead child, and to press for his restoration demonstrated the prophet's identification with the covenant people's deepest longing.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 5:15 teaches, 'And now behold, I ask of you, my brethren of the church, have ye spiritually been born of God? Have ye received his image in your countenances?' The restoration of the Shunammite's son is a spiritual birth in its fullest sense—the child is born not only from the womb but born again from death through the prophet's prayer. This foreshadows the spiritual rebirth that the Book of Mormon emphasizes throughout.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76:50-60 describes the glory of those who are part of the celestial kingdom. They are 'they whose names are written in the Lamb's book of life.' The Shunammite's son, restored from death through covenant relationship with the prophet and God, is emblematic of those who inherit the promises—their names are remembered, their lives are restored, their covenant relationships are eternal.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that through covenant relationships, we are bound to God in ways that transcend death. The Shunammite's hospitality created a covenant relationship with the prophet, who in turn stood in covenant with God. Through that chain of covenant, the son was restored. The temple endowment teaches a similar progression of covenants that bind us to God and each other, culminating in eternal life and the restoration of family relationships.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's resurrection appearance to His disciples includes the command for them to 'handle me, and see' (Luke 24:39). Like Elisha telling the Shunammite to take up her son, the risen Christ invites His followers to touch and receive the reality of His restored body. Both miracles move from the prophet/Messiah's private work (prayer, the closed chamber, the tomb) to the public witnessing and joyous reception by those who love them. The Shunammite's receiving of her son parallels the disciples' joy at receiving the risen Christ—grief transformed into indescribable joy through the prophet/Messiah's power over death.
commentary.application: When God restores what was lost—whether a relationship, a sense of divine presence, a lost opportunity, a renewed faith—do not hesitate to receive it. 'Take up' means grasp it, hold it, claim it as yours. The Shunammite could have doubted, could have tested Elisha's word, could have wept and turned away. Instead, she received. Her simple act of taking up her son completed the miracle—not by her power but by her faith and willingness to participate in what God had done. In your own life, when restoration comes, step forward and receive it with gratitude and full presence. Do not let fear or doubt prevent you from embracing the gift God has returned to you.

text_kjv: Then she went in, and fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground, and took up her son, and went out.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks the climactic resolution of the Shunnamite woman's story — the return of her dead son. Her response is not one of ecstatic joy or verbal acclaim, but of profound, silent reverence. She enters Elisha's chamber, and her body expresses what her voice cannot: she falls at his feet and bows to the ground. This is the posture of a vassal before a king, of a suppliant before a savior. The sequence is theologically significant — she honors the prophet and acknowledges the source of the miracle before she even reclaims her child. Only after this act of prostration does she take up her son and depart.

The TCR rendering emphasizes the wordlessness of this moment: 'Her response — falling at his feet, bowing to the ground — is wordless gratitude.' In Hebrew narrative, silence often speaks louder than speech. She does not cry out, does not thank him with words, does not ask questions. She simply bows, takes her son, and leaves. This restraint suggests mature faith — not the faith that demands explanation, but the faith that recognizes the holy work has been done and trusts in its permanence.

Va-tetze, 'and she went out,' returns her to ordinary life. The resurrection is not the end of her story; it is the restoration of her story. She will live with her son, raise him, watch him grow — all because she persisted in faith when the prophet's first gesture seemed to fail. Her departure from Elisha's chamber is not a retreat from covenant relationship but a return to covenant living.

word_study.meaning: The verb naphal ('to fall') in the reflexive form conveys not merely physical collapse but an act of deliberate prostration, a bowing of the body as an expression of submission, gratitude, and homage. The preposition 'al ('upon/at') marks the recipient of honor.
word_study.significance: This posture appears throughout scripture when mortals encounter divine power manifested through a covenant servant. It is the language of worship rendered not to the prophet himself but through him to the God whose power he channels.

word_study.meaning: Hishtachu is the Hithpael form of shachah ('to bow, to worship'). Artzah ('to the ground') intensifies the act — not a slight bow but a full prostration with the face toward the earth. This is the most complete gesture of honor in ancient Near Eastern culture.
word_study.significance: The verb hishtachu is used throughout scripture for worship — sometimes offered to God, sometimes to kings or prophets as representatives of divine authority. The Shunnamite's gesture acknowledges that what has occurred — the restoration of her son — is divine work, not human achievement.

word_study.meaning: Nasa ('to lift, to carry, to take up') is the verb used in Genesis 22:6 when Abraham carries the wood for Isaac's sacrifice. Here, it reverses the tragedy — instead of bearing her son to death, she bears him to life.
word_study.significance: The physical act of lifting and carrying her son is the ultimate confirmation of the resurrection. She does not ask for proof, does not test whether he is truly alive. She simply takes him up and goes. Faith does not demand verification; it receives the gift.

cross_references.connection: Jesus raises the widow's son at Nain and delivers him to his mother, echoing Elisha's miracle and prefiguring Christ's mastery over death.
Elijah's resurrection of the widow's son in Zarephath — the prototype for Elisha's sign and a model of prophetic intercession for the dead.
King Lamoni's experience of being 'overcome by the Spirit' and appearing dead — followed by his resurrection to restored covenant relationship — mirrors the Shunnamite's son's restoration.
The Lord's declaration that 'the spirit and the body are the soul of man' and that resurrection reunites them — the theological foundation for understanding why Elisha's work matters.

commentary.historical_context: The posture of falling at someone's feet was a standard gesture of deference in ancient Near Eastern royal and prophetic contexts. Cuneiform records from Mesopotamia and Egyptian tomb paintings show supplicants in exactly this position before kings and gods. The Shunnamite's response would have been immediately understood by her contemporaries as an appropriate acknowledgment of her benefactor's authority and the extraordinary nature of what has occurred. In a society where childbirth and infant mortality were constant dangers, the loss and recovery of a son represented not merely personal tragedy and joy but the restoration of the woman's status, security, and hope for her future.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's son Corianton experiences a kind of spiritual death through sin and is restored to covenant standing through Alma's intercession and teaching — a metaphorical parallel to the Shunnamite's physical restoration of her son through Elisha's intercession.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 76 and the vision of the resurrection describes the reuniting of spirit and body as the work of Christ. Elisha's miracle, while temporary, foreshadows that ultimate resurrection and the joy of reunion that it brings.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The act of prostration and bowing in Elisha's presence parallels the covenant gestures performed in the temple — a physical expression of submission to divine will and recognition of the sacred work taking place.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha, like Elijah before him, demonstrates prophetic power over death and resurrection. These miracles prefigure Christ's victory over death and His power to resurrect all mankind. The Shunnamite's wordless worship of Elisha reflects the response of all creation when Christ has completed His redeeming work. Her return to ordinary life with her restored son images the future resurrection when families will be together in the presence of God.
commentary.application: The Shunnamite woman teaches us that true faith in a covenant relationship expresses itself first in honor and recognition of the source of blessing, only then in the claiming of the blessing itself. In our modern covenant life, we often rush to claim the gifts God offers without pausing to acknowledge their source. This verse invites us to let our gratitude take physical form — whether through prayer, service, or the simple act of lifting our eyes to heaven in recognition. The miracle is not incomplete until we have bowed. And our lives are not restored until we have returned to living them with renewed awareness of their sacredness.

text_kjv: And Elisha came again to Gilgal: and there was a dearth in the land; and the sons of the prophets were sitting before him: and he said unto his servant, Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets.

commentary.narrative:
The narrative abruptly shifts from private miracle (the Shunnamite's son) to communal crisis. Elisha returns to Gilgal — a prophetic center and place of covenant renewal in Israel's history — during a severe famine. The scene is one of deprivation: the land is gripped by ra'av ('dearth, hunger'), and Elisha is surrounded by 'the sons of the prophets,' the prophetic community that depends on him for spiritual and now physical leadership. The vulnerability of the moment is palpable. These are not wealthy men with storehouses; they are prophets gathering before their leader, presumably hoping for guidance or sustenance.

Elisha's response is immediate and practical: he orders his servant to bring out the great pot and prepare stew for the community. This is not a miraculous multiplication yet — it is simply a leader taking responsibility for his people during crisis. The verb shefot ('set on,' literally 'cause to deport the fire') suggests urgency and command. Elisha does not wring his hands or declare that the famine is God's judgment; he begins to cook. The action itself is an act of faith — a statement that provision is possible even when resources are scarce.

The positioning of this scene is theologically significant. Immediately after the private, intimate miracle of resurrection, we see the prophet in his public role: feeding, sustaining, and caring for the prophetic community. Elisha's ministry is not confined to individuals seeking help; it extends to the institutional life of prophecy itself. The communal gathering before him suggests they are waiting not just for food but for the prophet's presence, his stability, his faith in a time of hunger.

word_study.meaning: Hunger, famine, a severe shortage of food. The noun appears throughout the Old Testament as a natural crisis or divine judgment (Genesis 12:10, Ruth 1:1). Here, it describes the condition of the land — a widespread deprivation affecting the entire nation.
word_study.significance: The famine sets the context for the miracle to follow. It is not abstract hunger but concrete, life-threatening scarcity. The prophets are not gathered out of curiosity but out of necessity. This is when faith is tested most severely — not in abundance, but in want.

word_study.meaning: A term for the prophetic community or school of prophets. 'Sons' here means 'members of' or 'students of' — not necessarily biological sons, but a cohort bound by prophetic calling and community. Similar communities appear in 1 Samuel 19:20 and elsewhere.
word_study.significance: This language emphasizes that prophecy in Israel is not merely individual but institutional — a living community with continuity, authority, and mutual obligation. Elisha's responsibility is not only to proclaim God's word but to sustain the prophetic order itself.

word_study.meaning: A cooked dish, typically a thick stew or soup made by boiling vegetables and sometimes meat. The verb nazal ('to boil, to cook') is the root. Nazid represents a common, economical meal — food for those without means for elaborate preparation.
word_study.significance: Elisha chooses to make nazid, not a festive meal. This is sustenance food, the kind that stretches limited resources and feeds many. The choice reflects the famine's reality and Elisha's practicality — feed the people with what can be made quickly and abundantly.

cross_references.connection: Elijah is fed by ravens during famine, demonstrating divine provision for prophets in times of want — a pattern Elisha follows by caring for his prophetic community.
Abram goes to Egypt during a famine, illustrating the biblical theme of famine as a crisis testing faith and covenant commitment.
Lehi's vision of those who hunger and thirst — Elisha's care for the prophetic community reflects Christ's promise to fill those who hunger after righteousness.
The Lord's law of consecration requires that those with plenty share with those who lack, echoing Elisha's response to the famine.
'Give us this day our daily bread' — Elisha's provision of stew during famine illustrates the reality of dependence on God's care for daily sustenance.

commentary.historical_context: Gilgal held special significance in Israel's history as the site of covenant renewal and the first encampment after crossing the Jordan (Joshua 5:9-10). By the time of Elisha, it was established as a prophetic center. Ancient sources (the Tel el-Amarna letters and Mesopotamian records) document several severe famines in the Levant during the 9th century BCE. Archaeological evidence suggests that during such crises, communal cooking and shared meals became survival strategies — multiple families or a community would combine resources and prepare food communally to stretch scarce resources. Elisha's action reflects this practical wisdom within an ancient Near Eastern context while simultaneously marking it as an act of prophetic leadership.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The prophet Alma gathers with the righteous in the land of Helam and they share in communal life and sustenance together (Mosiah 18-24), echoing the prophetic community's dependence on its leader for both spiritual and practical care.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 52:40 describes the Church as a body where 'all things [are] common unto them.' Elisha's gathering of the prophetic community around a communal meal prefigures the law of consecration and the principle of stewardship that binds the covenant community together.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gathering of the prophetic community before Elisha and the sharing of food parallels temple worship and the sacred meal of covenant — the spiritual communion that binds the community to God and to one another.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha, gathering the prophetic community and preparing to feed them, prefigures Christ's role as shepherd and provider. The famine sets the stage for a sign of Christ's multiplication of loaves and fishes — both demonstrate that the prophet-king has power over scarcity and the authority to provide for the people's needs.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that prophetic leadership includes practical care for the community. Elisha does not spiritualize the hunger away or declare that famine is merely a test of faith — he acts to feed his people. For us, this means that covenant community is not merely a matter of doctrinal agreement but of mutual support in material need. The verse invites us to ask: Who in my community is hungry — spiritually or physically? What is my responsibility to those who gather with me? Do I see the prophetic community (the Church) as dependent on me, and am I willing to use what I have to sustain it?

text_kjv: And one went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full, and came and shred them into the pot of pottage: for they knew them not.

commentary.narrative:
As Elisha prepares the communal meal, one of the prophets goes out into the field — presumably beyond the city walls or encampment — to forage for herbs and greens to supplement the stew. Foraging during famine was a survival necessity; wild plants were free and could be gathered to stretch scarce resources. The man finds a wild vine (gefen sadeh, 'field vine') and from it plucks what the KJV calls 'wild gourds' — the Hebrew paqqu'ot sadeh. According to ancient sources and modern botanical knowledge, these were likely colocynth gourds (Citrullus colocynthis), a plant that grows wild throughout the Near East.

Colocynth is intensely bitter and highly toxic. The fruit contains alkaloid compounds that cause violent gastrointestinal distress and can be fatal in sufficient quantities. Yet to an unfamiliar eye, the round gourds might appear edible. The man, in his ignorance, gathers them eagerly — filling his lap with what he believes is food — and returns to the cooking pot. The phrase ki lo yada'u ('for they knew them not') is key. This is not malice, not carelessness born of negligence, but simple lack of knowledge. In a famine, when hunger is acute, one eats what one can find.

What the verse establishes is both the precariousness of the situation and the innocence of the error. The prophetic community is reduced to foraging. The source of sustenance could become a source of death through no one's intention. This is the reality of famine — it strips away normal food systems and forces people to gamble on unfamiliar plants. The miracle that follows will not address the famine itself (that remains a backdrop throughout), but will address this immediate crisis: the poisoning of the only food being prepared for the hungry community.

word_study.meaning: Gourds of the field. Paqqu'ah refers to a gourd or squash-like fruit; sadeh means 'field' or 'wild.' These are undomesticated gourds growing wild in the landscape. The specific identification as colocynth (a bitter, poisonous melon) is based on ancient Near Eastern botanical knowledge and modern identification of plants in the region.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering note emphasizes that these are not merely unfamiliar vegetables but dangerous ones — the man's lack of knowledge is not a character flaw but an understandable gap in a time of crisis when desperation overrides caution.

word_study.meaning: Palachah means 'to slice, to cut into pieces.' The man chops the gourds and drops them into the cooking pot. This is a natural action — chopping vegetables for stew — made sinister only by what the vegetables contain.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes the normalcy of the action. Nothing in the man's behavior is unusual; the danger lies entirely in the hidden nature of what he is adding. This sets up the miracle as a restoration of knowledge — making known what was hidden.

word_study.meaning: Yada ('to know') here means not merely intellectual awareness but practical, experiential knowledge — the ability to recognize and distinguish one thing from another. The negative ('not knew') emphasizes ignorance born of unfamiliarity, not of foolishness.
word_study.significance: This phrase absolves the man and the community of blame while establishing the seriousness of the situation. The danger is real, the poisoning is real, but it is not the result of anyone's sin or disobedience. This is the natural consequence of living in deprivation — a consequence that only a prophet can reverse.

cross_references.connection: The manna given in the wilderness is compared to coriander seed and tastes like wafers made with honey — miraculous food provided when natural sources fail, paralleling the need that Elisha's miracle will address.

Paul's principle that whatever is not of faith is sin — yet the man's action is clearly not sin, establishing that ignorance in crisis is not culpable while still creating a genuine danger that must be addressed.

When Lamoni's servants feast and then fall into a spiritual death-like state, the word is later 'carried about from place to place' — like poison spreading — yet restoration through the king's faith is possible.

The Lord declares that calamities shall fall upon the inhabitants of the earth because of their transgressions — yet Elisha's miracle shows that not all calamity is punishment, and the prophet can intervene to save the innocent.

commentary.historical_context: Famine in the ancient Near East forced populations to forage for wild plants. Archaeological evidence from Iron Age sites shows that during periods of scarcity, the diet shifted dramatically from staple grains and livestock to gathered plants, seeds, and roots. The practice of eating wild gourds and other unfamiliar plants during famine is documented in ancient texts. The Sumerian poem 'Eridu Genesis' describes famine conditions where people resort to eating plants normally considered inedible. The particular danger of colocynth is well-documented in ancient Egyptian and Mesopotamian medical texts, which warn of its poisonous properties. The man's action reflects the real dietary shifts that occurred during historical famines — the blurring of the line between food and poison when hunger becomes acute.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 18, Nephi's family experiences hunger at sea and must sustain themselves on what they can find — their desperation parallels the prophets' foraging during famine, though their circumstances are not their fault.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 29:15-20 describes the nature of opposition and the natural consequences of living in a fallen world — the poisoned gourds are part of that order, yet the covenant community has access to prophetic power to overcome natural hazards.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The principle of ignorance and the need for prophetic knowledge to navigate the complexities of mortality parallels the temple's function as a place where knowledge is revealed that cannot be discovered through ordinary experience alone.

commentary.christological_typology: The poisoned gourds that unknowingly enter the community's meal prefigure the hidden dangers that threaten the human soul — false doctrine, unrecognized sin, spiritual poison entering through ignorance. Only the prophet (and ultimately, Christ) can identify the danger and restore the source of life.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a profound truth about the limitations of individual knowledge and the necessity of communal accountability and prophetic guidance. The man meant no harm; he acted with good intent during a crisis. Yet his action endangered the entire community. Modern application: we live in an age of information overload and ideological diversity. It is easy to consume ideas, teachings, media, and philosophies that appear nourishing (filling our intellectual hunger) but contain hidden poison. We may act with perfect innocence. Yet the verse invites us to trust the prophet's role to identify what is safe and what is dangerous — and to test our sources of nourishment against revealed truth. The remedy, as the next verse shows, is not shame or judgment but wisdom and the word of the prophet.

text_kjv: So they poured out for the men to eat. And it came to pass, as they were eating of the pottage, that they cried out, and said, O thou man of God, there is death in the pot. And they could not eat thereof.

commentary.narrative:
The stew is served to the gathered community. As they begin to eat, they immediately recognize something is wrong. The bitter taste of the colocynth is unmistakable — a sharp, acrid flavor that triggers an instinctive rejection. Their response is visceral: they cry out in alarm and call upon Elisha with the formal address 'O man of God.' The phrase mavet ba-sir ('death in the pot') is both literal and archetypal. This is not merely bad-tasting food; it is poison. It is food that kills. The crisis is immediate and acute — the very meal intended to sustain the prophetic community has become a vessel of death.

The narrative captures the terrifying moment of recognition. Hunger has brought them to the point of eating unfamiliar plants. Elisha has responded with immediate, practical leadership, preparing a communal meal. The gathering has been assembled. And then — in the moment of eating — death is discovered. The TCR rendering emphasizes the vivid urgency: 'as they tasted the stew, they cried out, "There is death in the pot, man of God!" They could not eat it.' The inability to eat is both physical (the taste is unbearable) and spiritual (eating would be to accept death). This is a moment when the community's survival depends entirely on the prophet's ability to act.

The positioning of this cry is significant. The prophets do not turn to each other; they turn to Elisha. They do not attempt to solve the problem themselves; they call out to the man of God. In doing so, they demonstrate the very faith that the miracle requires. They do not know how he will fix it. They have no rational expectation that poison can be reversed. Yet they cry out to him with full confidence that he is capable of addressing the crisis. This is the faith that precedes the miracle.

word_study.meaning: Mavet ('death') is absolute. It does not mean 'illness' or 'sickness' but death itself — the ultimate consequence of consuming the poisoned stew. The pot, which should be a vessel of nourishment, has become a vessel of death. The simple, direct phrasing conveys the starkness of the recognition.
word_study.significance: This is the language of crisis and judgment. The word 'death' appears in the context of covenant warnings (eat and live, or eat and die — Deuteronomy 30:15-20). Here, the prophets face the reality that what they are about to consume will kill them. The recognition is clear and irrevocable.

word_study.meaning: A formal title for a prophet — literally, 'a man of God,' one who stands in God's presence and represents divine authority on earth. The title appears throughout the Elijah-Elisha narratives and elevates the prophet above ordinary human status.
word_study.significance: The use of this formal title in the moment of crisis indicates that the prophetic community recognizes Elisha not as a friend or colleague but as a representative of God's power. Their appeal is fundamentally an appeal to God's authority working through the prophet. This is not a social gesture; it is a theological stance.

word_study.meaning: Yachal ('to be able, to have strength') in the negative. The community lacks the ability — or the willingness, given the danger — to consume the stew. They cannot eat because it would be to accept death.
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes not mere disgust but actual incapacity in the face of known poison. No amount of hunger can overcome the body's recognition of threat. The miracle that follows must therefore be one that removes the actual poison, not merely one that changes the taste or persuades them to eat despite the danger.

cross_references.connection: The waters of Jericho are healed when Elisha casts salt into them — a parallel in which what is ordinarily poisoned or unfit for use becomes purified through the prophet's word and symbolic action.

Moses presents the choice: 'I have set before you life and death, blessing and curse... choose life.' The poisoned pot literalizes this covenant language — death is real, and only the prophet's intervention can restore the option of life.
A warning about wine that 'biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder' — describing how good things can hide poison. The colocynth gourds similarly disguise danger in the appearance of food.
Jesus warns against false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but inwardly are ravening wolves — the poisoned pot is a type for the hidden danger of false doctrine disguised as nourishment.
Alma warns that 'the word of God is more powerful than the word of a devil' — Elisha's word will prove more powerful than the poison.

commentary.historical_context: The immediate recognition of the poison's taste reflects the real biology of colocynth, which is so bitter that a small amount renders any food unpalatable. The bitter principle (a compound called colocynthin) produces an immediate and intense gastrointestinal response. Ancient Near Eastern texts and modern ethnobotany confirm that colocynth poisoning causes violent vomiting and diarrhea within minutes of consumption. The fact that the community recognizes the danger before fatal consumption occurs indicates that the very bitterness of the poison is, paradoxically, a protection — it triggers rejection before lethal doses can be taken. The historical record confirms that such accidental poisonings from wild plants occurred during ancient famines, and that the recognition and rejection of poisoned food was a matter of immediate survival awareness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 32:28 describes receiving the word as like a seed planted in the heart — the stew is the opposite, a poisoned substance passing through the lips. The contrast illustrates the principle that what enters our spiritual diet shapes our spiritual health.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:34 teaches that 'wo be unto him that crieth all day long, except it be for a broken heart and a contrite spirit.' The prophets cry out, not in rebellion, but in recognition of their mortal helplessness — the posture in which God can work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The recognition of death and the cry for salvation prefigure the covenant seeker's acknowledgment of mortality and absolute dependence on the Savior for redemption. The pot becomes a type for the human condition before the atonement — under a sentence of death, needing intervention.

commentary.christological_typology: The poisoned pot is a type for the fall of man — all of humanity has partaken of what appears to be nourishment but carries death within it (Romans 5:12, 'sin entered the world, and death by sin'). The cry to the man of God prefigures the cry of all humanity to Christ, the true Man of God, for deliverance from death. The poison that cannot be overcome by human effort or reasoning becomes the occasion for prophetic — and ultimately divine — intervention.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the necessity of recognizing danger swiftly and seeking help immediately. The prophetic community does not debate whether the taste is really problematic. They do not attempt to neutralize the poison themselves. They cry out to the man of God. For us, this means: cultivate spiritual sensitivity to distinguish between nourishment and poison (sound doctrine and false doctrine, healthy relationships and toxic ones, true promptings and deceptive ones). When you recognize danger, do not hesitate or debate — cry out to God and His authorized servants. The shame of vulnerability is incomparably smaller than the price of trying to handle a deadly crisis alone. Moreover, the verse teaches that recognition of danger is not a sign of weakness or failure of community — it is the necessary first step toward healing.

text_kjv: But he said, Then bring meal. And he cast it into the pot; and he said, Pour out for the people, that they may eat. And there was no harm in the pot.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha's response to the crisis is immediate and characteristic: he does not explain the poison away; he removes it. He commands that qemach ('flour' or 'meal') be brought to him. This is not a natural antidote. Flour has no chemical properties that would neutralize colocynth poison. What Elisha is performing is a prophetic sign — an action that embodies and enacts the divine word of restoration. As the TCR rendering notes, 'The flour (qemach) is not a natural antidote to the poison — it is a prophetic sign, like the salt thrown into Jericho's spring (2:21).'

Elisha casts the flour into the pot. The act is simple, direct, and accompanied by no incantation or prayer recorded in the text. He then instructs his servant to serve the community: 'Pour out for the people, that they may eat.' The command is absolute and assumes complete success — not 'try serving them and see if it works,' but 'serve them.' The response comes immediately: 'And there was no harm in the pot.' The Hebrew ve-lo hayah davar ra ba-sir ('there was no evil thing in the pot') indicates total purification. The poison is gone. The stew is safe. The community can eat.

What occurs here is a prophetic miracle based on the word of God working through a covenant servant. The flour itself is powerless; the miracle lies in the prophet's authority and God's response to his word. This is consistent with other signs in the Elisha cycle: the multiplication of loaves (verse 42-44), the raising of the dead (verses 32-37), the healing of the waters (2:21). In each case, Elisha performs a simple physical action (throwing salt, throwing meal, calling on God over the child) that becomes the vehicle for divine power. The miracle is not the action; the action is the medium through which the miracle flows.

word_study.meaning: Ground grain, typically barley flour in the ancient Near East. Qemach was a staple food, used in daily bread-making and in offerings at the sanctuary. It was one of the most basic and valuable commodities, especially during famine.
word_study.significance: The choice of flour is itself symbolic. In a time of famine, flour is precious and scarce. Elisha uses precious resources to cleanse the community's food supply. The gesture demonstrates that the prophet's priority is the community's survival, even at the cost of wasting scarce grain. Moreover, flour as a purifying element echoes the use of flour in the ritual ordeal (Numbers 5:15-31) and in sanctuary offerings — it is a substance connected to holiness and restoration.

word_study.meaning: Shalach ('to throw, to cast') in the simple past. The verb is used in Genesis 37:20 for throwing Joseph into the pit, and in Jonah 1:15 for throwing Jonah overboard. Here, it is the act of a prophet commanding fate itself — casting flour into poison and transforming it.
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes the decisive, almost authoritative nature of the action. This is not a tentative gesture or a hopeful experiment. Elisha throws the flour into the pot as one who knows the outcome. The action is decisive because the prophet's word is backed by divine authority.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'there was no evil thing.' Davar ra ('evil thing,' 'harmful thing') is a comprehensive term for anything that would cause injury, death, or dysfunction. The negation (lo hayah) affirms the complete absence of harm.
word_study.significance: The phrase indicates total restoration. Not 'some harm remained' or 'it was less poisonous' but a complete elimination of the dangerous element. The stew is no longer merely edible; it is safe. This affirms the totality of the prophet's power to restore what has been corrupted.

cross_references.connection: Elisha heals the water of Jericho by throwing salt into it, declaring 'Thus saith the Lord, I have healed these waters.' The flour cast into the poisoned pot parallels this — a simple substance becomes the vehicle for prophetic purification.
Immediately following this passage, Elisha multiplies twenty loaves of barley bread for a hundred men — the flour used here to purify poison prefigures grain used to multiply nourishment.
The 'meal offering of jealousy' uses flour as an instrument of divine judgment and truth-revelation. Here, flour becomes an instrument of restoration and mercy.
Jesus teaches that the kingdom of heaven is like leaven hid in meal — a small agent hidden in grain that transforms the whole. Elisha's flour transforms the entire pot of stew.
The Lord declares that those who have shall give to the poor and needy — Elisha's use of precious flour during famine to restore communal food reflects the law of consecration.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern ritual practice, various substances were used symbolically in purification ceremonies. Salt and grain were particularly significant in this role — both appear in sanctuary rituals and in prophetic signs. The use of flour or grain in ritual contexts is well-documented in Egyptian and Mesopotamian sources. The fact that Elisha uses flour — a precious commodity in famine — to purify food reflects the logic of sacrifice: something valuable is offered to restore something essential. The community's ability to eat depends on the consumption of resources that cannot easily be replaced. This would have been immediately understood by the community as an act of extraordinary generosity and an affirmation of faith that God would continue to provide.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 32:26-43, Alma teaches that a word from the Lord, planted in the heart, grows and bears good fruit — and can be tested by its fruit. The poisoned pot bore bitter, deadly fruit; the flour cast by the prophet transforms it to produce nourishing fruit.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 105:5 teaches that 'all things that have been given to children of men are the heritage of children of men.' Elisha's flour belongs to the community; he uses it to restore the community's ability to eat. This prefigures the consecration of all things to the Church of the living God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The casting of flour into the poisoned pot is a type for the atonement of Christ — through His sacrifice and word, that which was corrupted by poison (sin) is made whole and clean. The flour, once lost in the pot, is gone but accomplishes complete restoration. So Christ's sacrifice accomplishes redemption at the cost of His own substance.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's action is a prophetic foreshadowing of Christ's atonement. As the flour is cast into poison to transform it completely, Christ takes upon Himself the poison of sin and death, transforming it through His resurrection into the possibility of eternal life. The word of the prophet that accompanies the flour — 'Pour out for the people, that they may eat' — anticipates Christ's words at the Last Supper: 'Take, eat; this is my body.' Both moments establish that what was deadly becomes nourishing through the prophet's word and sacrifice.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to trust that the prophet has access to solutions beyond our understanding and our ordinary resources. The prophets in the pot did not know how to neutralize the poison. They had no chemical knowledge, no rational explanation for how flour could help. Yet they trusted. For us, this means: cultivate faith in prophetic leadership even when the solution seems inadequate or unclear. The prophet does not always explain why a particular course of action will work. Sometimes we are simply called to act on faith, trusting that divine authority has access to remedies we cannot see. Moreover, the verse teaches that restoration is not only possible but complete. When the prophet acts, the harm is not merely reduced or managed — it is fully removed. This should give us hope about the power of repentance, redemption, and the healing available through the atonement of Christ.

text_kjv: And there came a man from Baalshalisha, and brought the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley, and full ears of corn in the husk thereof. And he said, Give unto the people, that they may eat.

commentary.narrative:
Immediately after the purification of the poisoned pot, a man arrives from Baal-shalishah, a town in the hills of Ephraim (located about twelve miles north of Jericho, in the territory of the northern kingdom). He brings a gift to Elisha: lechem bikkurim ('bread of the firstfruits') — specifically, twenty loaves of barley bread and fresh grain in the husk. This is remarkable timing. The community has just been saved from poison, and now provision arrives.

The gift itself is significant. Firstfruits — the earliest and choicest portion of the harvest — were sacred in Israel's covenant law. According to Leviticus 23:20 and Deuteronomy 26:1-11, firstfruits were to be brought to the priests as a confession that God owned the land and the harvest. That this man brings firstfruits to Elisha, not to a priest in the Jerusalem temple, is theologically loaded. It indicates either that the northern kingdom's religious practice had shifted (the prophets serving in place of or alongside the priesthood), or that this man recognized in Elisha an authority equivalent to the priesthood — a covenant authority that made him a fitting recipient of the firstfruits.

The amount — twenty loaves and fresh grain — is generous but limited in the context of the famine and the community Elisha feeds. This sets up the miracle that follows (2 Kings 4:43-44), where Elisha multiplies the meager gift to feed one hundred men. But even here, in verse 42, the gift itself teaches a lesson: in a time of want, when Elisha and the prophetic community face deprivation, a stranger arrives bearing not ordinary bread but the finest bread — the firstfruits. God's provision comes through the generosity of the faithful, and the prophetic community is sustained not by its own resources but by the covenant gifts of those who recognize and honor their authority.

word_study.meaning: Bikkurim literally means 'firsts' or 'first fruits' — the earliest produce from a harvest. In covenant law, bikkurim were offered to God, typically through the priestly system, as a recognition of God's sovereignty over the land. Lechem bikkurim is bread made from the finest grain, offered first.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering notes: 'The man from Ba'al Shalishah brings lechem bikkurim ('bread of the firstfruits') — grain from the first harvest, which under the Torah was to be brought to the priests (Leviticus 23:20).' The gift represents a covenant act — acknowledging God's ownership through the prophet, recognizing Elisha as one who stands in a covenantal relationship with the divine.

word_study.meaning: A town or location in the hill country of Ephraim, in the northern kingdom of Israel. The name appears only here and in 1 Samuel 9:4. Ba'al often indicates a place of significance or ownership; shalishah may refer to a third part of a region or to 'three' (shloshah). The exact location is uncertain but is generally placed north of Jericho.
word_study.significance: The man comes from a distance, traveling to bring his gift. He is not part of the regular prophetic community but a believer who recognizes Elisha's authority and responds with generosity. His willingness to travel and bring firstfruits during a famine is itself a sign of faith and covenant commitment.

word_study.term_english: full ears of corn in the husk
word_study.meaning: Karmel refers to fresh grain, newly ripened grain still in the ear — tender, succulent grain. Tziklon refers to the husk, the outer covering. The phrase 'fresh grain in his sack' emphasizes that these are new, precious portions of the harvest, still in their natural covering.
word_study.significance: The gift includes both processed food (bread made from flour) and fresh produce (grain still in the husk). This variety suggests genuine abundance — not merely a symbolic offering but substantial nourishment. The man has gathered the best of what he has.

cross_references.connection: The law of firstfruits: 'ye shall bring out of your habitations two wave loaves of two tenth deals... they shall be of fine flour baken with leaven; they are the firstfruits unto the Lord.' The man from Baal-shalishah honors this law by bringing firstfruits to the prophet.

The ceremony of bringing firstfruits to the place where God chooses to cause His name to dwell — though the location has shifted in the northern kingdom, the principle remains: firstfruits are brought to honor God's authority working through a covenant servant.
When seeking Samuel the prophet, Saul and his servant bring a small gift — it was customary to honor prophets with tangible tokens of respect and covenant relationship.
The widow of Zarephath gives her last meal to Elijah, and it is multiplied — a parallel act of faith and generosity in famine that enables the prophet's ministry.

'Will a man rob God?... Bring the whole tithe... and see if I will not throw open the floodgates of heaven and pour out so much blessing.' The man from Baal-shalishah's gift of firstfruits exemplifies the covenant principle of faithful giving that releases divine blessing.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of bringing gifts to prophets was well-established in ancient Israel. First Samuel 9:7-8 mentions a customary gift when seeking a prophet's guidance. The phenomenon of prophetic communities being supported by voluntary gifts from the faithful appears throughout the biblical period and in extra-biblical sources. The firstfruits offering was a central element of Israelite religious practice, documented in the laws of Deuteronomy and Leviticus. During the northern kingdom period (when Elisha prophesied), the Jerusalem temple and priesthood were not accessible to most Israelites. The shift of firstfruits offerings to prophets reflects a real historical development — prophets in the northern kingdom began to function in roles traditionally reserved for priests, receiving offerings that would ordinarily go to the temple. The location 'Baal-shalishah' is tentatively identified as Artas, about twelve miles north of Jericho, in the hill country of Ephraim, making the journey to Elisha a significant act of pilgrimage.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 18:6, Nephi's family is led into the wilderness and sustained by the Lord's hand — yet they also depend on the work of Nephi's hands and on the cooperation of the family. The man from Baal-shalishah cooperates with God's purposes by bringing his firstfruits to sustain the prophet.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:34 teaches the principle of giving: 'Wo be unto him that crieth all day long, except it be for a broken heart and a contrite spirit... But he that doeth the works of righteousness shall receive his reward, even peace in this world, and eternal life in the world to come.' The man's gift is an act of righteousness; the multiplication of his gift is the reward.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The bringing of firstfruits to the prophet parallels the bringing of offerings to the temple — both are covenantal acts of acknowledgment that God owns all and that we are stewards of His abundance. In the restored Church, members bring their gifts (including tithes and offerings) to sustain the prophetic office.

commentary.christological_typology: The man from Baal-shalishah bringing his firstfruits prefigures the wise men bringing gifts to Christ — both honor the one who stands in God's stead. The multiplication of the bread (which follows in verses 43-44) foreshadows Christ's multiplication of loaves and fishes and His ultimate role as the Bread of Life who sustains all people. The gift of firstfruits specifically points to Christ as the firstfruits of the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20-23) — the first and finest offering from the human family to God.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that God sustains His covenant community not through their own resources alone but through the generosity of the faithful. The man from Baal-shalishah did not have to bring his firstfruits to Elisha. He lived in a different region, faced the same famine, and could have kept his precious grain for his own family. Yet he brought it. This teaches us several things: First, recognize and honor prophetic authority, even at personal cost during times of scarcity. Second, understand that giving to the Church and to those who serve God is not a loss but a covenant act that taps into God's multiplication and blessing. Third, trust that when we give our 'firsts' — our best, our earliest abundance — God ensures that we do not lose by it. Fourth, recognize that the prophet and prophetic community depend on the generosity of the Saints. Each member bears some responsibility for sustaining the institutional work of God.

text_kjv: And his servitor said, What, should I set this before an hundred men? He said again, Give it unto the people, that they may eat: for thus saith the LORD, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof.

commentary.narrative: The servant's objection is entirely reasonable and grounded in practical arithmetic. Twenty loaves of bread cannot feed a hundred men—the math simply does not work. This moment captures a tension fundamental to miracles: they begin with the collision between human limitation and divine power. The servant is not faithless; he is realistic. He sees an impossible situation and says so aloud. Elisha does not rebuke him for doubt but instead provides something the servant lacks—the word of the Lord. The phrase 'thus saith the LORD' (ko amar YHWH in Hebrew) signals that this is not Elisha's optimism or personal confidence, but a prophetic oracle. God himself guarantees the outcome.

word_study.meaning: Servant, attendant, one who ministers or renders service. The root שׁרת (sharat) means to serve, minister, or wait upon. This is a person in active service—not a slave in bondage, but one attending to the needs of another.
word_study.significance: The servant's question is not rebellion but genuine perplexity. He is closely enough connected to Elisha to voice concern, yet he lacks the prophetic knowledge that would resolve it. This underscores a key theme: access to God's word transforms perspective.

word_study.meaning: To give, place before, or present. From the root נתן (natan). The servant asks: what shall I give this before a hundred men? The word encompasses both the physical act of placing food and the metaphorical act of offering or presenting.
word_study.significance: The servant's question uses the same verb Elisha will use in his command. The difference: Elisha commands it be done in faith; the servant questions it in doubt. Yet both recognize the action as an offering—something presented to fulfill a need.

word_study.meaning: A prophetic formula declaring divine speech. Literally: 'Thus says Yahweh.' This phrase appears throughout the prophetic books as the marker of authentic revelation—not the prophet's opinion, but God's word.
word_study.significance: This formula is used 415 times in the Hebrew Bible. It is the signature of prophecy. When Elisha uses it, he is not expressing a hope or a guess—he is announcing what God has declared. The servant's objection is answered not with argumentation but with the authority of divine speech itself.

word_study.meaning: To eat (akhol) and to have left over, remain (hoter from the root יתר, yatar, meaning to exceed, be surplus, remain). The phrase combines the action of eating with the promise of abundance—not bare sufficiency but abundance.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering clarifies the force of this promise: 'they will eat and have some left over.' This is not merely 'there will be enough.' It is 'there will be more than enough.' God's provision characteristically exceeds the need. This becomes a theological signature of divine generosity throughout scripture.

cross_references.connection: Jesus feeds five thousand with five loaves and two fish, and twelve baskets of fragments remain. The Elisha miracle is the Old Testament type; this is the New Testament fulfillment on a vastly greater scale.

In the feeding of the four thousand, seven baskets remain after all eat and are satisfied. The pattern of miraculous provision with surplus is consistent across both Old and New Testament—God gives abundantly, not scarcely.

In the wilderness manna provision, 'he that gathered much had nothing over; and he that gathered little had no lack.' Like Elisha's multiplication, manna demonstrates God's ability to provide equitably from supernatural means.

Earlier in this chapter, Elisha multiplies oil for a widow in debt, with the surplus enabling her economic recovery. The pattern of miraculous increase for those in need is Elisha's characteristic ministry.

Elijah multiplies flour and oil for the widow of Zarephath during famine, with the supplies not running out. This Elijah miracle establishes the precedent that Elisha now repeats, showing continuity in the prophetic office.

commentary.historical_context: The multiplication of food miracles reflect ancient Near Eastern understanding of divine power. Fertility, increase, and abundance were the prerogatives of the gods. A prophet who could cause provision to multiply demonstrated access to divine power that transcended ordinary natural law. The servant's objection reflects the realistic resource management of the Iron Age Levant, where famine was frequent and food security fragile. That Elisha performs this miracle in a context of famine (as established in 2 Kings 4:38) makes the surplus especially remarkable—not a time of plenty that could hide the miracle, but a time of scarcity that throws it into sharp relief. The hundred men may be prophetic disciples (the 'sons of the prophets' mentioned earlier in the chapter) who gathered for teaching and sustenance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 17:37-39 records that Ammon was invited to a feast where the king of the Lamanites manifested concern about the provision, similarly showing how a ruler's care for guests and concern about adequacy frames divine provision.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 84:85 teaches 'whatsoever ye ask the Father in my name it shall be given unto you, that is expedient for you.' The principle of divine provision—that God gives what is needful and appropriate—is fundamental to covenant relationship.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The multiplication of bread echoes temple practice: the showbread in the Holy Place represented God's covenant provision for His people. Elisha's miracle transforms the ritual symbol into actual abundance. In restoration perspective, Christ is 'the bread of life' (John 6:35), and the eucharistic understanding of breaking bread and distributing it for sustenance connects the Old Testament multiplication to the sacrament in the New Testament and in latter-day covenant practice.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's multiplication of bread prefigures Jesus' feeding miracles and his identity as 'the bread of life.' The prophetic oracle 'thus saith the LORD' announces the certainty of provision in the same way Jesus' acts of feeding declare God's care for His people. Elisha as the conduit of miraculous provision—standing between human insufficiency and divine abundance—typifies Christ as the mediator through whom God's provision flows to humanity. The surplus left over in both Elisha's and Jesus' miracles emphasizes that God's abundance is never just enough; it is always more than required, reflecting the character of divine generosity.
