commentary.application: Modern covenant members face moments like this servant's objection constantly: situations where what we have seems inadequate for what is required. The verse teaches that the answer to 'what shall I give?' is not calculation but obedience. When Elisha says 'Give it to the people,' he is not denying the servant's realistic assessment; he is calling him to act on faith in God's word. The phrase 'thus saith the LORD' is the game-changer. In modern application, when members encounter seeming insufficiency—inadequate time for family prayers, insufficient resources for service, limited personal strength for the work—the principle is the same: obedience to God's command, spoken through His authorized servants, transforms apparent lack into sufficiency. The surplus promised by God is not a happy accident; it is part of the promise. When we are obedient to divine direction in giving, serving, and sacrificing, God's provision exceeds what we calculated we needed. The practical takeaway: hear the word of the Lord through His servants, obey it fully, and trust that the result will exceed the insufficiency we feared.

text_kjv: So he set it before them, and they did eat, and left thereof, according to the word of the LORD.

commentary.narrative: The verse moves from promise to fulfillment with a stark simplicity: it happens exactly as spoken. Elisha sets the bread before them. They eat. And there is left over. The formula 'according to the word of the LORD' (kidvar YHWH in Hebrew) is crucial: this is not a lucky accident or a happy surprise. This is the vindication of prophecy. What God said through His prophet came to pass. The servant's practical doubt has been answered not by argument but by fact. One hundred men ate from twenty loaves, and there were leftovers. The miracle is complete and witnessed by all who received it. This verse demonstrates a cardinal truth of the prophetic office: when a prophet speaks 'thus saith the LORD,' the word does not return void (Isaiah 55:11). It accomplishes what God sent it to do.

word_study.meaning: He gave/placed before them. The verb יתן (natan, to give) in the simple past tense (Qal wayyiqtol). The preposition לִפְנֵי (lifnei) means before, in the presence of, or in front of. The action is both physical (placing food) and relational (presenting it to meet their need).
word_study.significance: This is the same verb the servant used when he objected ('what shall I set before them?'). Elisha's obedience transforms the servant's question into action. The miracle begins not with sudden multiplication but with the simple act of giving what they have, trusting God's word.

word_study.meaning: They ate. The verb אכל (akal, to eat) in the plural third-person past tense. The simple statement masks the miracle: a hundred men ate from a supply that should have been exhausted after feeding far fewer.
word_study.significance: The plain language of fulfillment is part of the power of the verse. Scripture often describes miracles in straightforward terms, as if they were the most natural thing in the world. This understates nothing; it emphasizes that when God acts, the impossible becomes ordinary.

word_study.meaning: And they had left over, remained, had surplus. From the root יתר (yatar, to exceed, be more than, have left over, remain). The verb is in the simple past tense, plural form.
word_study.significance: This verb is the fulfillment of verse 43's promise of hoter (having something left over). The word emphasizes not merely adequacy but abundance. They did not eat until it was gone and barely satisfied. They ate and had surplus. This surplus is not accidental; it is the confirmation that God's word has been fulfilled exactly as spoken.

word_study.term_english: according to the word of the LORD
word_study.meaning: According to the word, statement, or decree of Yahweh. The preposition כ (ki) means 'according to,' 'like,' or 'as.' דבר (davar) means word, matter, thing, or decree. This phrase signals that what has occurred is the precise fulfillment of divine speech.
word_study.significance: This formula appears throughout the historical books of the Old Testament to mark the vindication of prophetic words. It is the theological statement that God's word has power. What was declared came to pass. This is the ultimate validation of the prophet's authority: not that he is clever or that luck favored him, but that he speaks on behalf of God, and God's word is reliable.

cross_references.connection: Isaiah teaches that God's word will not return void but will accomplish what He purposes. Elisha's fulfilled word is a practical demonstration of this principle of divine speech.

The entire passage from verses 42-44 forms one complete narrative: the gift brought, the servant's objection, Elisha's faith-command, and the miraculous fulfillment. This verse is the conclusion of a three-fold structure (gift, promise, fulfillment).

Samuel says to Saul: 'The Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent.' The reliability of God's word is central to covenant faith; Elisha's miracle demonstrates God's integrity.

King Hezekiah's provision of food for priests and Levites is described in language similar to Elisha's miracle: abundance that exceeds expectation, blessed by the Lord. Divine blessing on provision is a recurring theme across the historical books.

In Jesus' feeding of the five thousand, 'he distributed to the disciples, and the disciples to them that were set down; and likewise of the fishes as much as they would. When they were filled, he said unto his disciples, Gather up the fragments that remain, that nothing be lost. Therefore they gathered them together, and filled twelve baskets.' The parallel structure (distribution, eating, gathering surplus) mirrors Elisha's miracle.

commentary.historical_context: The formula 'according to the word of the LORD' is how ancient Near Eastern historians and scribes recorded the validation of a prophet's authority. In the broader ancient Near East, prophets and diviners were common figures, but their credibility rested on whether what they predicted came to pass. The Hebrew Bible uses this precise language to distinguish the God of Israel from other deities: His word has efficacy. What He speaks comes to be. In the context of 2 Kings, written during or after the Babylonian exile, this assertion of God's reliable word would have been especially meaningful to a people who had experienced the prophetic warnings of judgment come true. The surplus left over reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding that divine blessing manifests as abundance—more produce, more herds, more provision than naturally expected. The hundred men may have been gathered from the broader prophetic community or from a town in famine, making this a public miracle with multiple witnesses—strengthening its authority.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 9:22 states that the signs and wonders shown among the people would testify of Christ's coming, and that by the power of the Holy Ghost are all things done. Elisha's miracle, as a sign and wonder, points toward this principle: prophetic power demonstrates the reality of divine presence and covenant relationship.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 68:4 teaches concerning the words spoken by authorized servants: 'What I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken, and I excuse not myself.' The fulfillment of Elisha's word reflects this principle of divine accountability—God stands behind the words of His prophets. D&C 1:14 similarly asserts the binding nature of the Lord's word: 'Search these commandments, for they are true and faithful, and the predictions which are contained in them shall all be fulfilled.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In restoration theology, the authority to act in the name of the Lord and have one's words fulfilled is a function of priesthood covenant and standing in the temple. Elisha acts as a covenant officer of the Lord, and his word is validated by God's own power. In latter-day understanding, those who hold priesthood authority and keep their covenants similarly act as instruments through which God's word is fulfilled. The consumption of bread and the surplus remaining connect typologically to the sacrament, where members covenant to take upon themselves the name of Christ and have His Spirit always with them—a covenant of provision and abundance.

commentary.christological_typology: Verse 44 confirms the fulfillment of Elisha's prophetic word in the same way that Jesus' resurrection fulfilled His own words ('the third day he rose again'). Just as Elisha's word proved reliable through the evidence of satisfied hunger and surplus provision, Jesus' word proved reliable through the resurrection and through His ongoing provision to the Church. The figure of the prophet whose word is validated before the people points toward Christ as the ultimate Prophet whose every word will be fulfilled. The surplus left over—evidence that God's provision exceeds what the law of nature would allow—foreshadows Christ's superabundant grace, which Paul describes as 'exceeding abundantly above all that we ask or think' (Ephesians 3:20).
commentary.application: When members read 'according to the word of the LORD,' they should pause and reflect on what it means to stand on God's word in their own lives. The miracle occurred because (1) the word was spoken by a servant of God, (2) the people obeyed the command given, and (3) God fulfilled what was promised. In modern covenant life, this sequence repeats: we hear God's word through authorized servants (the prophet, apostles, and leaders), we obey the command given (even when it seems insufficient), and God fulfills His promise. The practical application is to trust in God's word spoken through His servants more than in our own calculations of what is possible. When Church leaders counsel members to sacrifice, to serve, to give, to live certain principles—these are not suggestions to be weighed against personal preference or circumstance. They are words spoken in God's name, and God Himself stands behind them to validate and fulfill them. The surplus promised—a fulfilling life, answered prayers, increased spirituality, family strength—comes not through our arithmetic but through our obedience to God's word. The takeaway: hear God's word, obey fully without the servant's hesitation, and watch as He provides not just sufficiency but abundance.

text_kjv: Now Naaman, captain of the host of the king of Syria, was a great man with his master, and honourable, because by him the LORD had given deliverance unto Syria: he was also a mighty man in valour, but he was a leper.

commentary.narrative: The opening of this chapter presents one of scripture's most profound paradoxes: a man of extraordinary power and status is utterly powerless against his own condition. Naaman is not introduced as a villain or a foreigner to be despised; he is described with seven superlatives that establish him as the most honored military leader in Aram's court. The phrase 'a great man with his master' and 'honourable' (nesu fanim, 'lifted of face') indicates not merely official rank but genuine personal favor. More remarkably, the text tells us that the LORD—Israel's God—gave victory to Israel's enemy *through* Naaman's leadership. This shatters any tribal or nationalistic theology: the God of Israel operates outside ethnic or religious boundaries to accomplish His purposes. He uses whoever He chooses, however He chooses, to bring about His will. The dramatic irony, however, cuts deepest in the final clause: despite all his greatness, Naaman 'was a leper'—afflicted with a skin disease that would have rendered him ritually unclean and socially isolated even within the protective sphere of the king's court.
commentary.narrative_2: The Hebrew word metzora (from tzara'at) refers to a range of skin conditions that rendered a person ritually impure according to Levitical law, not the modern diagnosis of Hansen's disease. The ancient Near Eastern mindset would have perceived such a condition as especially tragic in Naaman's case: he is a man of action, valor, and achievement, yet he is progressively separated from normal social and religious participation. His wealth, status, and military genius cannot heal him. This verse establishes the central theological tension of the narrative: human power and resources are insufficient for certain kinds of affliction. The name Naaman itself—meaning 'pleasant' or 'gracious'—carries ironic weight: the man whose name speaks of pleasantness bears a condition that makes him ritually and socially unpleasant in the eyes of his community. By the end of verse 1, the reader understands that we are about to witness not a military victory but a very different kind of triumph.

word_study.meaning: a man of stature, greatness, importance; someone of high social rank and influence
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes not merely official position but genuine personal greatness. In biblical usage, gadol often connotes spiritual as well as material significance. That Naaman is 'great' yet afflicted sets up the narrative's central tension.

word_study.meaning: literally 'lifted of face'; an idiom for high social standing, favor, and respect from superiors
word_study.significance: This phrase suggests not just rank but the personal favor and regard of the king himself. It indicates that Naaman has earned honor through accomplishment and character, not merely inherited status. The Covenant Rendering preserves this nuance better than 'honourable.'

word_study.meaning: salvation, deliverance, victory, rescue; fundamentally refers to God's saving action
word_study.significance: The use of teshu'ah is theologically significant: it is the term for God's redemptive action. That God gave 'teshu'ah' (a work of divine salvation) *through* Naaman to the pagan kingdom of Aram illustrates that the LORD's sovereignty transcends national and religious boundaries. God accomplishes His purposes through vessels of His own choosing, regardless of their faith commitments.

word_study.term_english: mighty man in valour / mighty warrior
word_study.meaning: a warrior of strength and valor; a man of military prowess, courage, and martial excellence
word_study.significance: The phrase emphasizes martial skill and demonstrated courage. Yet even this warrior—mighty in every physical and martial sense—cannot overcome his condition through strength or will. The word gibbor appears throughout scripture to describe mighty men and warriors, but here its conventional meaning proves inadequate.

word_study.meaning: one afflicted with tzara'at; a condition of ritual impurity covering various skin disorders, not modern leprosy (Hansen's disease)
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'skin disease' avoids the medical anachronism of 'leprosy.' In the Levitical system (Leviticus 13-14), tzara'at rendered a person ritually unclean and required separation from the community. The condition could be contagious and was deeply stigmatizing. That Naaman, despite his greatness, must address this condition is the driving force of the entire narrative.

word_study.meaning: derived from the root n-'-m, meaning 'pleasant, lovely, gracious'
word_study.significance: The irony of the name is fundamental to the narrative's theological message: the man whose name means 'pleasant' is afflicted with a condition that would be repellent and isolating. This suggests a latent grace or redemptive possibility in Naaman despite his present condition—a divine irony hinting at his eventual restoration.

cross_references.connection: Establishes the Levitical protocols for identifying and managing tzara'at (skin disease), which determines how Naaman's condition would have been understood as rendering him ritually impure and requiring isolation from community worship.
Later in this same period, the king of Aram will besiege Israel and Samaria, showing the political context of Aramean-Israelite conflict within which Naaman's healing occurs.

Reflects the principle that God's glory is manifested through His deeds rather than through human or national might, paralleling how the LORD gives victory through Naaman despite Aram's antagonism to Israel.
Paul echoes this principle—that God is God of both Jews and Gentiles—establishing a New Testament parallel to the theological claim that the LORD's sovereignty operates without ethnic restriction.
Later references to Naaman in the narrative of Hazael provide continuity to Aramean political history and show the lasting impact of Naaman's encounter with the prophet.

commentary.historical_context: In the 9th century BCE, Aram (modern Syria) was a significant regional power frequently in conflict with Israel. Aramean military campaigns into Israelite territory were documented, including the taking of prisoners and spoils. The mention of raiding parties (v. 2) reflects standard ancient Near Eastern military practice: smaller strike forces conducted raids to capture prisoners, livestock, and valuables. Naaman's titles and gifts in verse 5 reflect actual Aramean court practices. The talent of silver and pieces of gold mentioned represent genuine weights of precious metals used in ancient commerce. The 'ten changes of raiment' (ten sets of clothing) were luxury items indicating high status; in the ancient world, fine clothing was a form of wealth and a diplomatic gift. The king-to-king correspondence in verse 6 reflects actual diplomatic protocols of the period—major requests would move through official channels. Naaman's assumption that healing would be a royal prerogative (v. 6) reveals the ancient Near Eastern understanding that kings possessed access to divine power or special privileges not available to common people. The prophet, by contrast, operated outside the royal apparatus, deriving authority directly from the God of Israel.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Nephite encounter with Jesus Christ in 3 Nephi 11:1-18 parallels the pattern where a foreign or unexpected approach to divine power must be redirected and refined. As Jesus appears to the Nephites outside Jewish expectation and institutional structures, so Elisha's healing operates outside Aramean royal channels. The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes that God's power is not bound by human institutions or expectations (Alma 37:7-8).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:41 ('the earth abideth the law of a celestial kingdom') and D&C 1:38 ('what I the Lord have spoken, I have spoken, and I excuse not myself') establish that God's power operates according to divine law, not human arrangement—a principle reflected in Elisha's later insistence on the specific protocol for Naaman's healing (2 Kings 5:10).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Levitical protocols governing tzara'at (Leviticus 13-14) are temple-related laws of ritual purity. Naaman's healing will require not merely physical cure but restoration to a state of ritual cleanliness—a symbolic death and resurrection through immersion in the Jordan River that foreshadows later temple and covenant understanding of sanctification.

commentary.christological_typology: Naaman is a proto-type of the gentile who, despite having no covenant claim on Israel's God, receives grace and healing through Israel's prophet. Just as Naaman must abandon his assumptions about power and status to receive healing, so humanity must abandon reliance on earthly greatness and come to Christ in humility and faith. His eventual healing through washing in the Jordan prefigures baptismal regeneration and the principle that healing and salvation come through ordinances and divine power, not through human status or wealth.
commentary.application: This verse establishes a foundational principle for modern covenant living: status, accomplishment, and worldly greatness cannot resolve our deepest afflictions. Naaman represents anyone who brings their full resume of achievements and resources to the foot of spiritual healing, only to discover that none of those things matter. The verse invites honest self-assessment: what in my life am I trying to solve through my own strength or resources that actually requires divine intervention? Like Naaman, we may be greatly honored in the world while spiritually compromised. The verse also establishes that God's power works through unexpected channels and in behalf of unexpected people—a reminder that divine grace is not earned by nationality, status, or institutional membership, but flows according to God's own sovereign will.

text_kjv: And the Syrians had gone out by companies, and had brought away captive out of the land of Israel a little maid; and she waited on Naaman's wife.

commentary.narrative: This verse introduces one of scripture's most remarkable figures: an unnamed slave girl, young, powerless, and displaced from her homeland. She enters the narrative as the collateral damage of warfare—one of countless captives taken in the Aramean raids against Israel. The text gives her no name, no tribal affiliation, no family history. She is identified solely by her age ('little maid'), her nationality ('from the land of Israel'), and her status ('she waited on'—served—Naaman's wife). By all appearance, she is the least significant person in this story: a child slave in a foreign household, with no legal rights, no voice in her community, and no apparent influence. Yet she becomes the pivot point on which the entire narrative turns. Her one asset is her knowledge of Israel's prophet and her faith that he can heal Naaman's condition.
commentary.narrative_2: The passage's mention of raiding parties 'by companies' reflects the actual military practice of the period: smaller strike forces conducted rapid raids into enemy territory to capture prisoners and spoils. Such raids were intended both to gain wealth and to weaken the enemy through displacement. This slave girl represents thousands of Israelite captives who would have been taken during the Aramean-Israelite conflicts of the 9th century BCE. The vulnerability of her position cannot be overstated: separated from her family, language, and religious community, enslaved in a foreign household, with no prospect of rescue. Yet within this desperate circumstance, she demonstrates extraordinary faith and, more remarkably, genuine compassion for her master's affliction. She does not express bitterness that her master is suffering; rather, she expresses concern for his welfare and knowledge of how he might be healed. This is the beginning of a reversal: the powerless will become the instrument of salvation; the slave will teach the master the way to healing.

word_study.meaning: bands, companies, raiding parties; small military units organized for strikes or raids
word_study.significance: The term indicates organized military action—not random violence but deliberate raids conducted as part of the Aramean strategy against Israel. The use of 'companies' rather than a single army suggests the coordinated nature of Aramean military operations.

word_study.meaning: they took captive, they brought away, they led away as prisoners
word_study.significance: The verb emphasizes forced removal and enslavement. This was standard practice in ancient Near Eastern warfare: conquered populations or captives were taken as slaves to serve in the victor's household and labor force.

word_study.meaning: a young girl, a maiden, a female child or adolescent; qetannah emphasizes smallness, youth, and vulnerability
word_study.significance: The double emphasis (young + small) underscores her defenselessness and powerlessness. In the ancient world, such a young captive would have been particularly vulnerable. Yet this is precisely the vessel through which God works. The diminutive status is theologically significant: God often accomplishes His purposes through the least likely, least powerful, and least esteemed.

word_study.meaning: literally 'before'; idiomatically 'in the presence of, in the service of, attending to'
word_study.significance: The phrase indicates her role as a domestic servant in Naaman's household, specifically serving his wife. This proximity will prove crucial: she will have direct access to her mistress and thus be able to convey her knowledge of the prophet.

cross_references.connection: As a mixed multitude went out of Egypt with the Israelites, so captive Israelites were taken into foreign lands during wartime, creating diaspora communities that carried knowledge of Israel's God to foreign territories.
References captive women and maidens as the spoils of war in ancient Near Eastern conflict, establishing the historical and cultural context of slave-taking in the region.
The grief of losing a child combined with loss of the ark shows how captivity and displacement represented multiple layers of loss for Israelite families.

Though set in a different context, Peter's instruction about wives winning unbelieving husbands through their conduct parallels the slave girl's approach: faithful witness to someone of different faith without accusation or confrontation.

Alma's experience of remorse and the divine intervention that follows establishes a Book of Mormon parallel to how the slave girl, despite her captivity, maintains faith and becomes an instrument of divine healing.

commentary.historical_context: The mention of Aramean raiding parties reflects documented military campaigns of the 9th century BCE. Aramean kingdoms (particularly Damascus under Ben-Hadad and later Hazael) conducted systematic military operations against the northern kingdom of Israel to gain territory, wealth, and captives. Ancient Near Eastern warfare consistently included the taking of prisoners, who were enslaved and incorporated into the victor's labor force. Slavery in this period was not the racial slavery of later eras but typically involved people of the same geographic region, taken in war or through debt. Captives were often domestic servants in royal or elite households, as this slave girl was. Women and children captives in particular were vulnerable to exploitation. The mention of her service to Naaman's wife indicates her placement in the household hierarchy—she was valuable enough to be assigned to the wife of a high-ranking official, suggesting she was young, healthy, and possibly trained in domestic service. That she retained knowledge of Israel's prophet despite her captivity speaks to the effectiveness of religious memory transmission even under conditions of displacement.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The theme of diaspora faith appears throughout the Book of Mormon: Lehi and his family were removed from Jerusalem but carried the scriptures and covenantal understanding with them (1 Nephi 1-2). Later, captured Lamanites sometimes became instruments of conversion and healing (Alma 24). The principle is consistent: geographical displacement and captivity do not separate God's covenant people from their knowledge of His ways or their faith in His prophets.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 1:30 affirms that the Lord's kingdom includes all people called by His name. The slave girl, though captive and enslaved, remains within the scope of God's knowledge and purpose. D&C 121:34-36 establishes that God's power flows through unexpected channels and that human oppression cannot prevent divine work.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The theme of captivity and redemption is central to temple theology. As Israel was captive in Egypt and redeemed, and as later Israelites were taken captive to Babylon, so the slave girl represents the captive who retains covenant consciousness and becomes a channel for healing. The principle of redemption through divine intervention (not human power) runs throughout temple symbolism.

commentary.christological_typology: The slave girl's position—powerless, displaced, enslaved, yet possessing knowledge that can bring salvation—foreshadows the role of Israel itself in God's redemptive plan: a nation taken captive by sin, yet bearing witness to the Savior and possessing the knowledge of His way. She becomes a type of the faithful remnant through whom God works to accomplish His purposes in the world.
commentary.application: This verse challenges modern assumptions about power, status, and influence. The slave girl has none of the resources Naaman possesses: no wealth, no authority, no freedom. Yet she becomes the agent through which divine healing enters Naaman's life. For modern covenant members, this raises profound questions: What knowledge do I possess that might heal others? Am I willing to speak, even from a position of powerlessness or perceived insignificance? The verse also addresses those who experience circumstances they did not choose—captivity, displacement, loss of freedom or opportunity. Despite your circumstances, what knowledge of Christ, of healing, of the gospel do you retain? How might your witness, expressed simply and faithfully, become an instrument of healing in someone else's life? The slave girl's compassion for her captor—her willingness to seek his healing despite his role in her captivity—establishes a standard of Christian charity that transcends self-interest and circumstance.

text_kjv: And she said unto her mistress, Would God my lord were with the prophet that is in Samaria! for he would recover him of his leprosy.

commentary.narrative: The slave girl now speaks. This is her only appearance in the text, and her brief utterance sets in motion a chain of events that will involve two kings, international diplomacy, and the ultimate demonstration of divine power outside the structures of human authority. Her statement to her mistress—Naaman's wife—is remarkable for several reasons. First, it expresses genuine compassion for her master's condition despite her own captivity and enslavement. She does not harbor resentment or wish harm upon Naaman; rather, she expresses concern for his welfare. Second, it reveals her knowledge of Israel's prophetic tradition: she knows of a prophet in Samaria (the capital of the northern kingdom of Israel) and has faith that this prophet possesses the power to heal tzara'at. Third, and most significantly, her words are based not on hearsay or vague hope but on confident faith: 'he would recover him'—not 'he might,' but an assertion of the prophet's power. Her statement uses the Hebrew conditional 'achalei' ('would that,' 'if only'), expressing a wish that her master could access this healing.
commentary.narrative_2: The significance of her identifying the prophet as being 'in Samaria' cannot be missed. Samaria was the capital of Israel, the northern kingdom—the enemy territory from which she herself was taken captive. Yet she speaks of Samaria and its prophet with complete confidence, as though divine power resides there. This is the voice of faith speaking across national boundaries and military enmities. She knows—or has been taught, or has herself experienced—that God's power in Israel extends beyond tribal identity or national allegiance. Her confidence in the prophet's ability to heal is absolute. She does not say the prophet might help or could attempt to heal; she states definitively that 'he would recover him,' using a verb (ye'esof, 'would gather away') that indicates complete removal of the condition. This is not tentative faith but certain knowledge. The verse exemplifies the principle that God's power is not bound by national borders, military conflict, or the social status of those who witness to it. An enslaved child's word becomes the catalyst for salvation.

word_study.meaning: an exclamation expressing desire or wish; 'would that,' 'if only,' expressing longing for something not presently possible
word_study.significance: The term indicates a conditional desire: she wishes it were possible for her master to access the prophet. It is not merely a hopeful suggestion but an expression of genuine longing for his healing, suggesting her concern for his welfare transcends her enslaved status.

word_study.meaning: a spokesman for God; one who speaks on behalf of the divine; in Hebrew prophecy, the prophet serves as God's representative and conduit for divine word and power
word_study.significance: The slave girl's identification of a prophet in Samaria indicates her knowledge of Israelite religious institutions and her belief in prophetic power as a vehicle for divine action. This suggests she retained religious memory and understanding despite her captivity.

word_study.meaning: to gather, to collect, to remove; in this context, to gather away, to remove the disease, to cure completely
word_study.significance: The verb suggests complete removal or restoration, not merely temporary relief. The girl does not hope for management of the disease but for its complete removal. This reflects an understanding that prophetic power operates at the level of complete restoration and healing.

word_study.meaning: mistress, lady of the house; the wife of an important man or head of household
word_study.significance: She addresses her remarks to the person most likely to have influence over Naaman: his wife. This demonstrates practical wisdom in her approach—she uses her access and the relational dynamics of the household to communicate her message.

word_study.meaning: the capital city of the northern kingdom of Israel; the city sits on a strategic hill in central Palestine and was built by Omri, king of Israel
word_study.significance: By naming Samaria specifically, the girl demonstrates knowledge of Israel's geography and institutions. Samaria was Israel's capital and the center of its religious and political life—a fact that an enslaved Israelite captive would know.

cross_references.connection: When Elisha hears of the king of Israel's distress about healing Naaman, he responds, 'Let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel'—echoing the slave girl's identification of the prophet and validating her faith.
Jesus emphasizes that faith spoken boldly—especially by the least and most vulnerable—witnesses to God's power: 'What I tell you in darkness, speak in light.'

Paul writes that God chooses 'the foolish things of the world to confound the wise' and 'the weak things to confound the mighty,' a principle exemplified in the slave girl's faith becoming the catalyst for divine healing.

The young Nephite soldiers demonstrate faith without fear, speaking truth in their circumstances; similarly, the slave girl speaks her knowledge of divine power despite her captivity and powerlessness.

The woman with the issue of blood demonstrates faith that if she can but touch the hem of Jesus' garment, she will be healed—a parallel to the slave girl's confident assertion that the prophet can heal Naaman.

commentary.historical_context: The reference to 'the prophet that is in Samaria' almost certainly refers to Elisha, who was active during this period and was known to operate in the northern kingdom. Prophets in ancient Israel were recognized as conduits for divine power and were consulted for healing, guidance, and prophecy. The reputation of prophetic figures would have spread even to foreign territories, and it is plausible that an Israelite captive would have retained knowledge of a famous prophet's location and reputation. Samaria was indeed the capital of the northern kingdom, built by King Omri on a defensible hilltop. The city was the political, military, and religious center of Israel. That the slave girl could name the city and confidently place a prophet there indicates she retained knowledge of her homeland's geography and institutions despite her captivity. In the ancient world, prophetic healing was recognized across cultures: both Egyptians and Mesopotamians had figures who claimed healing power through divine agency. However, the particularity of the Israelite prophet—operating directly from the God of Israel rather than through priestly institutions or divination—was distinctive. The slave girl's confidence in the prophet's ability reflects the Israelite understanding of prophetic power as a direct channel to divine healing.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 8:19-24, Alma is sent specifically to the city of Ammonihah to preach. When the people of that city reject him, he leaves with sorrow—but later, an angel tells him that his word will be the means of salvation to that very city. Similarly, the slave girl's word, spoken in obscurity and captivity, becomes the word that sets in motion Naaman's path to healing. The principle is consistent: God uses the faithful witness of those in difficult circumstances to accomplish His purposes.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 11:21 ('Seek not to declare my word, but first seek to obtain my word, and then shall your tongue be loosed') establishes the principle that those who retain knowledge of God and His prophets will be enabled to speak that knowledge at the proper time. The slave girl has obtained knowledge of the prophet and now speaks it.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The theme of covenant witness persisting despite exile and captivity appears throughout temple theology. In the endowment narrative, covenants made in the temple persist even when the individual is removed from the temple setting. The slave girl represents the covenant consciousness that persists despite physical displacement: she carries knowledge of God's prophet even in captivity.

commentary.christological_typology: The slave girl's faith in the prophet's power foreshadows faith in Christ. Her statement—'he would recover him'—asserts healing power beyond the capacity of human resources or social status. This prefigures the faith required to approach Christ: a confidence that His power extends to complete restoration and healing, available to those who approach Him regardless of their social status or perceived worthiness.
commentary.application: This verse raises searching questions about our witness: What knowledge do we possess about divine power and healing? Are we willing to speak it, even from positions of apparent powerlessness or insignificance? The slave girl's brief statement demonstrates that faithful witness does not require eloquence, authority, or status—it requires only genuine knowledge and genuine conviction. For modern covenant members, her example challenges us to examine our own faith in prophetic power and in the capacity of the Lord's chosen instruments to bring healing. Do we speak confidently of divine healing and prophetic power, or do we hesitate, allowing social status or cultural skepticism to silence us? Additionally, her compassion for her master despite her captivity sets a standard for Christian charity: the ability to wish healing and good for those who have harmed us, maintaining faith in divine power while transcending our own grievances. Her faith also establishes a pattern for diaspora believers: regardless of where we are displaced or captive, knowledge of God's prophets and power persists and empowers our witness.

text_kjv: And one went in, and told his lord, saying, Thus and thus said the maid that is of the land of Israel.

commentary.narrative: The slave girl's words now ascend the ladder of power. Someone in the household—most likely a servant or attendant—carries her message to Naaman himself. The text does not name this intermediary, but his role is crucial: he becomes the transmission mechanism by which the powerless girl's voice reaches the powerful commander. The phrase 'thus and thus said the maid' (kazot ve-khazot) is a summary formula indicating the substance of her message was reported, though not necessarily with every word preserved. What matters is that Naaman receives the core claim: there is a prophet in Samaria who can heal his condition. Remarkably, Naaman does not dismiss this report with mockery or anger. Instead, verse 4 shows him acting on what an unnamed slave girl has said. This is astonishing: a commander of armies, honored by kings, accepts guidance from a captive child. The text does not explain his acceptance or willingness to pursue this course—it simply presents it as fact. This silence is theologically significant: it suggests that God works on human hearts in ways not always visible to us, preparing receptiveness before the word arrives.
commentary.narrative_2: The movement of the message from slave girl to Naaman marks a fundamental reversal of the power structure. In the ancient world, the word of a slave was worthless in any official context; slaves had no standing, no credibility, and no authority. Yet Naaman, at the apex of power, listens and acts. This is not because of her status but despite her lack of status. Her knowledge—her faith that a prophet in Israel can heal—proves more valuable than all the wealth and status Naaman possesses. The text now begins to show the progressive involvement of more and more significant figures: the message moves from the slave girl to an unnamed servant to Naaman himself, and from verse 4 onward it will move to the king of Aram, then to the king of Israel, and finally to the prophet Elisha. Each figure in this chain must make a decision: will they trust what they have heard? Naaman's decision to pursue healing based on a slave girl's word sets the pattern for what follows. He does not wait for official channels or royal permission; he brings the matter to his lord, the king.

word_study.meaning: and he went, and he came; a simple narrative movement indicating the passage from one sphere to another
word_study.significance: The anonymity of the messenger emphasizes that the message, not the messenger, carries significance. Anyone could have carried this word, but the substance remains: the slave girl has identified a source of healing.

word_study.meaning: and he told, and he reported, and he made known to his master
word_study.significance: The verb nagid (to tell, to make known) is used for both trivial reports and significant announcements. Here it carries weight: the anonymous servant brings significant news to Naaman.

word_study.term_english: Thus and thus / such and such
word_study.meaning: thus and so, such and such; a summarizing phrase indicating the substance was conveyed though not necessarily verbatim
word_study.significance: The phrase acknowledges that while the exact words may have shifted through transmission, the essential content remained consistent: the slave girl spoke of a prophet who could heal.

word_study.meaning: the young girl, the maiden; the same term used in verse 2, now with the definite article indicating she is a known figure in the household
word_study.significance: By verse 4, the slave girl is recognized as a specific, identifiable person within the household. She is no longer anonymous; Naaman knows of her. The fact that a slave girl's words carry enough weight to be reported to Naaman suggests she has already established credibility or at least has established a reputation for knowledge.

word_study.meaning: from the land of Israel; a phrase identifying her origin and, by implication, her connection to knowledge of Israel's religious institutions
word_study.significance: Her Israelite origin is specifically noted as the source of her credibility. She knows about Israel's prophet because she is from Israel. This explains how she came to possess knowledge that would be crucial to Naaman's healing.

cross_references.connection: 'By long forbearing is a prince persuaded, and a soft tongue breaketh the bone,' paralleling how the slave girl's simple, soft testimony persuades Naaman, a prince of his nation.
Elisabeth, though older and in a different circumstance, responds to Mary's word with immediate faith and recognition: similarly, Naaman responds to the slave girl's word without requiring proof.

After the Samaritan woman at the well speaks of Jesus, 'many of the Samaritans believed on him for the saying of the woman.' The pattern is parallel: a person of low status brings a word that moves others to seek healing or salvation.

Young Samuel hears the word of the Lord, and though he is a child, his word is taken seriously by Eli and eventually by all Israel. The slave girl, though a child and a slave, carries a word that moves a commander of armies.

The Lord promises that the president of the Church 'shall receive all the words of warning which have been given by the prophets'; similarly, Naaman receives the words of a prophetess (the slave girl's prophetic knowledge) and acts upon them.

commentary.historical_context: The transmission of message through household servants and intermediaries reflects the actual structure of ancient Near Eastern elite households. Naaman, as commander of the king's forces, would have maintained a substantial household with numerous servants and officials. Information within such a household would typically flow through recognized channels: servants reporting to higher officials, who report to the master. The fact that a report originating with a slave girl could reach Naaman suggests either that the girl had established credibility within the household or that the matter was remarkable enough that it moved through normal channels despite her low status. Ancient Near Eastern history documents numerous cases where individuals of low status provided crucial information that influenced decisions of powerful figures. The willingness of a powerful person to act on information provided by a slave reflects either desperation (Naaman's disease) or a cultural context where certain kinds of knowledge (religious knowledge, healing knowledge) transcended normal status hierarchies.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 5:41-51, Nephi and Lehi's testimony, delivered in the context of their imprisonment and powerlessness, is received by the jailer, Coriantumr, leading to his conversion and eventual influence on thousands. The principle is parallel: the testimony of those in captive or powerless circumstances carries power when received with faith.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:4 ('the light which is in all things') suggests that truth and knowledge transmitted through any source—even the least esteemed—carries the light of Christ. The slave girl's word, though she is powerless, carries the light of prophetic knowledge.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In covenant understanding, no message from God is disqualified by the status of the messenger. The temple theme of ascending from one level of knowledge and power to another is reflected in this verse: the message ascends from the slave girl through the servant to Naaman to the king, each level adding authority and power to the initial testimony.

commentary.christological_typology: The flow of testimony from the humble servant through intermediaries to those in authority foreshadows the pattern by which Christ's gospel moves through the world: beginning with simple testimony from the least esteemed (fishermen, women, the poor) and eventually reaching kings and principalities. The principle is that divine truth does not require elite status to carry it; indeed, it often flows most powerfully through the humble.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that our testimony, however humble our station, can carry weight with those of far greater power and status. It also teaches us to listen for truth wherever it originates. Naaman, despite his rank and accomplishment, does not dismiss a slave girl's word out of pride or status consciousness. For modern covenant members: First, if you are in circumstances of powerlessness or captivity (whether literal or metaphorical), know that your witness still carries weight and can move those in positions of greater power. Speak what you know of divine healing and prophetic power without waiting for permission or status to validate your voice. Second, if you occupy positions of power or authority, maintain Naaman's humility: be willing to hear truth from unexpected sources and unexpected people. The slave girl represents the voice that institutional structures often silence—and sometimes it is precisely that voice that carries the word of salvation. Third, recognize that our testimony ascends through the household of faith just as the slave girl's word ascended through Naaman's household. What we speak in humility may move others to seek healing and salvation.

text_kjv: And the king of Syria said, Go to, go, and I will send a letter unto the king of Israel. And he departed, and took with him ten talents of silver, and six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of raiment.

commentary.narrative: The king of Aram responds to Naaman's report with decisive action. He grants Naaman permission to journey to Israel in search of healing and provides him with both a letter of introduction to the king of Israel and extraordinary gifts: ten talents of silver, six thousand pieces of gold, and ten changes of fine clothing. These gifts represent wealth on a scale that illustrates both Naaman's importance to the Aramean king and the king's desperation to restore his valued commander's health. The dispatch of such wealth alongside the formal letter indicates that the Aramean king understands the healing as requiring a royal transaction: he is offering payment to the king of Israel in exchange for healing services. This reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of how divine power operates. The Aramean king assumes healing is a commodity that one king can purchase from another, analogous to trading for military services, territory, or other royal prerogatives. He does not conceive of healing as flowing directly from God through a prophet; instead, he envisions it as a royal service that the king of Israel can provide.
commentary.narrative_2: The gifts are described with precision for theological reasons. Ten talents of silver represented approximately 300-340 kilograms of silver—a staggering sum in the ancient world, representing years of a laborer's wages. Six thousand pieces of gold represents an equally enormous sum. Ten changes of raiment (sets of fine clothing) were luxury items that served as indicators of wealth and status. These gifts demonstrate that Naaman is not approaching healing as a suppplicant but as a distinguished dignitary bearing appropriate diplomatic gifts. The Aramean king's instruction to 'go' is direct and authoritative, befitting his status. The decision-making moves now from the slave girl to Naaman to the king of Aram. At each level, the decision is to pursue healing through the prophet. Yet the framing has changed: what began as a slave girl's expression of faith in the prophet's power has now become an official state mission involving international diplomacy and the transfer of massive wealth. The irony is that this escalation of power and resources obscures the simplicity that will eventually be demanded: washing in the Jordan River.

word_study.term_english: king of Syria / king of Aram
word_study.meaning: the king of Aram (Syria); the ruler of the Aramean kingdom
word_study.significance: The formal identification by title and kingdom emphasizes the official nature of the action. This is not a private favor but a state matter involving two kingdoms.

word_study.meaning: and I will send a letter, and I will dispatch a written communication
word_study.significance: The formal letter serves as an official diplomatic communication between sovereigns, establishing the gravity and official nature of the request that will be made of the king of Israel.

word_study.meaning: ten talents of silver; a talent (kikkar) was a unit of weight representing about 34-39 kilograms
word_study.significance: This quantity of silver represents enormous wealth—approximately 340-390 kilograms. In perspective, a laborer's annual wage was typically measured in fractions of a talent. This demonstrates the value the Aramean king places on Naaman's restoration and suggests his understanding that healing requires proportional payment.

word_study.meaning: six thousand pieces/pieces of gold; the exact value of each piece is uncertain, but collectively this represents another enormous sum
word_study.significance: Gold, more precious than silver, is offered as additional payment. The combination of silver and gold emphasizes the wealth involved and reinforces the understanding that healing is being treated as a commodity to be purchased.

word_study.meaning: ten sets of clothing, ten changes of garment; fine clothing served as both practical goods and indicators of wealth and status
word_study.significance: Clothing in the ancient world, especially fine clothing, was a valuable commodity and a marker of elite status. That ten complete sets are provided indicates luxury items intended for diplomatic gift-giving.

word_study.meaning: and he took in his hand; the phrase indicates personal possession and presumably responsibility for safeguarding
word_study.significance: Naaman carries these gifts personally, indicating their importance and his role as their guardian. They are not sent separately but accompany him on his journey.

cross_references.connection: The centurion approaches Jesus with profound humility ('I am not worthy'), asking for healing for his servant. Though a Roman officer of rank, he recognizes that healing comes from Jesus' word, not from wealth or status. Naaman, by contrast, initially approaches with gifts and status expectations.
Jesus warns, 'A man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.' Naaman's enormous wealth cannot secure his healing; healing requires a different understanding of value.
Paul writes that 'the love of money is the root of all evil.' Naaman's initial approach treats healing as a commodity to be purchased, reflecting reliance on wealth rather than faith.

The Lord teaches principles of stewardship and warns against being 'unequally yoked together with unbelievers.' The Aramean king and Naaman, operating from assumptions of secular power and wealth, approach healing differently than God intends.

Peter teaches that redemption is 'not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold,' but with the precious blood of Christ. The gifts Naaman carries, though vast, cannot purchase what only faith in divine power can access.

commentary.historical_context: The mention of the king of Aram's authorization of this mission reflects actual diplomatic protocols of the ancient Near East. Kings maintained correspondence with one another, and official missions to foreign courts required royal sanction and resources. The wealth provided—ten talents of silver and six thousand pieces of gold—reflects the enormous resources available to ancient Near Eastern monarchies. Archaeological evidence indicates that ancient kingdoms engaged in regular diplomatic exchanges, including the sending of envoys with gifts. The assumption that healing or other services could be purchased reflects a transaction-based understanding of power: kings exchanged gifts, territories, military services, and various forms of expertise as part of diplomatic commerce. The Aramean king's assumption that healing could be acquired through the right diplomatic channel and gift would have seemed logical within his cultural framework. However, it reflects a fundamentally pagan understanding of power: power is exercised through wealth, status, and institutional authority. The Israelite understanding, by contrast, is that power flows from God through prophetic channels, independent of wealth or institutional status.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 22:1-18, the king of the Lamanites seeks to know God but initially approaches through institutional channels and status assumptions. Only when he humbles himself and seeks directly (verse 18: 'O God, I will give away all my sins to know thee') does he find the path to salvation. Naaman similarly must learn that status, wealth, and institutional authority cannot purchase what faith alone can access.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 35:1-3 establishes that God's work is not advanced through human strength or resources but through divine power. The Lord's way of healing Naaman will not be through the wealth and status Naaman brings but through obedience to the prophet's seemingly humble instruction.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple theology, all earthly status and wealth must be left outside. The endowment strips individuals of their worldly markers of status, teaching that before God, all stand equal. Naaman's journey from reliance on wealth and status to obedience in a simple act (washing in the Jordan) mirrors this progression toward spiritual equality before God.

commentary.christological_typology: Naaman represents all humanity approaching divine healing with the wrong assumptions. We bring what we have—our accomplishments, our resources, our status—expecting them to purchase salvation or healing. Christ, however, teaches that 'Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God' (John 3:3). The new birth is not purchased but received through faith and obedience. Naaman's journey will require him to surrender his assumptions about the nature of power and learn that divine power operates according to God's logic, not human economics.
commentary.application: This verse confronts the modern tendency to treat spiritual reality as though it operated under the same logic as material reality: the assumption that money, status, resources, and power can purchase or access what only faith can reach. If we are facing spiritual affliction or seeking divine healing—whether physical, emotional, or spiritual—we must examine whether we are attempting to solve it with the equivalent of Naaman's gifts: reliance on our own strength, wealth, status, or accomplishment. The verse teaches that such reliance, however impressive, cannot access what the prophet can offer. It also teaches that we must surrender our assumptions about power: we may need to do what seems inadequate or foolish (as Naaman will later be asked to do) because divine power operates according to divine logic, not human reason. For leaders and those in positions of authority: the verse warns against assuming that institutional power can deliver what only prophetic power—what only direct communication with and obedience to God—can accomplish. The Aramean king's error was in believing he could purchase healing through official channels. Modern institutions of all kinds make similar errors when they assume their authority and resources can substitute for prophetic wisdom and divine power.

text_kjv: And he brought the letter to the king of Israel, saying, Now when this letter is come unto thee, behold, I have therewith sent Naaman my servant to thee, that thou mayest recover him of his leprosy.

commentary.narrative: The formal letter from the king of Aram to the king of Israel represents the apex of official, institutional action in this narrative. The king of Aram writes not as a supplicant but as an equal sovereign addressing another sovereign, commanding that his servant Naaman be healed of his skin disease. The letter's content reveals the profound misunderstanding that frames this entire approach: the Aramean king assumes that healing is a service one king can command another king to perform. He places the responsibility for healing squarely on the king of Israel: 'thou mayest recover him' ('asafto—gather away, remove, cure his disease). The king of Aram does not ask the king of Israel to help find a healer or to recommend a prophet; he instructs him to perform the healing itself. This is not a request for assistance but a demand cast in diplomatic language. The phrase 'I have therewith sent' (shalachti eleicha) uses language of sending a servant or subordinate—treating the healing as a task to be accomplished by the king of Israel as a royal service. The entire apparatus of state—diplomatic correspondence, massive gifts, official sanction—has been deployed to accomplish what will ultimately require only humility, faith, and obedience to the prophet's simple instruction.
commentary.narrative_2: The letter arrives at the court of the king of Israel, and the impact will be seismic. Unlike Naaman and the king of Aram, who approach this as a matter of royal prerogative and resource management, the king of Israel will recognize that what is being demanded of him is impossible—not because of lack of power or wealth, but because healing from tzara'at is not a royal prerogative at all. It is a work of God, flowing through the prophet. This verse represents the climactic moment of misunderstanding before the narrative shifts toward the true source of healing. The letter demonstrates how far the message has traveled from the slave girl's simple faith: 'If only my master could go to the prophet!' Now it has become an official state demand, backed by gifts and diplomatic authority. Yet all of this power and resource and institutional machinery is pointed in the wrong direction. It seeks healing from the king when healing comes from the prophet; it assumes healing can be purchased when it can only be received through faith; it treats healing as a commodity when it is an act of divine grace. The verse's power lies partly in its dramatic irony: the more authority and resource are brought to bear, the further the approach moves from the simple source of healing.

word_study.meaning: and he brought the letter, and he delivered the written document
word_study.significance: The letter is treated as a formal, significant object. Its delivery marks the official entry of the matter into state diplomacy between two kingdoms.

word_study.term_english: Now when this letter is come unto thee
word_study.term_original: ve-atta ke-vo hassefer hazeh eleicha (וְעַתָּה כְּבוֹא הַסֵּפֶר הַזֶּה אֵלֶיךָ)
word_study.meaning: and now when this letter reaches you, and when this very letter comes to you
word_study.significance: The phrase marks a transition point: the letter's arrival signals the moment when the king of Israel must respond. The present tense ('is come') indicates the moment of reading.

word_study.meaning: behold, look, know, understand; an imperative form calling attention to something important
word_study.significance: The term demands the king's attention: 'Know that I am sending to you.' It is not a polite request but an assertion of action.

word_study.meaning: I have sent, I am sending; the completed action indicates that Naaman is already in motion toward Israel
word_study.significance: The verb indicates decisive action already taken. The king of Aram has already committed to the course; he is informing the king of Israel after the fact, not requesting permission.

word_study.meaning: my servant, my servant; a term of respect when one monarch refers to an official or valued subordinate to another monarch
word_study.significance: The Aramean king refers to Naaman as 'my servant,' establishing his identity and importance. Yet 'servant' also indicates subordination—appropriate for the king of Aram to use in referring to his own official, but it also carries resonance with the theme of servitude that runs through the narrative (the enslaved girl is also 'servant' to Naaman's wife).

word_study.meaning: and you shall gather away, you shall remove, you shall cure; the verb places responsibility for healing directly on the king of Israel
word_study.significance: The verb asaf (to gather, to remove) is the same verb used in verse 3, where the slave girl expressed faith that the prophet would 'asaf' (remove) Naaman's disease. But here it is directed at the king of Israel, not the prophet. This reveals the king of Aram's misunderstanding: he assumes the king of Israel can perform what only the prophet can do.

word_study.meaning: from his skin disease, from his condition of ritual impurity
word_study.significance: The final word of the verse returns to the central reality: Naaman's affliction. All the diplomatic machinery, wealth, and authority exist to address this one condition. Yet none of those worldly resources can touch it.

cross_references.connection: The king of Israel's response immediately follows: 'Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man doth send unto me to recover a man of his leprosy?' showing his recognition that what is demanded is impossible for any king to accomplish.

Jesus teaches His disciples about the nature of kingdom power, contrasting human authority ('the Gentiles exercise dominion over them') with divine power that operates through service. Naaman's journey will move him from reliance on political power to submission before divine power.
Samuel tells Saul that 'to obey is better than sacrifice,' establishing a principle that obedience to God's way is more valuable than all the resources and offerings human power can bring.

The Lord teaches that 'the rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven,' which cannot be exercised outside divine law. Naaman seeks healing through the powers of earthly kingship, but healing flows from the priesthood and prophetic power.

'The king's heart is in the hand of the LORD, like the rivers of water: he turneth it whitehithersoever he will.' The king of Aram directs his resources toward healing, but it is the Lord who will direct the outcome through the prophet.

commentary.historical_context: The formal letter between kings reflects actual diplomatic practice in the ancient Near East. Archaeological discoveries, including the Tel Fekheriye bilingual inscription and other diplomatic correspondence, show that ancient kings communicated through official letters, often carried by official envoys. These letters were formal documents that established the terms of diplomatic interaction. The assumption that one king could command another to perform a service (healing) reflects the understanding that powerful monarchs had influence and resources that extended beyond their borders. However, this assumption also reveals a fundamental misunderstanding of the nature of prophetic power in Israel. While kings in pagan societies were often viewed as intermediaries between divine and human realms (in Egypt, for instance, the pharaoh was understood as divine or semi-divine), Israelite kingship was more limited. Kings could not perform priestly functions or prophetic acts outside their proper sphere. Healing from diseases of ritual impurity fell squarely within prophetic and priestly domains. The letter's arrival at the king of Israel's court represents a moment of diplomatic crisis: an Aramean king is making a demand that the king of Israel cannot possibly fulfill through any earthly means. This sets up the necessity for a different kind of power—prophetic power—to resolve the situation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Helaman 10:1-10, Nephi receives the sealing power—the power to bind and loose on earth and in heaven. The king of Israel, by contrast, has no such power. He is asked to do what only a prophet can do. The contrast illuminates the distinction between political authority and spiritual authority, between the power to command armies and the power to access divine healing.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 15-16 and the specific callings given to individuals by revelation establish the principle that God calls specific individuals to specific tasks, and no amount of institutional authority can substitute for proper calling. The king of Israel cannot heal Naaman because he has not been called to that work; only the prophet has.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, understanding the limits of earthly authority is central to covenant theology. The king of Aram represents all earthly power operating without knowledge of God's law and God's way. The temple teaches that earthly power must be submitted to divine authority. Naaman's journey will move him from reliance on the king (the earthly authority figure) to reliance on the prophet (who represents God's authority).

commentary.christological_typology: The king of Israel's predicament—faced with a demand he cannot fulfill—parallels the human condition before Christ. Humanity is afflicted with a condition (sin) that no earthly power can remedy. We cannot save ourselves; our own efforts and resources, however impressive, cannot achieve salvation. Only through the Mediator—Christ, the ultimate Prophet—can healing come. The letter demands the impossible; Christ's gospel offers the impossible made possible through faith in divine power.
commentary.application: This verse teaches several truths for modern covenant living: First, recognize the limits of human authority and worldly power. When facing spiritual affliction, we cannot solve it through institutions, wealth, status, or earthly authority structures. A spiritual problem requires a spiritual solution accessed through faith and obedience to divine instruction. Second, examine whether you are attempting to approach spiritual reality through institutional channels that cannot reach it. Are you seeking healing from an authority structure that, however impressive and resource-rich, cannot deliver divine healing? Are you offering payment (of time, effort, money, reputation) as though spiritual reality operated as a commodity market? Third, if you occupy a position of authority or leadership, recognize the limits of your authority. You cannot demand that others accomplish what lies outside the scope of your stewardship. You cannot substitute institutional power for divine power. The king of Aram's error in demanding what the king of Israel cannot deliver is a warning to all leaders: know your limits, and point people toward the source that can truly heal. Finally, observe that the narrative has moved from the slave girl's simple faith through escalating layers of worldly power and authority—and the problem has not been solved. It will be solved only when all this worldly apparatus is bypassed and Naaman stands before the prophet, then before the river, in radical simplicity.

text_kjv: And it came to pass, when the king of Israel had read the letter, that he rent his clothes, and said, Am I God, to kill and to make alive, that this man doth send unto me to recover a man of his leprosy? wherefore consider, I pray you, and see how he seeketh a quarrel against me.

commentary.narrative:
The king of Israel's reaction to Naaman's request reveals both theological insight and political paranoia. He correctly recognizes that healing leprosy is a divine prerogative, not a human one—it belongs to God alone. His rhetorical question, 'Am I God, to kill and to make alive?' demonstrates genuine understanding that such miracles are beyond mortal power. However, his interpretation of the request itself is fundamentally wrong. Rather than seeing an opportunity for God to demonstrate His power through His prophet, the king interprets the request as a deliberate provocation—a pretext for war. This panic reveals the fragile political relationship between Israel and Syria (Aram), and the king's assumption that such an impossible demand must be a scheme to justify military aggression.

The tearing of clothes (a sign of deep distress) shows the king's emotional state, but it also reveals his failure to think beyond himself or to recognize God's hand in this situation. He does not consider consulting his own prophet, Elisha. Instead, he immediately assumes the worst of the Aramean king's motives. This is a critical moment: the king has the letter describing an incurable disease but lacks the faith to believe God can heal it.

word_study.meaning: literally, 'tore his garments.' In ancient Hebrew practice, this was a standard expression of grief, mourning, distress, or extreme emotional disturbance. It signaled to others that something catastrophic had occurred.
word_study.significance: The king's instinctive reaction shows the depth of his alarm. This is not a calculated political response but an emotional one—the physical act of tearing clothes broadcasts his panic to his court. The gesture signals that he sees the request as a crisis.

word_study.term_english: Am I God, to kill and to make alive
word_study.meaning: This rhetorical question asserts that only God has the power over life and death. The pairing of 'kill' and 'make alive' encompasses the full spectrum of divine power—God alone controls the boundary between death and life.
word_study.significance: The king's theological statement is accurate; he correctly identifies healing as a divine monopoly. Yet his accuracy in theology does not lead to faith. Instead of seeking God's prophet, he remains trapped in political calculation. This shows the danger of correct doctrine without corresponding action.

word_study.meaning: literally, 'he is seeking an excuse' or 'he is being stubborn/obstinate.' The root suggests looking for a pretext or justification. The sense is deliberate provocation.
word_study.significance: The king interprets the impossible request as a deliberate trap—a way for the Aramean king to manufacture justification for war. This reveals political anxiety and a failure to see beyond military frameworks. The king cannot imagine that this is simply a cry for help.

cross_references.connection: The affirmation that God alone has power to 'kill and make alive' echoes Hannah's song, establishing this as a foundational truth about God's exclusive dominion.
God Himself declares, 'I kill, and I make alive,' reinforcing that this power belongs to God alone—a truth the king correctly states but fails to act upon.
The young girl's confidence in Elisha's power to heal stands in sharp contrast to the king's despair, showing the difference between faith and fear.
The principle that Christ took upon Him the infirmities and sicknesses of His people illustrates how healing power ultimately emanates from God through His appointed servants.

commentary.historical_context: The Aramean-Israelite relationship during this period (9th century BCE) was volatile, marked by sporadic warfare and uneasy truces. The king of Israel's immediate assumption that this request is a military pretext reflects genuine historical tension. In the ancient Near East, diplomatic letters were formal documents, and an impossible demand could indeed be interpreted as a deliberately offensive escalation. The king's panic is not irrational given the geopolitical context—it shows how easily international misunderstandings could trigger conflict. The mention of leprosy (צָרַעַת, tzara'at) likely refers to various skin conditions, some contagious and some not, that rendered a person ritually and socially unclean according to Levitical law.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The king's failure to recognize God's power working through a prophet parallels the hardness of heart seen in the Book of Mormon when people refuse to believe the signs and wonders wrought by God's servants (see Alma 10:24-25). The opportunity to witness God's power is lost through pride and fear.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The principle in D&C 8:8 ('And now, verily, verily, I say unto thee, put your trust in that Spirit which leadeth to do right') applies here. The king fails to trust the Spirit and instead relies on political calculation, missing the chance to see God's hand.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of ritual cleansing appears here (the king's understanding that leprosy renders someone unclean), which connects to temple purification practices. Healing in this narrative is ultimately about restoration to covenant community, not merely medical recovery.

commentary.christological_typology: The king's acknowledgment that only God can 'kill and make alive' foreshadows Christ's ultimate claim to this power. In John 5:26, Jesus asserts that the Father 'hath given to the Son to have life in himself,' and in John 11, Jesus demonstrates His power over death through raising Lazarus. The king recognizes divine prerogative but lacks faith to see it manifested.
commentary.application: This verse challenges us to examine the gap between correct doctrine and genuine faith. We may affirm that God has power over sickness, death, and impossibilities, yet when faced with a personal crisis, we often respond with the king's panic rather than seeking God's means of deliverance. The lesson is to move beyond acknowledging God's power in the abstract and actually seeking His prophets and servants when faced with seemingly impossible situations. Our first instinct should be to consult God's representatives, not to assume the worst of circumstances.

text_kjv: And it was so, when Elisha the man of God had heard that the king of Israel had rent his clothes, that he sent to the king, saying, Wherefore hast thou rent thy clothes? let him come now to me, and he shall know that there is a prophet in Israel.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha's intervention marks the pivot point of the narrative. The prophet hears news of the king's distress and immediately responds—not to comfort the king, but to redirect both the king and Naaman toward the true source of healing. His opening question, 'Wherefore hast thou rent thy clothes?' is gently corrective; it suggests there is no need for such despair if faith is properly placed. More importantly, Elisha's message reframes the entire situation: this is not a political crisis but a revelatory opportunity. The specific purpose of the healing, as Elisha states it, is not merely to cure a disease but to establish a truth—'that there is a prophet in Israel.'

This statement is profoundly theological. The existence and activity of a prophet is evidence of God's presence and engagement with His covenant people. When Elisha says, 'there is a prophet in Israel,' he is declaring that God has not abandoned Israel, that communication between heaven and earth remains open, and that divine power is available through His appointed servant. The healing will not be merely medical; it will be a sign and witness. Naaman's cure will testify to the reality of Israel's God and His prophet.

word_study.meaning: A phrase used throughout 1 and 2 Kings to designate a prophet—one who is defined by his relationship to God and his authority from God. It emphasizes that the prophet's identity and power derive from God, not from political office or human authority.
word_study.significance: When Elisha is identified as 'the man of God,' it signals his unique standing and legitimacy. He operates from a source of authority higher than any earthly king.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew word for prophet literally means 'one who is called' or 'one who speaks forth.' A navi is God's spokesperson—one who receives divine communication and delivers God's word. The Covenant Rendering's translator notes emphasize that the prophet's role is to represent God's presence and word to the people.
word_study.significance: Elisha's self-identification as a navi establishes him as God's voice in Israel. The phrase 'there is a prophet in Israel' (yesh navi be-Yisrael) is not merely a statement of fact but a declaration of God's active engagement with His covenant people. The healing will prove this reality.

word_study.meaning: The Hebrew root yadah means 'to know' in the deep sense of experiential knowledge, not mere intellectual awareness. This is the kind of knowledge that comes through direct encounter and experience.
