word_study.significance: Naaman will not merely learn a fact; he will come to know—to experientially understand—that there is a prophet in Israel. The healing will be transformative knowledge, not abstract information.

cross_references.connection: After Elijah raises the widow's son, she declares, 'Now by this I know that thou art a man of God, and that the word of the LORD in thy mouth is truth.' Healing serves as proof of prophetic authenticity and God's word.
God gives Moses signs and wonders to perform so that 'they may believe that the LORD God of their fathers hath appeared unto thee.' Signs authenticate God's messenger and God's message.
The Book of Mormon teaches that we must experiment upon the word of the prophet and observe the results—like Naaman coming to know through experience that the prophet speaks truth.
Christ designates the president of the Church as 'a seer, a revelator, and a prophet,' establishing the pattern of God's ongoing communication through prophetic authority.

commentary.historical_context: The historical Elisha was active during the reign of Joram in Israel (roughly 852-841 BCE), a period of intermittent conflict with Aram. Elisha's prominence as a miracle-worker and prophetic figure is well attested in the biblical narrative. The political context makes the interaction between Israel and Aram significant—these were not distant nations but neighbors, sometimes allies, sometimes enemies. The fact that a high-ranking Aramean general would seek healing from an Israelite prophet suggests that Elisha's reputation as a healer had reached beyond Israel's borders. In the ancient Near Eastern context, a miracle performed on a foreign dignitary would have diplomatic and religious significance.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma 37:6-7 teaches that 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass.' Elisha's simple, direct message ('go and wash in Jordan') contrasts with Naaman's elaborate expectations, just as the Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that God's ways work through simplicity and faith rather than worldly pomp.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 42:11 states that the elders of the Church should understand 'all things concerning the kingdom of God.' Similarly, Elisha represents the living prophet who understands God's will and can direct others according to divine knowledge. The prophet is God's means of communicating His purposes.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The concept of the prophet as God's representative and the means through which God's power is accessed relates to temple ordinances and covenants. In the temple, we encounter God's representatives (the priesthood) as mediators between ourselves and God's power. Elisha functions in a similar role here.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha, as God's prophet, is a type of Christ as God's ultimate prophet and spokesman. In Hebrews 1:1-2, the writer establishes that God spoke through the prophets, but in these latter days has spoken through His Son. Elisha's role as mediator of divine healing points forward to Christ as the ultimate healer whose power extends to all nations (as Naaman will come to understand).
commentary.application: When we face impossible situations, do we first seek God's prophet and God's word, or do we panic like the king? Elisha's calm, faithful response shows that the faithful remnant know where to turn in crisis. The principle is that God provides channels through which His power flows—through His prophets and servants. We should cultivate the habit of seeking prophetic guidance rather than relying solely on our own understanding. Additionally, the purpose of God's miracles is not merely to fix our problems but to strengthen our testimony that God is real and His servants are true.

text_kjv: So Naaman came with his horses and with his chariot, and stood at the door of the house of Elisha.
text_kjv_alt: So Naaman came with his horses and with his chariot, and stood at the door of the house of Elisha.

commentary.narrative:
Naaman arrives at Elisha's house in full military regalia—with his horses and chariot—the material trappings of his status and power as commander of the Aramean army. The very specificity of this detail (horses and chariot) emphasizes the contrast between his earthly power and his need for divine power. A man accustomed to being served, obeyed, and honored now stands at the door of a humble prophet's house. He 'stood at the door'—the text does not say he entered, was invited in, or was greeted according to the protocol due to a man of his rank. He arrives expecting to be received as a dignitary, yet what follows will completely overturn his expectations about how divine healing works and how a man of God conducts himself.

This moment is freighted with cultural significance. In ancient Near Eastern society, when a great man came to the home of someone of lower status, the lower-status person typically came out to greet him, show deference, and facilitate his needs. Naaman is about to learn that the prophet operates according to different rules—that the spiritual realm has its own hierarchy and protocol that supersedes earthly rank and power. He has traveled from Syria to Israel expecting a certain kind of encounter, but what he will receive instead is a lesson in humility.

word_study.meaning: The repeated use of possessive pronouns ('his horses, his chariot') emphasizes these as Naaman's personal belongings and symbols of his authority. Horses and chariots were the high-tech military equipment of the ancient Near East, used by commanders and kings.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on Naaman's military equipment underscores what he brings with him: earthly power, status, military might. These symbols of worldly authority will prove irrelevant to the healing he seeks. He cannot heal himself with horses or chariots; he needs to divest himself of reliance on these things.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'he took his stand at the entrance of the house.' The verb amad ('to stand') can imply a formal stance or position. The petach ('entrance' or 'door') is the threshold—the boundary between outside and inside, between being received and waiting.
word_study.significance: Naaman's physical position at the door is symbolic of his spiritual position: outside looking in, waiting for recognition, not yet admitted into the house of God's representative. His standing at the door shows he is not yet integrated into the world of faith and divine healing.

cross_references.connection: The young slave girl had already identified Naaman's need and pointed him toward Elisha, so his arrival fulfills the chain of events she set in motion through her simple, faithful words.

When Saul sought Samuel, they asked if he was at home and how to approach him properly. Similarly, Naaman is seeking a 'man of God,' but unlike Samuel's situation, Elisha will maintain distance and not emerge to greet the visitor.
The proverb states that 'humility comes before honor.' Naaman is about to learn this lesson as his status and earthly authority are rendered irrelevant.
Like the centurion who comes to Jesus seeking healing for his servant, Naaman is a military commander seeking healing. Both will learn lessons about humility and faith that transcend social rank.

commentary.historical_context: Naaman's arrival with military escort was likely not unusual for a man of his rank traveling internationally in the 9th century BCE. Such an impressive retinue would be expected for diplomatic and military missions. The presence of horses and chariot also suggests he came prepared for a significant event. Aram (Syria) and Israel during this period had various points of contact—trade, conflict, and occasional cooperation. Archaeological evidence from the region shows that military commanders of this era were wealthy and powerful figures, often granted considerable autonomy. Naaman's rank as 'commander of the host' (sar tzava'o) would have made him one of the most powerful men in Aram, second only to the king. His arrival at a prophet's simple house represents an extraordinary reversal of normal social expectations.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The story of Limhi and the Lamanites (Mosiah 7-8) presents a parallel of seeking help across hostile lines. Just as Naaman must go to Israel despite it being a foreign and potentially hostile land, so Limhi and his people must negotiate with their enemies for understanding. Both stories show that truth and help can come from unexpected sources.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 64:34 teaches that 'he that is willing to take upon him my name, and endureth to the end, the same shall be saved.' Naaman must be willing to take upon himself the ways of Israel's God, which requires laying aside his own status and expectations—a form of taking upon oneself a new identity.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is a place where all people, regardless of earthly rank, stand equal before God. Just as Naaman must come as a suppliant to a humble prophet's house, all who enter the temple must divest themselves of worldly status and come as children of God seeking His ordinances and blessings.

commentary.christological_typology: Naaman's coming to Elisha's door parallels the requirement that all who seek healing and salvation must come to Christ. Luke 14:11 states that 'whosoever exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.' Naaman's journey will require him to humble himself before receiving exaltation (healing).
commentary.application: This verse invites reflection on how we approach spiritual help. Do we come to God's representatives (prophets, priesthood leaders, and servants) with humility, or do we come expecting to be served according to our worldly status? Naaman's standing at the door illustrates a crucial principle: before we can receive divine help, we must acknowledge that we are outsiders to that help and that we need what only God can provide. True spiritual progress begins with recognizing our need and our powerlessness to fix ourselves, no matter how powerful or accomplished we are in worldly terms.

text_kjv: And Elisha sent a messenger unto him, saying, Go and wash in Jordan seven times, and thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean.

commentary.narrative:
Elisha's response to Naaman is remarkable for what it is not: there is no dramatic invocation of God's power, no physical gesture, no laying on of hands, no grand pronouncement. The prophet does not even come to the door. Instead, he sends a messenger with simple instructions. This is the antithesis of what Naaman expected—he anticipated a ceremonial healing performed by the prophet himself, something visible and impressive. Instead, he receives instructions that require obedience and faith. The command itself is straightforward: 'Go and wash in Jordan seven times.' The promise is equally clear: 'thy flesh shall come again to thee, and thou shalt be clean.'

The specificity of 'seven times' connects to Levitical purification rituals found in Numbers 19 and elsewhere, linking Naaman's healing to Israel's covenantal framework. His cleansing is not arbitrary or generic; it follows the pattern of Israel's law. The Jordan River is specified—not just any river, but Israel's river, the boundary of the promised land, the river of Israel's identity. To be healed in the Jordan means to be healed on God's terms, in God's place, according to God's covenant. The healing power, according to this instruction, lies not in Elisha's intercession or the prophet's gesture, but in obedience to God's word given through His prophet.

word_study.meaning: The verb halokh means 'to go' or 'to walk,' indicating movement and action. Rachatz means 'to wash' or 'to bathe.' Together, they form a command to take action—to go physically to the Jordan and perform the ritual action of washing.
word_study.significance: The emphasis is on Naaman's agency and obedience. He must act; he cannot remain passive. Healing requires his participation, not merely Elisha's intercession. This breaks the pattern where a powerful figure (king or commander) receives service from others.

word_study.meaning: The number seven in Hebrew has deep symbolic significance. In covenant contexts, seven often represents completeness, perfection, or sacred completion (as in the Sabbath, the seventh day). Seven immersions may also connect to Levitical ritual washings prescribed in the law.
word_study.significance: The number is not arbitrary. Seven times suggests a complete, ritual action—a sacred completing of the healing process. Naaman cannot do it five times or ten times; the specific number emphasizes that this is divine instruction with divine authority.

word_study.meaning: The Jordan River, the major river system of the Levant and the eastern boundary of the promised land. The Jordan was laden with covenantal significance in Israelite tradition—it was the boundary crossed to enter the land, and it became a symbol of God's covenant territory.
word_study.significance: The choice of the Jordan is theologically significant. It is not a generic river but Israel's river. Naaman's healing in the Jordan means his restoration occurs within Israel's covenantal space. The river connects healing to covenant identity.

word_study.term_english: thy flesh shall come again to thee
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'your flesh will return to you.' The verb shub ('return' or 'restore') is used. The phrase emphasizes restoration and return to wholeness—not the creation of new flesh but the restoration of what was corrupted.
word_study.significance: The promise uses language of restoration rather than mere healing. Naaman will not become someone new; his own flesh will be restored to him. This emphasizes wholeness and the recovery of his former state.

word_study.meaning: To be clean or pure, both physically and ritually. In Levitical law, being 'clean' means being fit to participate in the community and in worship. Conversely, being 'unclean' (tameh) meant being excluded from covenant participation.
word_study.significance: Cleansing is not merely medical but covenantal. To be clean means to be restored to full participation in the community—to be able to touch others, enter the temple, participate in worship. Naaman's healing will restore him to covenant community.

cross_references.connection: The Levitical law for cleansing from leprosy prescribed washings and sprinkling, establishing the ritual framework that Elisha's prescription follows. Seven immersions parallels the repeated washings in the purification ritual.

The ritual for cleansing from contact with the dead involved washing with water, establishing water's role in covenant purification practices. Naaman's washing follows this pattern of ritual cleansing.

The Israelites crossed the Jordan to enter the promised land, establishing the Jordan as the threshold of covenant blessing. Naaman will cross its waters (through washing) to enter healing and covenant community.

'For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD.' Elisha's simple, indirect method contrasts with Naaman's expectation, illustrating how God's ways differ from human understanding.
The Book of Mormon teaches that Christ will take upon Him the infirmities and sicknesses of His people. Similarly, healing comes through God's appointed servant, not through human might or status.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, ritual bathing and washing were common practices in various religious traditions. The Jordan River held particular significance for Israelites as the boundary of their promised land and as a site of covenant renewal. Archaeological evidence suggests that water rituals were important in both Israelite and surrounding Near Eastern religions. The prescription of seven washings would have been understood within the framework of Levitical purification law (though the specific context of leprosy purification in Leviticus 14 prescribes different ritual elements). For Naaman, coming from a Syrian/Aramean background, being instructed to wash in Israel's sacred river would have been surprising and, as the text will show, offensive to his national pride.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The principle of obedience to a small instruction leading to great blessings appears in the Book of Mormon. In Alma 37:40, Alma teaches Helaman that 'by small and simple things are great things brought to pass.' Naaman's simple obedience to wash will result in complete healing—a perfect illustration of this principle.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 58:26-29 teaches the principle of working by faith: 'For behold, it is not meet that I should command in all things; for he that is slothful and cannot obey my voice shall not have place in the kingdom of my Father.' Naaman must act in faith; he cannot receive healing through passive waiting.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The seven-fold washing recalls the preparation for entering sacred space. In the temple, we undergo ritualistic preparation (including washing and anointing) to prepare us for receiving sacred ordinances. Naaman's washing prepares him to receive healing and restoration to community—a parallel to temple preparation.

commentary.christological_typology: The pathway to healing requires obedience to God's appointed representative and the willingness to follow instruction that may not make immediate sense. In John 9, Jesus instructs the blind man to wash in the pool of Siloam—another instance where healing comes through obedience to a specific instruction. Naaman's seven washings may also prefigure the completeness of Christ's atonement, which makes us wholly clean.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that God's methods are often simpler than we expect and require our active obedience. We cannot be passive recipients of healing or spiritual growth; we must be willing to follow counsel given through God's servants, even when it seems strange, insufficient, or beneath our dignity. The Jordan is not a magical healing pool; the healing power comes from God and is accessed through obedience. In our own lives, when spiritual leaders counsel us to do simple things—pray, study the scriptures, keep the commandments, serve others—these are not suggestions but pathways to spiritual healing. Our willingness to humble ourselves and follow such counsel determines whether we receive the promised blessings.

text_kjv: But Naaman was wroth, and went away, and said, Behold, I thought, He will surely come out to me, and stand, and call on the name of the LORD his God, and strike his hand over the place, and recover the leper.

commentary.narrative:
Naaman's immediate response to the instruction is anger and rejection. The word 'wroth' (qatzaf) indicates not mere disappointment but furious indignation. His response reveals what he expected: a dramatic, public healing ceremony in which the prophet would personally come out, perform visible actions, invoke God's name with great ceremony, and restore him in a way that displayed the prophet's power. Naaman had mentally scripted the entire encounter, and when reality diverges from his expectations, he rejects it entirely. This is the critical test of faith.

Naaman's expectations are not inherently wrong—they reflect a reasonable understanding of how prophetic miracles might work. Yet they also reveal his misunderstanding of where healing power truly originates. He wants to see the prophet's power displayed; he wants visible evidence of the prophet's authority. What he fails to understand is that the prophet's power is not his own but God's, and God's power operates through faith and obedience, not through spectacle. The simplicity of the instruction is actually the test: will Naaman believe the word of God spoken through the prophet, or will he insist on visible demonstration that satisfies his own expectations?

word_study.meaning: To be angry, wrathful, or indignant. The root qatzaf carries the sense of quick, hot anger. This is not cold calculation but emotional reaction.
word_study.significance: Naaman's anger is instinctive and immediate—the response of someone used to being obeyed and honored who suddenly encounters an affront to his dignity. His emotion reveals his character and his reliance on earthly status rather than faith.

word_study.term_english: He will surely come out to me
word_study.meaning: Literally, 'he will go out to me' or 'he will come forth to me.' The repetition of the verb (yetze yatzo—'come out, come forth') emphasizes the emphatic expectation. Naaman expected the prophet to personally emerge.
word_study.significance: The emphasis on the prophet 'coming out' shows Naaman expected to be met in person, honored with the prophet's physical presence. In his mind, a great man deserves to be received by the prophet in person.

word_study.meaning: To 'call on the name of God' means to invoke God's presence and power through speaking God's name. This was understood as a powerful ritual action that demonstrated the speaker's authority to access God's power.
word_study.significance: Naaman expected the prophet to perform a public, verbal invocation—a ritual pronouncement that would demonstrate the prophet's access to divine power and would be visible proof of the miracle.

word_study.term_english: strike his hand over the place
word_study.meaning: To wave or lift the hand over a location. This gesture conveys blessing, power, or miraculous action. Naaman expected the prophet to make a visible, dramatic gesture.
word_study.significance: Again, Naaman's expectations center on visible, physical action that would demonstrate power. He wants a ceremony, not a command. He wants to see the healing happen through the prophet's visible action.

word_study.meaning: To gather, collect, or restore. The word asaf can mean to cure or heal in the sense of restoring to wholeness. Ha-metzora ('the leper') is the person with skin disease.
word_study.significance: Naaman thought the prophet would 'gather up' the disease, removing it and restoring wholeness through visible action. He expected the healing to be a dramatic event, not a quiet obedience.

cross_references.connection: In his hometown, Jesus 'did not many mighty works...because of their unbelief.' Conversely, faith enables miracles. Naaman's anger represents a failure of faith that threatens to prevent his healing.

Jesus mentions that there were many lepers in Israel in Elisha's time, but 'none of them was cleansed saving Naaman the Syrian.' The passage emphasizes that Naaman will be healed, but the narrative shows his healing is contingent on his willingness to obey.
'Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall.' Naaman's pride in his status and his haughtiness before the prophet nearly prevents his healing.

Nephi's brothers murmur against the lord and fail to receive blessings, while Nephi's obedience and faith enable him to accomplish the impossible. The Book of Mormon demonstrates repeatedly that faith and obedience are prerequisites for God's power to work.

commentary.historical_context: Naaman's expectation reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding of how divine power is manifested and accessed. Magical practices in surrounding cultures often involved invocation of divine names, gestures, and visible ritual actions. From Naaman's perspective as a Syrian general, the simple instruction to wash seemed inadequate and insulting. It lacked the ceremonial grandeur that would befit his status and that he believed would be necessary to move God to action. The tension between Naaman's expectations and Elisha's instructions also reflects a difference in spiritual understanding: Naaman thinks healing comes through the prophet's power and performance; the text will reveal it comes through obedience to God's word.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 3-4, Laman and Lemuel repeatedly question Nephi's obedience to the Lord's commands, expecting more dramatic or visible confirmation before committing to action. Like Naaman, they expect signs before faith rather than faith leading to manifestation. Naaman's anger parallels their murmuring.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 50:24 states, 'That which is of God is light; and he that receiveth light, and continueth in God, receiveth more light, and that light groweth brighter and brighter until the perfect day.' Naaman's rejection of the simple instruction represents a failure to receive light; continuing in anger and expectation prevents him from receiving more.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple requires patrons to follow specific instructions and ordinances as prescribed, not as they imagine them. Faith in the temple process means trusting that the prescribed way leads to the promised blessings, regardless of whether it matches our expectations.

commentary.christological_typology: Naaman's rejection of God's simple word through the prophet foreshadows the broader human tendency to reject God's plan of salvation. Christ Himself noted that people often expect a messiah who comes in power and glory, not in humility. The expectation of a grand, visible display of power rather than simple obedience mirrors humanity's resistance to God's actual way of working.
commentary.application: This verse confronts us with an uncomfortable mirror: In what ways do we reject God's guidance because it doesn't match our expectations? Do we expect dramatic confirmation before obedience, or are we willing to follow counsel that seems simple or insufficient? Naaman's anger reveals that pride and preconceived notions can prevent us from receiving the very blessings we seek. The lesson is that faith means trusting God's way, even—especially—when it differs from what we would have scripted. True faith is demonstrated not when circumstances match our expectations but when we obey despite our expectations being violated.

text_kjv: Are not Abana and Pharpar, rivers of Damascus, better than all the waters of Israel? may I not wash in them, and be clean? So he turned and went away in a rage.

commentary.narrative:
Naaman's objection reveals the fundamental misunderstanding at the heart of his rejection. He believes the healing power resides in the water itself—in its quality and purity. The rivers of Damascus, he argues, are superior to Israel's Jordan; therefore, he should be able to wash in them and achieve the same result. This reflects a materialistic understanding of healing power: if the goal is to remove disease from the body through water, then the best water should suffice. What Naaman fails to grasp is that the Jordan's significance is not hydraulic but theological. The healing power is not in the water's mineral content or clarity but in God's covenant relationship with Israel and in obedience to His word spoken through His prophet.

Naaman's comparison of rivers also reveals national pride. He cannot accept that healing must come through Israel's river, in Israel's way, according to Israel's covenant. Accepting this would mean acknowledging Israel's God and Israel's prophet as superior to his own nation's resources and wisdom. His rage (chemah—a burning anger) drives him away. He chooses his dignity and his national pride over his healing. The entire narrative pivots on this moment: will Naaman be willing to humble himself, to acknowledge Israel's God, and to follow simple instructions? Or will he return home unhealed, his pride intact but his flesh still ravaged by disease?

word_study.meaning: Two major rivers of Damascus. The Abana (modern Barada) is the primary river of Damascus, known for its clear, cold water flowing from the Anti-Lebanon mountains. The Pharpar (possibly the A'waj) is another significant river in the region. Both were important for irrigation and water supply in the Damascus oasis.
word_study.significance: Naaman invokes the rivers of his own homeland, the rivers he knows and trusts. By naming them specifically, he grounds his objection in the familiar. The rhetorical question 'Are not these better?' appeals to what he can measure and see—the physical properties of water.

word_study.meaning: Good, excellent, superior. The root tov implies quality, excellence, or preference. Naaman is making a comparative judgment about water quality.
word_study.significance: Naaman's use of 'better' reveals his thinking: he believes healing is a matter of physical or material quality. Better water equals better healing. He is unable to conceive of healing as a covenant matter rather than a material one.

word_study.meaning: Literally, 'shall I not wash in them?' The rhetorical question implies that surely washing in the superior waters of Damascus should accomplish the same result. Naaman is arguing by logic: if washing heals, and Damascus waters are better, then Damascus waters should work.
word_study.significance: The rhetorical question shows Naaman attempting to use reason and logic to override the prophet's instruction. He cannot accept that healing is not a matter of logic and material quality but of faith and obedience.

word_study.term_english: turned and went away in a rage
word_study.meaning: The verbs suggest a deliberate physical turning away (phen) and departure (yelekh). Chemah ('rage,' 'heat,' or 'wrath') is a burning anger—an emotional state that overrides reason. The phrase 'he turned away' suggests he literally turns his back on the healing.
word_study.significance: Naaman's physical turning away is a symbol of his spiritual rejection. He chooses anger over submission, dignity over healing. The description of his emotional state emphasizes that pride and wounded self-image drive his decision more than rational assessment.

cross_references.connection: 'For my thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways my ways, saith the LORD...as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways.' Naaman learns this truth the hard way—God's way (the Jordan) is not what human reason would choose.

'Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding...Be not wise in thine own eyes.' Naaman's reliance on his own reasoning about water quality prevents him from trusting the prophet's instruction.
Jesus says, 'Except ye see signs and wonders, ye will not believe.' Naaman similarly demands visible demonstration rather than simple obedience, and his demand threatens to cost him his healing.

'Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men.' The simple instruction to wash seems foolish to Naaman, yet it contains divine wisdom superior to his reasoning.

Jacob teaches that the 'wise of the world' are caught in a snare because they 'suppose that they are wise, and hearken not unto the counsel of God.' Naaman's reliance on his own understanding and pride in his nation's wisdom prevent him from heeding the prophet.

commentary.historical_context: The specific mention of Damascus and its rivers emphasizes the geographical contrast. Damascus was one of the great city-states of the Levant, and its rivers were well-known and celebrated. The Abana/Barada is spring-fed and provides abundant, clear water—superior in conventional terms to the Jordan in many aspects. From a purely material standpoint, Naaman's objection makes sense. However, the narrative is teaching a spiritual rather than practical lesson. In the ancient Near Eastern context, rivers were often associated with deity and national identity. The Jordan was Israel's river; the rivers of Damascus belonged to Aram. Naaman's objection reflects not merely practical skepticism but a resistance to acknowledging Israel's God and accepting healing on Israel's terms.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Nephi's brothers repeatedly rely on what they can see and measure rather than faith in the unseen word of the Lord (1 Nephi 2:12). Naaman's reasoning about water quality parallels their reasoning about the feasibility of their mission—both rely on earthly measurement rather than faith.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 1:37-38 teaches that God's word is sure and His promises are fulfilled, and that those who listen will be blessed while those who turn away will fall. Naaman's turning away from the prophet's word parallels turning away from God's word itself.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple teaches that certain ordinances must be performed in specific ways and places. One cannot substitute other waters or other methods; covenant blessing comes through following the prescribed way. Naaman learns this principle through his healing narrative.

commentary.christological_typology: Just as Naaman must humble himself and accept God's way through Israel's covenant and Israel's river, all humanity must accept salvation through Christ—God's appointed way. The human tendency to argue for alternative paths (Pharisaic self-righteousness, works without grace, reliance on human merit) parallels Naaman's insistence that Damascus water would suffice. Christ is the only way, just as the Jordan was Naaman's only way to healing.
commentary.application: This verse challenges our own tendency to judge spiritual matters by earthly standards. We may ask: 'Why must I attend Church when I can pray at home?' 'Why must I follow the prophet's counsel when my own reasoning suggests a better way?' 'Why must I accept this calling when I have other plans?' The answer lies in understanding that spiritual power and blessing do not operate according to materialistic logic. We receive them through trusting God's word spoken through His servants, even when—especially when—it contradicts our expectations and our reasoned judgments. Pride in our own understanding, nationality, status, or wisdom can prevent us from receiving the very blessings we desperately need. True healing (spiritual and otherwise) requires us to abandon the assumption that we can reason our way to truth and instead submit to the pathway God has established.

text_kjv: And his servants came near, and spake unto him, and said, My father, if the prophet had bid thee do some great thing, wouldest thou not have done it? how much then when he saith to thee, Wash, and be clean?

commentary.narrative: Naaman stands at a crossroads. He has been told to wash in the Jordan to be healed of his leprosy—a command so absurdly simple that his pride has already rejected it. He expected the prophet to perform some dramatic ritual, to invoke his God with ceremony and power. Instead, he was given water and a word. His servants now approach him with a wisdom that cuts through his offense. They do not challenge his status or his army; they appeal to his logic through what Hebrew rhetorical tradition calls a qal va-chomer argument—if the greater (doing something difficult), then certainly the lesser (doing something easy). Their address as avi ('my father') is significant: it softens the rebuke with affection while still correcting him. These servants, unnamed in the narrative, understand something their master does not: obedience does not require understanding, and healing does not depend on human dignity.
commentary.narrative_continued: The TCR rendering brings out the force of the servants' argument even more clearly: 'How much more when he simply tells you, Wash and be clean?' The word 'simply' captures the contrast between what Naaman expected and what Elisha actually said. The prophet did not demand a great thing; he made an offer of grace dressed in the simplest possible language. The servants recognize that the obstacle to Naaman's healing is not the command but the commander's unwillingness to comply with something that seems beneath him. This verse reveals a pattern that runs through the entire Naaman story: the humble understand what the powerful resist. The slave girl saw what Naaman could not. Now his own household servants see what he cannot. The narrative is training us to recognize that divine healing often comes through humility, which for a man of power means learning to obey simple instruction.

word_study.meaning: servants, attendants; those bound in service. In the context of military hierarchy, these would be officers and aides in Naaman's command structure.
word_study.significance: The narrative privileges the wisdom of the servants—those lower in rank than Naaman. They possess the clarity that status obscures. This is a consistent biblical pattern: the lowly see what the mighty cannot (cf. the slave girl in 2 Kings 5:2–3).

word_study.meaning: father; in social discourse, a term of respectful address conveying affection and authority. Used here not biologically but as a courtesy title for a superior.
word_study.significance: The servants call Naaman 'father' not to flatter but to soften their correction with intimacy. They are saying, in effect, 'Honored one, we must speak truth to you.' In the Restoration tradition, this echoes Alma's counsel to his sons and the tender way truth is spoken within covenant community (Alma 36–42).

word_study.meaning: a great word, a difficult matter. Gadol means great in size, significance, or difficulty.
word_study.significance: The servants posit a hypothetical: if the prophet had asked Naaman to do something gadol ('great, difficult, demanding'), he would have done it. The implication: why not do the easy thing? The rhetorical structure forces Naaman to confront the illogic of his refusal. The command is not great in difficulty; the resistance is great in pride.

cross_references.connection: Samuel tells Saul that obedience is better than sacrifice—the principle the servants here apply to Naaman: compliance with God's simple command matters more than the grandeur of what is asked.
The prudent see danger and take refuge; the servants see Naaman's spiritual danger (refusal of healing) and offer wise counsel to redirect him.
Alma teaches that we must be 'obedient to all the commandments'—paralleling the servants' logic that if obedience is commanded, obedience is required, regardless of difficulty.

The Lord tells the Saints to 'be anxiously engaged in a good cause' and do many things of their own free will—yet Naaman resists the good cause of his own healing because it seems insufficiently dramatic.

commentary.historical_context: The cultural context here involves ancient Near Eastern assumptions about magic, ritual, and divine action. Naaman expected a theurgic performance—visible, audible, dramatic invocation of divine power. The Israelite prophet offered something far more radical: invisible obedience. In the ancient world, healing often was associated with ritual specialists who performed complex ceremonies, invoked gods by name, and required elaborate preparations. Elisha's instruction—wash and be clean—stripped away all the ceremonial apparatus. This would have seemed almost impious to Naaman, who came from a religious context where the complexity of the ritual was proportional to its efficacy. The servants' argument, by contrast, reflects Israelite theological intuition: God's power operates through simple obedience, not through human impressiveness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The principle appears in Nephi's obedience to build a ship despite his lack of shipwright knowledge (1 Nephi 17:8–9). Nephi obeyed the voice of the Lord without requiring to understand the full method beforehand. Similarly, Alma the Younger's conversion came through obedience to preaching (Alma 36:24), not through grand signs. The servants' qal va-chomer argument reflects Nephite teaching found in Helaman 12:24–25, where small obediences lead to greater understanding.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants repeatedly emphasizes that obedience precedes understanding. In D&C 64:34, we learn that the Lord requires the heart and willing mind; in D&C 130:20–21, obedience to law brings corresponding blessing. Naaman must obey the law of the Jordan (the simple washing) to receive the blessing (healing). Section 93 teaches that light comes through obedience: 'All truth is independent in that sphere in which God has placed it' (D&C 93:36), and we must discover that truth through compliance with known law.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The washing here anticipates temple washings and anointings. In the endowment, candidates for the temple undergo preparatory washings as symbolic of spiritual cleansing—a private, simple act that precedes the more elaborate ordinances. Naaman must descend to the Jordan as a prerequisite to ascending in spiritual status.

commentary.christological_typology: The servants' insistence that Naaman perform the simple act foreshadows the gospel's central claim: salvation comes through a simple act of faith and obedience, not through human achievement or wisdom. Jesus taught that entering the kingdom requires becoming as a little child (Matthew 18:3–4), stripping away the pride and self-sufficiency that prevent reception of grace. Naaman's resistance to simple instruction mirrors humanity's resistance to simple redemption through the Atonement. The servants function as a type of the Holy Ghost, urging us to obey when we want to negotiate.
commentary.application: This verse asks us directly: what simple obedience are we resisting because it seems beneath us or insufficient? Naaman's resistance teaches that pride often wears the mask of discernment. We tell ourselves that we would obey if the command were more impressive, more mystical, more suited to our status or intelligence. The servants' challenge remains: if we would obey a difficult thing, why not obey the simple thing? Modern application might involve: simple daily prayer when we want a more sophisticated spiritual practice; honest conversation when we prefer to let resentment fester; basic scripture study when we crave esoteric doctrine; straightforward repentance when we want to negotiate the terms of our change. The verse invites covenant members to examine where they are like Naaman—waiting for a command that will make sense to them, when the path to healing lies in compliance with the already-given word.

text_kjv: Then went he down, and dipped himself seven times in Jordan, according to the saying of the man of God: and his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child, and he was clean.

commentary.narrative: Naaman obeys. The narrative shifts from resistance to compliance with a verb of descent: va-yered ('he went down'). This verb carries weight in Hebrew biblical narrative. To go down often means to descend in status, to humble oneself, to enter a liminal space. Naaman, the commanding general who arrived with horses and chariots and the pomp of Aramean power, goes down to the Jordan. He removes his armor, his insignia, the visible markers of his authority. He immerses himself—va-yitbol—not once but seven times. The number seven in biblical theology signifies completeness and divine action. Naaman does not dip himself once and wait; he goes down again and again, each immersion an act of surrendered obedience. And the healing is total and immediate: va-yashov besaro kivesar na'ar qaton ('his flesh returned like the flesh of a small child'). Not merely cleansed but renewed. The leprosy, which had consumed his skin and marked him as unclean, is erased. In its place is new skin—infant skin, unscarred, unblemished, innocent.
commentary.narrative_continued: The phrase 'his flesh came again like unto the flesh of a little child' is extraordinary in its specificity. The Hebrew na'ar qaton does not simply mean 'healed' or 'restored'—it means transformed into the flesh of a child. Naaman is not merely cured; he is made new. The disease consumed the exterior of his being; the Jordan restores it. And the verse closes with ve-yithar ('and he was clean'), a verb that carries both medical and ritual significance. He is tahor—ritually pure, able to enter the sanctuary, fit for covenant community. The healing is simultaneous and total: physical restoration and ritual purification happen in the same moment through obedience to the prophet's word. The Covenant Rendering captures this beautifully: 'His skin was restored like the skin of a young child, and he was clean.' What is remarkable is that nowhere in the text does Elisha perform any action during the immersion. There is no prayer recorded, no invocation of God's name, no miraculous phenomenon. The healing happens through obedience to instruction. The prophet has set the condition; Naaman has met it; God has acted.

word_study.meaning: descended, went down. The root ר-ד-ה speaks to downward movement, humiliation, or entry into a lower state.
word_study.significance: This verb is theologically loaded. To go down is often to be humbled (as in Egypt's descent into famine, or descent into Sheol). But in covenant theology, descent often precedes ascent. Naaman must go down to the Jordan to be raised up in his flesh. The pattern appears in Nephi going down to the ship-building site (1 Nephi 17:7) and in Christ's descent before exaltation.

word_study.meaning: immersed, plunged, submerged. The root is connected to tevilah, ritual immersion in Jewish practice.
word_study.significance: This is not casual washing but immersion—a complete submersion. In later Jewish practice, tevilah became the standard for ritual purification. The verb here anticipates the later rabbinic tradition. For LDS readers, the language of immersion resonates with baptism, the covenant act that is total and transformative.

word_study.meaning: seven times. Sheva (seven) is the number of completeness and perfection in biblical numerology. Paam (time, step, instance) indicates enumeration.
word_study.significance: Seven is the number of divine action and completion. The seven immersions parallel the seven days of creation, the seven-year cycles in the Torah's law, the seven blasts at Jericho. Naaman's healing requires not one immersion but seven—a complete, divinely-ordered action. This emphasizes that the healing is not accidental or partial but total and sanctioned by God's structure.

word_study.meaning: his flesh returned, his skin came back. Shav means to return, turn back, restore. Basar means flesh, skin—the body's exterior.
word_study.significance: The verb shav (to return, restore) indicates that what was lost is now recovered. But the comparison to a na'ar qaton (small child) suggests more than recovery—it suggests complete renewal. The disease that consumed his flesh is replaced with new, unblemished flesh. This is resurrection language applied to the body.

word_study.meaning: young child, small boy. Naar means boy or youth; qaton means small, little, young.
word_study.significance: The comparison is to a child's skin—unmarked, unblemished, innocent. It is not merely healthy skin but innocent skin. The disease marked Naaman's body with shame and separation; the healing restores him to a state of wholeness and innocence. In the context of covenant theology, this suggests restoration to a state before sin marred the body.

word_study.meaning: was clean, became pure. The root ט-ה-ר (tahor) indicates ritual and physical cleanliness.
word_study.significance: This verb is crucial. Naaman is not just healed medically; he is declared clean—tahor. In Levitical law, only the priest could declare someone clean after a skin disease (Leviticus 13–14). Here, Elisha (a prophet, not a priest) declares Naaman clean through his obedience to instruction. The healing is simultaneously physical and spiritual, medical and ritual.

cross_references.connection: The detailed laws of skin disease diagnosis and isolation; Naaman's tsara'at required this kind of examination and separation, making his restoration to cleanliness all the more significant.
Christ's baptism in the Jordan—immersion in the same river, an act of obedience that opens the heavens. Both immersions involve descent into water and divine action that follows obedience.
Israel called out by name but not with the fullness of understanding—paralleling Naaman's instruction to obey without complete comprehension of why the Jordan specifically would heal him.

Mormon's summary that Christ took upon himself the flesh and blood of his people and suffered that his bowels might be filled with mercy—Naaman's restoration of his flesh foreshadows Christ's bodily resurrection and the resurrection of all flesh.
The doctrine of resurrection applied to the elements themselves—'the elements are eternal'; Naaman's flesh is restored eternally new, suggesting the renewal of all creation.

commentary.historical_context: The Jordan River held deep significance in Israelite covenant theology. It was the boundary between the wilderness and the promised land; the Israelites crossed it to claim the inheritance (Joshua 3–4). It was where John the Baptist would later baptize (Matthew 3). Naaman's immersion in the Jordan is not arbitrary. For a Syrian general, this river is a foreign place, yet it is precisely in this foreign place—not in his home territory where his gods were worshipped—that healing comes. The cultural assumption of the ancient Near East was that gods were territorial. Naaman will later ask for Israelite soil to take home because he believed that the God of Israel was most powerfully active on Israelite land. The subversion of this expectation in Naaman's story is profound: the God of Israel acts through simple obedience to his prophet, regardless of place. Archaeology has identified the Jordan as a relatively modest river—not impressive in scale. Yet its waters, combined with obedience to prophetic instruction, bring about one of the most dramatic healings in the Hebrew Bible.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon emphasizes the principle of obedience preceding understanding. Nephi obeyed the voice of the Lord in building the ship without seeing the design beforehand (1 Nephi 17:8–11). Lehi's family followed the prophet without always comprehending the ultimate destination. Alma taught that the word is like a seed that you plant and nurture, and through faith and obedience, it grows into understanding (Alma 32:26–43). Naaman's immersion mirrors this pattern: obedience to the word of the prophet produces the promised result.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: The Doctrine and Covenants teaches that obedience is the law upon which all blessings are predicated (D&C 130:20–21). Naaman receives healing because he obeys the law—the law of the Jordan, the law of the prophet's word. Section 93 teaches that light and truth come through obedience: the more we comply with known law, the more we understand. Naaman immersed himself seven times; in D&C 76:51–62, the celestial glory is described in terms of light and knowledge that increase through obedience. The healing of Naaman's flesh anticipates the ultimate restoration of all flesh in resurrection (D&C 88:14–16).
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The Jordan immersion foreshadows the temple's preparatory washings and anointings. In the endowment, candidates are washed and anointed—private, ceremonial acts that precede the more elaborate ordinances. Naaman's seven immersions in the Jordan parallel the order of the priesthood, where preparation and purification precede advancement. The renewal of his flesh 'like a little child' echoes the temple teaching that we are born again through covenant, restored to an Edenic innocence. The phrase 'being clean' carries ritual significance that will climax in the temple ordinance of full cleansing and restoration.

commentary.christological_typology: Naaman's descent to the Jordan and emergence restored parallels Christ's descent into the waters of baptism (Matthew 3:13–17) and his descent to the grave and resurrection. The seven immersions suggest the completeness and divine ordering of Christ's redemptive work. Naaman's flesh 'returned like the flesh of a little child' foreshadows Christ's resurrection body—transformed, glorified, yet recognizable. The declaration of cleanliness (va-yithar) is a type of Christ's perfect obedience declaring all humanity clean through his Atonement. Just as Naaman's healing depended entirely on obedience to the prophet's word, so our healing depends entirely on obedience to the Savior's word: 'Follow me.'
commentary.application: This verse models what covenant obedience produces: total transformation. For modern members, the question is: what simple obedience is producing unexpected transformation in my life? Naaman's story suggests that when we obey the Lord's servants (prophets, apostles, parents, leaders) in matters that seem simple or even inexplicable, divine power works through us. The specific application involves recognizing that small, repeated acts of obedience (like Naaman's seven immersions) accumulate into profound change. This applies to daily prayer, scripture study, family home evening, temple attendance, repentance—seemingly 'small' obediences that, when performed with faith, work transformation as thorough as the renewal of Naaman's flesh. The verse also teaches that healing—spiritual and otherwise—often requires entering unfamiliar water, descending into vulnerability, and trusting a source outside our own power and status.

text_kjv: And he returned to the man of God, he and all his company, and came, and stood before him: and he said, Behold, now I know that there is no God in all the earth, but in Israel: now therefore, I pray thee, take a blessing of thy servant.

commentary.narrative: Naaman returns—va-yashav—now transformed in both body and understanding. He comes not alone but with his entire retinue, his 'mahane' (company, camp), the military escort that had arrived in such pomp. The change in his posture is marked: he 'stood before him' (va-ya'amod lefanav), suggesting submission, respect, the stance of a subject before a superior. His declaration—hinneh na yadati ki ein Elohim bekhol ha-aretz ki im be-Yisrael ('now I know that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel')—is the theological centerpiece of the entire narrative. This is not a tentative belief or a pragmatic admission that the Israelite God happened to heal him. This is an exclusive monotheistic confession from a pagan military commander. The word yadati ('I know') is not intellectual assent but experiential knowledge: Naaman knows because his own flesh has testified to him. His skin has become the evidence of God's reality. His offer of a berakhah ('blessing, gift') is his attempt to establish reciprocity, to repay what he has received, to transform grace into transaction.
commentary.narrative_continued: What makes this confession remarkable is the timing and the speaker. At the opening of the chapter, Naaman was a man of power and status, valued by his king and commander of his nation's armies. Yet leprosy has rendered him powerless, despite all his military might and political influence. He came to Elisha seeking a cure as a commercial transaction—implied in his offer of gifts and treasure at the outset (2 Kings 5:5). Now, having been healed through obedience rather than payment, Naaman understands something profound: healing is not a commodity to be purchased but a revelation of God's exclusive reality. The prophet Elisha operates not in service to Naaman's power but in service to the God of Israel, a God whose authority transcends military might, national borders, and human status. Naaman's confession that there is no God in all the earth except in Israel is a radical statement—it denies the legitimacy of all other gods, including the gods of Aram where he held high rank. His offer of a gift (berakhah) is simultaneously an expression of gratitude and a misunderstanding: he wants to reciprocate as if the healing were a commercial exchange, rather than understanding it as grace.

word_study.meaning: returned, turned back, came back. The root ש-ו-ב suggests turning around, repentance, restoration.
word_study.significance: The same verb used for the restoration of Naaman's flesh now describes Naaman himself returning to the prophet. He has been transformed and is now returning to acknowledge that transformation and its source. In covenantal language, returning to God is repentance. Naaman's return is his act of turning from reliance on human power and military might toward acknowledgment of divine authority.

word_study.meaning: I know, I have come to know. The root י-ד-ע indicates intimate, experiential knowledge, not mere intellectual assent.
word_study.significance: Yada in biblical Hebrew often implies intimate knowledge—as in 'Adam knew Eve' (Genesis 4:1). Naaman's knowledge of God's reality is not theoretical but embodied. His own skin has experienced what the Israelite God can do. This knowledge has come through his flesh and cannot be undone by argument or doubt.

word_study.meaning: there is no God, there exists no deity. Ein is the negative existential; Elohim is the general term for deity or the God of Israel.
word_study.significance: Naaman's statement goes further than henotheism (acknowledging other gods but worshipping one). He declares ein Elohim bekhol ha-aretz ki im be-Yisrael ('there is no God in all the earth except in Israel'). This is strict monotheism: the God of Israel is the only God that actually exists. The confession is absolute and exclusive. As the TCR note indicates, this is remarkable coming from a Syrian general whose own culture assumed the legitimacy of multiple deities.

word_study.meaning: blessing, gift, bequest. The root ב-ר-ך speaks to fertility, fruitfulness, and the transmission of blessing.
word_study.significance: Naaman offers a berakhah—a blessing-gift. The term is significant because it implies gratitude and relationship rather than mere payment. Yet Elisha will refuse it, indicating that prophetic healing cannot be reciprocated with wealth. The refusal teaches that grace operates outside the market economy. For modern covenant members, the concept of berakhah connects to the blessings of the temple and priesthood—spiritual gifts that cannot be purchased but flow from obedience and faith.

cross_references.connection: Pharaoh must acknowledge, 'There is none like unto the LORD our God'—similar to Naaman's confession, though Pharaoh's comes grudgingly while Naaman's comes from gratitude for personal healing.
After Elijah's contest on Mount Carmel, the people declare, 'The LORD, he is the God'—a national confession that parallels Naaman's personal confession of exclusive monotheism.
Paul teaches that confession with the mouth leads to salvation; Naaman's verbal acknowledgment of the Lord's exclusive reality mirrors the confessional act at the heart of Christian covenant.

Lamoni's father, a pagan king, comes to knowledge of the true God through the testimony of Ammon and experiences a spiritual conversion; like Naaman, he moves from power and pride to humble acknowledgment of divine reality.
The vision of the degrees of glory reveals that knowledge of God comes through revelation; Naaman's knowledge of God's exclusive reality is a form of personal revelation through his own experience.

commentary.historical_context: Naaman's confession of monotheism in a polytheistic cultural context was extraordinary. The ancient Near East assumed a multiplicity of gods, each with territorial jurisdiction, each commanding loyalty from specific peoples. The idea that only one God existed and that this God's power transcended national boundaries and ethnic identity was radically subversive. Naaman came from Aram, which worshipped gods like Hadad (the storm god, whom Rimmon may represent) and other Aramean deities. His confession that only the God of Israel exists is not merely theological; it is a renunciation of his entire cultural and religious identity as an Aramean. Historical records show that religious syncretism was common in the ancient world—one could acknowledge multiple gods simultaneously. Naaman's exclusive declaration that Israel's God is the only God who exists represents a remarkable conversion. His attempt to bring Israelite soil to Damascus (verse 17) reflects the ancient Near Eastern assumption that gods were territorial. Ironically, Naaman is trying to manage his new monotheistic faith through territorial categories—he wants to bring the land of God to his own land. The narrative will show the limitations of this understanding.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: King Lamoni's father, a pagan king, comes to a similar knowledge through Ammon's preaching (Alma 22:14–18). His confession mirrors Naaman's: upon understanding the nature of God, he desires to know how to repent. Zeniff, though an Israelite by birth, initially relied on his own power and understanding; only through experience and revelation did he come to acknowledge the supremacy of God's will (Mosiah 9:1–3). The principle is consistent: knowledge of God's exclusive reality comes through personal experience of divine power, not through abstract theology.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 76, Joseph Smith and Sidney Rigdon receive a vision of the degrees of glory and explicitly state that they 'saw the light and glory' of Jesus Christ's kingdom. Naaman's coming to knowledge of God's reality mirrors this pattern: knowledge of God comes through direct experience and revelation. Section 88:47 teaches that 'the light of the body is the eye'—Naaman has seen with his own eyes (his healed flesh) the power of Israel's God. D&C 101:77–80 speaks of bringing together those who acknowledge God's reality; Naaman's confession positions him among those who have come to know the true God.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple, covenant members stand and witness the testimony of Jesus Christ and make solemn covenants to follow him. Naaman's standing before Elisha and making his confession parallels the confessional aspect of temple worship. His willingness to renounce other gods and acknowledge only the God of Israel foreshadows the renunciation of the world made in the temple. The berakhah (blessing) he offers anticipates the blessings pronounced upon those who keep their covenants.

commentary.christological_typology: Naaman's public confession of the exclusive reality of the God of Israel is a type of the central Christian confession that Jesus Christ is Lord (Romans 10:9). His knowledge arising from personal experience of healing power—his transformed flesh—is a type of post-resurrection knowledge. Just as Naaman returns to acknowledge the prophet who mediated his healing, so believers return to acknowledge Christ, the mediator of all healing and redemption. Naaman's confession that there is 'no God in all the earth but in Israel' prefigures the universal acknowledgment of Christ's kingship that John saw in Revelation: 'Every creature which is in heaven, and on the earth, and under the earth, and such as are in the sea, and all that are in them, heard I saying, Blessing, and honour, and glory, and power, be unto him that sitteth upon the throne, and unto the Lamb for ever' (Revelation 5:13).
commentary.application: This verse asks: What personal experience of God's power has changed your theology? Naaman did not come to monotheistic faith through argument or instruction in doctrine. He came to it through his own body being healed. For modern covenant members, this suggests that the most powerful testimonies are built on personal experience with divine power. When we have been healed (physically, emotionally, spiritually), when we have experienced the Lord's protection or guidance, when we have seen impossible things made possible through faith—these experiences become unshakeable anchors for testimony. The verse also teaches humility in the face of divine power: Naaman came as a proud commander seeking to negotiate and purchase a cure; he returns as a humble suppliant acknowledging God's exclusive authority. The application for today: do we acknowledge, in our lives and in our communities, that there is only one God whose power matters, only one source of healing and redemption? Or do we functionally polytheize, dividing our loyalty between the Lord and the world, between divine authority and human power? Naaman's confession invites us to the same exclusive commitment.

text_kjv: But he said, As the LORD liveth, before whom I stand, I will receive none. And he urged him to take it; but he refused.

commentary.narrative: Elisha's refusal is absolute. The prophet speaks under oath: 'Chai YHWH asher amadti lefanav im eqqach' ('As the LORD lives, before whom I stand, I will not accept it'). This is not a polite demurral; it is a sworn statement, a solemn invocation of the divine name. The formula 'as the LORD lives' (chai YHWH) was an oath of binding force in ancient Israel. It appears elsewhere in the mouth of prophets and kings when the stakes are highest (1 Samuel 14:39, 1 Kings 1:29, 2 Kings 3:14). Elisha adds 'before whom I stand' (asher amadti lefanav), emphasizing his prophetic standing—he is one who stands in the presence of the LORD. This phrase identifies the prophet as one admitted to God's council (cf. 1 Kings 22:19–22, where prophets stand before the throne of God). Elisha refuses Naaman's gift not because he is ascetic or disinterested, but because accepting payment would fundamentally alter what has happened. The healing was not a transaction; it was a revelation of God's grace. If Elisha accepted payment, the transaction would be complete, the accounts settled, the relationship severed. By refusing, Elisha keeps the revelation open.
commentary.narrative_continued: The next sentence deepens the picture: 'And he urged him to take it; but he refused.' The Hebrew va-yiftzer bo laqachat va-yema'en suggests that Naaman presses (yiftzer—pressed, urged, insisted) but Elisha remains immovable (va-yema'en—refused, held back). This is not a matter of Elisha being too humble to accept gifts. Rather, accepting Naaman's berakhah would have transformed the entire character of the encounter. Naaman came to Elisha seeking to purchase a cure; Elisha insisted that the cure could not be purchased but only received through obedience. Now Naaman wants to complete the transaction by paying the prophet. Elisha's refusal maintains the spiritual purity of what has occurred. The healing remains a gift, an unveiling of divine grace, not a service rendered for compensation. The narrative is teaching a crucial lesson: true spiritual work cannot be monetized without losing its spiritual character. Elisha stands before the LORD; he answers to the LORD alone, not to Naaman's wealth or gratitude.

word_study.meaning: The LORD lives; an oath formula invoking the life of God as a binding guarantee.
word_study.significance: This is one of the most solemn oath formulas in the Hebrew Bible. To swear 'as the LORD lives' is to invoke the eternal existence of God as a guarantee of the truth of one's statement. The formula appears in contexts of utmost seriousness: David uses it when declaring Solomon king (1 Kings 1:29), and Elisha uses it here to bind himself to his refusal. The modern ear may miss how binding this statement is—Elisha is putting his prophetic credibility on the line.

word_study.meaning: before whom I stand, in whose presence I stand. Amad means to stand; lefanav means before him.
word_study.significance: This phrase identifies Elisha as a prophetic figure admitted to the divine presence. The standing posture before God is the position of the prophetic guild (cf. 1 Kings 17:1, where Elijah says 'As the LORD God of Israel liveth, before whom I stand'). It is the stance of those who have access to God's counsel and speak with divine authority. Elisha is saying, in effect: 'I stand before God, and from that position, I tell you I will not accept your gift.'

word_study.meaning: pressed, urged, insisted; from the root meaning to break through or press against.
word_study.significance: Naaman presses (patzar) because he wants to complete the transaction, to repay the prophet and feel that accounts are settled. The verb suggests persistence, even urgency. But Elisha's refusal is immovable. The contrast between Naaman's insistence and Elisha's steadfastness emphasizes that the prophet's authority supersedes even the healed man's gratitude.

word_study.meaning: refused, rejected, held back; from the root meaning to refuse or resist.
word_study.significance: Elisha's refusal is not reluctant or polite. The verb yema'en suggests a firm, unchanging resistance. Elisha will not accept the gift, and his refusal cannot be negotiated. This same word appears when Pharaoh refuses to let the Israelites go (Exodus 7:14, 8:2) or when Jonah refuses God's command (Jonah 1:3). It is strong language for an immovable decision.

cross_references.connection: Micaiah the prophet describes standing before the throne of the LORD in the divine council; like Elisha, he speaks from the authority of direct access to God's presence.

Samuel appeals to the people as witness that he has not taken anything from anyone, maintaining prophetic integrity; Elisha similarly refuses to allow his prophetic office to become a business transaction.
Paul discusses whether apostles should receive support for their work and concludes that spiritual authority must not be compromised by payment; Elisha's refusal embodies the same principle.
Peter exhorts elders not to shepherd the flock 'for filthy lucre's sake' but willingly; prophetic and pastoral authority must be exercised for love, not gain.

The Lord teaches the early Saints: 'No one can be received into the church of God...unless he has the spirit of Christ'; the principle applies here—spiritual gifts cannot be bought or sold without losing their character.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, gift-giving was a crucial aspect of social and diplomatic relations. A gift established reciprocal obligation and sealed relationships. When Naaman offers a berakhah to Elisha, he is following the ancient Near Eastern protocol: honor the person who has served you by offering gifts. Refusal of a gift was therefore unusual and potentially offensive. Elisha's refusal breaks the expected social protocol, and in doing so, he makes a theological statement. The healing is not a commercial service; it is a revelation of divine power. The prophet cannot accept compensation without suggesting that the Lord's work is for sale. Moreover, in the ancient world, prophets were sometimes suspected of being self-interested—using divine authority to accumulate wealth or power. Elisha's refusal guards his prophetic integrity and the integrity of the Lord's work. Historically, we know that in Israel, false prophets were sometimes motivated by gain (Micah 3:5–7). True prophets, by contrast, risked their lives and sacrificed personal benefit. Elisha's refusal aligns him with the tradition of the true prophet who serves God, not Mammon.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma exemplified refusal of worldly gain when he gave up the judgment seat to preach (Alma 4:19–20). King Benjamin taught his people that they should serve one another and not seek to 'serve God only' for the sake of earthly rewards (Mosiah 2:17). The Book of Mormon consistently illustrates that true spiritual power cannot be monetized—when Korihor tried to make gain from prophesying, he was struck dumb (Alma 30:41–43). Elisha's refusal of Naaman's gift embodies the principle that prophetic power operates outside the market economy.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: In D&C 42:11, the Lord instructs the Saints: 'Let him that is ordained of God be ordained of the church, in this manner, that he may know how to act and to perform his office.' Elisha knows how to act as a prophet of God—by refusing payment. Section 51 directs the Saints to care for the poor and needy, but the motive must be charity, not gain. Section 121:39–46 teaches that ecclesiastical authority cannot be exercised 'to cover our sins' or for personal 'unrighteous dominion.' Accepting Naaman's gift would constitute a form of unrighteous dominion—allowing wealth to attach to the exercise of spiritual authority.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In the temple covenant, those who receive ordinances covenant to consecrate their time, talents, and means to the Lord. Elisha's refusal of Naaman's gift is an exemplary act of consecration—he refuses personal benefit to maintain the purity of the Lord's work. The temple teaches that spiritual gifts are the Lord's to give and the member's to receive, not commodities to be traded. The principle extends to temple workers: those who serve do so without payment, in consecration.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's refusal of Naaman's gift is a type of Christ's refusal to establish an earthly kingdom or accumulate wealth and power. Christ consistently refused the temptation to use spiritual authority for personal gain (Matthew 4:1–11). His cleansing of the temple (Matthew 21:12–13) was a direct confrontation against those who had turned the sacred space into a marketplace. Elisha's insistence that healing is not for sale prefigures Christ's teaching that salvation is freely given: 'Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters: and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price' (Isaiah 55:1). The prophet's refusal guards the nature of grace itself—grace cannot be purchased, only received.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern covenant members with a question: In what areas of my spiritual life am I trying to 'pay my way' or complete a transaction with God? The principle here is that relationship with God—forgiveness, healing, spiritual power—cannot be monetized. We cannot buy our way to righteousness through tithing (though tithing is a commandment), to forgiveness through offerings, or to spiritual gifts through effort. Yet the modern world constantly encourages transactional thinking: we work to deserve blessings, we give to get, we serve to be recognized. Elisha's refusal invites us to recognize that the deepest blessings flow from grace, not transaction. For those in positions of spiritual authority (bishops, Relief Society presidents, home teachers, parents), the verse warns against allowing authority to become a basis for personal gain or status. For all members, it invites recognition that spiritual power is not ours to sell—we are conduits, not proprietors. The verse also applies to how we receive blessings. Do we accept the Lord's healing with gratitude, or do we immediately seek to 'even the score' through works, as if grace could be repaid? Elisha teaches that grace is received, not reciprocated.

text_kjv: And Naaman said, Shall there not then, I pray thee, be given to thy servant two mules' burden of earth? for thy servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice unto other gods, but unto the LORD.
text_kjv_alt: And Naaman said, Shall there not then, I pray thee, be given to thy servant two mules' burden of earth? for thy servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice unto other gods, but unto the LORD.

commentary.narrative: Naaman's request reveals the limits of his spiritual understanding, even after his healing and his confession of monotheism. Having been refused a monetary gift, he now requests something else: adamah ('earth, soil'), as much as two mules could carry. The request seems odd to the modern reader, but it reflects a deeply rooted ancient Near Eastern assumption: deities were territorial. The God of Israel was understood to be present and powerful on Israelite land; in Syria, other gods held dominion. Naaman faces a practical problem: having renounced all gods except the God of Israel and committed to offering sacrifice only to the LORD, how can he worship the God of Israel in Damascus? His solution is to bring Israelite earth with him so that when he stands on it to pray or offer sacrifice, he will be standing on God's own territory. The request is simultaneously faithful (he has genuinely committed to exclusive worship) and mistaken (he assumes that God's power is geographically limited). His vow is clear and strong: 'thy servant will henceforth offer neither burnt offering nor sacrifice unto other gods, but unto the LORD' (lo ya'aseh od avdekha olah va-zevach le-elohim acherim ki im la-YHWH). He will not return to Aramean gods. His worship will be exclusively devoted to the God of Israel. Yet his solution to the problem of worshipping in exile reveals that he has not fully transcended the territorial assumptions of the ancient world.
commentary.narrative_continued: The Covenant Rendering clarifies the request: 'Then please let your servant be given as much earth as a pair of mules can carry.' The Hebrew va-lo yutan-na le-avdekha massa tzemed peradim adamah is a polite request, not a demand. Naaman asks for permission and relies on Elisha's grace. He does not attempt to purchase the earth (that would repeat his earlier misunderstanding) but to receive it as a gift, as something graciously granted. This reveals progress: Naaman has learned that grace cannot be purchased. Yet the presupposition—that worship of the true God requires standing on the true God's soil—remains unchallenged. The narrative will move toward a deeper problem in verse 18, where Naaman must confront an even more painful tension: his commitment to exclusive worship of the LORD will put him in the position of appearing to worship another god when his political duties require him to accompany his king to the temple of Rimmon. For now, his plan (taking Israelite soil to Damascus) attempts to resolve the geographic problem.

word_study.meaning: burden, load, carrying capacity. The root נ-שׂ-א means to lift, carry, bear.
word_study.significance: Naaman measures his need in terms of what can be physically carried—two mules' worth of earth. The term massa is used throughout the Hebrew Bible for the burden one carries, including the burden of responsibility or obligation. Naaman's request is practical: how much earth do I need to carry my new faith back to my homeland? The question itself reveals his geographical assumptions about divinity.

word_study.meaning: a yoke/pair of mules; tzemed is a yoked pair, peradim (plural of pereh) are mules—hybrid animals prized for strength and steadiness.
word_study.significance: The specificity of 'two mules' suggests practical calculation. Naaman wants enough earth to be meaningful but transportable. The use of mules (hybrids, not pure-bred horses) may be significant—these are practical, useful animals, not the prized war horses Naaman initially rode. The request reflects a humble pragmatism replacing his initial military grandeur.

word_study.meaning: earth, soil, ground, land. The same word used for the earth in Genesis 1:25 and for the promised land in exodus narratives.
word_study.significance: Adamah carries theological weight in the Hebrew Bible. It is not merely dirt but the earth that God has made, the ground that connects human beings to the divine creation. In Genesis, Adam is formed from adamah (the earth). In the Torah, the promised land is consistently referred to as the adamah, the earth that the LORD has given to Israel. Naaman's request for adamah is a request for earth that has been touched by the God of Israel, that carries the holiness of the promised land.

word_study.meaning: burnt offering (olah—that which goes up, completely consumed on the altar) and sacrifice (zevach—offering, that which is slain).
