word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'log' is more evocative than KJV's 'beam' — it suggests raw, natural material that must be shaped by human hands. This is honest, tangible work, not abstract or ceremonial. The provision of one beam per man establishes an equitable order.

word_study.meaning: Place, location, space, dwelling-place. Root meaning is 'that which is fixed or established.' Can be literal (a physical place) or metaphorical (a station, position, role).
word_study.significance: The community seeks to establish a new maqom — a fixed place where they can settle and continue their communal life. In Hebrew thought, a maqom is not merely temporary shelter but an established dwelling, implying permanence and stability.

cross_references.connection: In this verse, Elisha's community is again at work preparing food together in a communal setting, showing that physical labor and communal sharing were central to the prophetic guild's life.
The apostle calls believers 'lively stones' being built into a spiritual house — echoing the image of individuals contributing materials to a shared dwelling place, as Elisha's community does here.

When Israel builds the tabernacle, artisans are called and gifted with wisdom to work with timber and other materials. Like that sacred project, the prophetic community's building work is structured, communal, and ordered.

Nehemiah rallies Jerusalem's people to rebuild the walls by appealing to their unity and shared need — a parallel to how Elisha's community approaches their expansion with collective action and mutual commitment.

The Lord teaches that in the covenant community, 'thou shalt not take thy brother's advantage of his wages,' establishing principles of fair labor and communal support that undergird scenes like this timber harvest.

commentary.historical_context: The Jordan River in the 9th century BCE supported rich forest growth, particularly in the areas south of the Sea of Galilee and near the Dead Sea. Timber from this region was valuable and was regularly harvested for construction. The prophetic community's decision to go to the Jordan was not sentimental but practical — it was the nearest reliable source of building material. Ancient Near Eastern communities regularly organized collective labor projects for shared buildings; this was a standard way to accomplish major construction. The fairness implied by 'every man a beam' reflects an egalitarian ethos within prophetic communities, distinct from the hierarchical structures of royal courts or formal priesthoods.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 10, the Lamanites work together to fortify their city — collective labor for the community's welfare. The Book of Mormon consistently shows that faithful communities organize their labor fairly and collectively, reflecting the principle of 'all things in common' (Mosiah 26:39).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:119 teaches that the Lord's house is 'a house of learning' and that it should be built according to specific principles. The prophetic community's organized, equitable approach to building mirrors how covenant communities should approach temporal projects — with order, fairness, and united purpose.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gathering of individuals to contribute equally to a shared sacred space anticipates the temple covenant experience, where distinct individuals unite in a common purpose to build and sanctify a house of the Lord.

commentary.christological_typology: The willing contribution of each person to a shared dwelling echoes the Pauline image of the Church as the Body of Christ (1 Corinthians 12), where each member supplies their particular gift to build up the whole. Elisha's simple 'Go ye' reflects Christ's commissioning of His disciples to 'go and teach all nations' (Matthew 28:19), trusting their agency and capability.
commentary.application: This verse teaches a principle central to covenant community life: shared projects require both permission from inspired leadership and the voluntary participation of faithful members. Modern disciples should not wait for perfect conditions or micromanaged directives before undertaking the work that builds up their communities. When we identify a genuine need, propose a fair and reasonable solution, and receive affirmation from those responsible to guide us, we should proceed with confidence — understanding that honest labor in service of community welfare prepares the ground for divine help and blessing. The one-word permission 'Go ye' teaches us that inspired leaders trust their people to act with integrity and wisdom.

text_kjv: And one said, Be content, I pray thee, and go with thy servants. And he answered, I will go.

commentary.narrative:
After Elisha grants permission for the community to undertake the building project, one member makes a personal appeal: he asks Elisha not merely to approve their work, but to come and be present with them. The phrase 'Be content, I pray thee' (ho'el na) is a deferential request — literally 'be willing, please consent.' This is the voice of a disciple addressing his master with respect and affection. The request 'go with thy servants' is not commanding but beseeching — this disciple knows that Elisha's presence would be a privilege and a blessing to the entire community. Elisha's answer is equally direct and personal: 'I will go' (ani elekh). Not 'You may go' but 'I myself will come.' The addition of the pronoun ani ('I') emphasizes Elisha's personal commitment to be with his community in their work.

This moment reveals the relational quality of Elisha's leadership. He does not remain distant or aloof from his disciples' labor. Despite being a famous prophet with other demands on his time, he chooses to join them in manual work at the Jordan. This sets a precedent for prophetic leadership that transcends mere authority — it is characterized by solidarity, presence, and willingness to share in the community's tasks. The narrative structure is significant: each verse moves closer to the actual miracle. First, Elisha granted permission (verse 2); now he commits his personal presence (verse 3). Only after he has invested himself in the community's work does the sign occur. This sequence teaches that divine intervention often comes through the prophet's willingness to be genuinely present with his people.

word_study.meaning: Be willing, be pleased, consent, be content. A polite, even beseeching form requesting compliance or favorable disposition. Related to the root 'alal, meaning 'to will' or 'to choose.' The particle 'na' appended ('ho'el na') softens the request further, making it a humble petition.
word_study.significance: This is the language of reverence and affection — a disciple speaking to a beloved master, not commanding but earnestly requesting. The TCR rendering 'Please, be willing' captures the mixture of respect and intimacy. In covenant community, leaders and members relate through such mutual respect and genuine requests rather than pure command.

word_study.meaning: Servants, attendants, workers. The masculine plural possessive form 'your servants' shows the prophetic community members identifying themselves as servants in relation to Elisha. 'Eved can mean servant, slave, worker, disciple — anyone in a subordinate or supporting role.
word_study.significance: The community calls themselves Elisha's servants, not out of self-abasement but as a statement of their covenant relationship. They are bound to him in service and learning. This echoes the pattern of Old Testament prophetic apprenticeship and anticipates the New Testament model of disciples as servants of the master teacher.

word_study.meaning: I myself will go. The use of the explicit pronoun ani ('I') before the verb is emphatic — it stresses personal commitment and active choice.
word_study.significance: Elisha does not simply grant permission; he commits his own presence. The pronoun ani ('I') is crucial — it shows that the prophet is choosing to be present, not being pressured or obligated. This models how leaders in covenant communities should approach the work of building up others: with willing, personal sacrifice.

cross_references.connection: In Gethsemane, Christ commits His will to the Father's: 'Not as I will, but as thou wilt.' Like Elisha, Christ's leadership is defined by personal presence and submission to the greater work, even through suffering.

Paul exhorts believers to 'encourage one another and edify one another.' The community member's request and Elisha's acceptance model this mutual encouragement and shared commitment to building one another up.
The principle of training up a child 'in the way he should go' is illustrated here — Elisha's willingness to be personally present in his disciples' work is an act of mentorship and modeling.
Nephi teaches that leaders should 'come unto' the Lord, echoing the pattern of followers making personal requests to their guides and leaders, as the prophetic community does here with Elisha.

The Lord teaches that 'the rights of the priesthood are inseparably connected with the powers of heaven,' and that those powers are used through 'persuasion, by long-suffering, by gentleness and meekness.' Elisha's willing, gentle response to his disciples' request exemplifies this priesthood principle.

commentary.historical_context: In ancient Near Eastern hierarchical societies, a master or teacher was not expected to engage in manual labor alongside subordinates. Such egalitarianism in work would have been unusual, especially for someone of Elisha's prominence and power. His willingness to go to the Jordan with his servants reflects either an intentional counter-cultural practice or a distinctive feature of Israelite prophetic communities. The fact that the community dares to request his presence suggests that Elisha had established a culture of accessibility and mutual regard, not one of distance and formality. Such relationships — where authority figures were willing to work alongside those they served — were not the norm in royal courts or pagan temple hierarchies, making Elisha's behavior noteworthy.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 6:2-3, Alma 'walked from house to house' and 'did not esteem himself above his brethren,' mirroring Elisha's choice to be present with his community in their work. Both leaders embody the principle that spiritual authority is exercised through presence and service.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 38:24-25 establishes that in the covenant community, leaders should 'preside over you with thanksgiving.' Elisha's willing participation in the community's work is an expression of this kind of grateful, humble leadership.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The acceptance of a disciple's request and the master's commitment to be present with them foreshadows the temple experience, where God covenants to be present with His people in the sanctuary and to bless those who come before Him.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's incarnation is the ultimate expression of this principle: the divine Master chose to be personally present with His disciples, sharing meals, labor, and suffering with them. His words 'I will go' parallel Elisha's commitment, but at an infinitely greater depth — Christ went to the cross in solidarity with fallen humanity.
commentary.application: Leaders in covenant communities — whether bishops, stake presidents, parents, or any who hold responsibility for others — should ask themselves: Am I truly present with those I serve? Do I only give permission and instructions from a distance, or do I invest my personal presence in the community's work? Elisha teaches that authentic spiritual leadership requires willingness to get your hands dirty, to work alongside those you serve, and to make yourself genuinely available. For members, this verse invites the recognition that respectful, humble requests to those who lead us — made with genuine affection and not demand — often receive a response of willing presence that strengthens the entire community.

text_kjv: So he went with them. And when they came to Jordan, they cut down wood.

commentary.narrative:
This is the briefest verse in the passage, yet it is structurally essential. It records the simple fact that Elisha followed through on his commitment: he went with them, they arrived at the Jordan, and they began their work. The verb 'cut down' (va-yigzeru, from gazar) indicates the felling of trees — the physical, strenuous labor of harvesting timber. There is no indication of any miraculous assistance at this stage, no divine intervention to ease the work. Instead, Elisha and the prophetic community engage in honest, ordinary labor. The community is in Elisha's presence, working together, doing exactly what they had planned to do. This moment of normalcy is the necessary prelude to the extraordinary sign that follows. The narrative rhythm is deliberate: permission (verse 2), commitment (verse 3), action (verse 4), and only then — in verse 5 — does the crisis and miracle occur.

There is a subtle teaching here about the relationship between human effort and divine power. Elisha does not wave a staff to make trees fell themselves, nor does he speak a word to create timber from thin air. Instead, he and his community do the work. Only after they are invested in the task, after Elisha has shown his solidarity with their labor, does the need for divine intervention arise. This sequence suggests that God's miracles are not arbitrary displays of power but responsive acts of grace that enter into and sanctify human faithfulness. The community is doing their duty; now something unexpected will happen that tests whether they truly trust in divine providence even when their own resources fail.

word_study.meaning: To cut, cut down, fell, sever. The Hebrew verb gazar carries the sense of deliberate, decisive cutting — not tentative or partial, but complete felling. In the qal imperfect form (yigzeru), it indicates repeated or ongoing action.
word_study.significance: The verb suggests vigorous, intentional work. There is no hesitation or divine assistance at this stage — just the honest labor of men felling trees for building materials. The TCR rendering 'began cutting down trees' captures the purposeful, ongoing nature of the work.

word_study.meaning: Wood, tree, timber. The Hebrew word can refer to the living tree or to timber (felled wood). In this context, the plural 'etsim' suggests multiple trees being harvested.
word_study.significance: The simple, concrete focus on trees emphasizes the physical, practical nature of the task. No mystical language, no hint of the extraordinary — just the work of gathering materials from nature.

cross_references.connection: The Preacher reflects on the fruits of labor: 'Then I looked on all the works that my hands had wrought, and on the labour that I had laboured to do.' Elisha's community experiences the satisfaction of purposeful work before the miraculous intervention.
Paul writes, 'We are labourers together with God.' Elisha and his community labor faithfully at the Jordan; their human effort becomes the ground on which God's miraculous provision will rest.

The proverb teaches 'He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich.' The prophetic community works diligently; their faithfulness in labor prepares them for blessing.

The Lord teaches Joseph Smith that he must 'study it out in your mind' and 'ask if these things are not true' — emphasizing that divine revelation works in partnership with human thought and effort, not as a substitute for it.

commentary.historical_context: The Jordan River valley supported dense growth of poplar, willow, tamarisk, and acacia trees. The area was known in antiquity as a source of timber for the region (see 1 Kings 7:2, referring to the 'house of the forest of Lebanon,' which was a later, grander project, but showing the Levantine appetite for wood construction). Archaeological evidence from Iron Age sites shows that timber was regularly harvested from riverine zones and transported for building projects. The work of felling trees would have been laborious and required coordination — multiple men using axes to fell trees, strip branches, and haul the logs to the riverside for transport. Elisha's participation in this common labor would have earned respect in the ancient world, despite the cultural expectation that a famous prophet might remain aloof.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In 1 Nephi 17:5-10, Nephi and his brothers work to obtain timber and materials to build a ship. Like Elisha's community, they labor faithfully at a task, and only as they are engaged in the work does the Lord provide the specific knowledge and resources needed. The pattern shows faith working through diligent effort.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 4 teaches that in the Lord's work, 'faith, hope, and charity' must accompany effort. The prophetic community's ordinary labor at the Jordan is the context in which faith will soon be tested and strengthened.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gathering to work on a shared structure recalls the temple-building efforts throughout scripture — communities gathered to build sanctuaries for covenant worship. This scene, though smaller and more informal, participates in that same sacred principle.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ worked as a carpenter, engaging in ordinary labor (Mark 6:3). His willingness to work with His hands, like Elisha here, demonstrates that physical labor is honorable and that divine power is not opposed to earthly diligence. Later, Christ would perform miracles that multiplied provision — like the feeding of the five thousand — working through human effort to accomplish divine purposes.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that spiritual maturity and divine blessing do not exempt us from hard work; rather, they call us to work more faithfully and in better community. When we undertake a worthy project in service of others — whether building, teaching, caring, or creating — we should expect to encounter obstacles. But those obstacles do not indicate that we have chosen wrongly; rather, they are often the testing ground where faith deepens and divine help becomes visible. Do the work. Show up. Be present. Trust that your faithful labor, however ordinary it seems, is the ground on which God will work miracles of provision and grace.

text_kjv: But as one was felling a beam, the axe head fell into the water: and he cried, and said, Alas, master! for it was borrowed.

commentary.narrative:
The crisis arrives suddenly. As the community works, one man's axe head flies off into the Jordan River. In ancient times, an axe head was the most valuable part of the tool — a piece of worked iron, expensive to replace and difficult to forge anew. The man's cry of distress — 'Alas, master!' (ahah adoni) — is heightened by the explanation that immediately follows: the axe was borrowed. This detail is crucial. The loss is not merely inconvenient; it represents a debt he cannot pay. In ancient Israelite law and custom, someone who borrowed an item and lost or damaged it was obligated to restore it or compensate the owner. The man faces not only embarrassment but a genuine financial and moral obligation. His cry is a cry of genuine distress — he has lost what was entrusted to him.

Why does the narrative include this specific detail? Why emphasize that the axe was borrowed? The detail reveals Elisha's character as the answer to a community member's genuine need. This is not a story about miraculous intervention for luxury or convenience; it is about divine care for the desperate situation of a poor man — one of Elisha's own disciples — who has lost what belonged to another. Iron in the 9th century BCE was valuable; replacing it would represent weeks of wages for a laborer. The man's distress is real and sympathetic. And his cry is directed to Elisha: 'Alas, master!' — an appeal to the prophet he trusts. The narrative is subtly asking: Will Elisha help? Will the divine power present in a prophet respond to the plight of an ordinary community member who has experienced loss through no real fault of his own?

word_study.meaning: One who is felling/causing to fall a beam. The participle 'mappil' (causing to fall) from the Hebrew root naphal (to fall) suggests the active process of felling a tree or log.
word_study.significance: The use of the participle rather than past tense emphasizes the ongoing action — in the midst of the work, while actively engaged in the task, the accident occurs. There is no negligence implied; it is a common accident of dangerous labor.

word_study.meaning: Iron, as a metal. In ancient Hebrew, barzel is sometimes associated with foreign or unusual material, as iron-working was not ubiquitous in early Israel. Iron tools were valuable commodities.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering emphasizes 'the iron axe head' — making clear that this is specifically the iron component, the worked metal part of the tool. In the 9th century BCE, iron was more expensive than bronze in many regions, and iron-working required specialized knowledge. Losing an iron axe head represented a significant loss.

word_study.meaning: An exclamation of distress, grief, or alarm (ahah) followed by the address 'my master' or 'my lord.' The exclamation is visceral and genuine.
word_study.significance: The man's cry is not a quiet complaint but an anguished appeal. He cries out to Elisha as his master and authority figure — the one who might have power to help. The directness of the appeal shows both the intimacy of the community and the trust that Elisha can intervene.

word_study.meaning: Borrowed, lent out, taken on loan. From the root sha'al (to ask, borrow, lend). The word indicates a temporary loan, with the expectation of return.
word_study.significance: The man is not a careless owner of his own tool; he is the trustee of another's property. His guilt and anxiety are therefore bound up not just with personal loss but with failure to honor another's trust. This detail shows why Elisha's intervention matters so deeply — it is not mere convenience, but vindication of an honest man who faces an impossible obligation.

cross_references.connection: The law of Moses addresses liability for borrowed property: 'Every one that loseth any thing of his, and it be found in the hand of another; then both of them shall come before the judges.' Elisha's act of recovery fulfills the spirit of justice that Mosaic law addresses.
Both miracles involve a prophet responding to a community's desperate need through an act that uses natural elements (wood, water) as vehicles of divine power.

Peter and the disciples fish all night without success, then at Christ's word cast their net and catch a great multitude. Like the lost axe head, the fish represent provision that becomes visible through obedience and trust in the divine word.

The Lord teaches Joseph Smith that He will 'be merciful unto [his] weaknesses,' affirming the principle that divine power responds compassionately to human need and limitation, as Elisha's response to his disciple shows.
Alma's emphasis on being 'bound by the cords of everlasting love' reflects how the disciples of Elisha feel toward their master — bound to him by relationship, and trusting him in their desperation.

commentary.historical_context: In the 9th century BCE Levantine world, iron tools were increasingly available but still costly. A smith's work to produce an iron axe head would require significant labor and expertise. The loss of borrowed iron would represent a serious obligation — possibly weeks or months of wages for a laborer. The man's distress is historically authentic: in a pre-industrial economy, the loss of an expensive tool through which one earned one's livelihood was catastrophic. Borrowing and lending were common economic practices in the ancient Near East, and the duty to return borrowed property or compensate for loss was legally and morally binding. The man's cry reflects the very real anxiety of someone facing a debt he cannot easily repay.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 7:25-26, Limhi and his people cry out in their affliction, and the Lord hears and remembers them. The pattern shows that God responds to the genuine distress of His people, particularly when they cry out in faith to a representative of divine authority.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 27:14 teaches that in the gathering of the righteous, 'My servant Joseph shall be privileged to come in and partake of the sacraments with us.' The inclusion of the lost and suffering in the community's welfare is central to covenant practice. Elisha's response to his disciple's loss reflects this principle.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The man's cry for help and Elisha's willingness to intervene reflects the covenant principle that the Lord hears the cries of His children in affliction (D&C 121:1). The temple is a place where such cries are heard and answered.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's willingness to be moved by the distress of common people is foreshadowed here. The man's cry 'Alas, master!' parallels the desperate appeals Jesus received: 'Lord, help me!' (Matthew 15:25), 'Jesus, Master, have mercy on us' (Luke 17:13). Christ's response to such cries demonstrated divine compassion for human need.
commentary.application: This verse invites us to see ourselves in the man who lost the borrowed axe. In life, we all lose things — whether material items, opportunities, or even our sense of moral standing. We all face obligations we cannot meet through our own strength. The question is: Will we cry out to the Lord, or hide in shame? The narrative suggests that Elisha's disciples were in a community where such honest, vulnerable confession was possible. We should ask whether our families, wards, and personal relationships create space for such honest admissions of need. And those of us in positions of leadership should ask: When someone comes to me in genuine distress, about to face an impossible obligation they cannot meet, am I moved to help? Or do I judge them for their carelessness? Elisha's response teaches that divine power and human compassion respond not to the perfect, but to the humble and honest.

text_kjv: And the man of God said, Where fell it? And he shewed him the place. And he cut down a stick, and cast it in thither; and the iron did swim.

commentary.narrative:
The sign-act itself is remarkably simple and strange. Elisha asks where the axe head fell — a practical question that seems almost mundane. The man shows him the spot. Then Elisha cuts a stick (or branch) from a nearby tree, throws it into the water, and 'the iron did swim.' This is the miracle: iron, which is heavier than water, floats to the surface. Nothing else happens. No elaborate prayer, no dramatic gesture, no invocation of God's name — just the casting of a stick, and the natural order reverses. Iron floats. The narrative's economy is remarkable: it reports the sign with no comment, no elaboration, no explanation of Elisha's source of power.

Why this particular sign? And why does the narrative reference Exodus 15:25 — where Moses throws wood into bitter waters to make them sweet? The TCR translator notes this parallel, and it is illuminating. In both cases, a prophet responds to a community's desperate need with a sign-act that involves casting wood into water. The sign reverses or corrects a deficiency: bitter becomes sweet; heavy becomes light. The sign also demonstrates something crucial about how divine power operates in the world: it is not a magical override of physical law, but a gracious entering into physical reality to accomplish what human power cannot. The stick Elisha throws does not magically make iron buoyant; rather, through the stick, the divine power present in the prophet manifests in a way that lifts the iron to the surface.

The power on display here is not primarily about dazzling miracles; it is about divine care for a disciple's distress. The man will get his borrowed tool back, restore it to its owner, and be released from an impossible debt. The miracle is oriented entirely toward justice, restoration, and the welfare of an ordinary community member. Elisha does not perform the sign to prove his power or to make a name for himself; he performs it because his disciple is in distress and he is moved to help.

word_study.meaning: Man of God; a prophet who operates as God's representative and channels divine power into the world. The title appears frequently for Elijah (1 Kings 17:18, 24; 2 Kings 1:9), Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Samuel (1 Samuel 9:6), and others.
word_study.significance: The title 'ish ha-Elohim' is used precisely in contexts where the prophet is about to perform a sign or speak a word from the Lord. It designates not merely a holy person but one whose agency has become a vessel for divine action. The TCR rendering 'the man of God' (with the definite article) emphasizes that Elisha has a recognized, specific role as God's spokesman.

word_study.meaning: Where did it fall? Anah is an interrogative ('where'), and napal is the root 'to fall.' The question is simple and direct.
word_study.significance: Elisha's question might seem unnecessary — he is a prophet with divine knowledge. Yet he asks. This detail humanizes the interaction and shows Elisha engaging the disciple's need with genuine attention. The question also has a symbolic dimension: identification of the lost thing, locating it precisely, is the first step toward restoration.

word_study.meaning: Tree, wood, stick, timber. The same root word used in verse 4 ('etsim, trees'), but here in the singular.
word_study.significance: Elisha cuts a single stick and casts it. The simplicity is striking. Not a grand staff or ceremonial object, but just a stick cut from a nearby tree. This reinforces the theme of divine power working through simple, available means. The TCR translator notes the connection to Exodus 15:25, where Moses cast wood (ets) into bitter waters. Both prophetic signs use the same Hebrew word and the same method.

word_study.meaning: To float, swim, buoy up. The verb suggests rising to the surface or staying afloat. It is not the normal word for 'float' in Hebrew (that would be tzif), but tzafaf, which carries a sense of movement and liveliness — almost as if the iron actively rises.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'floated to the surface' captures the sense of active, upward motion. Iron does not naturally float; its rising is a reversal of normal physical law. Yet the verb suggests something graceful and natural-seeming, not a violent upheaval. The divine power is exerted with gentleness.

cross_references.connection: Moses casts wood (ets) into bitter waters at Marah, and they become sweet. Elisha casts wood (ets) into the Jordan, and iron (which should sink) floats. Both signs involve a prophet using a stick to reverse or correct a deficiency affecting the community.

Elijah provides for the widow of Zarephath, multiplying her flour and oil so she will not experience want. Like that sign, Elisha's recovery of the borrowed axe is motivated by compassion for someone facing deprivation.

Christ blesses bread and fish, multiplying them to feed five thousand. The sign involves taking ordinary material (bread and fish) and through a prophet's prayer transforming it into abundance — like Elisha's stick transforming the law of nature for the iron.
Peter walks on water at Christ's command — another reversal of natural law, demonstrating that divine power transcends physical limitation and can elevate what naturally would sink.

In the Kirtland Temple dedication, Joseph Smith prays that the Lord will 'enable those who minister in [this] house to understand thy Spirit, and to be worthy of thy trust.' Elisha's ability to work divine signs shows how thoroughly his spirit is aligned with God's will and concern for His people.

commentary.historical_context: The Jordan River in the 9th century BCE was a significant boundary and resource for the region, but it was also dangerous — swift currents, deep pools, and potentially treacherous conditions made it a place where tools and materials could easily be lost. The recovery of the axe head at the Jordan where it was lost demonstrates Elisha's power operating in a specific place where the community had gathered. The miracle occurs not in a temple or at an altar, but at a work site where ordinary people are doing ordinary labor. This is theologically significant: divine power is not confined to sacred spaces but operates wherever the prophets of God are present to invoke it. The ancient world knew of water-magic and purification rituals involving wood, so the Israelite audience would have understood that Elisha's action — casting wood into water — had symbolic weight, even if the outcome (iron floating) was extraordinary.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 37:35-36, Alma teaches Helaman that divine power flows to the righteous through keeping covenants and seeking wisdom. Elisha's sign flows from his covenant relationship with God and his alignment with God's character — concern for the poor and vulnerable. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that miracles arise from faithful obedience and genuine charity (Ether 12:12).
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 34:10 teaches that the Lord will work through His servants to bring about 'signs and wonders.' The sign of the floating iron is not self-aggrandizing but oriented toward restoring justice and relieving the distress of a covenant community member. This aligns with D&C 64:10, teaching that the Lord will 'freely forgive' and that His servants should embody the same forgiveness and restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The reversal of natural law — iron floating — prefigures the temple covenant, where we are lifted above our natural fallen state and exalted through ordinances and covenants. The sign is a miniature version of what the temple accomplishes spiritually: reversing what naturally would drag us down, elevating us through divine power.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ's command of natural law — 'Peace, be still' (Mark 4:39), His walking on water (Matthew 14:25), His multiplication of loaves and fishes (John 6:11) — all parallel Elisha's miraculous sign. Christ is the ultimate 'man of God' who manifests divine power not for display but for mercy toward those in need. The axe head is recovered; the broken, lost thing is made whole — a type of Christ's redemptive work, which restores what sin has broken and makes whole what was lost.
commentary.application: This verse teaches several interconnected principles for modern covenant life. First, it shows that divine power is not reserved for grand, public moments but flows toward ordinary people facing real distress. If you are struggling with an impossible obligation, a loss you cannot repair, a burden you cannot lift — cry out. God hears. Second, it demonstrates that prophetic authority is not about self-promotion or dazzling displays but about genuine care for community members' welfare. If you hold any kind of leadership, ask: Am I moved to help people in my community who face loss or distress? Third, it invites us to understand miracles not as violations of nature but as gracious interventions by divine power that can reverse what naturally would destroy us. The stick Elisha cast is small and simple, yet through it flows the power of heaven. Our own faithfulness, our own repentance, our own small acts of obedience are similarly vehicles through which divine grace operates to restore and elevate us. Finally, the sign assures us that what we have lost through accident, carelessness, or circumstance is not beyond the reach of divine mercy. The man who lost the borrowed axe is fully restored. We, too, are offered restoration — if we cry out in faith and align ourselves with God's purposes.

text_kjv: Therefore said he, Take it up to thee. And he put out his hand, and took it.

commentary.narrative: This verse concludes the miracle of the floating axe head. Elisha's command is deceptively simple: 'Pick it up.' Yet it carries profound theological weight. The miracle itself—the restoration of the lost iron head—has already occurred through Elisha's prayer and the work of God. What remains is for the man to act. This is the pattern throughout scripture: God works, but His people must respond in faith and obedience. The man's reaching out his hand and taking the restored axe represents the crucial human cooperation with divine grace. Without this action, the miracle would remain external, unappropriated. The TCR rendering 'The man reached out his hand and took it' emphasizes the concrete, physical nature of the response—faith must be embodied in action.
commentary.narrative_continued: This moment also reflects the principle that miracles are not given to replace human responsibility but to enable it. The axe head belonged to the man; it was his tool for his work. God restores it, but the man must take possession of it again. In the broader context of Elisha's ministry, we see a prophet who does not simply pronounce blessings from a distance. He engages in the immediate, practical concerns of ordinary people. A widow's sons are about to be enslaved; Elisha provides oil. An army loses an axe in a river; Elisha recovers it. These are not grand theophanic moments but tender acts of divine care for the vulnerable and the working poor.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The simplicity of the command—'Take it up'—also teaches that once God has done His part, we must do ours without hesitation or doubt. The man does not question whether the axe will float, does not ask for further assurance. He simply reaches out and takes what has been restored. This is the kind of trust Elisha cultivates throughout his ministry: not a passive waiting for God to do everything, but an active reception of what God provides.
commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's restoration of the axe head prefigures Christ's redemptive work. Just as the man had lost his tool through no sin of his own and Elisha restored it without cost to the man, Christ restores humanity's capacity for righteousness that was lost through the Fall. Yet the parallel also holds in the requirement for response—salvation comes through Christ's atonement, but individuals must 'reach out' in faith, repentance, and covenant-making to appropriate its power.

word_study.meaning: To lift, raise, take up; in this context, to appropriate or claim possession. The root carries the sense of elevation and active engagement. The TCR rendering 'Pick it up' captures the colloquial directness of the command—a simple instruction to take action.
word_study.significance: Harem is not passive receipt but active appropriation. The man must 'lift' the axe from the water, making it his own again through a deliberate act. This parallels the spiritual principle that grace must be accepted and incorporated into one's life through conscious choice.

word_study.meaning: Sent forth his hand; extended his hand. The verb shalach ('to send, stretch out') is used throughout scripture for reaching toward, grasping, and taking hold. Here it describes the physical gesture of faith—the outstretched hand is both practical and symbolic.
word_study.significance: The hand is the instrument of human agency. To stretch out one's hand toward God's provision is to demonstrate readiness to receive and participate. This phrase echoes other instances in scripture where people must physically reach for what God provides (Exodus 15:12, Deuteronomy 4:34).

cross_references.connection: The widow's oil miracle follows the same pattern: God provides supernatural provision through Elisha, but the widow and her sons must actively participate (gathering vessels, pouring oil) for the miracle to be realized.
New Testament exhortation to 'be not slothful, but followers of them who through faith and patience inherit the promises'—active reception of divine provision requires human cooperation and effort.

Modern revelation emphasizing that the Lord 'cannot look upon sin with the least degree of allowance' but also that His children must 'be anxiously engaged in a good cause' and 'do many things of their own free will.'
Lehi's teaching that 'ye are free to act for yourselves'—God provides options and blessings, but humans must choose to receive and act upon them.

commentary.application: In modern covenant life, this verse teaches that receiving God's blessings requires both trust in God's power and active participation. We cannot simply pray and wait passively; faith includes taking the concrete steps necessary to receive what God has prepared. Whether seeking guidance, healing, or restoration after loss, we must ultimately 'reach out our hand' through obedience, effort, and deliberate choice. The verse challenges the notion that spirituality is purely internal or that divine blessings automatically overflow without our engagement. Our responsibility is to recognize God's provision and actively claim it.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon repeatedly emphasizes the principle of responsive faith—that grace operates through human agency. In Alma 26:16-17, Ammon testifies that the Lord's work cannot be accomplished 'except through the works of the children of men' and that God provides the opportunity but humans must 'exercise faith in Christ.' Similarly, the Nephite emphasis on personal accountability aligns with the principle that God restores, but we must receive and act.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 58:26-27 teaches that those who serve the Lord must 'be anxiously engaged in a good cause' and 'do many things of their own free will.' The restoration principle extends beyond doctrinal clarification to behavioral expectations—we are agents in receiving and implementing divine blessings.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The pattern of divine provision followed by human participation mirrors covenant ceremony, where God's ordinances are presented and individuals must enter into them through their own choice and action. The extended hand reaching for blessing resonates with temple themes of reaching upward toward God's highest blessings.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of working in water—whether for irrigation, washing, or harvesting materials—was common in ancient Near Eastern societies. Iron tools were valuable and relatively rare in this period (the Iron Age was still establishing itself in the Levant during the 9th century BCE). The loss of an iron axe head would represent significant economic hardship for a laborer or young man. Archaeological evidence from sites in Israel/Palestine shows that metallurgical practices involved working near water sources for cooling and tempering. The miracle's restoration of the tool speaks to God's concern for the economic welfare of ordinary working people, not just kings and the wealthy.

text_kjv: Then the king of Syria warred against Israel, and took counsel with his servants, saying, In such and such a place shall be my camp.

commentary.narrative: The scene shifts abruptly from personal miracles to international military conflict. The Aramean king is actively conducting military campaigns against Israel. This is the historical context that had been building throughout the Omride period and into the reign of Jehoram: sustained military pressure from the Syrian (Aramean) kingdom to the northeast. The king convenes his war council, consulting with his officers about military strategy. His statement about setting up camp at 'such and such a place' reflects the kind of detailed operational planning required for military campaigns—choosing supply routes, defensible positions, and locations for ambush or engagement. The Hebrew phrase 'peloni almoni' (such-and-such, a certain place) is a deliberate withholding of information; the narrator knows these sites exist but chooses not to name them, emphasizing that the specificity of the location matters only to those involved in the campaign.
commentary.narrative_continued: What makes this verse crucial to the narrative is its contrast with what comes next. The Aramean king believes his war councils are private, that his strategic decisions are known only to his inner circle of trusted officers. Yet somehow, every plan reaches the ears of the king of Israel. From the king of Aram's perspective, this is inexplicable and maddening. From the narrator's perspective (and the reader's), the explanation is already clear: Elisha has access to divine knowledge that transcends ordinary intelligence networks. The verse sets up the tension that will drive the next four verses—a military commander whose plans are perpetually compromised by an enemy he cannot identify or eliminate.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The historical backdrop is important: the 9th-century relationship between Israel and Aram was characterized by intermittent warfare, trade conflicts, and occasional alliances. This particular passage suggests a period when Aram held military advantage and was conducting regular raids or campaigns into Israelite territory. The king's confidence in his ability to execute surprise attacks suggests he expects military success, yet his plans are consistently thwarted. This introduces an element of the supernatural into what appears to be ordinary military history.
commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's role as a revealer of hidden counsels and thwarter of enemy designs prefigures Christ's resurrection and ascension, whereby He gained access to all knowledge and authority. In John 2:24-25, the gospel declares that Jesus 'knew all men, and needed not that any should tell him of any man: for he knew what was in man'—a capacity Elisha demonstrates on a smaller scale through prophetic insight into the Aramean king's private deliberations.

word_study.meaning: Waged war, fought, engaged in combat. The niphal (passive) form suggests being in a state of ongoing war rather than a single decisive battle. This king is perpetually at war with Israel—warfare is his condition.
word_study.significance: The niphal form implies a habitual state rather than isolated incidents. The king of Aram is characterized by constant military engagement, suggesting that military conflict defined the political relationship between Aram and Israel during this period.

word_study.meaning: Conferred, deliberated, took counsel. The hitpael form suggests mutual deliberation with his officers. This is not an autocrat issuing orders but a commander consulting with his generals and strategists.
word_study.significance: Even kings rely on counsel and strategy. The verb emphasizes that military operations require planning and the input of experienced officers. Yet all this deliberation will be rendered useless by divine knowledge.

word_study.term_english: In such and such a place
word_study.meaning: To a certain place, to such-and-such a place; an idiom meaning an unnamed, unspecified location. The TCR rendering emphasizes this is 'such-and-such a place'—the reader is not meant to know its identity. This is a Hebrew idiom for deliberate anonymity.
word_study.significance: The narrator uses this formulaic phrase to indicate that while the specific location matters for the campaign, the reader need not know it. What matters is that these plans, whatever their specifics, will be known to Elisha and communicated to the king of Israel. The anonymity of the location underscores that the precise geography is less important than the theological principle: no human strategy escapes divine omniscience.

cross_references.connection: An earlier episode where the king of Aram (Ben-hadad) makes military threats, but the prophet provides strategic guidance that ensures Israel's victory—establishing the pattern of prophetic knowledge informing military affairs.

The psalmist declares that 'the Lord bringeth the counsel of the heathen to nought: he maketh the devices of the people of none effect'—here Elisha becomes the instrument of God's frustration of Aramean strategy.

Isaiah proclaims that human counsel will be brought to nothing: 'Take counsel together, and it shall come to nought; speak the word, and it shall not stand'—an echo of the principle illustrated through Elisha's prophetic knowledge.

In latter-day revelation, the Lord teaches that 'it is the nature and disposition of almost all people, as soon as they get a little authority, as they suppose, they will immediately begin to exercise unrighteous dominion'—yet the righteous are preserved by superior knowledge.

commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse illustrates that human schemes and strategies, however carefully planned and confidently executed, are known to God and subject to His overarching purposes. When facing opposition or persecution, there is comfort in knowing that those working against righteousness operate without divine knowledge or ultimate authority. The verse also teaches that those who serve God's purposes—like Elisha—are given insight and wisdom that exceeds ordinary intelligence. In practical terms, this suggests the importance of seeking divine guidance for decisions rather than relying solely on human reasoning, and trusting that God's knowledge of our circumstances and our adversaries' intentions exceeds our own.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains parallel episodes where divine knowledge supersedes human military intelligence. In Alma 16:5-8, Alma inquires of the Lord regarding the Lamanite army's movements and receives specific knowledge about their location and intentions. Like Elisha, Alma serves as a conduit for divine intelligence that preserves his people from ambush and destruction. Both narratives demonstrate that the Lord's knowledge extends to the plans and movements of His people's enemies.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-6 teaches that the president of the Church will receive revelations to guide the Church, as Joseph Smith was promised divine guidance 'in all things that pertain to this kingdom.' The principle that God reveals enemy designs and strategies to His chosen servants extends from ancient times through the Restoration.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple ceremony and covenant language, the righteous are taught that God's knowledge surpasses that of all nations and powers. The endowment teaches that the righteous are equipped with knowledge and power beyond what the world possesses—a principle illustrated through Elisha's supernatural awareness of enemy movements.

commentary.historical_context: The mid-9th century BCE was marked by significant Aramean expansion under dynasties centered in Damascus. Archaeological evidence from inscriptions (such as the Tel Dan Stele mentioning the 'House of David') and administrative records shows that Aramean kings conducted regular military campaigns through the Levantine corridor. The setting of military camps and supply lines was standard ancient Near Eastern military practice. Kings would deliberate with officers regarding routes, terrain, defensible positions, and seasonal timing. The phrase 'took counsel with his servants' reflects authentic military procedure—commanders in the ancient world relied on the advice of experienced officers and strategists. The mention of specific encampment locations suggests knowledge of terrain and established routes through Israel, consistent with the military campaigns documented in both biblical and extra-biblical sources.

text_kjv: And the man of God sent unto the king of Israel, saying, Beware that thou pass not such a place; for thither the Syrians are come down.

commentary.narrative: Elisha now acts on the knowledge he has received. Rather than simply knowing the Aramean plans privately, he immediately conveys this intelligence to the king of Israel. He is not a prophet who hoards revelation for spiritual prestige or personal advantage; he is a deliverer of divine warnings meant to protect the nation. The TCR rendering 'The man of God sent word to the king of Israel: Be careful not to pass through that place, because the Arameans are positioned there' emphasizes the practical, urgent nature of the communication. This is not mystical pronouncement but concrete tactical intelligence. Elisha warns specifically against passing through certain locations because enemies are 'positioned there'—the Hebrew verb nechittim suggests they have taken up ambush positions, lying in wait for Israelite forces to enter their territory.
commentary.narrative_continued: The interaction between Elisha and the king is mediated—Elisha 'sends' his message; he does not appear in person to make the statement. This may reflect the political reality that a prophet did not automatically have direct access to the king, but it also illustrates an important principle: Elisha's prophetic word does not require his physical presence to be effective. The word itself, conveyed through a messenger, carries divine authority and must be obeyed. The king's response to this repeated warning (as verse 10 will clarify) is not skepticism but action—he heeds the warnings and sends scouts to verify or avoid the warned locations. This suggests that Elisha's credibility with the king is already established before this episode begins.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What emerges from this verse is the role of the prophet as a guardian of the nation's survival. Elisha is not content to perform miracles for individuals; he exercises his prophetic office in service of the state's security and the people's welfare. He stands between his nation and destruction, using supernatural knowledge to prevent ambushes and military disaster. This expands significantly the scope of Elisha's ministry beyond the personal miracles of earlier chapters.
commentary.christological_typology: Elisha's warning to the king prefigures Christ's role as intercessor and guardian of His people. In John 10:27-28, Christ declares, 'My sheep hear my voice... and no man is able to pluck them out of my Father's hand.' Like Elisha warning the king to avoid ambush, Christ warns and protects His people from spiritual destruction and deception. The theme of the prophet as sentinel guarding against danger resonates with Isaiah 62:6, where watchmen are appointed to 'give the Lord no rest' through persistent intercession for protection.

word_study.meaning: Man of God; a prophetic title emphasizing that the prophet is identified and empowered by God. The phrase appears frequently in Deuteronomistic literature and in prophetic narratives, denoting one who represents and acts on behalf of God.
word_study.significance: The title 'man of God' establishes Elisha's authority. He does not speak merely as a political advisor but as one whose words carry divine weight and authenticity. The same title is used for Moses (Deuteronomy 33:1), Elijah (1 Kings 17:18), and other prophets.

word_study.meaning: Guard yourself, take heed, be on guard. The reflexive form indicates active vigilance and protective action. This is a command to heighten awareness and take precautions.
word_study.significance: The verb conveys urgency and necessity. This is not merely information but a command to act protectively. The king must be vigilant, must guard himself against the threatened danger.

word_study.meaning: Do not pass through, do not cross over. A negative command preventing movement through a specific region.
word_study.significance: The simplicity of the command—avoid this place—reflects the practicality of Elisha's intelligence. The solution is straightforward: the king need only refrain from moving through the ambush site.

word_study.meaning: Have positioned themselves, have descended into position, are lying in wait. The verb suggests tactical positioning—the Arameans have taken up strategic positions, perhaps in elevated terrain or concealed locations.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'are positioned there' captures the sense better than the KJV's 'are come down,' which could imply merely arrival. Nechittim suggests active, deliberate positioning for military advantage—they are waiting to ambush. The verb choice conveys not just presence but hostile readiness.

cross_references.connection: Saul seeks out Samuel the prophet, and he is told 'he is an honourable man; and all that he saith surely cometh to pass.' Elisha, like Samuel, is a prophet whose words prove reliable and whose advice proves protective.

King Jehoshaphat seeks prophetic counsel before military engagement, and Elijah's representative brings unwelcome but true counsel that protects the king from disaster—a parallel pattern of prophetic warning preventing military catastrophe.

Jeremiah receives divine direction to warn the people against taking a particular course of action, just as Elisha warns against passing through a particular place. In both cases, the prophetic word is meant to preserve life.

The Lord promises that a prophet called to lead the Church 'shall receive my law, and shall keep my commandments; and in his heart shall keep all the covenants'—the prophet is given divine knowledge for the protection and guidance of the covenant people.

commentary.application: In modern covenant life, this verse teaches the critical importance of heeding prophetic warning. The king of Israel prospered in his military campaigns specifically because he listened to Elisha's counsel and took evasive action. Similarly, members of the Church are blessed when they heed the warnings of living prophets and apostles regarding spiritual dangers and false paths. The verse also suggests that prophetic guidance is often practical and actionable—not vague spiritual platitude but specific direction about what to avoid and what to pursue. Just as the king could 'pass not through such a place,' modern believers are counseled to avoid specific behaviors, media, relationships, and philosophies that pose spiritual hazard. The principle is clear: the prophet's role includes warning against danger before it arrives, allowing the faithful to take preventative action rather than suffering consequences after harm is done.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 43:22-25, Alma receives from the Lord knowledge of Lamanite military movements and positions his forces strategically in response. Like Elisha, Alma combines divine knowledge with military wisdom to protect his people. The Book of Mormon repeatedly shows that prophetic knowledge extends to enemies' plans and movements when necessary to protect the Lord's covenant people.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 38:29 teaches that 'I, the Lord, will make known unto you what things are expedient for you'—the principle that God reveals necessary knowledge for the survival and protection of His people. The modern Church similarly relies on prophetic leadership to provide guidance that protects the Saints from spiritual and temporal dangers.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: Covenant ceremony teaches that the Lord provides protective knowledge and guidance to those who enter into covenant with Him. The endowment includes instruction that the righteous are given knowledge that surpasses what the world possesses, enabling them to avoid deception and harm.

commentary.historical_context: In the ancient Near East, military intelligence and reconnaissance were critical aspects of warfare. Commanders relied on scouts, spies, and informants to gather information about enemy movements and terrain. The practice of setting ambushes in strategically advantageous locations (passes, defiles, river crossings) was standard military strategy. Archaeological evidence from military campaigns and inscriptions shows that commanders studied terrain, identified choke points, and planned ambushes accordingly. The prophet Elisha's provision of tactical intelligence would have been understood in the ancient world within the context of divine favor and blessing—a king blessed by the gods (or in Israel's case, by Yahweh) would have access to foreknowledge through divine intermediaries. Aramean military operations in the 9th century BCE are documented in Assyrian records and other Near Eastern sources, confirming the historical plausibility of sustained campaigns in the region.

text_kjv: And the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God told him and warned him of, and saved himself there, not once nor twice.

commentary.narrative: This verse marks the culmination of the pattern established in verses 8-9: Elisha provides intelligence, the king acts on it, and the result is that Israel is saved from Aramean ambush. Critically, the TCR rendering makes clear that this was not a single incident—'not once or twice, but repeatedly'—the Hebrew idiom lo achat ve-lo shtayim indicates that this pattern occurred many times. The king of Israel did not simply react once to Elisha's warning; he established an ongoing practice of sending scouts or reconnaissance forces to the locations Elisha had warned about, and in each case, he was able to protect himself and avoid disaster. The phrase 'saved himself there' suggests both personal safety for the king and, by extension, the safety of his forces and the avoidance of military catastrophe.
commentary.narrative_continued: The repeated nature of this pattern is essential to the narrative arc. A single successful prediction might be dismissed as coincidence or lucky guessing. But repeated, pattern-based warnings that consistently prevent military disaster establish an undeniable pattern of divine knowledge and intervention. By the time we reach verse 11, when the king of Aram becomes enraged and suspicious, the reader understands fully why: the Aramean king's military plans have been consistently and inexplicably compromised. From his perspective, someone in his inner circle must be a traitor; there is no other rational explanation for why every campaign plan is discovered before execution.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: What is also notable is the king of Israel's response. He does not demand proof from Elisha or hesitate in implementation. Rather, he 'sent to the place' with what appears to be trusting obedience. The TCR rendering 'sent scouts to the place' (implied by context) shows that the king took Elisha's warnings seriously enough to verify them and adjust his military movements accordingly. This is the posture of a wise ruler—he does not blindly follow every rumor, but he respects Elisha's credibility enough to investigate and protect himself. Over time, as the pattern repeated, the king's confidence in Elisha's warnings would only deepen.
commentary.christological_typology: The king's repeated salvation through heeding prophetic warning prefigures the salvation available to humanity through Christ. Just as the king is 'saved' from military destruction through accepting Elisha's guidance, humanity is saved from spiritual destruction through accepting Christ's teaching and intercession. The repetition ('not once nor twice') emphasizes that salvation is not a one-time event but an ongoing process of accepting guidance and protection.

word_study.term_original: וַיִּשְׁלַח מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶל־הַמָּקוֹם (va-yishlach melekh israel el-hammakom)
word_study.meaning: The king of Israel sent [forces/scouts] to the place. The verb shalach ('send') in military context typically implies sending troops or reconnaissance to investigate, secure, or avoid a location.
word_study.significance: The king's action is both protective and verifying. He sends scouts to confirm Elisha's warning and to protect himself if the warning proves accurate. This demonstrates the king's practical wisdom—he does not require absolute faith but uses prudent verification.

word_study.meaning: And he guarded/preserved himself there. The reflexive verb form indicates active protection and vigilance. The king does not passively wait but takes protective measures in the warned location.
word_study.significance: The reflexive form emphasizes human agency combined with divine knowledge. The king learns where danger is positioned and takes active steps to avoid it. He is not passively rescued but actively uses divinely-provided information to protect himself.

word_study.term_original: לֹא אַחַת וְלֹא שְׁתָּיִם (lo achat ve-lo shtayim)
word_study.meaning: Not one time and not two times; an idiomatic expression meaning 'many times, repeatedly, not just once or twice.' This is a Hebrew way of saying the pattern happened multiple times—more than two occasions, establishing a consistent pattern.
word_study.significance: The TCR rendering 'not once or twice, but repeatedly' captures the idiom's force. The repetition transforms what might be coincidence into undeniable pattern. The Aramean king's frustration (in verse 11) is now fully justified—his plans have been compromised not once but systematically, repeatedly, inexplicably.

cross_references.connection: The proverb teaches, 'A prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself: but the simple pass on, and are punished.' The king of Israel demonstrates prudence by heeding Elisha's foresight and taking protective action.

David repeatedly narrowly escapes Saul's pursuit, and the narrative attributes his safety to divine intervention and providence. Like the king of Israel, David is 'saved' through a combination of human prudence and divine protection.
The psalmist declares that the righteous are protected under God's wings and will see the destruction of the wicked—the king of Israel experiences this protection through Elisha's prophetic warnings.

The Kirtland Temple prayer includes the petition 'that Zion may flourish and be established in righteousness, and that all our borders may be enlarged'—reflecting the principle that God's covenant people are protected and preserved when they heed divine counsel.

commentary.application: For modern members, this verse teaches the cumulative power of trusting prophetic guidance. The king did not need to see all future Aramean campaigns to develop confidence in Elisha; each verified warning built his trust. Similarly, members who observe that prophetic counsel proves true on multiple occasions in their own lives develop deeper faith and more willingly accept guidance in untested areas. The verse also illustrates a practical approach to faith: the king used intelligence to verify the prophecy and took actionable steps based on it. Modern believers can similarly expect prophetic guidance to be both spiritual and practical, and can respond through both faith and prudent action. The principle of 'not once nor twice' suggests that patterns matter—a single experience might be coincidence, but repeated patterns establish reliability and deserve trust.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: Alma's pattern of military success described in Alma 44:19-20 similarly rests on the foundation of divine knowledge and wisdom. Alma wins battles 'by stratagem' and foresight, much as the king of Israel avoids ambushes through Elisha's intelligence. The Book of Mormon teaches repeatedly that the righteous who heed prophetic counsel experience temporal and spiritual preservation.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-6 promises the Church president that 'he shall be blessed, for all those who receive the sayings of my servant shall know that his words are true and that light and truth shall be established.' The king of Israel's repeated verification that Elisha's warnings prove true builds his confidence, just as the Doctrine and Covenants promises that prophetic words will be verified as true.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The endowment teaches that those who enter covenant with God receive not only spiritual promises but practical protection and guidance for navigating worldly dangers. The principle of being 'warned' and taking protective action, as the king did, is central to covenant theology—the Lord provides knowledge necessary to avoid spiritual and temporal pitfalls.

commentary.historical_context: Military reconnaissance and intelligence gathering were essential practices in ancient Near Eastern warfare. Commanders would send scouts or advance forces to investigate reports of enemy movements, to verify intelligence, and to secure advantageous positions. The practice of fortifying or preparing defenses at strategic locations was standard. Archaeological evidence from fortified settlements and military outposts shows that armies stationed watchers and guards at vulnerable points to provide early warning of attack. The repeated success of the king of Israel in avoiding Aramean ambushes suggests that over a period of time, multiple coordinated campaigns were planned and thwarted. This pattern would be historically plausible during a period of sustained military tension between Israel and Aram, consistent with the 9th-century BCE context in which Elisha's ministry is set.

text_kjv: Therefore the heart of the king of Syria was sore troubled for this thing; and he called his servants, and said unto them, Will ye not shew me which of us is for the king of Israel?

commentary.narrative: The Aramean king's mounting frustration now comes to a breaking point. The TCR rendering 'The king of Aram was enraged over this' captures the escalation from mere military setback to personal fury. The Hebrew verb va-yissa'er ('was stormy, was agitated') describes an internal turbulence—his heart is in turmoil. This is not the calm deliberation we saw in verse 8; this is the rage of a commander whose plans are repeatedly thwarted. The king's logic is straightforward: his military strategies are secrets shared only with his inner circle of officers and servants. Yet somehow every plan reaches his enemy before implementation. The only rational explanation he can conceive is that one of his own people is a traitor, leaking information to the king of Israel. His question—'Which of you is working for the king of Israel?'—expresses both accusation and desperation. He is demanding that his officers identify the spy in their midst.
commentary.narrative_continued: What is particularly poignant about this moment is the king's blindness to the true explanation. He assumes human treachery because he cannot conceive of divine knowledge. His entire worldview is materialist, bounded by what human agents can know and communicate. The very concept that an enemy prophet might have supernatural access to his private conversations does not occur to him—or rather, it will occur to him only when his officers provide the explanation in verse 12. The king's question reveals the limits of natural explanation and sets up the moment when the supernatural dimension enters his consciousness. His question also reveals his authority and power: he can demand answers from his officers, can threaten and investigate for disloyalty. Yet his power is powerless against the one true source of his problem—Elisha and the God who empowers him.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: There is also a tragic element here. The king of Aram is wise in military affairs, capable of strategic planning and execution. Yet his very rationalism blinds him to spiritual reality. He cannot see what his own officers will soon explain: that the prophet Elisha operates in a realm beyond military strategy or human loyalty. This moment sets up the dramatic reversal of power that will culminate in Elisha's capture and subsequent miraculous escape (verses 13-23).
commentary.christological_typology: The king of Aram's rage at being unable to understand or defeat Elisha's prophetic knowledge prefigures the rage of those who opposed Christ. In John 8:46-47, Christ asks His opponents, 'Which of you convinceth me of sin?' and observes that they cannot hear His words because they are not 'of God.' Like the king of Aram, Christ's enemies sought to identify the source of His power and authority within purely natural frameworks, unable to conceive that it transcended human explanation. Christ's power, like Elisha's, operated in a realm their categories could not encompass.

word_study.term_original: וַיִּסָּעֵר לֵב מֶלֶךְ אֲרָם (va-yissa'er lev melekh aram)
word_study.meaning: His heart was stormy, was agitated, was turbulent. The verb sa'ar ('to storm, to rage') is used of wind and tempests—here it describes the king's interior state as a raging tempest. The heart (lev) in Hebrew anthropology is the seat of will, intention, and emotion.
word_study.significance: The verb choice is vivid and visceral. The king is not merely displeased; he is internally stormy, agitated to the point of rage. His rational military planning has given way to emotional turbulence. The image of the heart as a storm conveys loss of composure and control.

word_study.meaning: Called to his servants, summoned his servants. The verb kara ('to call') in the imperative sense means to summon for immediate audience and response.
word_study.significance: The king immediately takes action, using his authority to gather his officers. The urgency is evident—this is not a planned meeting but an emergency summoning, driven by the king's agitation.

word_study.meaning: Will you not tell me? The negation halo ('not') in a question form is rhetorical, conveying obligation or strong expectation. The verb nagad ('to tell, to inform, to make known') carries the sense of revealing something hidden.
word_study.significance: The king is not politely asking; he is demanding revelation. The rhetorical question implies that his officers have a duty to tell him. His tone suggests that if one of them is guilty of treason, they should confess or accuse the guilty party.

word_study.term_original: מִי מִשֶּׁלָּנוּ אֶל־מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל (mi mi-shellanu el-melekh israel)
word_study.meaning: Who from among us is [sided with/working for/belonging to] the king of Israel? The phrase mi mi-shellanu ('who from among us') expresses both accusation and demand for identification. To be 'for' the king of Israel is to be disloyal to the king of Aram.
word_study.significance: The king frames this as a loyalty question. The traitor has sided with Israel's king against Aram's king. The assumption is that one of the officers has been purchased, bribed, or coerced into providing information to the enemy.

cross_references.connection: Saul, enraged and suspicious, demands that his servants identify the conspirator against him—a similar moment where a king's paranoia and frustration lead to accusations of betrayal within the court.

King Nebuchadnezzar demands his wise men reveal his dream, and when they cannot, he becomes enraged and orders their execution—another example of a ruler's anger at inability to understand or control a situation.
Eliphaz describes receiving a revelation in the night, trembling with fear—contrasting with the king of Aram's inability to receive or understand divine revelation.

Joseph Smith cries out from Liberty Jail, 'O God, where art thou? And where is the pavilion that covereth thy hiding place?'—expressing the profound alienation of one cut off from divine knowledge and protection, as the king of Aram is cut off from understanding Elisha's supernatural knowledge.

commentary.application: For modern believers, this verse offers both warning and comfort. The warning is against the king of Aram's blindness—the tendency to interpret spiritual events through purely material lenses and to miss the divine reality operating behind apparent circumstances. The comfort is in recognizing that those who operate by divine knowledge and power may face opposition and accusation from those who cannot perceive the source of their success, but their power comes from a source beyond the reach of purely natural opposition. Members might also reflect on the king's rage as the response of worldly wisdom confronted with spiritual truth it cannot explain or control. The verse teaches that being guided by prophetic knowledge will sometimes place faithful members at odds with those who operate by purely secular reasoning, and that such opposition, while uncomfortable, is not ultimately threatening.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 16:5-7, Alma inquires of the Lord regarding the location of captive Nephites, and the Lord reveals to him that they have fled into the wilderness. Alma then knows more than any scout could know, and his enemies are frustrated by his seemingly supernatural knowledge of their movements. Like the king of Aram, Lamanite leaders would be mystified by how their plans are discovered.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:45-46 teaches that the righteous are endowed with power and authority that the world cannot perceive or understand. The king of Aram is experiencing the frustration of one operating in the natural realm confronted by someone operating in the spiritual realm. Modern revelation teaches that spiritual knowledge transcends human explanation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In covenant theology, the righteous are taught that they are endowed with 'power from on high' (D&C 38:32) that enables them to accomplish things beyond natural explanation. The king of Aram's rage at not being able to understand Elisha's knowledge parallels the inability of those outside covenant to comprehend the power of those within it.

commentary.historical_context: The practice of demanding loyalty and investigating suspected spies was common among ancient Near Eastern rulers. Kings maintained courts of officers, generals, and administrators, all of whom had access to sensitive military information. The discovery or suspicion of a mole within one's inner circle was a serious threat to military security and royal authority. Ancient inscriptions record instances of kings conducting investigations into disloyalty and espionage. The assumption that military secrets could only be compromised through human treachery was universal in the ancient world—the concept of supernatural knowledge transcending human intelligence networks would have been outside the king of Aram's immediate framework of understanding. This makes the officers' explanation in verse 12 all the more shocking: the explanation must move beyond espionage into the realm of prophecy and divine knowledge.

text_kjv: And one of his servants said, None, my lord, O king: but Elisha, the prophet that is in Israel, telleth the king of Israel the words that thou speakest in thy bedchamber.

commentary.narrative: One of the king's officers steps forward and provides the answer that the king of Aram cannot conceive of himself: the explanation is not espionage but prophecy. The officer's opening—'None, my lord, O king'—directly answers the king's accusation: there is no traitor among the officers. But then comes the revelation that must have shaken the king's understanding of reality: 'It is Elisha, the prophet in Israel.' The officer does not suggest that Elisha has human spies; he states that Elisha himself knows the private contents of the king's bedchamber—the most intimate, most secret location of his palace. This elevates the threat from the level of military espionage to the level of supernatural penetration. An enemy who had merely obtained information through spies might be countered by improved security and counter-intelligence.
