The horrifying inversion here—mothers surrendering children, agreements to cannibalize—represents the complete opposite: the loss of all sacred bonds. This is what happens when God's covenant is rejected.

commentary.christological_typology: The breaking of the mother-child bond through cannibalism in famine is the opposite of Christ's self-giving. Christ offers His own flesh and blood voluntarily, for the feeding and salvation of all. He enters into a covenant where He is the one offered, not the vulnerable child. The woman's report of cannibalistic agreement shows the world's hunger and desperation; Christ alone can satisfy that hunger in a way that does not destroy the bonds of love.
commentary.application: This verse presents the ultimate consequences of covenant-breaking: the dissolution of the bonds we hold most sacred. A mother-child bond is among the most fundamental of human relationships. When famine (literal or spiritual) becomes severe enough, that bond breaks. For modern Latter-day Saints, the application is urgent: What are you doing to maintain covenant standing? It is not possible to flirt with covenant violation and assume that family bonds remain intact. The spiral goes: covenant breach → loss of God's protection → external pressure (siege/famine) → internal collapse of moral boundaries → the breaking of family bonds themselves. The question is not academic. Ask yourself: Are my family relationships sturdy enough to survive famine? Or have I allowed compromise and drift to weaken the covenants that hold them together?

text_kjv: So we boiled my son, and did eat him: and I said unto her on the next day, Give thy son, that we may eat him: and she hath hid her son.

commentary.narrative:
The woman now confirms that the agreement was carried out on her side: 'So we boiled my son, and did eat him.' The past tense, the matter-of-fact tone, the domestic image of boiling—all combine to create a narrative that is almost unbearably stark. She has eaten her own child. The verb tense and narrative voice leave no ambiguity: this is not hypothetical, speculative, or exaggerated. The woman is reporting an accomplished fact to the king.

But the real complaint emerges in the second part: 'I said unto her on the next day, Give thy son, that we may eat him: and she hath hid her son.' The woman kept her end of the bargain; the other woman did not. This is not a lament about the moral horror of cannibalism—the woman does not seem to view it that way. It is a complaint about breach of contract. The woman upheld her obligation (she gave her own son) but her partner has hidden her son and broken the agreement. She has been cheated. In a world of complete moral collapse, there is only one thing left: the expectation that agreements will be kept.

This is perhaps the most devastating detail in the entire passage. The woman is not grieving her child or confessing to a horrendous act. She is asserting that she fulfilled her obligation and now demands that the other woman do the same. The narrator does not tell us what happened to the hidden son, or whether the other woman feared the woman's anger, or any moral judgment. The narrative simply states the fact: agreement was made, one side performed, the other side defaulted. And the woman brought her complaint to the king.

The reader is meant to feel the total inversion of values here. In a functioning society, such an agreement would be unthinkable. In a besieged city at the point of starvation, it becomes a binding contract that can be adjudicated. The woman's appeal to the king is no longer a plea for help but a demand for justice in enforcing an agreement about cannibalism.

word_study.meaning: From bashel, 'to cook, boil, prepare food.' The qal form is simple past. This is the ordinary word for cooking food; there is no special term used to distance or euphemize the act.
word_study.significance: The use of the everyday word for cooking emphasizes the mundane, domestic nature of the act. This is what happens in a kitchen when food is prepared—except the food is a human child. The ordinariness of the language against the horror of the referent is the point.

word_study.meaning: From chaba, 'to hide, conceal.' The qal perfect form indicates a completed action. The verb is used throughout Scripture for hiding things from discovery.
word_study.significance: The act of hiding her son suggests the other woman's revulsion at what she had agreed to, or her calculation that she could renege. Either way, the breaking of the agreement is the issue being adjudicated.

cross_references.connection: This verse reports the completion of what was agreed to in verse 28—the woman kept her part of the agreement by providing her son.

The covenant curse specifies that a woman will hide (chaba) her afterbirth due to starvation in siege. The word here echoes the hiding of the son, showing that complete loss of maternal care is the curse being fulfilled.

During the famine in Elijah's time, the widow of Zarephath tells Elijah she has only enough meal and oil to make one last cake before she and her son die. The parallel shows repeated cycles of famine testing maternal bonds, but always within God's plan of provision.
Similar report of mothers eating children during siege judgment, with the same matter-of-fact tone: the atrocity is documented without emotional commentary.

commentary.historical_context: The specific detail about boiling suggests the method by which meat would normally be prepared in an Israelite household. Boiling required fuel (wood or dung) and water, both presumably still available even under siege. The attention to such domestic detail grounds the horror in the real: this is not mythological or legendary, but the actual behavior of real people under extremity. Historians note that during extended sieges in the ancient world, cannibalism did occasionally occur, though it was rare and typically involved the dead before it involved the living. The detailed report here suggests either eyewitness testimony or a historical record compiled from what people reported. The element of breach of contract—one party performing and one reneging—is psychologically realistic. People under extreme stress often make irrational agreements, and then one party, when faced with the actual requirement, withdraws. The woman's complaint suggests a legal sensibility still functioning even in extremity: she appeals to the king for justice, as though there were still a law and a legal system, even though the content of what is being adjudicated shows the collapse of all law.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The Book of Mormon contains warnings about what happens when people break covenants. In Alma 62:39-40, after periods of war and turmoil, the Nephites repent and rebuild. The implication is that without repentance, the destructive spiral would continue. Here in Samaria, there is no sign of repentance, and the spiral continues unto complete dissolution.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 88:37-38 speaks of law and order as divine principles. 'For the earth is full of the riches of the mysteries of the kingdom by the keys...And the order of the Son of Righteousness shall be the law of the celestial and terrestrial kingdoms.' When covenant is broken, order collapses, and what remains is the parody of order shown here—contracts about cannibalism.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The temple is the place where covenants are made binding and eternal. The contrast between temple covenant-making and the covenant made here between two starving women is stark. In one, bonds are sealed for eternity with divine authority; in the other, bonds are broken through deception. The lesson is that all covenants depend on the reality of God's authority and blessing.

commentary.christological_typology: The woman has offered her own son, fulfilled the agreement, and now demands justice. This is the opposite of what Christ offers. Christ does not bargain or make agreements; He gives freely. He does not hide His son; He openly surrenders Him. He does not demand justice from others or accuse them of breach; He receives unjust treatment and forgives. The woman's complaint shows the logic of the fallen world: you must perform, agreements must be kept, breach must be punished. Christ enters into a different logic entirely: grace, forgiveness, undeserved mercy.
commentary.application: This verse forces a confrontation with how far people will go when deprived of basic needs. It also reveals something about human nature: when society collapses and basic survival is at stake, people do not become noble; they become transactional. The woman is not trying to save her child; she agreed to have him cooked and eaten. She is only complaining because someone else broke faith with her. For modern readers, the application is this: What happens to your values when you face deprivation or extremity? Do you hold fast to core covenants, or do you begin to rationalize increasingly questionable agreements? The fact that the woman brought her complaint to the king—still expecting justice, still operating within a framework of law—shows that even in the depths of degradation, humans retain the sense that there should be order and fairness. The tragedy is that the king, to whom she appeals, is powerless to establish real justice. Only God can truly order justice. The application: Maintain your covenant with God now, while you still have the capacity to think clearly. Do not wait until desperation forces you into agreements and compromises you cannot recover from.

text_kjv: And it came to pass, when the king heard the words of the woman, that he rent his clothes; and he passed by upon the wall, and the people looked, and, behold, he had sackcloth within upon his flesh.

commentary.narrative:
The king's response to the woman's report is visceral and immediate: he tears his clothes. The rending of garments was a standard gesture of mourning, grief, and sometimes penitence in Israelite culture. It was a public sign that something catastrophic had been witnessed or learned. But what is remarkable here is what this tearing reveals: 'he had sackcloth within upon his flesh'—literally, 'sackcloth on his flesh underneath.' The Covenant Rendering's translator notes highlight the significance: the king has been wearing sackcloth—a sign of mourning and possibly penitence—under his royal garments, hidden from public view. He has been grieving in secret.

This detail complicates the narrative. Earlier, we saw the king deflect the woman's plea with a question about threshing floors and winepresses, suggesting hardness or evasion. We might have concluded he was callous or unmoved by his people's suffering. But now we learn he has been wearing sackcloth against his skin, which means he has been in a state of private mourning throughout the siege. He has not been unaware of the crisis; he has been grieving it, fasting, and performing acts of penitence. Yet this private grief has not translated into effective action or into public acknowledgment of the need for repentance.

The king's tearing of his outer garment reveals the sackcloth beneath. In a sense, his private anguish is suddenly made public. The people see what was hidden. This is a moment of vulnerability where the king's inner state—his awareness of the crisis, his sense of loss—becomes visible. Yet the narrative suggests this will lead not to repentance and prayer, but to violence against the prophet (as verse 31 reveals). The king's grief, though genuine, has not led to turning toward God. Instead, it seems to be driving him toward a desperate attempt to find someone to blame.

word_study.meaning: From qara, 'to tear, rend, split.' The qal form indicates a sudden, forceful action. When applied to clothing, it signifies a dramatic gesture of grief or anguish.
word_study.significance: Rending garments was a culturally coded action in Israel. It communicated that the person had been confronted with overwhelming tragedy. The action was not merely emotional but performative—it was meant to be witnessed and understood.

word_study.meaning: A rough, coarse fabric, usually made from goat or camel hair, worn as a sign of mourning or penitence. Sackcloth was uncomfortable and was worn next to the skin as part of the discomfort of mourning.
word_study.significance: The wearing of sackcloth was both a private act of self-mortification and a public sign of status change. A king wearing sackcloth underneath his royal robes was performing secret mourning—he had withdrawn from normal royal dignity but had not yet made this public.

word_study.term_english: upon his flesh / next to his skin
word_study.meaning: Literally 'upon his flesh.' The preposition 'al' indicates proximity or direct contact. Besaro (flesh) emphasizes the direct contact of the rough material with the skin.
word_study.significance: The detail that sackcloth was worn next to the skin rather than over outer garments emphasizes that this was a private act of mortification. The discomfort was not theatrical; it was experienced in solitude. The king was suffering physically and privately.

word_study.meaning: From bayit, 'house, inside.' The preposition mi- makes it 'from inside' or 'from within,' suggesting hidden, inner, not outward-facing.
word_study.significance: The Covenant Rendering uses 'underneath' to capture the sense that the sackcloth was interior, hidden from casual observation. This was not a public performance but a private grief.

cross_references.connection: The king of Nineveh, upon hearing of judgment, tears his robe and puts on sackcloth, then calls for repentance. Unlike the king of Israel, he moves from personal grief to public repentance and national turning.

David tears his clothes and wears sackcloth for Abner's death: 'And David said to Joab...Rend your clothes, and gird you with sackcloth.' Grief is made public in order to call others to accountability and mourning.
King Ahab, upon hearing his judgment, tears his clothes and puts on sackcloth and fasts. Like the Ninevite king, this is part of genuine (if incomplete) repentance that moves God to respond.

The prophet calls the people: 'Turn ye even to me with all your heart...and rend your heart, and not your garments.' True repentance is internal, not merely performative. The king's sackcloth is meaningless if it does not lead to a rending of the heart.

When the high priest hears Jesus' words about the Son of Man, he tears his garments in outrage and claims blasphemy. The gesture of tearing garments can signify either genuine grief or performative condemnation.

commentary.historical_context: Wearing sackcloth was a documented practice in the ancient Near East, both in Israel and in surrounding cultures. Mesopotamian texts describe rulers wearing sackcloth as a sign of mourning or seeking the gods' intervention. The practice was particularly associated with fasting and prayer during crises. That the king wore sackcloth beneath his royal garments suggests he was performing private religious mourning while maintaining the appearance of normal royal function. This was not uncommon—rulers would sometimes observe personal fasts or acts of mourning while continuing public duties. The detail that the people could see the sackcloth when his outer garment was torn suggests that either the king's sackcloth extended down to his legs in a way that was visible when the upper garment tore, or that the people understood from the gesture itself what was beneath. The public revelation of private mourning could have served either as vindication of the king's care for his people (look, he grieves with you) or as indication that his personal mourning had not led to effective action (he grieves, but what does that accomplish?).

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Mosiah 11:25-26, King Noah initially appears to be immune to the preaching of the prophets. But later (Mosiah 18), we learn that some of his people, including eventually his son Limhi, do repent. The difference between private sorrow and public repentance is crucial. The Book of Mormon emphasizes that repentance must be real and complete, not mere performance.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 58:42 teaches: 'Behold, he who has repented of his sins, the same is forgiven, and I, the Lord, remember them no more.' True repentance requires action and turning, not merely wearing the external signs. The king's sackcloth, if worn without genuine turning toward God and His prophets, is empty.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: In temple covenant, the person strips off outer garments and is clothed anew. The detail of the king's hidden sackcloth may suggest something about the gap between outward form and inward reality. Covenant requires that the whole person—inside and outside—be dedicated to God, not just the parts no one sees.

commentary.christological_typology: Christ did not hide His suffering or grief. He wept openly at Lazarus' tomb (John 11:35), and He agonized in Gethsemane with His suffering known to His disciples. Unlike the king of Israel, who kept his sackcloth hidden, Christ made His anguish visible and made it purposeful—His suffering was redemptive, not merely expressive of sorrow. The king wore sackcloth but was powerless to change the situation; Christ's suffering led to the redemption of all mankind.
commentary.application: This verse asks several uncomfortable questions: Can private grief exist alongside public failure? Can a person mourn genuinely and yet make wrong choices? The king is clearly not unmoved by the suffering around him; his sackcloth proves that. Yet his private mourning has not led to repentance, prayer, or turning back to God and His prophets. In fact, verse 31 will show that his next action is to blame and threaten the prophet Elisha. For modern readers, the application is: Beware of performing the outer signs of repentance without the inner reality. Do not let private sorrow substitute for actual change. Do not wear sackcloth while refusing to turn to God. Do not grieve the consequences of sin while continuing to sin. More positively: If you are grieving, let that grief drive you to genuine repentance, not to blame-seeking or evasion. The king's sackcloth might have been the beginning of real change. Instead, it appears to remain hidden, private, ineffectual. Let your sorrow for the state of your covenants lead you to actually change your covenants, not merely to hide your distress beneath outer dignity.

text_kjv: Then he said, God do so and more also to me, if the head of Elisha the son of Shaphat shall stand on him this day.

commentary.narrative: The king of Israel, driven to desperation by the siege of Samaria and the resulting famine, has reached the breaking point of his faith. In this verse he swears a binding oath—using the formal self-cursing formula—that he will behead Elisha before the day ends. The irony is devastating: the king wears sackcloth (the outward sign of humility before God) even as he swears to murder God's prophet. He appears to blame Elisha for the siege, either because Elisha counseled against surrender or because the king holds the prophet responsible as God's representative for the city's suffering. The oath itself is a moment of profound spiritual rebellion disguised as decisive action.
commentary.narrative_continued: What makes this moment particularly tragic is that the king misdiagnoses the source of his affliction. He sees famine and siege and assumes God has abandoned Samaria. Rather than repent or seek divine wisdom through the prophet, he chooses to eliminate the messenger—a deeply human but spiritually fatal response. The oath 'God do so and more also to me' literally calls divine judgment upon his own head if he fails to kill Elisha. He is doubling down on rebellion, not merely threatening violence but swearing before God that he will commit it. This verse sets up the tension that drives chapters 6–7: will Elisha be protected? Will the king's oath be fulfilled or broken? The answer comes swiftly—not through Elisha's death, but through divine intervention that will humble the king and vindicate the prophet.

word_study.term_english: God do so and more also
word_study.term_original: כֹּה־יַעֲשֶׂה־לִּי אֱלֹהִים וְכֹה יוֹסִף (koh ya'aseh li Elohim ve-koh yosif)
word_study.transliteration: koh ya'aseh li Elohim ve-koh yosif
word_study.meaning: This is the standard Israelite oath formula expressing self-cursing—literally 'thus may God do to me and thus may he add [more punishment] if [condition].' The speaker invokes divine judgment on himself as a guarantee of his sincerity. The formula appears throughout the Hebrew Bible when someone swears a binding vow.
word_study.significance: The king is not merely expressing anger; he is making a formal, legally binding oath before God. By using this language, he transforms a death threat into a sacred vow. The tragic irony is that he swears this oath while wearing sackcloth, the garment of repentance—showing a man outwardly humbling himself before God while inwardly rebelling against God's prophet.

word_study.meaning: The physical head, but in covenantal language, often represents the person himself, authority, or the seat of judgment. To remove a man's head is the ultimate violation of his personhood and dignity.
word_study.significance: The king's threat to behead Elisha echoes ancient Near Eastern practices of desecration and dishonor—beheading was not merely execution but a way of erasing someone's identity and denying them a proper burial. For a prophet, this would be especially abhorrent.

word_study.meaning: Literally 'to stand upon/over.' The preposition 'alav' ('upon him') suggests domination, rule, or remaining in place. The Covenant Rendering captures the sense: 'stays on his shoulders,' emphasizing that the king swears to remove Elisha's head from his body.
word_study.significance: The verb 'to stand' in covenantal contexts often means to endure or persist. Here it underscores that the king is swearing to act before sunset—to use the remaining hours to accomplish Elisha's death.

cross_references.connection: The LORD threatened to judge Eli's house for their rebellion against His covenant. Like the king of Israel, Eli's family rejected God's prophet; here the king swears to kill God's prophet, another form of covenant violation.
Elijah complained that Israel had sought to kill the prophets. The king's oath against Elisha continues this pattern of persecution that prophets have endured throughout Israel's history.
The people and priests sought to put Jeremiah to death for his prophecies. Like the king here, they rejected the prophet's message and sought violent retribution.

Jesus prophesied that Israel would kill and persecute the prophets He would send. The king's oath here exemplifies the tragic pattern of covenant people rejecting and seeking to destroy God's messengers.

commentary.historical_context: The siege of Samaria was a brutal military campaign, likely by the Aramean forces under Ben-hadad. Ancient siege warfare typically lasted months and caused mass starvation within city walls. Excavations at various Levantine sites show evidence of siege conditions: depleted grain stores, animal remains consumed down to the bone, cannibalism during extreme famine. The king's desperation is historically plausible—a starving population would demand radical action. In the ancient Near East, it was not uncommon for desperate leaders to blame priests or prophets for divine displeasure, sometimes resorting to their execution as a means to appease the gods. The king's logic, though perverted, reflects a known pattern: if the gods are angry, eliminate their representatives. The self-cursing oath formula was a legally binding mechanism in Israelite and broader Semitic culture, taken with utmost seriousness.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of covenant leaders rejecting God's prophets appears throughout the Book of Mormon. In Helaman 13, the people of Zarahemla sought to kill Samuel the Lamanite, who prophesied their destruction. Like the king of Israel, they preferred comfortable lies to divine truth, and sought to silence the messenger.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 21:4-5 promises that the president of the Church will receive revelation to lead the Saints, with the warning that 'they who receive my law and my commandments shall keep them.' The king of Israel rejected this principle—he refused to hear Elisha's counsel and instead swore to kill him. D&C 1:14 similarly warns that 'the weak things of the world shall come forth and break down the mighty and strong ones.'
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The wearing of sackcloth while swearing murder represents a profound violation of the principle of integrity in covenant making. In the temple, covenants are made with the whole heart. The king makes his oath while in a state of ritualistic mourning (sackcloth), but his heart is fixed on rebellion. This invokes the principle that outward observance without inward commitment is spiritual death (see also Alma 31:23).

commentary.christological_typology: The king's oath against Elisha prefigures the false oaths sworn against Jesus during His trial. Just as the king invoked God's judgment on himself while swearing to kill God's prophet, the Jewish leaders swore oaths of false witness against Jesus (Matthew 26:59-61). Both involve covenant-breakers using formal legal language to condemn the innocent. Elisha's deliverance through divine intervention (which follows in verse 33 and chapter 7) parallels Christ's resurrection—the ultimate vindication of God's prophet against human violence.
commentary.application: Modern covenant members face subtle temptations similar to the king's. When circumstances grow difficult—sickness, financial hardship, relational strain—there is a temptation to blame God's representatives or to reject prophetic counsel that calls for patience and faith. The king wanted a solution on his timeline; the prophet offered trust in God's timeline. We are called to distinguish between outward religiosity (sackcloth) and genuine faith. If we find ourselves angry at prophets or resistant to prophetic guidance during trials, we should pause and examine our hearts. Are we truly seeking God's will, or are we seeking a convenient answer that lets us remain in control? The remedy is not to swear oaths against the messengers, but to 'wait upon the Lord' as Elisha will counsel in chapter 7.

text_kjv: But Elisha sat in his house, and the elders sat with him; and the king sent a man from before him: but ere the messenger came to him, he said to the elders, See ye how this son of a murderer hath sent to take away mine head? look, when the messenger cometh, shut the door, and hold him fast at the door: is not the sound of his master's feet behind him?

commentary.narrative: While the king swears in verse 31 to have Elisha beheaded, this verse shows Elisha in a posture of calm authority—seated in his house surrounded by the elders of Israel (likely civic or religious leaders who had gathered to seek his counsel). The contrast is stunning: the king is frantic and oath-bound; Elisha is composed and prophetic. The messenger is sent ahead as an executioner, but before he arrives, Elisha announces his coming to the elders and gives them tactical instructions. This is Elisha's prophetic gift in full display: he knows what the king intends before the messenger even knocks on his door. His supernatural knowledge of coming events is not a passive mystical gift but an active knowledge that allows him to respond with both wisdom and authority.
commentary.narrative_continued: Elisha's instructions to the elders are twofold: first, shut the door against the messenger to delay him; second, hold him at the threshold until 'the sound of his master's feet' arrives. Elisha anticipates that the king will follow close behind his messenger—likely because the king could not wait for a report of Elisha's death but was compelled to come himself. The prophet is essentially saying, 'Do not let this messenger execute me. Stall him. When the king himself arrives, he will see that I am alive, and his heart may soften.' Elisha's strategy is not defensive violence but a confidence that facing the king directly will be more effective than fighting off an executioner. This reveals a deep trust in God's protection and in the possibility of the king's repentance.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: Elisha's address to the elders includes a sharp rebuke: 'See ye how this son of a murderer hath sent to take away mine head?' The title 'son of a murderer' (ben ha-meratstsech) is a loaded accusation. It likely refers to Ahab's judicial murder of Naboth to seize his vineyard (1 Kings 21), or more broadly to the violence inherent in the royal house. By naming the king as a 'murderer's son,' Elisha is saying, 'This is what happens when a people abandon God's law. They have a king whose family blood is stained with innocent blood, and now he seeks to add a prophet's blood to that stain.' Yet even as Elisha makes this condemnation, he is also protecting the king from committing an irreversible sin. The elders are witnesses to Elisha's supernatural knowledge and moral clarity.

word_study.meaning: To sit, dwell, or be established. In prophetic contexts, sitting often indicates a position of authority, judgment, or rest. Elisha sits in his house (as opposed to the king pacing in anger); the elders sit with him (gathering as supplicants or students).
word_study.significance: The verb choice emphasizes Elisha's stability and spiritual centeredness. While the king is in motion, driven by rage and oath, Elisha is seated—grounded, unmoved, and in control of the situation through prophetic insight.

word_study.meaning: A descendant or inheritor of murder; one whose family legacy is bloodshed. The term meratstsech (from ratsach, 'to murder') specifically refers to deliberate, unjust killing—not war or execution, but covenant violation through assassination.
word_study.significance: Elisha's use of this title is both a condemnation and a diagnosis. The king is not acting in isolation; he is the product of a dynasty that has repeatedly violated God's law and murdered the innocent. This is spiritual inherited guilt manifesting in the present moment.

word_study.meaning: To close, bar, or seal the door. The verb sigru is a strong, decisive action—not gently closing but firmly shutting, often with a connotation of exclusion or defense.
word_study.significance: Elisha's instruction is tactical but also symbolic: a closed door is a boundary, a refusal of entry, a protection of the prophetic space. The door becomes the line between the king's murderous intent and Elisha's divinely protected life.

word_study.term_english: hold him fast at the door
word_study.meaning: To press, squeeze, or confine someone at the door. The verb lachats conveys pressure or constraint; ba-dalet ('at/in the door') specifies the place. Together, the phrase means to physically restrain someone at the threshold.
word_study.significance: This is not a request for polite resistance but for physical action. Elisha is asking the elders to become human barriers, delaying the executioner until the king arrives. The door becomes a battleground where faith and obedience are tested.

word_study.meaning: The voice/sound (qol) of the feet (raglei) of his master (adonav). Qol often refers to audible sound but can also mean 'news' or 'report'; here it is the literal sound of footsteps—Elisha hears or senses the king's rapid approach.
word_study.significance: Elisha's prophetic perception extends beyond the immediate moment. He not only knows the messenger is coming but senses the king's urgent approach. This multilayered prophetic knowledge—of events not yet manifested, of thoughts not yet spoken—elevates Elisha's authority over every earthly power.

cross_references.connection: Elisha detects a woman's hidden sorrow ('her soul is vexed within her'). Here again, he perceives what is invisible to others—a pattern of prophetic sensitivity that extends to both emotional and material realities.

Michal warned David of Saul's plot to kill him, enabling his escape. Like Elisha, David was protected by supporters who warned him of the king's murderous intent, though David fled while Elisha stands firm in prophetic confidence.
Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear. Elisha's calm in the face of the king's threat mirrors this psalmist's trust in divine protection despite human enmity.

Jesus told His disciples not to fear those who can kill the body but cannot kill the soul. Elisha's fearlessness in the face of the executioner reflects this same priority: the body may be threatened, but the prophet's life is secure in God.
The apostles were beaten for their testimony but rejoiced, continuing to teach. Like Elisha, they faced persecution from earthly powers yet remained unmoved in their commitment to God's message.

commentary.historical_context: The reference to 'elders' sitting with Elisha suggests a formal gathering, possibly a council or assembly seeking the prophet's guidance during the siege crisis. In ancient Israel, elders were civic and religious leaders who would have legitimate authority and influence. That they are present with Elisha indicates he held significant status—not a fugitive hiding but a leader around whom the community gathered. The tactic of closing a door and physically resisting an executioner is historically plausible; in ancient Near Eastern contexts, the threshold of a house was a sacred space where sanctuary could be claimed. The mention of 'hearing footsteps' is interesting archaeologically: houses in Iron Age Levant were typically built on stone or packed earth floors, and footfalls of a hurrying man—especially in urgency—would be quite audible to those inside. Elisha's assertion that he hears the king coming suggests not merely supernatural knowledge but also practical awareness of the sounds of someone approaching.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 8:4-11, Alma was driven from city to city and beaten by mobs, yet he remained faithful. Like Elisha, Alma was protected by God even when surrounded by those who sought to destroy him. The principle is the same: a prophet's life is held secure in God's hands, not in the approval of earthly powers.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 100:16 states: 'Therefore, let your minds be girded up, keep all my commandments, and be faithful.' The king is failing at this very point—he is not keeping God's commandments but breaking them by swearing to kill a prophet. Elisha exemplifies the opposite: calm, obedient, and trusting in God's protection. D&C 122:5-6 promises that even if the prophets face 'all manner of afflictions, they may be made perfect through sufferings'—Elisha faces affliction but remains steadfast.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The closed door in Elisha's house takes on covenantal significance. In the temple, sacred space is protected by doors and boundaries. Elisha's instruction to bar the door symbolizes the protection of sacred covenant space against the intrusion of evil intent. The elders physically defending that boundary mirrors the temple's principle of guarding sacred truths from those who would defile them.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha seated with the elders, calmly awaiting the executioner who has been sent against him, prefigures Jesus in the upper room with His apostles, knowing that Judas has gone to betray Him, knowing the chain of events that will lead to His execution, yet remaining unmoved and at peace. Both Elisha and Jesus are aware of the death sentence against them before it is carried out, yet both remain in authority over their circumstances. Elisha's instruction to the elders to bar the door parallels the locked doors of the upper room (John 20:19)—spaces of revelation protected from hostile powers. Ultimately, Elisha's deliverance through the king's sudden appearance and change of heart mirrors Christ's resurrection: the human plan to eliminate the prophet fails, and God's plan triumphs.
commentary.application: We live in times when truth and prophetic counsel are frequently rejected. When we bear witness to prophetic truth and face resistance or mockery, Elisha's example teaches us to remain centered, calm, and grounded in our conviction. Like Elisha, we are not called to defend ourselves through aggression or cunning, but to stand in the truth and allow God to vindicate it. The instruction to 'shut the door' and protect sacred space is relevant to modern covenant members: we are called to guard our testimonies, our families, and our commitments from the intrusion of hostile ideologies. We do this not through fear or isolation, but through deliberate, faithful boundaries. Most importantly, Elisha's serene confidence in the face of death is a model for spiritual unshakableness. When circumstances seem to conspire against us, when powerful voices demand our compromise, we can remember that a prophet was once alone in a besieged city, facing the king's executioner—and God's plan prevailed.

text_kjv: And while he yet talked with them, behold, the messenger came down to him: and he said, Behold, this evil is of the LORD; what should I wait for the LORD any more?

commentary.narrative: The final verse of this passage marks a dramatic shift. While Elisha is still speaking to the elders, the messenger arrives—but more significantly, the king himself appears. The phrasing of the KJV obscures the actual speaker; the TCR rendering makes clear that it is the king who makes the statement, 'This disaster is from the LORD. Why should I wait for the LORD any longer?' The king has reached a spiritual and psychological nadir. He has made his oath against Elisha (verse 31), sent an executioner (verse 32), and now—seemingly—comes to witness or oversee the deed himself. But in the moment of confrontation, something shifts. The king stops and, rather than order the execution, speaks a statement of spiritual despair. He is no longer angry but defeated. He has arrived at a moment of terrible theological clarity: he recognizes that the siege, the famine, the calamity are the work of the LORD (YHWH).
commentary.narrative_continued: The king's statement is crucial: 'This evil is of the LORD.' He has identified the correct source of his suffering—God, not chance, not military miscalculation, not even the prophet's failure. In that recognition lies a glimmer of truth. Yet immediately the king draws the wrong conclusion: 'What should I wait for the LORD any more?' The logic is perverted. If God has sent this suffering, then—the king reasons—hope is futile. Trust is pointless. Why continue to expect deliverance from a God who is clearly inflicting judgment? This is the spiritual temptation that follows upon the heels of correct theological diagnosis: the king knows God is responsible, but instead of repenting, he despairs. He moves from rage against Elisha to despair toward God. Both emotions are forms of covenant-breaking—the first through violence, the second through loss of faith.
commentary.narrative_continued_2: The verse ends in mid-narrative: the king makes his statement of despair, but there is no closure, no divine response. We must wait for chapter 7 to see how God will answer this moment of lost hope. But even in the silence of verse 33, a profound lesson emerges. The king came to kill the prophet but finds himself face-to-face with the truth of his own condition. The siege is real. The famine is real. His power is helpless. His oaths are hollow. And the source of it all is the God he has been running from. In this moment, before Elisha speaks another word, the king has already begun to be broken of his self-will. The verse closes with a question—'What should I wait for the LORD any more?'—that demands an answer. And that answer will come, not from the king's strength, but from God's power.

word_study.meaning: Evil, disaster, calamity, harm. The term can refer to moral evil (wickedness) or consequential evil (affliction, suffering). Here it encompasses the siege, the famine, the death, the despair—everything that has befallen Samaria.
word_study.significance: The king uses ra'ah to describe not a moral failing on his part, but the affliction sent against him. He has not yet achieved the repentance required to see that his own covenant-breaking is the root of the disaster. He knows the disaster comes from God but does not yet understand why.

word_study.meaning: From before/from the face of the LORD; originating with, sent by the LORD. The preposition me-et ('from') indicates direct divine agency. This is not bad luck or human error—it is God's action.
word_study.significance: The king's recognition of divine agency is the first step toward repentance. He cannot repent until he admits that God is at work. But he stops there, failing to proceed to the next step: asking why God is acting, and what repentance would look like. The Covenant Rendering brings out the horror of the situation: 'This disaster is from the LORD'—a recognition that lands like a hammer.

word_study.meaning: What should I hope for, expect, or wait upon? The verb chil (or chakah) means to wait with expectation, to hope, to endure. The interrogative mah ('what') is rhetorical—the king is not truly asking but lamenting.
word_study.significance: The word ochil is particularly poignant because it recalls the language of patient waiting that is so central to faith. In the Psalms and prophetic literature, waiting upon the LORD is the mark of covenant fidelity. The king's question inverts this: he is asking why he should continue to hope. He has lost faith not because God has failed to act, but because God has acted—and the action is judgment. He confuses judgment with abandonment.

word_study.meaning: Still, yet, again, anymore. The adverb od indicates continuance or its cessation. 'What should I wait for the LORD any more?' means 'Why should I continue hoping?'
word_study.significance: The word od opens a subtle possibility. In chapter 7, the king will indeed wait for the LORD—not through his own effort, but through the miraculous deliverance God will send. The very word od, which the king uses to express the cessation of hope, will be answered by divine action that far exceeds what any amount of human waiting could produce.

cross_references.connection: Why is light given to a man whose way is hid, and whom God hath hedged in? Job, facing inexplicable suffering, asks similar questions of despair. Like the king, he has recognized God's hand but interprets it as judgment without mercy.

My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? This psalm expresses the king's anguish—not that God is absent, but that His face seems turned away, His help delayed. Yet the psalm ultimately resolves in trust (verse 24).

They that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength. The very act of waiting that the king despairs of—waiting upon the LORD—is here revealed as the source of renewal. The king's question in verse 33 will be answered by this principle in chapter 7.

The LORD is my portion, saith my soul; therefore will I hope in him... It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait. Elisha exemplifies this waiting; the king is tempted to abandon it. These verses offer the prophetic answer to the king's despair.

Whatsoever things were written aforetime were written for our learning, that we through patience and comfort of the scriptures might have hope. The king's question in verse 33 is meant to drive us—and him—back to the scriptures and to faith that transcends circumstance.

commentary.historical_context: The siege of Samaria is historically attested, though details vary among sources. The famine conditions described in chapter 6 are consistent with siege archaeology: excavations at Iron Age Levantine sites show evidence of severe food shortage, including the consumption of non-food substances (clay, bones) during extreme distress. The king's psychological state—moving from rage to despair—reflects the documented experience of besieged populations. Despair is a well-attested military effect of prolonged siege; it was used strategically by ancient commanders, who would sometimes delay final assault to allow starvation and demoralization to weaken resistance. The king's theological statement—'This evil is of the LORD'—reflects an ancient Near Eastern understanding that calamity is divine punishment. This was the dominant theological framework across the ancient Near East: if a city fell or a kingdom suffered, it was because the gods had withdrawn their favor. The king's statement would not have been unusual in its theology; what is unusual is what happens next in chapter 7, where God acts in a way that defies expectation.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: In Alma 32:13-16, the people of Antionum are described as humble because they were 'brought low by the hand of the Lord.' The king of Israel is being brought low, but has not yet achieved the humility that would allow him to receive the seed of faith. Alma 31:10 describes those who had fallen away and 'did not believe in the spirit of prophecy'—the king is on the verge of this very state, about to lose faith in both God and His prophets.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: Doctrine and Covenants 121:7-8 promises that 'your adversity and your afflictions shall be but a small moment; And then, if ye endure it well, God shall exalt you on high.' The king, in verse 33, has not yet endured his affliction well; he is tempted to abandon hope. But God's promise holds: his small moment of siege is about to be transformed by a miracle that will turn the siege to victory.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The king's despair represents a breaking of covenant—specifically, the covenant to trust God in all things. In the temple, we covenant to 'obey the law of Christ.' That law includes both obedience to commandments and faith in God's timing and wisdom. The king has broken the second part of this covenant by refusing to 'wait for the LORD.' Chapter 7 will show that waiting—though it feels futile—is precisely what brings deliverance.

commentary.christological_typology: The king's despair—'What should I wait for the LORD any more?'—echoes the despair of the disciples after Jesus's arrest. In Matthew 27:20, the crowds and leaders demanded His death; in Matthew 27:50, Jesus cried out in apparent abandonment. The disciples similarly faced a moment where their hopes seemed dashed, where God's plan appeared to have failed, where continuing to 'wait for the LORD' seemed pointless. Yet the resurrection answered their despair just as the miracle of chapter 7 will answer the king's. Both the king and the disciples faced a test: would they continue to hope when circumstances suggested hopelessness? Both would learn that God's deliverance transcends human timing and human wisdom. Elisha, standing calmly in the prophet's office, prefigures the risen Christ—alive and victorious when all seemed lost.
commentary.application: This verse captures a moment that many modern members have faced: the point of spiritual crisis where you acknowledge that God is real and at work, but despair that He will ever help you. The king's statement is dangerous because it is half-true. He is correct that 'this evil is of the LORD'—that afflictions come within God's purview. But he is catastrophically wrong to conclude that because God has sent affliction, hope is gone. The application is twofold. First, when you recognize God's hand in your circumstances (whether through trial or through quiet revelation), do not make the king's leap from 'God is acting' to 'God has abandoned me.' God may be testing, refining, or redirecting you. Second, commit to wait upon the LORD as the Psalmist describes. The waiting is not passive resignation but active faith—continuing to pray, to serve, to trust, even when deliverance is not visible. Chapter 7 will demonstrate that in less than twenty-four hours, everything changes. The same is true in our lives. The spiritual assignment of verse 33 is to refuse the king's despair and instead affirm: 'I will wait for the LORD, though I do not see the way, because He is worthy of trust.'

text_kjv: Wherefore they arose and fled in the twilight, and left their tents, and their horses, and their asses, even the camp as it was, and fled for their life.

commentary.narrative:
This verse marks the climactic moment of divine deliverance. The entire Syrian army abandons its encampment in panic at twilight—the moment between day and night when visibility is poorest and fear most easily takes hold. The Hebrew phrase va-yanusu el nafsham (they fled toward their own souls) emphasizes the totality of their terror: they flee for their very lives. What is remarkable is not merely that they fled, but what they left behind: everything. The tents remain standing, the horses and donkeys remain tethered, supplies are untouched. An entire military force, gripped by a divinely induced panic at the sound of chariots and horses (as the previous verses explain), abandons its equipment wholesale and flees into the darkness.

This abandonment was complete and immediate. The camp sits exactly as it was (ka-asher hi)—frozen in time by the supernatural fear that seized the Syrian soldiers. The strategic implications are devastating for the besiegers and salvific for the starving city of Samaria. Elisha's prayer for the Lord to open the eyes of his servant (6:17) has been answered not through military confrontation but through psychological terror that accomplishes what swords could not. The Lord did not need the Israelites to fight; He needed only to reveal the supernatural army already arrayed on their behalf.

word_study.meaning: Neshef denotes twilight or dusk—the liminal time between day and night when vision is obscured and fear is amplified. The verb nus means 'to flee' with urgency and panic, not orderly retreat.
word_study.significance: The choice of twilight for the flight is both practically strategic and theologically significant. It is the moment of greatest vulnerability and darkness—a fitting time for God's enemies to be routed by unseen forces.

word_study.meaning: Ohel (plural ohalim) is 'tent'—the basic shelter of nomadic and military forces. The verb azav means 'to abandon' or 'to leave behind,' suggesting both desertion and irretrievable loss.
word_study.significance: The abandonment of tents represents the abandonment of the siege itself. A military force without its camp is a force in complete disarray. This detail emphasizes the totality of the rout.

word_study.meaning: Nefesh literally means 'soul' or 'life-breath,' but idiomatically 'fled for their lives' or 'fled for their own souls' conveys desperate self-preservation. El-nafsham ('toward their own souls') is an intensive expression emphasizing the urgency.
word_study.significance: The phrase underscores that survival became the sole motivating force. Every soldier fled solely for his own preservation, abandoning unit cohesion, command structure, and military objectives. This is panic in its purest form.

cross_references.connection: Elisha's servant is initially afraid when surrounded by the Syrian army; now that same supernatural protection manifests as terror that scatters the enemy without a sword being drawn.
The Egyptians flee in panic when the Lord manifests His presence through supernatural signs; similarly, the Syrians flee at the sound of the Lord's invisible army.
The Lord defeats the Canaanites at Gibeon by casting great hailstones; here, the Lord defeats the Syrians through divinely induced panic—demonstrating various means of deliverance.
Alma's forces pursue fleeing Amlicites who abandon their weapons; the pattern of a routed army leaving behind its equipment parallels this Book of Mormon narrative.
The Lord promises deliverance without the need for His people to lift weapons; the Syrians' flight demonstrates this principle that God's strength accomplishes what human strength cannot.

commentary.historical_context: The twilight flight reflects the reality of ancient warfare. Darkness was a natural moment for armies to be most vulnerable; visibility affected both navigation and morale. A panicked flight at twilight would have been disorienting and rapidly catastrophic as discipline broke down. The complete abandonment of a military camp—tents, animals, supplies—was economically devastating to the besieging force and would have been understood by ancient audiences as a sign of overwhelming defeat. The psychological phenomenon of mass panic is real; the addition of the supernatural auditory hallucination (the sound of chariots and horses) would have been sufficient to shatter the cohesion of any ancient military force, especially one already weakened by doubt and fatigue from a siege. The Aramean soldiers, hearing what they believed were reinforcements for Samaria, would have had no way to verify the sound and every reason to fear being trapped between the city's garrison and an approaching army.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of the Lord delivering His people through supernatural means rather than military superiority appears throughout the Book of Mormon. Alma 2:27-28 describes a similar sudden routing of enemies, and 1 Nephi 4:6 emphasizes that the Lord prepares a way for His people through means beyond their own strength.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 35:8 teaches that the Lord 'shall go forth' among His people and 'shall lead you to and fro' in a way that confounds His enemies. The Syrians' confusion and flight exemplifies how the Lord's purposes are accomplished often through psychological and spiritual means rather than physical force.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The removal of the siege and the opening of the city gates parallels the temple theme of deliverance and the opening of the way. The protection of Samaria prefigures how the Lord preserves His covenant people through supernatural means.

commentary.christological_typology: Elisha functions as a type of Christ in his intercessory role. Just as Elisha prayed for the servant's eyes to be opened (6:17), Christ opens the spiritual eyes of all who believe on Him. The deliverance of the city through the prophet's intercession prefigures Christ's redemptive work, which saves all who come unto Him. The supernatural rout of the enemy anticipates the final victory of Christ over all opposing powers.
commentary.application: This verse teaches that the Lord's deliverance often comes through unexpected means and at unexpected times. The Syrians fled at twilight, not at dawn when a conventional army might have attacked. Modern believers often expect deliverance to come in predictable ways—through visible means, through our own strength, through conventional solutions. This narrative invites us to trust in God's ability to deliver in ways we cannot foresee or engineer. When facing sieges of our own (financial pressure, illness, spiritual darkness, family conflict), we are invited to recognize that God may have already sent deliverance we have not yet perceived. Our role is to listen, to believe, and to act on what God has already prepared.

text_kjv: And when these lepers came to the uttermost part of the camp, they went into one tent, and did eat and drink, and carried thence silver, and gold, and raiment, and went and hid it; and came again, and entered into another tent, and carried thence also, and went and hid it.

commentary.narrative:
The four men with leprosy become the instruments of God's revelation. Having discovered an empty camp, they initially respond as desperate, starving men do: they eat and drink. Their rapid consumption reflects months or years of deprivation—they were not merely hungry but at the threshold of death. The verbs cascade in breathless succession: they ate, drank, carried away goods, went, hid them, returned, entered another tent, carried off more, and hid again. This is not the measured looting of soldiers following conquest; it is the frantic hoarding of men who have known scarcity and fear having it return.

The lepers' actions reveal a psychological pattern. First comes survival (eating and drinking), then opportunism (carrying away wealth), then preservation (hiding it). They repeat this cycle deliberately, moving from tent to tent, taking silver, gold, and clothing. These men, who had been ritually unclean and cast out from society, are now at the center of events that will determine the fate of the city. They are, in a sense, reclaiming wealth and dignity that their condition had denied them. Yet their actions remain morally ambiguous at this point—they are gorging themselves and hoarding treasures while a city starves. This will trouble their consciences by verse 9.

word_study.meaning: Ketseh means 'edge,' 'end,' or 'extremity.' The lepers approach from the margins, literally at the edge of the encampment, which is fitting for men whose disease had already marginalized them.
word_study.significance: The spatial detail reflects their social position: they enter the camp from its margins, as they themselves have always lived at society's margins. Their physical approach mirrors their social status.

word_study.meaning: Simple verbs of consumption—to eat and to drink—but in the context of starvation, these acts represent the most urgent human need. The lepers' first action is survival.
word_study.significance: The eating and drinking come before the looting, indicating that physical survival is the immediate priority. Only when hunger is briefly sated do they turn to accumulating wealth.

word_study.meaning: Nasa means 'to carry' or 'to lift'; tamun means 'to hide,' 'to bury,' or 'to store away.' The verb tamun appears frequently in contexts of burying treasures or hiding valuables.
word_study.significance: The deliberate hiding of wealth suggests both security against loss and perhaps a subconscious acknowledgment that this wealth belongs to the city, not to them. They hide it rather than openly displaying it, indicating some awareness of moral complexity.

word_study.meaning: Halak ('to go') + tamun ('to hide') forms the idiom of deliberate concealment. The repetition of this pattern—'and went and hid'—appears twice in this verse, emphasizing the systematic nature of their hoarding.
word_study.significance: The repetition creates a rhythm of panic-driven accumulation. Each tent is methodically plundered and each cache carefully hidden, suggesting both fear of loss and guilty conscience.

cross_references.connection: The lepers will immediately recognize the moral problem with their actions and will correct course, choosing to report good news rather than hoard it.
The lepers, like the prodigal son, experience the joy of access to abundance after deprivation; their immediate consumption reflects the relief of survival, not merely greed.
Wealth gained hastily (as the lepers are gaining it) tends to diminish, while the lepers will learn that sharing brings greater blessing than hoarding.
The lepers' initial focus on self-satisfaction parallels the tendency to seek 'their own ways' rather than the Lord's ways, a condition corrected by conscience and revelation.
The root of evil is the love of money; the lepers must overcome the urge to hoard wealth if they are to act righteously in the next verse.

commentary.historical_context: The behavior of the lepers reflects the reality of survival psychology. Men on the brink of starvation, suddenly finding abundant food, would consume it rapidly without restraint. The hoarding of valuables—silver, gold, and clothing—reflects not mere greed but the mentality of those who have experienced deprivation and fear its return. In the ancient Near East, portable wealth (precious metals and fine garments) was a form of security and status. For men who had been stripped of social standing by disease, the accumulation of such goods represented a reclamation of dignity. The Covenant Rendering notes that the verbs 'pile up in rapid sequence,' creating a sense of breathless urgency that matches the psychological reality of desperate men gorging after starvation and hoarding after deprivation. The Syrian camp contained supplies meant to sustain an entire army, so the wealth and food available would have been extraordinary from the perspective of four starving men.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of receiving abundance and being tested regarding how to use it appears in Helaman 12:1-2, which warns that prosperity often leads to pride and forgetting God. The lepers' immediate concern for their own welfare before the welfare of others mirrors this pattern.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 56:16-17 warns against using wealth for selfish purposes; the lepers must learn that the good news they have discovered is meant to be shared, not hoarded. D&C 82:18 teaches that the Lord's abundance is meant to sustain the covenant community, not individuals in isolation.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The removal of ritual impurity (the lepers becoming spiritually 'clean' through their righteous action in the next verse) parallels temple themes of purification and transformation. Their initial selfishness must be overcome before they can become instruments of salvation.

commentary.christological_typology: The lepers' transformation from self-focused consumption to self-sacrificing proclamation prefigures the spiritual transformation that comes through Christ. Just as the lepers must overcome their instinct to hoard in order to become bearers of good news, believers must overcome the natural human tendency toward selfishness to become witnesses of Christ's salvation.
commentary.application: This verse presents a mirror to our own instincts. When we experience blessing—financial gain, health recovery, spiritual experience—our first impulse is often to enjoy it privately, to hoard it, to secure it against loss. But the narrative trajectory suggests that this impulse, while natural, is incomplete and ultimately unsatisfying. The lepers' pattern (eating, hiding, repeating) would have continued indefinitely except for their conscience stirring them toward a better way. Modern believers should examine whether they are hiding their blessings from others. Have you experienced deliverance from a habit and kept quiet about it? Have you received spiritual insight and shared it only with the closest circle? Have you received financial blessing and focused only on personal security rather than community welfare? The lepers' shift in verse 9 suggests that true satisfaction comes not from consumption or hoarding, but from proclaiming good news.

text_kjv: Then they said one to another, We do not well: this day is a day of good tidings, and we hold our peace: if we tarry till the morning light, some mischief will come upon us: now therefore come, that we may go and tell the king's household.

commentary.narrative:
The lepers' conscience awakens. Their internal dialogue—'We do not well'—marks a moral turning point. The Hebrew phrase yom besorah hu ('this is a day of good news') uses the word besorah, which carries the connotation of gospel, evangelion, salvation news. The lepers recognize intuitively that they are holding back information about deliverance. This is not merely withholding facts; it is withholding salvation. Their conscience warns them: 'If we tarry till the morning light, punishment will come upon us.' This is a stunning theological statement. The lepers grasp that hoarding good news of salvation is itself a sin that brings judgment. They understand that moral obligation requires them to share the deliverance they have discovered.

The shift from verse 8 to verse 9 is remarkable. The same men who were frantically hoarding now voluntarily abandon the spoils of their discovery to proclaim good news. This is not because they fear being discovered; it is because their conscience has convicted them that good news about deliverance cannot ethically be kept silent. The lepers will go from social outcasts to saviors of their city. Their recognition that this day is 'a day of good tidings' suggests they understand the significance of what has happened: the Lord has opened a way of escape and salvation, and that way must be proclaimed. By verse 10, they will be reporting to the city gatekeepers, and by verse 11, the news will reach the king himself.

word_study.meaning: Lo ('not') + ken ('thus,' 'in this manner') + osim ('doing') literally means 'we are not doing thus/in this manner/well.' It expresses moral disapproval of their own actions.
word_study.significance: The lepers' self-awareness of moral failure is the turning point. They are capable of recognizing right from wrong and choosing to change course.

word_study.meaning: Besorah literally means 'good news,' 'gospel,' or 'glad tidings.' It is the same root later used for 'gospel' (evangelion) in Greek translations. This is news of deliverance, salvation, or victory.
word_study.significance: The lepers' use of 'besorah' suggests they understand the theological significance of their discovery. This is not merely military intelligence; it is news of God's deliverance. The Covenant Rendering emphasizes that this word carries the semantic weight of 'gospel'—salvation news that must be proclaimed.

word_study.meaning: Machshim means 'to be silent,' 'to keep quiet,' or 'to be still.' It denotes deliberate withholding of speech. The same word appears in 1 Kings 22:3, where Israel 'sits idle' without action.
word_study.significance: The lepers' silence is presented as culpable—they are actively withholding speech when they should be speaking. Keeping peace about good news is not virtuous; it is negligent.

word_study.term_english: some mischief will come upon us
word_study.meaning: Avon means 'iniquity,' 'guilt,' or 'punishment.' The verb matzao means 'to find' or 'to overtake.' The phrase means 'guilt/punishment will find us' or 'we will be held responsible.'
word_study.significance: The lepers understand that silence regarding good news of salvation is itself a sin that will be judged. This reflects a sophisticated moral theology: withholding salvation is an act of commission, not merely omission.

cross_references.connection: Paul quotes Isaiah: 'How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?' The lepers grasp this principle—Samaria cannot be saved without someone proclaiming the good news.
Peter and John declare: 'For we cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard.' The lepers similarly cannot remain silent about what they have witnessed.
Ammon teaches that to withhold testimony of God's deliverance is itself a transgression; the lepers embody this principle by choosing to proclaim rather than conceal.
The Lord teaches that those who have received truth have a responsibility to share it; withholding knowledge of salvation brings judgment. The lepers' conscience aligns with this doctrine.
Jesus teaches that light (good news, gospel) cannot be hidden under a bushel but must be set on a hill to give light to all. The lepers apply this principle by going public with their discovery.

commentary.historical_context: The lepers' moral reasoning reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding of divine judgment and social obligation. In the cultural context of the ancient Near East, those who received favor from the gods (or the God of Israel) were often understood to have obligations to the wider community. Withholding news of deliverance would have been seen as a breach of covenant obligation. The lepers' shift from self-interest to community welfare also reflects the transition from survival mode (immediate physical need) to moral reasoning (future consequences). Additionally, the lepers' recognition that the morning will bring a different situation suggests they understand that the opportunity to act righteously is time-limited. By morning, soldiers or officials might discover the empty camp, and the lepers' testimony would then appear self-serving rather than sacrificial.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of witnesses chosen from unexpected sources to proclaim salvation appears throughout the Book of Mormon. In Alma 26:12-13, Ammon marvels that the Lord used him, a man of little learning, to bring souls to repentance. The lepers, like many unlikely prophets in the Book of Mormon, become instruments of God's will through humility and obedience.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 88:81 teaches: 'He who receiveth light and continueth in God, receiveth more light, and that light groweth brighter and brighter.' The lepers' choice to share their discovery rather than conceal it will result in greater light and blessing. D&C 33:9-11 emphasizes the responsibility of those who have received truth to proclaim it openly.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The lepers' transition from isolation (unclean, cast out) to becoming messengers of salvation mirrors temple progression from outer court to inner sanctum, from separation to communion with God's purposes. Their willingness to serve the community rather than themselves makes them fit vessels for God's message.

commentary.christological_typology: The lepers function as types of the apostles after the resurrection. Just as the apostles were transformed from fearful disciples into bold proclaimers of salvation, the lepers are transformed from desperate men seeking self-preservation into willing witnesses of deliverance. Their recognition that 'this is a day of good tidings' parallels the disciples' recognition that Christ's resurrection is good news (evangelion) for all humanity. The lepers' willingness to sacrifice their own gain for the sake of sharing good news prefigures the apostolic commitment to preach the gospel even at cost to themselves.
commentary.application: This verse confronts modern believers with a challenging question: What good news have you received that you have not shared? Perhaps you have experienced healing (physical, emotional, spiritual) that you have kept private for fear of seeming self-aggrandizing. Perhaps you have received spiritual insight in a patriarchal blessing or personal revelation that you have shared only with close family. Perhaps you have felt the witness of the Spirit testifying of truth, yet you have remained silent in conversations where that truth was being questioned. The lepers' conscience teaches that silence about salvation is itself a sin. They had every reason to keep quiet (fear of discovery, desire to enjoy spoils, uncertainty about reception), yet they recognized that good news about deliverance cannot ethically be withheld. The application is not to compel belief or manipulate others, but to recognize that the good news we have experienced comes with a moral obligation to witness. The lepers' change of mind from verse 8 to verse 9 suggests that this recognition often comes through conscience—an internal awareness that the right thing to do is to share what we have discovered.

text_kjv: So they came and called unto the porter of the city: and they told them, saying, We came to the camp of the Syrians, and, behold, there was no man there, neither voice of man, but horses tied, and asses tied, and the tents as they were.

commentary.narrative:
The lepers follow through on their moral conviction and immediately report to the city gatekeeper. Their testimony is factual, specific, and compelling: they went to the Syrian camp, found no people, heard no human voice, but discovered horses and donkeys tied up and tents standing intact. The repetition that the animals remain 'tied up' is strategically significant—it proves the departure was panicked and total, not a tactical withdrawal. A military force that intended to return would have taken its horses and donkeys. The fact that these animals remain secured suggests either that the Syrians fled so suddenly they had no time to gather them, or they fled in such disorder that no one was responsible for collecting them.

The lepers approach the gatekeeper (sho'er ha-ir), the official responsible for controlling access to the city. This is the proper authority to whom such intelligence should be reported. The chain of communication has now begun: from the margins of society (the lepers) to the official guardians of the city (the gatekeepers) to the rulers within. The lepers' report is straightforward and free of conjecture. They do not speculate about why the Syrians fled or what it means strategically; they simply report what they observed. This restraint makes their testimony more credible. They are eyewitnesses to fact, not interpreters of meaning.

word_study.meaning: Sho'er literally means 'one who watches' or 'one who keeps/guards.' The sho'er ha-ir is the official gatekeeper responsible for controlling entry and exit and for maintaining communication with the city's leadership.
word_study.significance: The lepers understand hierarchy and approach the appropriate authority rather than spreading rumors. This demonstrates both wisdom and respect for order.

word_study.meaning: Ein ('there is not') + ish ('man,' 'person'). This double negation emphasizes complete absence—not merely that some people had fled, but that no people remained at all.
word_study.significance: The absolute negation is key to the significance of the testimony. This is not a report of strategic repositioning; it is a report of total abandonment.

word_study.meaning: Kol ('voice,' 'sound') + adam ('man,' 'humanity'). The absence of human voice confirms the absence of human presence. Silence itself becomes evidence.
word_study.significance: The lepers understand that human presence leaves auditory traces. The absence of any sound of human activity (speech, footsteps, activity) corroborates the complete evacuation.

word_study.term_original: הַסּוּס אָסוּר וְהַחֲמוֹר אָסוּר (ha-sus asur v-ha-chamor asur)
word_study.meaning: Asur means 'bound,' 'tied,' or 'secured.' The repetition of the word (horses asur, donkeys asur) emphasizes that the animals are deliberately restrained, not merely present.
word_study.significance: Tied animals are evidence of hasty departure. An army that intended to move would have untied and collected its mounts. The fact that animals remain secured proves the flight was unplanned and total.

word_study.meaning: Ka-asher ('just as,' 'as') + hemah ('they are,' 'they were'). This phrase describes the tents standing exactly as they were abandoned, undisturbed and intact.
word_study.significance: The tents remaining 'as they were' is final proof of abandonment without opportunity for orderly withdrawal. All the material infrastructure of the camp remains, literally frozen in place by panic.

cross_references.connection: The gatekeeper will immediately relay this information to the king's house, continuing the chain of communication from society's margins to the center of power.
The lepers are eyewitnesses who 'have heard' and 'have seen' and now 'declare' what they have witnessed. Their testimony is based on direct experience, not hearsay.
Rahab similarly reports factual intelligence (the condition of the Canaanites' morale and military readiness) to the Israelite spies, demonstrating that God uses witnesses from unexpected sources.
Alma calls for witnesses to come forward and testify of what they have 'felt' and 'known' to be true. The lepers similarly testify factually of what they have observed.
The Lord teaches that bishops (city authorities) should receive reports from members. The lepers follow this principle by reporting to the proper city authority rather than spreading rumors.

commentary.historical_context: The gatekeeper was an official of some standing in ancient Near Eastern cities. Gates were fortified positions and control points, and the gatekeeper was responsible for security, taxation of goods, and communication with city leadership. The lepers' approach to this official rather than directly to the king shows understanding of proper hierarchy. Additionally, the specific details the lepers provide—no people, no voice, animals still tied, tents intact—are the kind of intelligence a military commander would find credible. The report is neither sensationalized nor under-stated; it is factual and specific. Ancient audiences would have recognized this as competent eyewitness testimony. The progression from the lepers (social outcasts) to the gatekeeper (official authority) to the king (political power) reflects the way information moved through hierarchical societies.

restoration_lens.bom_parallels: The pattern of testimony moving through proper channels appears in Alma 17:3-4, where Alma's sons report to him before the congregation. Good news and important intelligence flow upward through established authority structures.
restoration_lens.dc_connections: D&C 21:4-5 teaches that the Lord's organization has proper channels for communication and decision-making. The lepers demonstrate respect for this principle by reporting to the appropriate authority.
restoration_lens.temple_connections: The gate is a liminal space—between outside and inside, between wilderness and civilization. The lepers, having been cast out beyond the gate, now become messengers at the gate, bringing news that will restore life to the city. This mirrors temple themes of passage from darkness to light, from separation to integration.

commentary.christological_typology: The lepers as witnesses mirror the role of John the Baptist as a witness to Jesus. John's testimony was simple, factual, and pointed beyond himself to the one he was witnessing of. Similarly, the lepers' testimony is straightforward and factual, pointing to the deliverance God has provided rather than to themselves.
commentary.application: This verse teaches the power of simple, factual testimony. The lepers do not embellish, do not speculate, do not preach a sermon. They simply report what they have seen and heard. Modern believers often feel they must add interpretation, explanation, or persuasive rhetoric to their testimonies. This verse suggests that powerful testimony is often simply truthful report. When you have experienced something spiritually real, it can be more powerful to simply state the fact clearly than to add layers of interpretation. For example: 'I was depressed and prayed, and my burden was lifted' is more powerful than a lengthy theological explanation of depression. 'I felt the Spirit testify of the Book of Mormon' is more powerful than apologetic arguments. Like the lepers, we should approach the proper authorities (priesthood leaders, family members, trusted friends) with our testimony rather than spreading it as rumor. And we should be precise and factual rather than exaggerated or speculative. The lepers' restrained, factual approach to their testimony gives it credibility.

text_kjv: And he called the porters; and they told it to the king's house within.

commentary.narrative:
This brief verse marks a crucial transition in the flow of information. The gatekeeper does not merely listen to the lepers' report; he acts on it by calling other gatekeepers (or guards) and passing the message inward to the king's house. The word 'penimah' (within, inside) suggests the inner chambers of the palace where the king and his officials reside.
